artigo.texto: 247 – Em uma contundente análise sobre os rumos da revolução tecnológica e da geopolítica mundial, o neurocientista e professor Miguel Nicolelis alertou que o entusiasmo desmedido em torno da inteligência artificial generativa atingiu o ápice de uma bolha especulativa que já dá claros sinais de ruptura. Durante participação no programa Giro das Onze, conduzido por Gustavo Conde e transmitido ao vivo pela TV 247, o cientista desmontou os mitos propagados pelo Vale do Silício e classificou os chamados data centers de hiperescala como “parasitas digitais” que ameaçam recursos hídricos, a soberania nacional e a estabilidade climática do planeta. Para Nicolelis, o atual modelo de desenvolvimento da IA no Ocidente não se sustenta financeiramente nem ecologicamente. O neurocientista comparou a euforia do mercado a uma pirâmide financeira bilionária, cuja conta já começa a ser cobrada na economia real. A miragem financeira e o custo ecológico Segundo Nicolelis, enquanto as grandes corporações tecnológicas investiram quantias estimadas em cerca de 5 trilhões de dólares na corrida armamentista dos modelos de linguagem e processadores gráficos de última geração, o retorno financeiro dessa infraestrutura segue infinitamente desproporcional. A consequência direta é uma extrema volatilidade nos mercados globais, marcada por oscilações violentas no valor de mercado de gigantes como Nvidia e Google. Contudo, é no território físico e no cotidiano das comunidades que a tecnologia cobra seu preço mais destrutivo. Nicolelis frisou que não se deve confundir os servidores comuns de internet com os hyperscalers dedicados ao treinamento contínuo de IA. “Esses parasitas digitais não geram empregos, exigem incentivos fiscais bilionários, consomem quantidades astronômicas de água e energia e desestabilizam os sistemas elétricos locais. Além disso, criam um calor residual insuportável no solo e poluição sonora ininterrupta de 24 horas por dia.” O cientista chamou atenção para a onda de protestos populares que já varre cidades na Europa, Ásia e Estados Unidos contra a instalação dessas estruturas, destacando plebiscitos locais onde comunidades rejeitaram massivamente novas licenças para plantas de processamento de hiperescala devido ao impacto nos aquíferos, na fauna e na saúde mental dos moradores do entorno. O perigo para o Brasil: soberania ou submissão colonial? No centro de suas críticas ao debate nacional, Nicolelis condenou com veemência iniciativas e políticas de isenção fiscal — a exemplo dos moldes discutidos no programa Redata — desenhadas para atrair essas megaestruturas para o território brasileiro. Citando planos de instalação de complexos de processamento em regiões vulneráveis, como o semiárido nordestino e o Porto do Pecém (CE), o pesquisador advertiu para a contradição de subsidiar gigawatts de eletricidade e reservatórios de água doce para companhias multinacionais enquanto a população local convive com riscos de crise hídrica crônica. “Soberania digital não se conquista cedendo nosso solo e nossa água para abrigar data centers de empresas estrangeiras. Conquista-se investindo em universidades públicas, em ciência da computação nacional e na capacitação dos nossos próprios cientistas para desenvolver modelos adequados às nossas necessidades reais.” Nicolelis pontuou que 90% do capital anunciado nesses projetos sequer circula na economia interna: vai para a compra de chips importados e obras civis temporárias. Concluída a infraestrutura básica, os complexos passam a operar de forma quase inteiramente automatizada, mantendo apenas dezenas de técnicos no local e deixando um passivo socioambiental permanente. China vs. Ocidente: a busca pela eficiência real Para ilustrar alternativas a essa lógica predatória, o cientista traçou um paralelo com a estratégia da China. Enquanto os Estados Unidos contam com milhares de centros de processamento voltados a treinar grandes modelos proprietários com custos exorbitantes — frequentemente voltados à publicidade direcionada, entretenimento fútil e vigilância —, o ecossistema chinês priorizou modelos abertos (open-source), compactos e focados na automação produtiva de processos industriais e de suporte ao trabalho humano. De acordo com Nicolelis, esses modelos consomem frações mínimas de energia e rodam em máquinas mais acessíveis, desmistificando a tese de que apenas a queima desenfreada de recursos naturais viabiliza o progresso técnico. “O cérebro consome 20 watts; o universo é analógico” Ao aprofundar a discussão para além da economia política, Nicolelis ressaltou os limites fundamentais da própria disciplina computacional. Diferente do cérebro humano, que opera em modo analógico, contínuo e consome cerca de 20 watts de energia metabólica — o equivalente a uma lâmpada fraca —, a IA moderna exige gigawatts de infraestrutura e multiplicações colossais de matrizes estatísticas para simular, de forma ruidosa, aspectos triviais da inteligência. O neurocientista alertou ainda para as consequências cognitivas da terceirização do pensamento humano para sistemas preditivos, citando estudos recentes na Noruega e Suécia que documentam a erosão do vocabulário, do raciocínio lógico e da capacidade de interpretação de texto entre estudantes viciados em interfaces digitais. Ao encerrar, Nicolelis fez um apelo para que a liderança política e a sociedade brasileira não se deixem seduzir pelo canto da sereia tecnocrata: “O Brasil precisa definir um projeto de desenvolvimento que aposte no seu recurso mais valioso: a criatividade e a capacidade cognitiva do seu povo. Não podemos aceitar o papel de mero quintal de energia barata e água para a especulação de meia dúzia de conglomerados globais.”

artigo.texto: Quincy, Wash. — Quincy's long-running push for data centers has brought jobs, tax revenue, a new hospital and a new high school, while also fueling concerns about water, farmland and a planned high-voltage transmission line. NonStop Local spoke with residents and officials in Quincy to get a closer look at what operating data centers mean for that community. At L and R Cafe II, owner Ibis Ortiz says main street businesses, like hers, are doing well in Quincy. "Probably our biggest in the morning is our breakfast burritos," said Ibis Ortiz. Quincy once leaned on food manufacturing and field work, but city leaders said that was not enough to keep people from leaving. "We survived on a food manufacturing plant and field work. That's what drove the city of Quincy. And we were seeing lots of people leaving," said Quincy City Administrator Joe Harris. The city then worked to recruit fiber companies and build around key amenities the area offers. "... low-cost power, from the hydropower, easy planning and permitting nothing to it, and the land," said Port of Quincy Commissioner for Dist. 1, Curt Morris. That effort helped bring eight data center campuses now operating in Quincy, each with multiple buildings. Expansions are expected. Various officials say those centers store online information tied to banking, medical records, insurance, airline ticketing, entertainment and other services people use every day. Morris said Quincy's facilities were not built as superscale artificial intelligence, generative AI or bitcoin mining sites. "This Microsoft plant isn't considered a mega, super-scale data center. I don't think that'll necessarily fit here because infrastructure will dictate how big you can make it. No, but having another one the size of 80-acres, 100 acres, Yeah, we take all those all day, There's just too much confusion between AI and data centers," said Morris. Water use is one concern. Quincy told NonStop Local the city's data centers use 8% of the city's water, but more water sources are needed for expected residential and industrial growth. "...either more re-use water, or water out of the Columbia Basin Irrigation District, or the Columbia River itself," said Quincy Q-1 Water Program Manager, Bob Davis. Officials said Microsoft already has a re-use water system that it funded, and the city runs for Microsoft. Quincy aims to have another re-use plant operating in 2029. "Most of the cooling water will come from re-use water," said Morris. The port explained that reuse water is treated and sent to data center campuses and to other non-potable uses such as park irrigation. Companies started building these data centers 20 years ago. Now, older facilities are being replaced with more efficient ones. "They will be replacing them with higher efficiency and lower energy use and water use. They will be much more efficient," said Quincy Municipal Services Director, Carl Worley. Davis said newer data centers are also using less water to cool their systems. "Data centers today are installing non-evaporative cooling systems. They're using mechanical chilled systems," said Davis. "So, is the turnaround that they use more electricity?" asked Meili. "Yes, mechanical-chilled uses more electricity," answered Davis. The Port of Quincy said nearby farmland that might sell for $15,000 an acre for agriculture could bring about eight times that amount, if it's within the technology growth management map. "As industrial property, with the services we're working on, it'll be $125,000 an acre," said Morris. City officials said the much higher valuation of the city, and tax revenue from the data centers have drastically cut what citizens pay for many levies and bonds. "When we go out to the community and we say, hey, we need to build a new hospital, a new high school, a new police department, a new city hall, whatever that whatever that build, that ask is we're asking the citizens to fund that using $0.88 per $1,000 of their assessed value instead of $3.12 per thousand," said Harris. The city administrator adds that revenue linked to data centers helped Quincy more than double its police force. "A lot of cities in Washington don't even have one officer per thousand residents. Quincy has got 2.3 officers per thousand," said Harris. That same tax base also helped build new city, police and fire facilities, an aquatics center and a new high school. Quincy Recreation Director Russ Harrington pointed to the aquatics center's family features. "Youve got your lazy river, the slides and the kids' area that goes to the box pool," said Harrington. Quincy Public School Superintendent, Dr. Nik Bergman toured us around the new high school and said the bond support reshaped local campuses. "The voters passed a $108 million bond that would support the brand-new high school that we're being interviewed in today. It also built brand new elementary gyms. Every single one of our elementary schools has a new gym. It also helped us renovate the existing high school to make it into a middle school," said Dr. Bergman. Quincy Public Schools also partnered with Microsoft on a Data Center Technician Program. "A kiddo can leave Quincy High School and go right to work the data centers and earn a family sustaining income." said Dr. Bergman. "It starts over $60,000 plus. We have students who have come out from a year ago with the Data Center Technician Program and are going into jobs with that," said Lisa Karstetter with Microsoft Community Outreach. Quincy estimates data centers employ about 1,000 full-time workers, with more than half at Microsoft. This does not include contractors. Quincy estimates that each data center job creates four more good paying jobs. Back at the historic L and R Cafe II, one farmer told NonStop Local he sees the data center industry as a stronger job option for his son. artigo.texto: Com venda de elétricos em alta, BYD antecipa terceiro turno na fábrica de Camaçari, na Bahia Novo horário de produção, que estava marcado para começar no final deste ano, iniciou nesta segunda Atualizado Com vendas de carros elétricos em alta e demanda pelo seu novo modelo Atto 2, a chinesa BYD antecipou do final do ano para esta segunda-feira, dia 9, o início do terceiro turno de produção na unidade de Camaçari, na Bahia, que passa a operar 24 horas. Com a contratação de mais dois mil trabalhadores para este turno, o complexo industrial baiano alcança mais de dez mil funcionários desde o início da produção, no ano passado. As vendas de carros eletrificados têm crescido a um ritmo de dois dígitos no Brasil. Em outubro passado, foram emplacados 54.486 veículos eletrificados, um crescimento de 154,9% em relação ao mesmo mês de 2025, quando foram comercializados 21.369 exemplares, segundo a Associação Brasileira do Veículo Elétrico (ABVE). Entre janeiro e outubro, foram vendidos 436.809 veículos elétricos e híbridos no Brasil, uma alta de 158,8% em relação ao mesmo período de 2025. O Dolphin Mini e o Dolphin, ambos da BYD, lideram o ranking dos carros elétricos puros mais vendidos no varejo, e a marca chinesa já é a quarta que mais vende carros no país, atrás de Fiat, Volkswagen e General Motors, segundo ranking elaborado pela Bright Consulting, consultoria especialista no setor automotivo. O recém-lançado híbrido plug-in flex Atto 2 registrou 10.329 pedidos e 5.012 unidades emplacadas em pouco mais de 40 dias úteis, segundo a BYD. Além do terceiro turno, a BYD está concluindo os testes finais das áreas de soldagem e pintura — etapas decisivas para a produção 100% nacional. Na Bahia, são produzidos o elétrico Dolphin Mini, o sedã BYD King (híbrido plug-in) e o SUV BYD Song Pro (híbrido plug-in), e agora com a expansão, o Atto 2. — Estamos acelerando a produção porque o consumidor brasileiro está respondendo, e os números do Atto 2 deixam isso muito claro. Temos uma demanda expressiva para atender e uma fábrica preparada para acompanhar esse crescimento — afirmou Alexandre Baldy, vice-presidente sênior da BYD do Brasil e head comercial e de marketing da BYD Auto do Brasil, que lembra que os novos turnos já foram estruturados com jornada semanal de 40 horas. Um estudo do Observatório da Indústria (Sistema FIEB) em parceria com a BYD mostrou que o impacto da retomada das operações na unidade de Camaçari, depois que a Ford saiu do país e deixou a unidade, retomou cerca de 22 mil empregos (diretos, indiretos e induzidos) e a operação vai movimentar cerca de R$ 1,03 bilhão por ano em salários. O investimento total anunciado pela BYD para o complexo industrial de Camaçari é de R$ 11,3 bilhões, nos próximos anos, com capacidade inicial de produção de 150 mil veículos por ano. Já foram investidos R$ 5,5 bilhões. A BYD está anunciando ainda uma parceria com a TIM para fornecer soluções de conectividade embarcada para toda a frota de veículos leves da marca em circulação no Brasil. A parceria terá a implantação também de infraestrutura de redes 5G e 4G na fábrica de Camaçari, com sete pontos de cobertura externa e 63 equipamentos distribuídos entre os galpões e as áreas operacionais, permitindo conectar colaboradores, visitantes, sistemas operacionais e os próprios veículos ainda durante a fabricação, facilitando a comunicação entre diferentes etapas da produção.

artigo.texto: LITHONIA, Ga. — Longtime South DeKalb environmental and civic organizers brought residents together Saturday, Nov. 7, to question the rapid growth of artificial intelligence data centers and how much say communities should have before these facilities arrive in their neighborhoods. The Nov. 7 “AI Data Center Reveal” at Rockland United Methodist Church was organized by Renee Cail, president of Citizens for a Healthy and Safe Environment (CHASE), and Cheryl Moore-Mathis, president of the Klondike Area Civic Association (KACA). Both have been involved in environmental and land-use issues in South DeKalb for years. CHASE grew out of opposition to industrial development in the area and has been involved in fights over projects including the Metro Green Recycling facility in Stonecrest. KACA has roots going back decades to neighborhood organizing over quarry and industrial activity around the Klondike community. The Nov. 7 gathering brought that history into a newer fight over data centers, an increasingly prominent issue in DeKalb County and across Georgia. The panel included Dr. Yolanda Whyte, an Atlanta pediatrician and environmental-health advocate; Jessica Owens, director of data and mapping for Science for Georgia; and Andrea Young Jones, director of government relations and public policy for Georgia Women’s Action for New Directions (Georgia WAND). A sustained hum Organizers had planned for the panelists to give individual presentations, but audience questions quickly turned the event into a more open discussion. With time running short, the presentations were ultimately skipped as attendees and panelists continued talking through concerns ranging from health and noise to water use, electricity demand, tax incentives and local zoning. At one point, organizers unexpectedly played a sustained mechanical hum through the room as part of the program, asking attendees to consider what it might be like to live near continuous industrial noise. Whyte focused more broadly on potential health effects from pollution associated with large industrial facilities, including emissions from backup generators. She raised concerns about respiratory illness, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and cardiovascular effects in communities already exposed to pollution. Drawing on her work as a pediatrician, Whyte described seeing children who come into her clinic for unrelated issues but show signs of breathing problems during examinations. The discussion repeatedly returned to what communities receive in exchange for hosting large developments. Panelists questioned how many permanent jobs data centers create after construction is finished and whether companies should bear the full cost of the electricity, water and other infrastructure required to support their facilities. Shahnawaz Rafi, a visiting assistant professor in Emory University’s Environmental Sciences Department, pushed the discussion in a different direction. Rafi asked how communities should account for the potential financial benefits of a large development, including whether they could direct additional revenue toward needs such as health care or other public services. That prompted a broader exchange about whether economic benefits could offset environmental or infrastructure impacts and what protections should be built into projects before approval. Jones argued that communities should require companies to account for those costs at the beginning rather than relying on compensation later. Water usage concerns The conversation also touched on water concerns surrounding data center development elsewhere in the country and in Georgia, as well as the electricity needs of some large facilities. Owens focused much of her discussion on the tools residents and local governments have before a project reaches that point. “The biggest power that a municipality has in envisioning your future is zoning,” Owens said. She encouraged residents to follow zoning cases, special-use permit requests and local government meetings rather than waiting until projects are already approved. Owens works for Science for Georgia, a nonprofit science and public-policy advocacy organization that has become active in Georgia’s data center debate. The group has developed a statewide map of data center projects and has advocated for measures including environmental reviews, greater disclosure of resource use, community benefit agreements and requirements for companies to plan for facilities that are eventually abandoned or become obsolete. Science for Georgia has also been involved in DeKalb County’s ongoing discussion over how data centers should be regulated. Earlier this year, commissioners considered having the organization assist with a health and environmental review before the proposal developed into a broader call for an independently selected third-party study. County debates how to regulate data centers The Nov. 7 forum comes as DeKalb continues debating its own approach. The county has a moratorium on accepting applications for new or expanded data centers while officials study potential impacts and consider additional regulations. Two data center-related items are scheduled to return to the DeKalb County Board of Commissioners on Nov. 10, including a proposal requiring an independent health and environmental study before the moratorium can be lifted and another calling for broader definitions and classifications for data centers. The discussion Saturday ranged beyond the physical facilities themselves. Panelists and attendees discussed how companies collect and use personal data, targeted advertising, algorithmic pricing and the growing role of artificial intelligence in workplaces. Jones discussed concerns about algorithms determining compensation for gig workers, while Owens described how collected information can predict consumer behavior. artigo.texto: Cabinet Approves Rs. 145 bn Scheme for 92 GWh Energy Storage 09 Nov 2026 2 Min Read CW Team Share The Union Cabinet has approved a Rs. 145 bn viability gap funding (VGF) scheme to support the development of 92 GWh of grid-scale energy storage capacity by FY31. The initiative is intended to expand storage infrastructure and help India integrate a larger share of renewable energy into its electricity grid. The scheme will support 60 GWh of pumped hydro storage, 30 GWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS) and 2 GWh of alternative storage technologies. The projects are expected to involve total investment of Rs. 976 bn, with government financial support provided between FY27 and FY31. The programme is aimed at improving the financial viability of large-scale storage projects, which can help manage intermittent solar and wind generation and provide round-the-clock electricity. The planned addition represents 170 per cent of India’s existing grid-scale storage capacity and is intended to contribute to the country’s projected requirement of 411 GWh by FY32. The Central Electricity Authority’s National Electricity Plan estimates that India will require 411.4 GWh of energy storage capacity by 2031-32, including 236.22 GWh of BESS and 175.18 GWh of pumped hydro storage. The 92 GWh covered by the new scheme would meet around 22 per cent of the projected requirement. Capacity will be allocated through tariff-based competitive bidding. Public and private sector electricity distribution companies will be eligible for VGF support for battery storage and pumped hydro projects, while alternative storage projects can be implemented by public and private sector entities. Battery projects will also require at least 40 per cent domestic content, supporting local manufacturing and reducing reliance on imported components. The approval builds on earlier government measures. In September 2023, the Cabinet approved Rs. 37.6 bn to develop 4 GWh of battery storage capacity, later expanded to around 13.85 GWh. In June 2025, the Power Ministry extended VGF support to another 30 GWh through Rs. 54 bn from the Power System Development Fund. The Union Cabinet has approved a Rs. 145 bn viability gap funding (VGF) scheme to support the development of 92 GWh of grid-scale energy storage capacity by FY31. The initiative is intended to expand storage infrastructure and help India integrate a larger share of renewable energy into its electricity grid. The scheme will support 60 GWh of pumped hydro storage, 30 GWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS) and 2 GWh of alternative storage technologies. The projects are expected to involve total investment of Rs. 976 bn, with government financial support provided between FY27 and FY31. The programme is aimed at improving the financial viability of large-scale storage projects, which can help manage intermittent solar and wind generation and provide round-the-clock electricity. The planned addition represents 170 per cent of India’s existing grid-scale storage capacity and is intended to contribute to the country’s projected requirement of 411 GWh by FY32. The Central Electricity Authority’s National Electricity Plan estimates that India will require 411.4 GWh of energy storage capacity by 2031-32, including 236.22 GWh of BESS and 175.18 GWh of pumped hydro storage. The 92 GWh covered by the new scheme would meet around 22 per cent of the projected requirement. Capacity will be allocated through tariff-based competitive bidding. Public and private sector electricity distribution companies will be eligible for VGF support for battery storage and pumped hydro projects, while alternative storage projects can be implemented by public and private sector entities. Battery projects will also require at least 40 per cent domestic content, supporting local manufacturing and reducing reliance on imported components. The approval builds on earlier government measures. In September 2023, the Cabinet approved Rs. 37.6 bn to develop 4 GWh of battery storage capacity, later expanded to around 13.85 GWh. In June 2025, the Power Ministry extended VGF support to another 30 GWh through Rs. 54 bn from the Power System Development Fund. artigo.texto: Technology giant Google will build its first data center in southeast Wyoming, and potentially invest $17 billion in computing centers here. The company confirmed its Equality State data center plans Thursday afternoon, “designed to deliver lasting benefits for Laramie County families and businesses.” “We’re committed to partnering with communities to build data centers the right way,” the company said in a prepared statement. “We will pay for 100% of the power we use, and when we build data centers, we’ll cover the infrastructure needs directly driven by our growth.” It was unclear as of press time Google’s timeframe for building the first facility and how long it might take to complete its $17 billion buildout near Terry Ranch Road in Laramie County. The news comes amid a whirlwind of data center speculation throughout much of the state, including in the Cheyenne area, where the industry is already established, with 10 in operation and more than a dozen on the planning books. The bevy of data centers has provoked a backlash in Wyoming and elsewhere. Prominent politicians, including Secretary of State and soon-to-be Congressman Chuck Gray, have come out in opposition to new AI data centers in Wyoming. A University of Wyoming poll published last week found only 30% of residents here supported allowing the construction of more large data centers for AI technology. Google says it is partnering with natural gas pipeline company Tallgrass Energy, electric utility Black Hills Energy, American Electric Power and data center developer Related Digital for the “long-term” investment plan. The first step is a 702-megawatt facility, powered by fuel-cell technology — converting natural gas into electricity — and a plan to permanently sequester electrical generation emissions deep underground, the company said. Tallgrass is already developing a carbon dioxide sequestration hub in Wyoming, it noted. Regarding water consumption — a major concern among Wyomingites — Google said, “our Wyoming data center will be air-cooled to minimize strain on local water resources.” “This is not speculative. This is happening,” Cheyenne Mayor Patrick Collins told WyoFile. “I’ve been talking to Google, for at least a year now, about looking at Cheyenne to see if we’re a good fit for them and they’re a good fit for us, and I think they have determined we’re a great fit for them.” Tallgrass is already prepping a one-square-mile area for the first phase of the project, he said. “They have spent millions of dollars already, and Google will break ground here soon.” Prior to Thursday’s announcement, Google officials met with “more than 200 residents in Laramie County” to gather feedback to tailor its plans, the company said. Cheyenne City Councilman Larry Wolfe said Google’s announcement feels like a confirmation. “You know, we’re not easily dazzled anymore,” Wolfe told WyoFile. “I will tell you that it’s $10 billion here, $20 billion there. What it’s done is it has made us really cynical about projects that aren’t of that magnitude.”

artigo.texto: Brussels, 9 November 2026 The European Commission has today published the 2026 EU Climate Action Progress Report and Carbon Market Report, showing that EU greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions continue to fall, clean technologies are expanding, and an increasing amount of ETS revenues are available to EU Member States for investments in decarbonisation. These developments show how the clean transition continues to support the EU’s wider objectives of strengthening competitiveness, enhancing energy security, reducing dependencies and becoming climate resilient. The Climate Action Progress Report confirms that EU net GHG emissions fell by 1.6% in 2025 compared to 2024, according to provisional data. Emissions covered by the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) decreased by around 2% in 2025, while emissions in sectors covered by the Effort Sharing Regulation (ESR) remained broadly stable, and provisional data show an improvement in the EU land carbon sink. Emissions are now 39% below 1990 levels, while the EU economy has grown by 74% over the same period, decoupling one more year the growth of our economy from its decarbonisation, further reducing emissions. This year’s Carbon Market Report also finds that EU ETS revenues grew to €43.2 billion in 2025, an 11% increase compared to 2024. The EU also strengthened its longer-term climate framework this year by establishing a legally binding target to reduce net GHG emissions by 90% by 2040 compared to 1990 levels, with the entry into force of the amended European Climate Law in April 2026. Stepping up 2030 implementation across the EU While the EU remains fully committed to reducing net GHG emissions by at least 55% by 2030, the slower pace of emission reductions in 2025 means that efforts will need to accelerate across the economy in the second half of the decade. The report indicates that emissions covered by the Effort Sharing Regulation (including domestic transport, buildings, agriculture and waste) are currently expected to fall by around 38.5% by 2030 compared with 2005, slightly below the EU-wide target of 40%. The assessment shows that nine EU Member States are not making sufficient progress towards meeting their 2030 ESR targets. The Commission will request that Austria, Croatia, Cyprus, Germany, Italy, Ireland, Lithuania, Malta and Sweden each submit a corrective action plan to accelerate the implementation and development of emission reduction measures and investments. Provisional data show that net carbon removals from the land sector increased by around 11% in 2025 compared to 2024. Despite this improvement, current projections for the land sector also indicate a gap of 40–55 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent towards the EU’s 2030 land-use target. Clean transition strengthens energy security and competitiveness The accelerated deployment of clean technologies in 2025 continues to help reduce Europe’s dependence on imported fossil fuels and limit the impacts of volatile fuel prices on citizens and businesses. While EU cleantech manufacturing has expanded significantly, the report highlights that further economic opportunities for European industry can still be captured, which will as a result mobilise investment. Registrations of battery-electric cars increased to 1.9 million in 2025, the equivalent of roughly one in six new car registrations. EU wind and solar capacity increased to 611 GW, or around 49% of total electricity generation capacity. The installation of heat pumps also accelerated, with estimated 41 GW of additional capacity installed in 2025, up from 26 GW in 2024. Climate resilience increasingly urgent Climate-related extreme events have caused an estimated €822 billion in economic losses in the EU since 1980. Around €70 billion per year will need to be invested in adaptation up to 2050. The reports emphasise the rapidly growing impacts of climate change, with severe impacts in 2026. The new EU Climate Resilience Framework, presented in October 2026, will strengthen Europe’s ability to anticipate, prepare for, and manage climate risks with a proposed Climate Resilience Law underpinned by a common reference trajectory for global warming. EU ETS continues to be a well-functioning carbon market The 2026 Carbon Market Report shows that EU ETS revenues amount to €43.2 billion in 2025. More than half this amount (€23.9 billion) went directly to EU Member States to finance decarbonisation measures for households and industry. Increasing the share of ETS revenues invested in decarbonisation, and maintaining the system’s integrity, will ensure that the EU ETS meets its 2030 target of a 62% emissions cut below 2005 levels. Emissions from industrial installations decreased by 3.3% from 2024, mostly driven by the iron and steel, cement, and chemical sectors. Maritime transport emissions decreased by 4% while aviation emissions grew by 0.2%, confirming the pressing need to decarbonise this sector. While overall ETS emissions remain below the cap, emission reductions have slowed compared to previous years. In July 2026, the Commission proposed a reform of the EU ETS for the decade 2030-2040. artigo.texto: Strengthening the Luzon grid: BESS at Magat supports flexible renewable integration Customer Story | 4 min read SN Aboitiz Power (SNAP) operates several of the Philippines' most important hydropower assets, including the Magat Hydroelectric Power Plant in Ramon, Isabela. The plant delivers up to 388 MW of dependable hydropower capacity to the Luzon grid. It is also a strong contributor to the Philippines’ Energy Plan 2023–2050, where the government aims to raise the country’s total share of renewable energy to 50 percent by 2050. To strengthen operational flexibility and support the country's clean energy ambitions, SNAP implemented a battery energy storage system (BESS) with grid-forming capability at the Magat site in two phases. The first 24-MW system entered commercial operation in January 2024 and demonstrated ancillary services performance under real operating conditions. Building on this result, SNAP launched a 16 MW expansion in 2025, which entered commercial operation in June 2026. The two battery energy storage systems operate independently, each with its own control architecture and operational boundaries. When dispatched together, they can inject up to 40 MW of fast-response power at the site’s common point of coupling, strengthening grid support for the Luzon system. As the share of Variable Renewable Energy (VRE) on the Luzon grid continues to increase, system operators require faster and more reliable resources to maintain frequency stability and ensure secure operation. For SNAP, this challenge was particularly acute at the Magat site, where hydropower plays a dual role in supporting both electricity supply and critical irrigation needs. Any additional grid support capability would need to perform reliably under real operating conditions and respond predictably during system events. At the same time, it had to integrate with existing plant infrastructure without introducing operational complexity or disrupting established processes at the site. SNAP required a solution that could deliver dependable contingency reserves, maintain stable behavior during grid disturbances, and provide clear visibility for operators. Just as importantly, the approach needed to be scalable and proven in a way that would allow future capacity decisions to be taken with confidence, based on performance rather than assumptions. To meet these challenges, SNAP adopted a phased deployment approach to strengthen grid support at Magat while managing risk and ensuring continuity of operations. The first phase, a 24 MW BESS commissioned in January 2024, demonstrated dependable ancillary services performance in day-to-day conditions, providing the firm operational basis for SNAP's 16 MW expansion, which entered commercial operation in June 2026. With two independently controlled BESS units operating at a shared single point of interconnection, Hitachi Energy supplied the power conversion solutions, plant-level controls, SCADA integration, and engineering support across both phases, establishing consistent response characteristics and sitewide visibility through cloud-based remote monitoring while preserving independent operation. Using a consistent system architecture across both phases reduced integration risk, supported lender confidence, a key consideration for project bankability, and established a repeatable approach for scaling storage within the existing site framework. Each unit maintains its own plant controller and operating parameters, and when dispatched together the two systems can inject up to 40 MW at Magat's common point of coupling, meeting the grid's requirement for fast response while keeping the assets logically separate for operations and maintenance. The phased deployment at Magat has strengthened SNAP's ability to provide fast, dependable grid support on the Luzon system, improving frequency response capability and enhancing stability during system events. Operationally, each system maintains independent control and clearly defined operational boundaries, preserving the ability to dispatch, maintain, or modify one unit without affecting the other. Both installations feed into SNAP's Integrated Remote Operations Center (iROC), providing centralized visibility that supports timely and informed operator decision-making without adding complexity to site operations. By building on the proven performance of the initial installation and maintaining continuity in system execution, SNAP has established a repeatable pathway for scaling energy storage at Magat. SNAP's decision to award both phases to Hitachi Energy reflects a partnership built on demonstrated performance, a practical indicator of confidence as the site scales its storage capacity. In doing so, SNAP has demonstrated that storage and hydropower can be scaled together in a way that is technically sound, commercially repeatable, and directly aligned with the Philippines' ambition to make renewables the backbone of its energy future.

artigo.texto: NEGÓCIOS NA COP31 JBNews Por José Teixeira O governador Otaviano Pivetta participa, a partir desta segunda-feira (9), da 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas (COP31), em Antália, na Turquia, com uma agenda voltada à abertura de oportunidades econômicas para Mato Grosso por meio da comercialização internacional de créditos de carbono e outros ativos ambientais. A missão ocorre em um momento em que o Governo do Estado busca estruturar instrumentos jurídicos e financeiros para transformar resultados de redução do desmatamento em receitas destinadas à conservação ambiental e à implementação de políticas de desenvolvimento sustentável. A COP31 será realizada de 9 a 20 de novembro, reunindo representantes governamentais, instituições financeiras, empresas e organizações internacionais para discutir medidas relacionadas às mudanças climáticas, ao mercado de carbono e ao financiamento da preservação ambiental. Pivetta integra a delegação mato-grossense acompanhado da secretária de Estado de Meio Ambiente, Mauren Lazzaretti, responsável pela condução das políticas ambientais estaduais. Entre os compromissos previstos estão reuniões com representantes de investidores internacionais ligados à Coalizão LEAF, iniciativa que mobiliza recursos públicos e privados para apoiar a proteção de florestas tropicais e a redução de emissões provocadas pelo desmatamento. A participação de países como Reino Unido e Noruega nesses mecanismos de financiamento representa uma oportunidade de aproximação de Mato Grosso com compradores internacionais de resultados ambientais certificados. A intenção do governo é ampliar a confiança dos investidores em créditos de carbono gerados a partir de reduções de emissões registradas no território estadual. Para que esses resultados sejam comercializados, entretanto, é necessário atender a exigências técnicas de certificação, monitoramento e verificação, além de demonstrar que as reduções de emissões são reais, mensuráveis e adequadamente contabilizadas. O trabalho está associado ao mecanismo conhecido como REDD+ Jurisdicional, que permite desenvolver programas de redução de emissões por desmatamento e degradação florestal em escala estadual. Durante a conferência, integrantes do Consórcio da Amazônia Legal também deverão apresentar ações realizadas pelos estados brasileiros para estruturar esse modelo de financiamento ambiental. Em Mato Grosso, uma das principais medidas relacionadas ao projeto é a proposta de criação da Companhia Mato-grossense de Ativos Ambientais S.A. (CMAA). O projeto de lei foi encaminhado pelo governador à Assembleia Legislativa e prevê a constituição de uma sociedade de economia mista destinada à estruturação, gestão e comercialização de créditos de carbono, créditos de biodiversidade e outros ativos ambientais gerados no território estadual. A nova companhia deverá funcionar como instrumento empresarial para organizar operações ligadas à economia ambiental, respeitados os limites estabelecidos pela legislação e pelas regras de certificação dos ativos negociados. A proposta também está associada ao compromisso anunciado pelo Governo de Mato Grosso de alcançar a neutralidade líquida de emissões de carbono até 2035. A criação da empresa, porém, ainda depende de autorização legislativa e dos procedimentos necessários à sua constituição. O encaminhamento do projeto não significa que a companhia esteja em funcionamento ou que já existam contratos internacionais firmados. A importância econômica desse modelo decorre da possibilidade de Mato Grosso obter receitas a partir de resultados ambientais, sem depender exclusivamente das atividades tradicionais de produção agropecuária e exploração de recursos naturais. O Estado possui áreas dos biomas Amazônia, Cerrado e Pantanal, que apresentam características ambientais diferentes e exigem estratégias específicas de conservação. Ao mesmo tempo, Mato Grosso ocupa posição de destaque na produção brasileira de soja, milho, algodão e proteína animal, tornando relevante a relação entre expansão econômica, preservação ambiental e exigências dos mercados consumidores internacionais. A criação de instrumentos de comercialização de carbono poderá ampliar as fontes de financiamento para projetos de prevenção ao desmatamento, recuperação ambiental, proteção da biodiversidade e valorização de comunidades que participam da conservação dos recursos naturais. No entanto, a dimensão financeira dessas oportunidades dependerá do volume de reduções de emissões que receber certificação, dos preços negociados, das condições contratuais e dos compromissos assumidos pelos compradores. Até a abertura da conferência, os comunicados oficiais consultados não apresentavam novos contratos assinados durante a COP31 nem confirmavam receitas efetivamente ingressadas nos cofres de Mato Grosso em razão da missão internacional. A programação da delegação também contempla discussões sobre riscos climáticos, prevenção e combate a incêndios florestais, economia florestal e estratégias para enfrentar crimes ambientais. Outro aspecto importante da conferência será a discussão sobre mecanismos capazes de ampliar o financiamento climático destinado a regiões que concentram grandes áreas de vegetação nativa. Essas negociações podem influenciar diretamente os interesses de Mato Grosso, especialmente em relação às condições de certificação, pagamento e reconhecimento internacional de resultados de conservação florestal. A cúpula de chefes de Estado e de governo está programada para os dias 11 e 12 de novembro, quando deverão ocorrer reuniões e pronunciamentos de alto nível sobre os compromissos internacionais de enfrentamento das mudanças climáticas. artigo.texto: Viridi and Good Carbon Deploy One of the Largest Indoor Battery Energy Storage Systems in an Occupied US Residential Building BUFFALO, N.Y., Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Viridi, the industry leader in fail-safe distributed energy storage systems, and Good Carbon Co., today announced the deployment of a 3.75MWh lithium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS) at Peace Bridge Place, a 105-unit affordable housing apartment building in Buffalo, New York. The project is one of the largest indoor lithium-ion battery systems in an occupied residential building in the United States. At Peace Bridge Place, Viridi’s RPSLinkIN indoor BESS is part of a broader clean energy strategy that includes geothermal heating & cooling, domestic hot water, and high efficient building envelope upgrades. The 3.75 MWh system is designed to provide extended backup power for the fully electrified building during outages, while also helping reduce demand on the local grid during peak periods. Good Carbon Co., which focuses on revitalizing multifamily properties in communities throughout Western New York, selected the system to strengthen energy resilience for residents and enable the property to enable flexible, grid-responsive energy management. Adam Serbert, CEO of Good Carbon Co, said: Energy is one of the biggest operating costs in multifamily housing, and how you manage it directly affects the long-term performance of a property “At Peace Bridge Place, Viridi’s battery and energy management technology will help us reduce peak demand, avoid higher-cost periods and participate in demand response programs. That means lower operating costs, new revenue opportunities and a stronger economic foundation for keeping the property affordable and well maintained. For us, this is not just about one building — it is about creating a model we can apply across future multifamily projects.” Viridi’s intelligent Energy Management System automatically stores and discharges electricity based on the needs of the fully electrified property and the local grid. It allows Peace Bridge Place to reduce electricity demand during peak periods and respond to utility signals when additional grid flexibility is needed, while providing greater energy resilience for residents. By reducing peak demand and participating in demand response programs, the system can help lower the property’s energy costs while creating new revenue opportunities. The New York State Energy Research and Development Agency (NYSERDA) is providing support to Good Carbon Co. for the Peace Bridge Place project through its Future Grid Challenge. The Peace Bridge Place project is a National Grid pilot focused on integrating flexible, grid-responsive technologies into its distribution network. Viridi’s energy storage and energy management technology will work in coordination with EnergyHub’s Edge Distributed Energy Resource Management System (DERMS), enabling the property to respond to National Grid signals during periods of peak electricity demand. Doreen M. Harris, President and CEO, NYSERDA, said: Peace Bridge Place demonstrates how forward-thinking energy storage solutions can ensure New York’s multifamily buildings are meeting the energy needs of its residents while creating a more reliable and resilient electric grid, “Projects like this embody NYSERDA’s mission to spur innovation that drives New York toward a clean energy future.” Distributed across seven battery rooms, the 3.75MWh system is integrated with Viridi’s proprietary Energy Management System (EMS), which optimizes the property’s electricity use while enabling it to respond to changing conditions on the local grid in two key ways: - Peak Shaving: As the building’s grid energy draw approaches a monthly peak, the battery automatically discharges to keep demand below a target threshold, reducing peak demand and associated $/kW demand charges. - Seasonal Demand Response: During peak events, National Grid dispatch signals are delivered through EnergyHub’s platform to Viridi’s energy management system, which then coordinates the response across the building’s battery and other energy systems. For participating residents, smart thermostat setpoints can be adjusted to “pre-cool” or “pre-heat” apartments before the event, enabling reduced HVAC consumption during the event while the battery discharges. Residents can opt out of individual events at any time. Together, these actions allow the property to reduce its net electricity demand while the local grid is under the greatest strain. Deploying lithium-ion battery storage indoors at this scale requires rigorous safety standards. The risk of thermal runaway — and its potential to propagate from cell to cell — has historically constrained where lithium-ion systems can be installed. The RPSLinkIN system is designed to address that challenge through Viridi’s proprietary Fail-Safe Anti-Propagation architecture, a passive safety layer designed to prevent thermal runaway from spreading between cells. That safety architecture has undergone industry-standard testing designed to evaluate how battery systems behave during a thermal runaway event. During UL 9540A testing, a cell was intentionally driven into thermal failure to determine whether the event would spread to surrounding cells. Viridi’s technology prevented cell-to-cell propagation, with no detectable release of heat, sparks, smoke, gas or flames. RPSLinkIN has also earned UL 9540 Listing from TÜV Rheinland, providing third-party certification of the complete energy storage system. Jon M. Williams, CEO of Viridi, said: This project demonstrates what becomes possible when energy storage is designed to serve the building and the grid at the same time, “Peace Bridge Place will now be able to reduce peak demand, respond when the grid needs support and strengthen resilience for the people who live there. Hyderabad-based energy storage company TREX Energy has begun lithium battery manufacturing at E-City in Maheshwaram, using an automatic module assembly line that produces 12 parts per minute. The plant will make 52S battery packs for 261 kWh and 5 MWh storage systems, supporting a product range that runs from 5 kWh home units to 5 MWh utility-scale BESS. The company has also received four acres of land from the Madhya Pradesh Government for a Phase 2 unit, though the plant’s capacity and timeline are yet to be confirmed. TREX Energy, an Indian energy storage company, has opened its lithium battery manufacturing facility at E-City, Raviryal, in Maheshwaram, Hyderabad. The plant was commissioned in late September, and the company formally announced its opening this week. It has a 12 PPM automatic module assembly line built to produce 52S battery packs, which are used in 261 kWh and 5 MWh energy storage systems. The plant comes at a time when India is adding renewable energy capacity quickly, and industries, utilities and households need more storage as a result. Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and other energy storage system (ESS) products help manage swings in power supply, handle peak loads and provide backup power. According to the India Energy Storage Alliance (IESA), India added 7.9 GWh of BESS capacity in the first half of 2026, taking its operational capacity to 8.5 GWh. TREX Energy said the Hyderabad unit will serve this demand through local manufacturing. It plans to build products suited to Indian operating conditions, reduce dependence on imports and shorten delivery times. Bharat S. Chhittarka, Director, TREX Energy, said the company was focused on lowering financing costs so that BESS becomes more affordable and reliable for the Indian market. He added that energy must be available when it is needed, and BESS was a key solution for this. The assembly line makes battery modules at a rate of 12 parts per minute. The company said automation will help keep production consistent, improve efficiency and maintain quality control as demand grows. Roshan Shaik, Technical Director, TREX Energy, said the line was a significant step forward for the company’s manufacturing capabilities. He said it allows the company to produce battery modules efficiently and consistently for BESS solutions ranging from 5 kWh to 5 MWh, and strengthens its ability to meet India’s rising storage demand with scalable and reliable products. The portfolio includes C&I BESS for factories, offices and commercial facilities looking to manage energy use, ensure backup power and improve operational resilience. It also covers utility-scale BESS for grid applications and large renewable energy projects, residential energy storage systems, home inverter batteries, and battery packs and ESS configurations, including the 52S packs for 261 kWh and 5 MWh systems. Earlier this year, the company launched its REX BESS, a liquid-cooled 125 kW/261 kWh cabinet system for commercial and industrial users. A few months later, IESA named it the C&I Company of the Year. For its next phase, TREX Energy has been allotted four acres of land by the Madhya Pradesh Government for a proposed Phase 2 facility. The expansion is expected to enlarge its manufacturing footprint and help it serve customers in more markets across India. Details of the facility’s capacity, development timeline and commissioning are yet to be confirmed. The company said it will continue to invest in manufacturing, technology and local talent as it expands. TREX Energy, which carries the tagline “We Store Electrons”, has registered offices in Hyderabad, Telangana, and Pune, Maharashtra. The new plant adds to a growing cluster of battery units around Maheshwaram, where Cygni Energy opened a 4.8 GWh BESS facility last year. India’s cell manufacturing is still at an early stage, so most local assembly units continue to depend on imported cells. Demand, however, is expected to keep climbing, with the Central Electricity Authority estimating a need for 236 GWh of BESS capacity by 2031-32. How quickly TREX firms up the capacity and timeline for its Madhya Pradesh unit will show how seriously it plans to compete for that demand. Source PTI 9th Nov, 2026 8th Nov, 2026 7th Nov, 2026

artigo.texto: Cabinet Approves Rs. 145 bn Scheme for Grid-Scale Energy Storage 09 Nov 2026 2 Min Read CW Team Share The Union Cabinet has approved a Viability Gap Funding (VGF) scheme with financial support of Rs. 145 bn for developing 92 GWh of grid-scale energy storage capacity. The scheme will run from FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31 and is intended to support capacity that has yet to be commissioned across India. The proposed capacity will represent 170 per cent of the country’s present grid-scale energy storage capacity and contribute towards the required 411 GWh capacity by 2031-32. The initiative is designed to support larger integration of renewable energy, improve grid stability and enable reliable, affordable and round-the-clock electricity supply. Under the scheme, 60 GWh will be allocated to Hydro Pumped Storage Plant (PSP) projects, 30 GWh to Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and 2 GWh to alternative energy storage technologies. The projects are expected to involve total investment of Rs. 976 bn, with VGF support intended to improve their financial viability and speed up the deployment of large-scale infrastructure. Capacity will be allocated through a tariff-based competitive bidding process. Public and private sector electricity distribution companies will be eligible for support for BESS and Hydro PSP projects, while projects using alternative storage technologies may be implemented by public and private sector entities. The scheme also includes a minimum Domestic Content Requirement of 40 per cent for BESS projects. The requirement is intended to encourage domestic manufacturing, create opportunities for Indian industry and reduce dependence on imported components, alongside existing supply-side incentives for battery manufacturing. The government expects the programme to improve the flexibility and resilience of the electricity system by addressing variations in renewable generation and reducing reliance on conventional generation for balancing power. It is also intended to strengthen energy security, support wider renewable energy utilisation and advance domestic manufacturing capabilities. artigo.texto: [SMM PV Flash] Tata Power Commissions 300 MW Solar Plant in Karnataka, Utility Portfolio Reaches 12 GW Tata Power announced on 5 November that Tata Power Renewable Energy, through wholly owned subsidiary TP Saurya, has commissioned a 300 MW solar project for the Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) at Koppal in Karnataka, with the plant now in commercial operation. The project uses solar trackers and TP580HG10NB bifacial modules, is expected to generate about 810 million units of electricity a year and mitigate around 103,820 tonnes of carbon emissions annually. With the commissioning, Tata Power Renewable Energy's utility-scale renewable portfolio has reached 12 GW, comprising about 7.2 GW operational, including 5.8 GW of solar and 1.3 GW of wind, another 4.9 GW at various stages of implementation and 0.7 GWh of battery energy storage. The company also disclosed 60 MWh of battery energy storage in operation across three locations in Mumbai at Mahalaxmi, Saki and Mankhurd, with a 200 MWh deployment across ten locations in the city approved by the Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission in April 2025.

artigo.texto: Tamil Nadu Mandates Battery Storage for Solar Projects Above 1 MW 09 Nov 2026 2 Min Read CW Team Share The Tamil Nadu government has mandated battery storage for every new solar project with a capacity of 1 MW or more under its Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Policy 2026. The policy aims to create 10 GWh of storage capacity by 2029, improve grid stability, support reliable peak-hour supply and increase the use of renewable power. New solar projects must install storage equivalent to at least 10% of their installed capacity, with the systems capable of discharging for four hours. The requirement applies to projects applying on or after the policy notification date and to projects commissioned from April 1, 2027. New substations pooling renewable power must install standalone storage equal to at least 10% of their sanctioned capacity. Existing substations must add storage equivalent to 5% in 2027-28 and a further 5% in 2028-29, as the state currently cannot utilise around 3,000-4,000 MW of solar power during the day. Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation will procure 2,500 MW, or 10,000 MWh, of battery storage in the first phase through competitive bidding. The prices will require approval from the Tamil Nadu Electricity Regulatory Commission, while Tamil Nadu Green Energy Corporation will act as the nodal agency for implementing the policy. The policy covers standalone storage facilities, systems integrated with solar and wind projects, and installations supporting transmission and distribution networks. Existing solar and wind projects can add storage without further approvals, while eligible projects commissioned during the policy period will receive a 10-year waiver of wheeling and transmission charges if the discharged energy is used within the state. The government has also launched a renewable energy application portal covering solar, wind, hybrid wind-solar and battery storage projects. Developers can register, submit documents, pay fees, complete technical scrutiny, undertake load-flow studies and obtain grid connectivity approvals online, while also tracking applications, correcting deficiencies and downloading approval orders. artigo.texto: CATL Backs Buyback With Aviation and Home-Storage Pacts as Margin Questions Linger Published on 11/08/2026 at 02:50 | Editorial boerse-global.de CATL has repurchased roughly 19.6 million A-shares through October 31, spending about RMB 5.4 billion, the company said on November 2. The figure sits well inside the RMB 20 billion to RMB 40 billion envelope authorized under its buyback program. The repurchase disclosure landed alongside a separate filing on the H-shares. UBS Group AG's disclosed long position in the Hong Kong-listed line fell to 4.82%, dropping it below the 5% reporting threshold. According to media reports, the decline stemmed from the return of shares under a securities lending arrangement rather than direct trading on the exchange. Aviation Battery Deal Adds a New Vertical Also on November 2, CATL signed strategic cooperation and product development agreements with Blue Vector. The two sides plan to jointly develop bespoke aviation batteries for the electric aircraft SKYLA V30, with Blue Vector naming CATL its exclusive battery partner. The aviation tie-up is the most unusual of a cluster of announcements that has broadened CATL's storage and transport footprint in recent weeks. On Tuesday, the company signed a memorandum of understanding with Octopus Energy and Ampace covering smart home-storage systems, with European markets as the initial focus. Under the plan, Octopus Energy's software and customer platform would be paired with battery technology from CATL and Ampace. The memorandum sets out a framework for joint exploration rather than a product already on sale. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? A second European storage initiative followed on October 27, when CATL and INTILION signed a memorandum to deploy CATL energy-storage systems totaling 3 GWh over five years. Germany, Switzerland and Austria are among the intended markets, and the agreement extends to additional territories beyond those three. Zeng Points to a Terawatt-Hour Era Chairman and chief executive Robin Zeng said on October 31 that CATL expects shipments of more than 1,000 GWh in 2026, up from 661 GWh the prior year. Zeng framed the forecast as the company's entry into the terawatt-hour era. The order pipeline is not the only variable in play. JPMorgan took a more cautious line a day earlier, cutting its earnings forecasts for Chinese battery makers, according to media reports, citing the difficulty of passing battery tax costs through to customers. The same cost-transfer squeeze was cited in coverage of the sector backdrop against which CATL's shares fell 3.7% on Friday, with the stock among battery names pulling back after an earlier rally in what reports described as a sector-wide retreat. CATL at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now. Melbourne Launch and Australian Alliances Outside Europe, CATL presented its TENER+ battery storage system, rated at 9 MWh, in Melbourne on October 28. It also announced memoranda with Hitachi Energy, EPEC Group and UNSW Sydney covering project delivery, grid connection and qualification. For investors, the buyback provides a concrete tally against a backdrop of announcements that range from signed supply frameworks to early-stage exploration. The UBS position change, tied to securities lending, is a technical adjustment in the H-share register and does not by itself alter the company's share count or the value held by other shareholders. artigo.texto: In early October, Joe Naff noticed a couple of guys with machinery across the street from his Smyth County home, climbing up the hillside. To him, it looked like core drilling to test the soil and stone in the rolling countryside of his neighborhood. What looked like noise testing followed a week later, he said in an interview, and Naff’s suspicions grew. Then, in late October, the town of Marion released a statement announcing a developer was interested in about 200 acres of government-owned property in the area — but council members and town staff wouldn’t say who the developer was or what it wanted to build. “If the council can just tell me that it is not a data center, I will back down,” Naff said during a town meeting Nov. 2. There was no reply from the council members. Concerns about the possibility of a data center are growing for Marion residents and Smyth County neighbors who live by the property, which lies just past the northeastern limits of Marion’s boundaries. The town, which is the county seat and has a population of about 5,500, has owned the land for five years and transferred the property to its economic development authority this past summer. When emailed questions about the developer and possible uses for the property, town manager Andrew Keen directed Cardinal News to the council’s October statement. The statement said Marion has been trying to find a good use for the property, even before it owned the land. The town has courted developers for housing, truck stops, distribution centers and manufacturing, according to the statement, but all attempts have been unsuccessful. Then a developer — unnamed in the statement — expressed interest early in 2026, which is why the town transferred the property to the development authority. “We don’t know if this property will pass environmental muster,” the statement said. “We don’t know if this company will select our site over others available. We don’t know if this developer will choose to pursue the purchase of this property.” The property is in a “due-diligence phase,” according to the statement. “Like other localities, we don’t make announcements based on anything short of certainties,” the statement said. A Cardinal News records request for nondisclosure agreements came up empty — the town attorney, Mark Fenyk, said in an email that neither the town or its development authority have any on file. Only one out of eight town council members, Hunter Atwell, responded to a request for comment. He said by email that Keen had already provided a response, and he confirmed he hadn’t signed an NDA. Since the property is in Smyth County, outside town limits, any kind of request to build a data center will have to go through its planning commission and board of supervisors, County Administrator Shawn Utt said in a video interview. The county passed an ordinance requiring a special exceptions permit for data center developments in September — though some residents have said officials haven’t gone far enough to protect the county’s ample agricultural land from data centers. Some also say the original zoning ordinance didn’t have data center language in the first place, so in their view, creating a special exceptions permit allows them into Smyth County. The county hasn’t received any requests for rezoning or a special exception permit for the property, Utt said. The process would probably take about a month and a half to come to a final vote, he said, between a public hearing and meeting discussions, if not longer. Eye on tax revenue The land could be a positive in terms of economic development and tax revenues, Utt said. Commercial use would be valuable, he said, and the county also has a need for housing. He is hopeful an interested developer means good things for Smyth County. “If it’s a data center — let’s put it this way, the bean counter in me wants the tax revenue,” Utt said. “The land has not been a tax generator for us, even though it’s got the potential. Anything would be great, anything commercialized.” But for Naff, the way Marion has handled the process has been disrespectful of residents who deserve to know what’s going to happen in their region, he said. His front porch looks out over the hills that he believes will become a data center. Should one be built, he and his neighbors are concerned about the toll on their utilities, property values and quality of life, as well as any potential environmental impact. A couple have broken down in tears while speaking to the town council about the issue. Their questions deserve answers, Naff said. He was born and raised in Marion, working in commercial real estate in the region. He moved into his house northeast of town in 2007. At the time, Walmart was considering building on the acreage now owned by the town, and he knew developers would be interested in the area, he said. But this result is not what he wanted, he said. “I don’t want a data center anywhere, but this?” Naff said. “This is not the highest and best use of this property.” He has had an issue with the town owning the land far before a data center came into the conversation, Naff said. The town bought the acreage for about $800,000 across three parcels. Marion did not do its due diligence, in his view, to figure out how much the land was worth or what resources it had to offer before signing the purchase agreement, he said. Now, this is the town’s last-ditch effort to make up for the misuse of public dollars buying the property, he said. “Nothing’s coming to fruition,” Naff said. “So, it’s my opinion that this is the Hail Mary.” ‘It’s just so pretty’ Sally Hash owns 90 acres across the road from the government-owned land. She and her daughters have raised cattle, sheep and goats there for over a decade, mostly as a hobby. artigo.texto: As data center developments continue to generate debate across Central Texas, one Killeen resident believes the industry could provide significant economic and workforce opportunities for the city. Olayinka Adelusi, who recently attended a Microsoft-related data center workshop in Southside, Virginia, is encouraging Killeen officials and residents to consider the potential benefits of attracting data center investments. “It’s something I really want us to have in Killeen here,” Adelusi said. “It’s going to open up our economy.” Adelusi said his visit demonstrated how data centers can support local businesses, create technical jobs and establish workforce partnerships with educational institutions. He described increased demand for construction materials, transportation services, hotels and food vendors in the Virginia community, which he attributed to data center development. Adelusi also addressed concerns about electricity consumption, water usage and noise. Based on the facilities he visited, he believes some concerns about noise are overstated and said operators are adopting cooling systems that recycle water and reduce energy consumption. However, the environmental impacts of data centers vary depending on their size, design and infrastructure requirements. Rather than opposing developments outright, Adelusi believes Killeen should negotiate agreements that provide measurable community benefits. “They need something from us. We should need something from them,” Adelusi said. He suggested that the city pursue commitments involving local hiring, workforce training and opportunities for area businesses. One example he highlighted was Microsoft’s partnership with Southside Virginia Community College and Hiring Our Heroes, which provides technical training for transitioning military personnel. In April, the college reported an 85% job placement rate within Microsoft over the preceding year through its Military Data Center Pathway program. Adelusi believes similar partnerships could be established with Central Texas College and Texas A&M University-Central Texas, particularly because of Killeen’s proximity to Fort Hood. “Imagine how many soldiers are transitioning every year,” Adelusi said. He said programs in HVAC, electrical maintenance, cybersecurity and data center operations could provide additional career opportunities for students and transitioning service members while reducing the need to commute to larger metropolitan areas. Killeen has already encountered opposition to data center development. In April, the Planning and Zoning Commission recommended denying a conditional-use permit for a proposed $30 million computing facility associated with ONMINE on South Fort Hood Street. During an Oct. 5 joint meeting, the City Council voted 6-1 to direct staff to develop alternative zoning standards for data centers rather than requiring individual conditional-use permits for every facility. Adelusi believes future discussions should balance infrastructure concerns with potential economic benefits, including tax revenue, local contracts and employment opportunities. For him, the priority is ensuring Killeen receives tangible benefits from companies seeking to invest in the community. “It’s really a good deal,” Adelusi said. “We just have to ask this company who is running this data center.”

artigo.texto: O Nature Investment Lab (NIL) iniciou, na sexta-feira, 6 de novembro de 2026, o processo de consulta pública direcionado à estruturação de um modelo de contrato padrão de compra e venda de créditos de carbono voltado a projetos de Soluções Baseadas na Natureza (SbN). A entidade informou que a rodada de coleta de contribuições técnicas segue aberta até o dia 27 de novembro de 2026, com a publicação da versão final de mercado projetada para março de 2027. O objetivo declarado pela articulação institucional consiste em colher subsídios de compradores, desenvolvedores, instituições financeiras e estruturadores de ativos ambientais para mitigar assimetrias jurídicas que encarecem e desaceleram as operações no país. Segundo os dados divulgados pelo NIL, a minuta preliminar do instrumento contratual foi construída após a realização de rodadas de consulta técnica com 25 instituições atuantes na cadeia de valor de finanças verdes e descarbonização. Entre os agentes envolvidos no desenho inicial constam organizações como Itaú BBA, Re.green, Petrobras, BNDES, Regia Capital e Systemica. A entidade afirma que o mecanismo tem como foco central os contratos de aquisição de longo prazo (conhecidos no jargão setorial como offtake agreements), apontados pela iniciativa como uma das principais ferramentas para a mitigação de volatilidade e risco de demanda em empreendimentos florestais e de restauração ecológica. A apresentação do modelo contratual ocorre em um momento estratégico de inserção internacional da agenda ambiental brasileira. De acordo com o cronograma detalhado pelo laboratório de investimentos, a minuta preliminar do documento, previamente apresentada na Semana do Clima de Nova York em setembro de 2026, será submetida a debates globais durante a COP31, realizada na Turquia. Na ocasião, representantes da liderança executiva da Climate Ventures integrarão o painel setorial sobre ampliação de investimentos em SbN promovido em conjunto pela Anbima, CNSeg e Febraban. Estrutura da arquitetura contratual proposta Conforme a documentação técnica submetida à consulta pelo NIL, as transações de ativos florestais e ecológicos no Brasil enfrentam entraves decorrentes do caráter estritamente bilateral e customizado de cada operação. Essa fragmentação eleva os custos de assessoria jurídica, estende prazos de diligência prévia (due diligence) e dificulta a comparabilidade entre portfólios para fins de precificação e garantia bancária. Para superar tais gargalos, o modelo arquitetado pelo NIL baseia-se em uma segmentação modular composta por cláusulas fundamentais, anexos comerciais customizáveis e apêndices operacionais. A entidade ressalta que os apêndices opcionais permitem às partes estruturar esquemas contratuais complexos, contemplando estruturas de financiamento fornecidas pelo próprio comprador corporativo, mecanismos de retenção em caso de não conformidade de certificação e salvaguardas voltadas às comunidades tradicionais afetadas pelos projetos territoriais. A padronização também estabelece balizas para a atribuição clara da titularidade dos créditos gerados, evitando bitributação, dupla contagem e conflitos dominiais que historicamente afastam investidores institucionais conservadores. De acordo com a avaliação transmitida pela gerência de projetos da Climate Ventures, a criação de contratos padronizados atua como catalisador de liquidez ao transformar ativos de descarbonização em instrumentos financeiros compreensíveis e securitizáveis. A entidade defende que a unificação das regras de compra e venda fortalece a previsibilidade operacional e jurídica, tornando viável a alocação de volumes substanciais de capital estrangeiro direcionados à restauração florestal em larga escala no território nacional. Gargalos de transação e ambiente de negócios para SbN O mercado de Soluções Baseadas na Natureza enfrenta o desafio estrutural de conciliar o horizonte temporal biológico da captura de carbono — que demanda décadas para consolidação de biomassa florestal — com as exigências de retorno e prazos regulatórios dos fundos globais de investimento. Na perspectiva defendida pelo NIL, a inexistência de uma base contratual amplamente aceita no Brasil atua como barreira de entrada para grandes aportes de capital intensivo, uma vez que cada projeto necessita de meses de negociações exaustivas entre departamentos jurídicos antes da assinatura do compromisso financeiro. A fragmentação de contratos acarreta custos transacionais desproporcionais, penalizando especialmente os desenvolvedores locais de menor porte e encarecendo a originação dos créditos. O modelo proposto visa estabelecer um vocabulário comum entre agentes da economia real, como companhias industriais com metas líquidas zero (net zero), e o sistema financeiro, englobando bancos comerciais, seguradoras e gestoras de fundos florestais. A modularidade do instrumento responde diretamente à demanda por padronização sem eliminar a autonomia das partes para precificar o risco inerente a cada bioma ou metodologia de crédito de carbono. Além da complexidade jurídica entre agentes privados, a conformidade de salvaguardas socioambientais e os critérios de adicionalidade climática figuram como elementos sensíveis na modelagem do NIL. O mercado internacional de créditos de carbono passou por revisões técnicas rigorosas nos últimos ciclos anuais, exigindo garantias verificáveis de integridade ecológica e governança territorial. Ao incorporar apêndices específicos voltados à mitigação de riscos regulatórios e integridade socioambiental, a minuta busca antecipar exigências de mercados jurisdicionais e fundos institucionais de alta governança. Articulação institucional e governança do projeto O Nature Investment Lab foi instituído em 2024 como uma rede técnica colaborativa focada em desobstruir gargalos financeiros e estruturar mecanismos de mercado para acelerar investimentos em Soluções Baseadas na Natureza.
