artigo.texto: CATL to Cancel Repurchased A-Shares as JPMorgan Trims Targets on Battery-Tax Squeeze Published on 11/08/2026 at 17:21 | Editorial boerse-global.de CATL plans to cancel the A-shares it has bought back under an existing repurchase programme, the battery giant disclosed, with the shares acquired through a plan authorised at between RMB20 billion and RMB40 billion. The cancellation has been flagged but not yet reported as completed. The buyback news lands alongside a round of target-price cuts from JPMorgan, which on Friday trimmed its earnings forecasts for Chinese battery manufacturers. The US bank pointed to battery-tax costs proving harder to pass on to customers than anticipated, and also assumed lower per-unit profits across the sector. Dual-listed targets move in opposite directions For CATL's A-shares, JPMorgan lowered its price target to RMB300 from RMB310 while keeping an "Overweight" rating. The H-share target came down to HKD420 from HKD440, with the rating held at "Neutral." CATL stock fell 3.7% on Friday. Media reports linked the pressure to the JPMorgan sector note, though no direct causal link between the day's decline and the analysis has been established. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? Europe and Australia storage agreements stack up On the operational front, CATL has rolled out a series of energy-storage agreements. A letter of intent signed on 27 October with INTILION covers the deployment of 3 GWh of CATL storage systems over five years, targeting Germany, Switzerland, Austria and other markets. Applications span utility-scale storage through to commercial and industrial installations, drawing on both sodium-ion and lithium-ion technologies. A day earlier, CATL subsidiary Ampace signed a letter of intent with Octopus Energy covering home storage, intelligent energy management and clean-energy services, including the possible use of sodium-ion batteries. Under the arrangement, Ampace is to handle development and manufacturing of the cells, battery management system and complete system, while Octopus Energy contributes sales channels and energy services. The partners will explore potential smart home-storage solutions for European households, with the UK, France and Spain as priority markets. CATL also used the All Energy Australia 2026 exhibition on 29 October to unveil its TENER+ storage system, signing partnership letters of intent with Hitachi Energy, EPEC Group and UNSW Sydney. CATL at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now. Aviation battery and a 1,000 GWh ambition Elsewhere, CATL agreed a strategic and product-related collaboration with Blue Vector on Monday. The company is to develop an aviation battery for Blue Vector's SKYLA V30 aircraft and has been named exclusive battery partner. Looking further out, chairman and chief executive Robin Zeng said on 31 October that CATL expects shipments of more than 1,000 GWh in 2026. artigo.texto: HOUSTON – Soaring water bills, massive data centers and how Texas handles students who repeatedly miss school could all become the subjects of new legislation as state lawmakers prepare to return to Austin. Monday, Nov. 9, marks the first day lawmakers can begin filing bills for the 2027 legislative session, offering Texans an early glimpse of the proposals that could eventually become state law. Recommended Videos And several Greater Houston lawmakers have already identified changes they want to pursue. The filing period also comes less than a week after Democrats flipped the Texas House and won the governor’s office, while Republicans retained control of the Senate. That means some proposals that struggled in previous sessions could get another chance, although lawmakers will still need to navigate a divided Legislature. Here’s what Houston-area representatives and senators have said they want to tackle. Data centers: Giving counties more authority State Rep. Cody Vasut, a Republican from Angleton, has committed to reviving legislation that would give counties greater authority over large developments, including data centers. The proposal would address concerns involving noise, public health and safety in unincorporated areas, where counties have fewer land-use regulatory powers than cities. Vasut introduced similar legislation during the previous session, but it never reached the House floor. “When you develop in the county, it’s been viewed kind of as the Wild West,” Vasut said during a public meeting in Brazoria County. He has argued that counties need additional tools as industrial projects increasingly move closer to residential neighborhoods. Not all Republicans agree. Houston-area Sen. Paul Bettencourt has argued that data center regulations should be established statewide rather than allowing individual communities to adopt different rules. Meanwhile, Houston Democratic Rep. Senfronia Thompson has raised another concern: Who should pay for the infrastructure needed to support the growing industry? During an August legislative hearing, Thompson questioned why residents should bear costs associated with data centers they had little say in approving. “Data centers are being pushed upon them, and they don’t have a choice to say no. But they’ve got to pay. I think that’s unfair. It’s undemocratic,” Thompson said. The issue could also overlap with Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa’s agenda. She has called for new restrictions on data center development and changes to industry tax incentives. RELATED COVERAGE: Water bills: New protections after Aqua Texas complaints State Rep. Tom Oliverson, a Republican representing northwest Harris County, wants changes to how private water utilities charge customers following complaints about soaring Aqua Texas bills. As KPRC 2 previously reported, some customers have received monthly bills exceeding $1,000, prompting lawmakers to question how the increases were allowed. “I am urging the Public Utility Commission to reject the proposed rate filing and furthermore to direct Aqua Texas to refund all of the excessive charges,” Oliverson told KPRC 2. The controversy could also lead to changes in how private utilities impose temporary rate increases, recover infrastructure costs and bill customers for wastewater services. Oliverson is not alone. Republican state Reps. Gary Gates and Cody Harris have also examined whether state regulations allow private utilities to impose substantial rate increases before regulators complete their reviews. Gates has questioned whether lawmakers need to close gaps in existing rules. Aqua Texas maintains that its rates reflect infrastructure investments intended to improve service and reliability. Its rate case remains under review. The lawmakers have not announced specific 2027 bill numbers, but their comments suggest utility regulation could receive renewed attention when the Legislature convenes. RELATED COVERAGE: KPRC 2’s Aqua Texas investigation School attendance: A renewed fight over truancy laws Houston Republican Sen. Paul Bettencourt has identified chronic truancy as a priority for the 2027 legislative session. Bettencourt previously pursued legislation to restore a civil truancy process for students who repeatedly miss school, but those efforts failed to pass. He told KPRC 2 Investigates last November that he intends to work with the Texas Education Agency (TEA) to refine the proposal for another attempt. “I’m going to be talking to TEA and say, ‘this is the focus.’ We tried to pass this bill twice. I want this bill tuned up to be the best it can be for the third pass,” Bettencourt said. The proposal could reignite a debate over how Texas should address students who are chronically absent. But Houston Democratic Rep. Gene Wu has questioned whether tougher truancy enforcement would address the circumstances keeping students out of classrooms. “Think about kids who are living in abject poverty, living in violent environments, living in difficult family situations. What are you going to do to them? Are you just going to punish them more than what life has already thrown at them?” Wu told KPRC 2 Investigates last November. Wu has instead advocated for additional resources to address barriers to school attendance, including transportation difficulties and family instability. RELATED COVERAGE: KPRC 2 Investigates school attendance School vouchers and Medicaid: Houston Democrats want another look Houston Democratic Rep. Christina Morales has identified repealing Texas’ private school voucher program and expanding Medicaid as priorities for the incoming House majority. Morales, who leads the House Democrats’ campaign arm, also wants lawmakers to revisit legislation she says unfairly targets immigrants and communities of color. The voucher program, approved in 2025, allows eligible families to use state funds toward private education expenses. artigo.texto: What to know: - Moratorium on new data centers: Michigan governor-elect Jocelyn Benson is proposing a pause on new data center construction until the state establishes regulations to protect communities and natural resources. - Community input required: Developers would have to hold public hearings before projects move forward, giving residents an opportunity to ask questions and voice concerns. - More transparency: Companies would be required to disclose information about proposed projects to prevent behind-the-scenes agreements that exclude residents. - Protecting water and land: Developers would have to demonstrate before construction that their projects would not harm Michigan’s natural resources. Recommended Videos Michigan governor-elect Jocelyn Benson is proposing a moratorium on new data center construction in the state until regulations require developers to meet specific standards for community transparency, environmental protections, and energy costs. Under the proposal, Michigan would not allow new data centers until rules require companies to negotiate openly with communities, protect natural resources, and cover the costs of their energy use. Benson’s plan calls for public hearings before projects move forward, allowing residents to ask questions and share concerns about proposed developments. It would also require transparency and disclosure reporting to prevent agreements between developers and government officials from excluding community members from the process. Another part of the proposal would require data center developers to demonstrate before construction that their projects would not negatively affect natural resources, including water and land. Benson also wants data centers to pay for the additional electricity they use rather than passing those costs on to residential and other consumers. Her proposal would prohibit data centers from receiving tax breaks. The plan also calls for union contracts to ensure data center projects create well-paying jobs for Michigan workers. Benson said companies that violate the proposed requirements would not be allowed to operate in Michigan. The proposal comes as data center development has become a growing concern for communities worried about energy demand, water consumption, environmental impacts, and the potential costs of large-scale facilities. Benson’s plan would establish requirements for how future data center projects are reviewed and approved, with an emphasis on community involvement and corporate accountability. During her one-on-one sit-down with Local 4 anchor Ty Steele, Benson said she supported a moratorium on new data centers until the state establishes safeguards to protect water and energy resources. Benson also said that companies should be required to pay for the energy they use and address noise pollution concerns. She proposed requiring community benefits agreements and creating an online portal where residents could track proposed and existing data center projects and provide input. Benson said the goal was to ensure communities benefit from development rather than simply absorbing its costs. More: Jocelyn Benson’s campaign promises as Michigan governor

The decline coincided with a fresh dose of caution from JPMorgan, which trimmed its earnings forecasts for China's battery sector, citing the difficulty of passing on tax-related battery costs to customers. The bank's more guarded stance accompanied the weakness in Hong Kong-listed battery stocks but was not established as the sole trigger for CATL's slide. Lower Price Targets Across Both Share Classes JPMorgan cut its target for the A-share line to RMB 300 from RMB 310, and lowered the H-share target to HKD 420 from HKD 440. The "Neutral" rating stayed in place on both counts. Buyback Progress and a Bullish Delivery Forecast On the capital-return front, CATL reported Monday that it had repurchased 19,605,919 A-shares through October 31, paying RMB 5,360,125,612.64 excluding transaction fees. The purchases fall under an already approved program worth between RMB 20 billion and RMB 40 billion, with the bought-back stock earmarked for cancellation and a reduction in registered capital. The update reflects execution of the existing plan rather than any new repurchase announcement. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? Chairman and CEO Robin Zeng offered a separate gauge of business momentum on October 31, projecting deliveries of more than 1,000 GWh for the current year. That would mark a substantial step up from the 661 GWh shipped in the prior year. European Home Storage in the Works CATL, Octopus Energy and Ampace signed a memorandum of understanding to explore smart home storage and energy-management solutions, with the UK, France and Spain as the first markets in view. Under the arrangement, Ampace would develop and manufacture the battery cells, battery management systems and storage systems, while Octopus Energy would contribute its customer channels along with energy supply and management services. Sodium-ion technology could also feature in the solutions under review. The agreement is aimed at exploring options, not at a confirmed full-scale market rollout. Aviation and Industrial Partnerships Round Out the Week CATL also closed strategic and product-related cooperation agreements with Blue Vector on Monday, becoming the exclusive battery partner for the SKYLA V30 aircraft and taking on custom development of the aviation battery for the program. Two days earlier, on November 1, the company agreed a strategic collaboration with Shanghai Electric spanning carbon-neutral industrial parks, energy storage, green transport and international business. artigo.texto: Trocar um carro a combustão por um carro elétrico pode parecer uma boa estratégia para quem trabalha como taxista. Afinal, gastar menos com combustível e reduzir algumas despesas de manutenção pode fazer diferença para quem passa boa parte do dia dirigindo. Mas existe um detalhe que precisa entrar na conta antes de assumir um financiamento de 60 meses: o preço da bateria. Em um cenário de compra de um veículo de R$ 160 mil parcelado em cinco anos, a economia com recargas precisa ser comparada com os custos de seguro, manutenção, financiamento e possíveis reparos depois do fim da garantia. LEIA TAMBÉM: - Aposentadorias do INSS podem chegar a R$ 8.893 em 2027 e novo salário mínimo promete aumentar pagamentos; veja quanto cada um poderá receber - Empregada doméstica tem direito ao 13º salário; patrão pode ser multado se atrasar pagamento - Imposto do Pecado começa em 2027: veja quais produtos terão novas alíquotas e como fica o preço A bateria de íon-lítio é um dos componentes mais caros de um automóvel elétrico. Levantamentos sobre o mercado brasileiro apontam que a substituição pode representar até 40% do preço total do veículo, embora o valor varie conforme a marca, o modelo e a capacidade do conjunto. Isso não significa que todo proprietário precisará trocar a bateria ao longo dos primeiros anos de uso. O desgaste acontece gradualmente, e a garantia oferecida pela fabricante pode cobrir determinados defeitos durante um período específico. Por que o carro elétrico pode ser vantajoso para quem trabalha como taxista? O principal atrativo está no custo de utilização. Um veículo elétrico não depende de gasolina ou etanol para rodar e pode apresentar despesas menores por quilômetro, dependendo do preço da energia, da eficiência do modelo e das condições de recarga. Para um taxista, que percorre distâncias elevadas diariamente, essa diferença pode ter impacto relevante no orçamento mensal. Outro benefício está na legislação tributária. A Lei 8.989/1995 prevê isenção do Imposto sobre Produtos Industrializados (IPI) para determinados automóveis adquiridos por motoristas profissionais que trabalham com táxi. A legislação inclui veículos elétricos e híbridos, mas estabelece condições. Entre elas estão a fabricação nacional, a utilização do automóvel na categoria de aluguel e o exercício da atividade por motorista profissional autônomo que seja titular da autorização, permissão ou concessão exigida. O benefício também tem prazo: o artigo 9º da lei estabelece efeitos até 31 de dezembro de 2026. Por isso, quem pretende comprar um automóvel com essa vantagem precisa conferir as regras e a autorização junto à Receita Federal antes de fechar negócio. Quanto tempo dura a garantia da bateria de um carro elétrico? Não existe um prazo único para todos os veículos elétricos. A cobertura depende da fabricante, do modelo, das condições de utilização e dos limites previstos no termo de garantia. Algumas empresas estabelecem prazos diferentes para veículos particulares e comerciais. Isso merece atenção especial no caso dos taxistas, porque o automóvel pode acumular quilometragem muito mais rapidamente do que um carro utilizado apenas em deslocamentos pessoais. A BYD, por exemplo, informa que seus veículos têm garantia geral de seis anos para uso particular. Para utilização comercial, como táxis e locadoras, a cobertura geral é de dois anos ou 100 mil quilômetros, o que ocorrer primeiro. Já a bateria de tração possui condições específicas: a fabricante informa garantia de oito anos ou 500 mil quilômetros para veículos de uso comercial, também considerando o limite que ocorrer primeiro. Esses prazos são exemplos de uma fabricante e não devem ser aplicados automaticamente a outras marcas. Antes da compra, o taxista precisa consultar o documento correspondente ao modelo escolhido e verificar se há exigências de manutenção ou restrições relacionadas ao uso profissional. O Código de Defesa do Consumidor também estabelece que a garantia contratual complementa a garantia legal. Pelo artigo 50, o termo deve informar claramente as condições, o prazo e os encargos que ficam sob responsabilidade do consumidor. A bateria pode custar até 40% do valor do carro? Sim, estimativas divulgadas sobre o mercado de veículos elétricos indicam que a bateria pode representar até 40% do preço total do automóvel. Em um veículo avaliado em R$ 160 mil, esse percentual corresponderia a R$ 64 mil. É importante, porém, não confundir essa estimativa com um orçamento de substituição. O preço efetivo depende do modelo, da disponibilidade de peças, da capacidade da bateria e do tipo de reparo necessário. Além disso, uma perda gradual de capacidade não significa necessariamente que o conjunto inteiro precise ser substituído. O diagnóstico técnico pode apontar outras possibilidades, conforme a estrutura do sistema e a orientação da fabricante. Por isso, antes de comprar, vale solicitar à concessionária um orçamento por escrito para a bateria e perguntar sobre a disponibilidade de reparos, módulos e peças de reposição. Também é importante lembrar que o fim da garantia contratual não elimina automaticamente todos os direitos do consumidor. Em caso de vício oculto, o artigo 26 do CDC prevê que o prazo para reclamar começa quando o defeito fica evidenciado. Como calcular se o financiamento de 60 meses realmente compensa? O preço anunciado do veículo não mostra sozinho quanto o taxista vai desembolsar. Para avaliar a compra, é necessário somar o valor das parcelas, os juros, o seguro, a manutenção e os gastos com recarga. A Calculadora do Cidadão, disponibilizada pelo Banco Central, permite simular financiamentos com prestações fixas. Com ela, é possível estimar o valor das parcelas a partir do montante financiado, da taxa de juros e do prazo escolhido. Outro documento importante é o Custo Efetivo Total (CET). Ele reúne os encargos da operação, incluindo juros, tarifas e impostos, e permite comparar propostas de diferentes instituições financeiras. O arti

O evento começa às 14h, no formato online, com transmissão pelo Youtube da FIERGS. As inscrições podem ser feitas neste link: https://xviiiseminariodetele.eventize.com.br/. O encontro ocorre em um momento estratégico para o Rio Grande do Sul, diante das perspectivas de novos investimentos em infraestrutura digital, como a instalação de data centers, e do avanço das aplicações de inteligência artificial. A programação reunirá especialistas e representantes de diferentes segmentos para discutir iniciativas, tecnologias e soluções que impactam a competitividade e o desenvolvimento do setor. Entre os participantes está Vinícius Borges Albernaz, coordenador-geral de Políticas Públicas para o Setor de Telecomunicações do Ministério das Comunicações. artigo.texto: Sixty percent of Americans reported not feeling comfortable having a data center in their community, according to a September Pew Research Center poll. The same poll also reported that 54% of Americans believe data centers are bad for the environment. This sentiment was reflected at the Leavenworth County Board of Commissioners meeting last month. "These developers are picking on small towns, and we want them to know a small town is not a pushover,” resident Dee Karleskint told KMBC during the meeting. “We've got educated people, we've got intelligent people, and we know what this is going to do to the community." The Kansas Legislature passed Senate Bill 98 in April 2025, that provided tax exemptions to corporations seeking to build data centers in the state. This is not a unique bill, but Kansas is in a unique spot this year as a key battleground state because of the Senate election. And, as it turns out, data centers are a bipartisan issue, one of great interest to the small community of Tonganoxie in Leavenworth County. After SB 98 passed, a firm called Cloverleaf proposed Project Bluestem, a data center situated near the Tonganoxie Business Park. According to Cloverleaf, the project would be fully committed to offsetting electricity and water prices that would usually affect the community. However, a financial analysis from Cloverleaf in May 2026 reported the project would cost $7 billion and create 50 jobs. Bluestem is only one of 15 proposed data center projects in Kansas, with five more already undergoing construction, according to the data center tracker from More Than Just Parks. Many Tonganoxie citizens have been vocal against this movement and said they feel like the local government has ignored their opposition. Among the outspoken is Richard Paz, who is running for state House District 38, which includes Tonganoxie. Paz advises Citizens Against Bluestem (CAB), an organization of Tonganoxie citizens protesting the new development. “It appears to me that a lot of the industry comes into small communities that don’t have the capability to address the overarching costs of these industry developments,” Paz said. According to Kansas Commerce, the goal of Bluestem, and of SB 98 in general, is to bring economic stability and higher-wage jobs to small communities such as Tonganoxie. But Paz, citing outcomes from other states, is concerned with the bandwidth of infrastructure to accommodate a sudden demand for resources. “I know a lot of the selling points have been that, ‘Hey, this could possibly lower rates,’ but that hasn’t been the case nationally,” Paz said in an interview. “The Southwest Power Pool simply does not have the capacity to provide for all these developments.” The Southwest Power Pool (SPP) is a nonprofit organization mandated by the federal government that ensures power supplies are distributed and able to be used reliably. SPP had multiple meetings this year to discuss how to accommodate and regulate large-scale projects. SPP President and CEO Barbara Sugg warned in summer 2024 of possible issues with power supply, especially from new data center projects. According to Sugg, new centers could worsen a power grid already strained by increasing demand and extreme weather conditions. The weather has been worsening and becoming more erratic within the past 10 years. All 10 of the hottest Julys on record have occurred since 2016, according to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). Climate change is also a factor in worsening weather events. Additionally, SPP said current power generators would need to be updated or replaced to accommodate larger-scale projects such as data centers. As Paz put it, in order to get millions, Kansas would have to spend billions. “I’ve never denied that the project is potentially bringing in millions of dollars of revenue, which the county needs,” he said. “But, again, with SB 98, when you look at the overall ledger of what’s being given up, we are giving up more than we receive.” The Kansan reached out to the Leavenworth County Commissioners' office for comment but did not receive a response. Conversation about resources and data centers has been focused on water, especially in Kansas. But Rex Buchanan, a local water expert and director emeritus of the Kansas Geological Survey, isn’t worried. “If you look at the amount of water that's used for data centers and compare that to, say, irrigation, the water used for irrigation dwarfs pretty much everything else,” Buchanan said. “Do data centers add to that? Well, maybe to a certain extent, but you also have to remember that, particularly out west, a data center, if it’s going to use water, has to have a water right.” A water right is a right granted by the state that allows people, whether individuals or companies, to pump and use water. Domestic use is exempt, but Bluestem would need a water right in order to pump its own water. “So, if you buy a water right from somebody that’s already using that water for, say, irrigation, then in some respects, it’s not like a data center is a huge new use,” Buchanan said. “It’s just a different use.” According to Bluestem’s website, the project would use a closed water loop, which loops and recycles water to cool down servers. However, the cost of a water right is not comparable to the cost of infrastructure. “If you live here in Lawrence, for instance, you're buying water from the city of Lawrence, and the city of Lawrence has water rights,” Buchanan said. “I would guess the cost of those water rights is really small compared to the cost of all the infrastructure it takes to move that water and get it to you in terms of pumping and treatment and that sort of thing.” Paz said he would rather that money and effort go to his constituents than a data center. “In order to attract industry, the de facto move is to provide tax exemptions," Paz said. artigo.texto: Mercado global de reguladores de tensão: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de reguladores de tensão até 2035: crescimento acelera com a demanda energética dos data centers e a modernização da rede elétrica Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de reguladores de tensão, o setor inicia 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compra mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta regionalmente mais diversificada. O mercado global de reguladores de tensão entra em uma fase de expansão sustentada, com a projeção de 2026 a 2035 apontando um crescimento anual composto de 5,8%, o que elevará o índice de mercado a 176 (2025=100). Esse avanço se apoia em dois pilares estruturais de demanda: a construção contínua de data centers e de infraestrutura de telecomunicações, que exige energia de alta qualidade e sem interrupções, e a modernização acelerada de redes elétricas envelhecidas, somada à rápida expansão das economias emergentes. Os reguladores de tensão — dispositivos que mantêm automaticamente um nível constante de tensão — tornam-se cada vez mais críticos à medida que a eletrificação se aprofunda nos setores industrial, automotivo e de energias renováveis. O mercado abrange uma gama diversificada de produtos, de reguladores lineares e chaveados a reguladores automáticos de tensão (AVRs), reguladores trifásicos e conversores CC-CC, cada um atendendo a faixas de potência e requisitos de aplicação específicos. A Ásia-Pacífico segue como a região dominante, sustentada por uma enorme produção industrial e por investimentos em infraestrutura, enquanto América do Norte e Europa apresentam demanda constante de substituição e modernização. O cenário competitivo reúne líderes globais de semicondutores e equipamentos elétricos ao lado de fabricantes especializados, com a inovação voltada para eficiência, miniaturização e integração com tecnologias de redes inteligentes. Este relatório oferece uma visão baseada em dados da dinâmica de mercado, das questões de cadeia de suprimentos e do caminho até 2035. O cenário-base para o mercado de reguladores de tensão projeta um CAGR de 5,8% entre 2026 e 2035, com o índice de mercado chegando a 176 em 2035 (2025=100). Essa perspectiva pressupõe a continuidade do crescimento econômico global, despesas de capital sustentadas em infraestrutura de data centers e investimentos progressivos em modernização de redes tanto em mercados desenvolvidos quanto emergentes. A trajetória da demanda não é uniforme entre os tipos de produto: reguladores chaveados e conversores CC-CC devem superar o mercado como um todo, impulsionados pelas exigências de eficiência da eletrônica de consumo e da eletrificação automotiva, enquanto os segmentos eletromecânico e de AVRs mantêm demanda estável de substituição em aplicações industriais e de concessionárias. Regionalmente, a Ásia-Pacífico deve manter a maior participação, embora seu ritmo de crescimento se modere à medida que a base se amplia; América do Norte e Europa devem registrar renovação dos investimentos em resiliência de rede e integração de renováveis, sustentando crescimento na casa dos dígitos médios baixos. América Latina e Oriente Médio e África oferecem potencial de alta vinculado a programas de desenvolvimento de infraestrutura e eletrificação, ainda que com maior volatilidade. Fatores do lado da oferta, como capacidade de semicondutores e disponibilidade de matérias-primas, devem permanecer amplamente equilibrados, sem grandes rupturas. O cenário-base não incorpora uma recessão global severa nem mudanças abruptas de política que possam alterar materialmente os ciclos de investimento. No conjunto, o mercado está posicionado para uma expansão constante e impulsionada por tecnologia, com a regulação avançada de tensão cada vez mais reconhecida como viabilizadora da eficiência energética e da estabilidade das redes. Vetores e restrições da demanda Principais vetores de demanda - Expansão acelerada de data centers e infraestrutura de nuvem, que exige regulação de tensão confiável para proteger equipamentos de TI sensíveis e garantir a disponibilidade dos serviços. - Modernização de redes elétricas e investimentos em redes inteligentes no mundo, motivados pela necessidade de integrar fontes renováveis e melhorar a qualidade da energia. - Aceleração da eletrificação automotiva e proliferação de sistemas eletrônicos nos veículos, ampliando a demanda por reguladores de tensão compactos e eficientes. - Automação industrial e adoção de tecnologias avançadas de manufatura, que exigem controle preciso de tensão para máquinas sensíveis. - Crescimento das instalações de energia renovável, sobretudo solar e eólica, nas quais a regulação de tensão é essencial para a integração e a estabilidade da rede. - Aumento da demanda por eletrônicos de consumo com padrões mais rigorosos de eficiência energética, impulsionando a inovação em reguladores lineares e chaveados. Possíveis restrições ao crescimento - A volatilidade dos preços de matérias-primas, especialmente de semicondutores e metais, pode pressionar as margens dos fabricantes e provocar oscilações de preços. - Ambientes regulatórios complexos e exigências de certificação em diferentes regiões podem atrasar lançamentos de produtos e elevar os custos de conformidade. - A concorrência intensa de fabricantes de baixo custo, sobretudo na Ásia, comprime os preços e limita a lucratividade de alguns segmentos. - A complexidade tecnológica e a necessidade de inovação contínua exigem investimentos significativos em P&D, o que representa uma barreira para empresas menores. - Interrupções na cadeia de suprimentos, como a escassez de semicondutores, pod

artigo.texto: The global long-duration energy storage (LDES) market is attracting billions of dollars in investment as renewable energy developers, utilities and industrial companies seek alternatives to conventional lithium-ion batteries. Iron-air batteries, vanadium redox flow batteries and thermal energy storage are emerging as competing technologies, with companies including Form Energy, ESS Tech, Invinity Energy Systems, Rongke Power, Rondo Energy, Antora Energy and Kyoto Group developing commercial projects. According to the BloombergNEF 2026 Sustainable Energy in America Factbook, approximately 2 GW and 9 GWh of novel long-duration energy storage capacity was installed globally in 2025, bringing cumulative deployment to 5 GW and 25 GWh. However, announced project pipelines substantially exceed commissioned capacity. Investment returns will depend on capital expenditure (CAPEX), storage duration, efficiency, operating costs, project utilisation and long-term electricity or industrial heat contracts. Iron-Air vs Flow Batteries vs Thermal Storage: Technology and Cost Comparison BloombergNEF’s 2026 analysis provides the levelised cost of storage (LCOS) benchmarks using 2024 cost assumptions. These figures are not directly comparable across every application. Thermal storage costs primarily reflect heat delivery, while battery costs reflect electricity storage. The modelling also assumes 365 annual cycles and limits counted discharge to 12 hours for longer-duration systems. Iron-air batteries remain at an earlier commercial stage, making verified project costs and operating performance particularly important. Form Energy Raises $750 Million for Iron-Air Battery Expansion Form Energy raised $750 million in Series G financing in August 2026, taking its total equity funding above $2 billion. The company is developing iron-air batteries capable of storing electricity for approximately 100 hours, targeting grid reliability during extended periods of low renewable generation. Form Energy reported an approximately 80 GWh project backlog under agreement, including a planned 300 MW/30 GWh system associated with Xcel Energy and Google in Minnesota. The investment will support manufacturing expansion, product development and commercial deployments. The company’s Series G financing announcement highlights growing investor interest in multi-day storage technologies. However, the reported backlog represents contracted and planned projects rather than commissioned storage capacity. Major Vanadium Flow Battery Projects and Vendors Invinity Energy Systems – United Kingdom: Invinity delivered a 20.7 MWh vanadium flow battery system for the Copwood Energy Hub in East Sussex in May 2026. The facility integrates battery storage with a 3 MWp solar installation, with grid connection and commercial operations planned for later in 2026. Invinity and Pacific Steel Group – United States: Invinity secured an order for a 32 MWh flow battery system at Pacific Steel Group’s Mojave Micro Mill in California. The battery will operate alongside a 40 MWp solar installation, supporting renewable electricity supply for steel manufacturing. Invinity and Dairyland Power – United States: Dairyland Power Cooperative ordered 43 MWh of vanadium flow batteries for deployment across multiple locations in the Midwest. Deliveries are expected to begin in 2027. Invinity and FlexBase – Switzerland: Invinity was selected to design a flow battery system of up to 1.5 GWh for the Technology Centre Laufenburg, integrating energy storage with an AI data centre and technology campus. The project remains in development. Rongke Power – China: Rongke Power is expanding vanadium flow battery manufacturing and electrolyte production. Its Dalian operations provide an important commercial reference for grid-scale storage, while its electrolyte manufacturing expansion supports future battery deployments. NTPC Renewable Energy – India: NTPC’s 16.7 MW/100 MWh vanadium flow battery project at Khavda, Gujarat, represents an important opportunity for non-lithium battery technology in India’s renewable energy market. Gujarat Industries Power Company – India: GIPCL’s 20 MW/120 MWh vanadium flow battery project at Vadodara adds another domestic reference for long-duration storage procurement. Other vendors developing flow battery technology include Sumitomo Electric, CellCube, VRB Energy, H2 Inc. and StorEn Technologies. Thermal Energy Storage Projects: Antora, Rondo and Kyoto Group Antora Energy – United States: Antora and POET commissioned Project Big Stone in South Dakota in May 2026. The project comprises approximately 5 GWh of thermal storage using more than 200 thermal batteries to supply industrial process heat. The development demonstrates the commercial potential of thermal storage in energy-intensive manufacturing. Its 5 GWh rating represents thermal energy capacity rather than electricity output. Rondo Energy – United States: Rondo commissioned a 100 MWh industrial heat battery in California in 2025. The technology stores electricity as high-temperature heat for continuous industrial steam production. Rondo Energy – Portugal: Rondo, EDP and Heineken are developing a 100 MWh thermal battery to deliver approximately 7 MW of steam to a brewery near Lisbon. Commercial operation is targeted for 2027. Kyoto Group – Hungary: Kyoto Group’s Heatcube technology uses molten-salt storage to supply industrial process heat and steam. Its commercial development demonstrates opportunities for replacing natural gas in industrial heating applications. Additional thermal storage vendors include Brenmiller Energy, Electrified Thermal Solutions, EnergyNest and Fourth Power, although their technologies, commercial maturity and output capabilities differ. The Antora Project Big Stone announcement provides a reference for industrial thermal storage deployment. artigo.texto: When I read in this newspaper that nearly 67% of Piqua voters supported banning large data centers, my first thought was, "Do we really understand what we're turning down?" I don't live in Piqua, and I certainly don't know all the concerns behind that vote. But with similar measures passing elsewhere in Ohio, I wonder whether we're looking at the bigger picture. Think about something as simple as swiping a credit card, calling 911, checking medical records, or Face-timing our grandchildren. Add GPS navigation, weather forecasting, online education, and countless other conveniences we take for granted. What do they have in common? They all depend on data centers somewhere. Data centers have become something of an invisible utility. We rarely think about them, but we'd certainly notice if they weren't there. And with artificial intelligence (AI) rapidly changing how we live and work, their importance will only grow. Consider Ohio's manufacturing industry. AI helps companies identify defective products, predict equipment failures, and improve efficiency. In aerospace and defense, advanced computing supports aircraft maintenance, logistics, intelligence analysis, and national security research. In the medical field, it has significantly helped in improving research and diagnoses. Think about the automobile. We didn't just build cars; we developed an entire economy (and building infrastructure) around them - manufacturers, parts suppliers, dealerships, repair shops, and thousands of supporting businesses because we understood the value of cars over horses and stage coaches. AI has similar potential, and data centers are an important part of the infrastructure that could help Ohio capture those opportunities. Now, consider what Piqua may be turning down. According to information published by the city, one proposed data center represented more than $1 billion in potential private investment, an estimated $180 million in community revenue over 30 years, and approximately 100 permanent jobs, plus construction employment. Those are projections, not guarantees. But they're hardly insignificant. There's also the tax revenue. Unlike large residential developments, data centers don't add hundreds of students to local schools or generate the same daily traffic. Yet they can contribute substantial property-tax revenue to support schools, police, fire protection, and other community services. Of course, the actual benefit depends on tax incentives, infrastructure costs, and agreements negotiated with developers. Communities should insist on knowing those numbers. Now, let's address the utility cost concerns. Data centers demand substantial electricity, sometimes significant water, and considerable land while creating relatively few permanent jobs. Those concerns are legitimate. But here's something many Ohioans may not know. In July 2025, the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio (PUCO) directed AEP Ohio to establish special rates requiring large data centers to pay for at least 85% of their contracted electricity capacity, even if they use less, with commitments extending up to 12 years. Why? To help protect everyday Ohioans from footing the bill for data center infrastructure. It's not a complete solution, but it's a significant step forward. Why not build on that approach. Require environmental safeguards, negotiate community benefits, and ensure developers pay their fair share of infrastructure costs. And involve residents early, before decisions appear to have already been made. Here's another consideration. Ohio businesses can use data centers located elsewhere. But if we consistently discourage these investments, we risk losing construction activity, tax revenue, technical partnerships, and opportunities to strengthen our technology industry. Imagine a manufacturer choosing between expanding in Ohio or another state. Reliable power, connectivity, technical talent, and computing infrastructure all matter. Why would we voluntarily weaken our position? Ohio has a remarkable history of innovation, especially in aviation, manufacturing, and national defense. I'd hate to see us embrace the benefits of technology while rejecting opportunities to build the infrastructure that supports it. I'm not suggesting we say yes to every data center. Far from it. I'm suggesting we understand what we're saying no to, ask the hard questions, and negotiate agreements that benefit our communities. Because tomorrow's businesses, investments, and jobs will go somewhere. I'd much rather see them come to Ohio.

artigo.texto: A expectativa é que a plataforma contribua para a criação de uma rede de processamento de dados mais segura, sustentável e eficiente TRANSFORMAÇÃO DIGITAL Governo prevê investimento de R$ 46,3 milhões em plataforma de inteligência artificial para data centers Por Redação O governo federal planeja investir R$ 46,3 milhões no desenvolvimento de uma plataforma de inteligência artificial (IA) destinada ao gerenciamento e à distribuição de dados entre mini data centers no Brasil. A iniciativa, anunciada nesta segunda-feira (9) pelo Ministério das Comunicações, busca reduzir custos operacionais, aumentar a eficiência energética e fortalecer a segurança das informações. Batizado de Prisma, o projeto utilizará inteligência artificial para identificar as melhores estruturas para o processamento de dados e distribuir automaticamente os recursos computacionais disponíveis. A tecnologia deverá permitir maior agilidade no acesso às informações e otimizar o funcionamento das infraestruturas digitais. Os recursos serão administrados pela Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep), enquanto o desenvolvimento ficará sob responsabilidade do Centro de Pesquisa e Desenvolvimento em Telecomunicações (CPQD). O prazo previsto para execução é de 36 meses, contados a partir da assinatura do convênio de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação entre as instituições. Além dos ganhos de eficiência, o governo pretende ampliar a autonomia tecnológica do Brasil e reduzir a dependência de soluções estrangeiras no tratamento de dados estratégicos. Segundo o ministro das Comunicações, Frederico Filho, o investimento em tecnologia nacional é fundamental para fortalecer a soberania digital e modernizar a infraestrutura do País. A expectativa é que a plataforma contribua para a criação de uma rede de processamento de dados mais segura, sustentável e eficiente, acompanhando a crescente demanda por serviços digitais e soluções baseadas em inteligência artificial.

artigo.texto: A technology that precisely controls the pathways of lithium ions inside lithium metal batteries to increase charging speed while extending battery life has been developed. Even after more than 100 cycles of charging and discharging under fast-charging conditions, the battery retained about 94% of its initial capacity. KAIST announced on the 9th that a joint research team led by Professors Dong Ki Yoon and Hye-Ryeong Byun of the Department of Chemistry has developed a next-generation battery separator technology that precisely controls the pathways of lithium ions by manipulating the molecular alignment of liquid crystal polymers. The research results were published on September 28 in the international journal "ACS Nano". Lithium-ion batteries use graphite as the anode and operate by allowing lithium (Li) ions to move between the cathode and anode, generating an electric current. Lithium metal batteries, which use lithium (Li) metal as the anode, are next-generation batteries capable of storing more energy than conventional lithium-ion batteries. In lithium metal batteries, lithium tends to concentrate in specific regions during charging and stack up into sharp, tree-like structures called “dendrites.” Dendrites shorten battery life and can damage the “separator,” which prevents contact between the cathode and anode, potentially causing internal short circuits and fires. The research team designed pathways along which lithium ions can move uniformly. When the pathways of lithium ion transport are tortuous, ions take detours and can concentrate in certain regions, forming dendrites. By designing straight and uniform pathways that guide ions directly toward the electrodes, it becomes possible to charge quickly while reducing the non-uniform deposition of lithium. The team used liquid crystal materials whose molecules align in a particular direction. Liquid crystals combine the orderly molecular arrangement of solids with the fluidity of liquids, allowing their molecular alignment to be controlled by factors such as electric current and surface treatment. The researchers fabricated a liquid crystal polymer separator containing nanoscale pores, only a few nanometers (nm; 1 nm is one-billionth of a meter) in size, and then attached polyethylene glycol chains to the liquid crystal separator. Oxygen atoms in the polyethylene glycol chains repeatedly form and break temporary bonds with lithium ions, guiding the lithium ions to move smoothly along the polyethylene glycol. When the liquid crystal molecules in the polymer separator were aligned vertically, they formed straight channels that directed lithium ions toward the electrodes. Applying this separator to lithium metal batteries, the cells retained 94% of their initial capacity even after 100 charge–discharge cycles under conditions that, in theory, allow full charging in 15 minutes. This study is expected to contribute to the development of next-generation high-energy-density batteries that can deliver long driving ranges and support ultra-fast charging, which are essential for future applications. Professor Yoon said, “This research demonstrates that by controlling the alignment of liquid crystal molecules, we can efficiently design lithium ion pathways and thereby improve both the performance and safety of batteries.” doi: 10.1021/acsnano.6c09591

artigo.texto: Fears over plans for battery site near school A group of parents whose children attend a rural primary school have said they are concerned by proposals to build a battery storage plant nearby. These sites, also known as battery energy storage systems (BESS), hold energy generated from wind or solar and release it when needed, but there are concerns about fire safety due to the lithium used in the batteries. Elgin Energy's plans for the site would put it less than one kilometre from St Lucia's Primary School and Nursery in Upton Magna, Shropshire. The firm has said it has "taken on board guidance from Shropshire Fire and Rescue Service and the National Fire Chiefs Council" when designing the site. Planning documents state that the school is 811 metres from a "potential fire source", although local residents have claimed 610 metres is a more accurate figure. Kryssy Sochacki's daughter is a student at the primary school, and feels "terrified" by the prospect. "My main focus has been around the safety of the school," she said. "We fully recognise the importance of renewable energy," Sochacki added, but said "the pursuit of renewable energy shouldn't come at the expense of children's safety". "This is just far too close to the school." The excess electricity is stored in BESS, usually inside lithium-ion batteries, so when conditions are calm and overcast it can be sent back into the power grid. Concerns around fire safety stems from the lithium within the batteries, which can cause an explosion when it overheats. A fire at a battery storage unit in Nottinghamshire in May 2026 saw residents advised to keep doors and windows closed. In planning documents, the school is noted to be one of the locations "at greatest risk" of being affected by smoke in the event of a fire. The smoke plume assessment suggests that "winds from the southwest" could carry smoke towards the school "approximately 18% of the time during a fire event". 'Safety a priority' In its planning application, submitted by agents Berry's, Elgin Energy said it had consulted both Shropshire Fire and Rescue Service and the National Fire Chiefs Council". It also said the plans for the 10-acre site had been drawn up with "safety as a priority". It said that included measures including "fire detection in each container, over-temperature protection, ventilation systems, and aerosol fire extinguishing system". Of the 87 public comments on Shropshire Council's planning portal, 85 are objections and just two are in support. According to the National Fire Chiefs Council, "BESS fires are challenging to extinguish and can continue to burn from several hours to several days." Its guidance adds that "smoke plumes from fires can also harm air quality" and that attempting to extinguish a BESS fire using water could "result in large volumes of contaminated fire-water runoff which can have a long-term impact on the environment". As such, the NFCC said the "prevailing view" was to adopt a "controlled burn to minimise runoff." Stef Thomas has two children at the primary school, and said the close proximity of the battery site was her main concern. "If there was a fire, the wind blows in [the direction of the school] more often than not," she said. "It's frightening, honestly, it's a massive worry. "Why would we want any sort of chance, any sort of risk to our children, even with like a 1% chance?" Laura Potts, another parent, said: "It's really concerning, and it's frightening." She added that she wanted to see more communication "on what would happen in an emergency". "The safety of the children is of the utmost importance," Potts said. "I think the safety of our children in the schools should be considered more important than even the education itself." The area is represented on Shropshire Council by Reform UK's Brendan Mallon, who said he had "many concerns" about the BESS plans. Mallon said he feared that a fire at the site could "shut down" the adjacent A5, which in turn could, he said, affect the ability of the emergency services to respond. He added that he believed battery storage plants should instead be built on "remote sites, preferably industrial sites". Mallon said that should the BESS be approved, he would feel "extremely let down," adding that the potential impact on the school "should have been applied at the start and rejected". A spokesperson for Shropshire Council said that "all planning applications are considered on their merits," with comments raised as part of the consultation taken into account. Elgin Energy, planning agent Berry's, and St Lucia's CofE Primary School and Nursery have all been contacted for comment.

artigo.texto: BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 9. Uzbekistan plans to increase its energy storage capacity to 4.5 gigawatts by 2030 and expand domestic production of electrical equipment, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev said during a visit to NURA Electric in Tashkent Region on Monday. The announcement was published on the official channel of Sherzod Asadov, the president's press secretary. Mirziyoyev said the next priority for the electrical engineering industry should be achieving a major technological leap rather than simply expanding production capacity. Foreign partners are ready to use locally manufactured products in energy storage projects, but some of the required equipment is not yet produced domestically, he said. Moreover, the president highlighted growing demand for video surveillance equipment in shopping centers, businesses, residential buildings and public spaces. Annual demand for such equipment in Uzbekistan is estimated at $200 million, while the market exceeds $600 million when neighboring countries are included. Companies such as Digital Security in Bukhara and Samvision in Samarkand currently produce around 2,000 cameras annually using their own software. Mirziyoyev emphasized the need to expand such projects to strengthen domestic manufacturing capabilities and capture a larger share of regional demand. Uzbekistan has been pursuing an energy sector transformation aimed at expanding generation capacity, diversifying its energy mix and improving energy efficiency. The country is investing in large-scale solar and wind power projects, modernizing electricity infrastructure and developing energy storage systems to integrate a growing share of renewable energy into the national grid. These efforts are part of its broader strategy to meet rising electricity demand while strengthening energy security and supporting industrial growth.

artigo.texto: U.S. utility-scale solar, wind, and battery storage hit new capacity records in Q2 2026, S&P Global finds The U.S. clean energy buildout hit a notable milestone in the second quarter of 2026. According to new analysis from S&P Global Market Intelligence, developers added nearly 7.5 GW of utility-scale solar — a 21% jump year-over-year — while battery storage set a quarterly record at 5.6 GW and wind posted its strongest quarter since 2021 with 5.1 GW of new capacity. All three sectors hit significant milestones in the same quarter. That’s not a coincidence — it points to something broader shifting in U.S. energy infrastructure. Q2 2026 capacity additions by the numbers The headline figures from S&P Global Market Intelligence are striking on their own. They carry even more weight when you look at them side by side. Cost trends helped too — solar panel prices and battery system costs have declined over time, making large-scale projects more financially viable at a faster pace. Solar led the way with nearly 7.5 GW of utility-scale capacity added during Q2 2026 — a 21% increase compared to the same quarter a year earlier. That’s a meaningful jump for a sector that was already growing steadily. Battery storage grabbed attention in a different way. The 5.6 GW added during the quarter set an all-time quarterly record for the technology in the U.S., reflecting how quickly storage has moved from a niche grid tool to a mainstream infrastructure component. Wind rounded out the picture. At 5.1 GW, Q2 2026 marked the technology’s strongest quarterly performance since 2021 — a real rebound for a sector that had faced supply chain disruptions and siting challenges in recent years. What makes this quarter stand out isn’t any single number — it’s that all three sectors hit significant milestones simultaneously, according to S&P Global’s data. Drivers behind the surge in renewable and storage deployment Several forces converged to produce these results. None of them is entirely new, but their combined effect appears to have pushed deployment into a higher gear. Investment momentum in utility-scale clean energy has stayed strong. Grid operators and corporate buyers have kept seeking reliable renewable capacity, and developers have responded by accelerating project timelines to meet that demand. Cost trends helped too — solar panel prices and battery system costs have declined over time, making large-scale projects more financially viable at a faster pace. Lower costs mean more projects can clear the financial hurdles required to reach construction. Federal tax credits have also played a meaningful role in pushing projects forward. Incentives tied to clean energy development motivated developers to move quickly, especially given uncertainty about whether those credits will stick around long-term. When expiration looms, activity tends to concentrate in the near term — developers race to qualify projects under current rules before anything changes. What the record additions mean for the U.S. grid These aren’t just impressive stats. They have real implications for how the U.S. power grid actually operates. Battery storage is the most consequential piece of the Q2 story from a grid reliability standpoint. Variable renewable sources like solar and wind produce power when the sun shines and the wind blows — not necessarily when demand peaks. Storage helps bridge that gap by capturing excess generation and dispatching it when it’s needed most. The combination of record solar and record storage additions in the same quarter suggests the industry is increasingly building the two together, producing something closer to dispatchable clean energy rather than purely intermittent generation. Wind’s strong quarter adds a different dimension. Wind resources are geographically distributed differently than solar — stronger in the Great Plains and parts of the Midwest, for example — so more wind capacity means more regional diversification in the renewable mix, which can strengthen grid resilience. Taken together, these additions suggest the U.S. energy transition may actually be picking up speed. Development pipeline and industry headwinds through 2031 If Q2 2026 shows where the industry is now, the development pipeline offers a glimpse of where it’s headed. S&P Global’s analysis identified nearly 300 GW of solar and more than 212 GW of storage targeted for completion between 2026 and 2031. Those are large numbers, and they suggest developers are planning for continued aggressive buildout over the next several years. The pipeline doesn’t guarantee delivery, though. Trade tariffs on imported components — including solar panels and battery materials — continue to pressure project costs. When input costs rise, projects that looked financially viable on paper become harder to finance and build. Expiring federal tax credits create a separate layer of uncertainty, complicating long-term financing and sometimes delaying final investment decisions altogether. Permitting constraints remain a structural bottleneck that hasn’t meaningfully improved despite the scale of the buildout. Even projects with financing in place can face years of delays navigating federal, state, and local approval processes — a problem that shows no signs of resolving quickly. What to take away from Q2 2026’s clean energy milestone Q2 2026 was a standout quarter for U.S. clean energy deployment. Solar hit a new year-over-year growth benchmark, battery storage set an all-time quarterly record, and wind posted its best performance in five years — all at once, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. Sustained investment, declining costs, and policy incentives motivating near-term action all contributed. The grid implications are real, particularly as storage and solar grow together into a more dispatchable pairing. artigo.texto: A crescente onda de protestos contra a instalação de data centers nos Estados Unidos, impulsionada pelo temor de aumento nas contas de energia, consumo excessivo de água e impactos ambientais, ganhou força nas disputas eleitorais e ampliou a pressão sobre candidatos republicanos e democratas. A reação dos moradores norte-americanos desperta questionamentos sobre os reflexos desse movimento na expansão dos centros de processamento de dados e inteligência artificial no Brasil, especialmente no Ceará, onde um empreendimento anunciado para Caucaia, na Região Metropolitana de Fortaleza, também foi alvo de manifestações de comunidades locais. Nos Estados Unidos, a resistência aos grandes centros tecnológicos deixou de ser uma discussão restrita ao meio ambiente e passou a integrar o debate político. O assunto ganhou espaço nas eleições de meio de mandato, realizadas no dia 3 de novembro, com candidatos pressionados a apresentar propostas para controlar os custos de energia, proteger os recursos hídricos e estabelecer limites à instalação dessas estruturas. A insatisfação popular se tornou um desafio para políticos dos dois principais partidos norte-americanos, especialmente em regiões onde moradores reclamam dos efeitos da chegada de grandes empresas de tecnologia. O movimento também provocou questionamentos sobre incentivos fiscais e benefícios concedidos pelos governos a empreendimentos que demandam enormes quantidades de eletricidade e água. QUESTIONAMENTOS SOBRE O CEARÁ O avanço dos protestos nos Estados Unidos chama a atenção para o Brasil, que busca ampliar sua participação no mercado internacional de inteligência artificial e processamento de dados. No Ceará, um dos principais exemplos dessa expansão é o projeto de instalação de um data center em Caucaia. O empreendimento recebeu apoio do prefeito Naumi Amorim, que defende a iniciativa como uma oportunidade de desenvolvimento tecnológico, atração de investimentos, geração de empregos, renda e arrecadação tributária para o município. A proposta, entretanto, também despertou resistência de comunidades locais, preocupadas com os possíveis impactos ambientais e com a utilização de recursos naturais, especialmente água e energia elétrica. EFEITOS NAS COMUNIDADES A experiência norte-americana coloca novas questões no debate cearense: quais serão os efeitos desses empreendimentos sobre o abastecimento de água? Quem arcará com os custos da infraestrutura energética necessária? Quantos empregos permanentes serão efetivamente criados? E quais contrapartidas ambientais e econômicas serão asseguradas às comunidades? São questionamentos que ganham importância diante da perspectiva de crescimento do setor no Estado. BRASIL TEM 169 DATA CENTERS MAPEADOS O Brasil já conta com 169 data centers mapeados, dos quais 132 estão em operação. Segundo levantamento do Maravalley, polo de inovação e tecnologia do Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo concentra 76 unidades, liderando a distribuição dessas estruturas no território nacional. A expansão é impulsionada principalmente pelo crescimento da inteligência artificial, dos serviços em nuvem, das redes sociais e de outras atividades digitais que exigem grande capacidade de armazenamento e processamento de informações. O Governo Federal também colocou o setor entre suas prioridades de desenvolvimento tecnológico. Durante a campanha presidencial de 2026, o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defendeu estímulos à instalação de data centers, associados a exigências ambientais, utilização de energia renovável e contrapartidas para o mercado brasileiro, como a reserva de capacidade computacional. CONSUMO DE ÁGUA E ENERGIA ESTÁ NO CENTRO DOS PROTESTOS A resistência à construção de data centers, registrada durante a campanha eleitoral nos Estados Unidos, se concentrou, principalmente, nos impactos sobre as contas de eletricidade e o meio ambiente. As instalações abrigam milhares de servidores que precisam funcionar continuamente. Dependendo do porte e da tecnologia utilizada, podem consumir volumes de energia comparáveis aos de cidades inteiras. Sistemas de resfriamento também podem exigir grandes quantidades de água, embora esse consumo varie conforme as tecnologias adotadas. Além da demanda energética e hídrica, moradores questionam a ocupação de áreas rurais, a perda de terrenos agrícolas, o barulho das instalações e a poluição provocada por geradores utilizados em situações de emergência. RESTRIÇÃO Segundo levantamento divulgado pela agência Reuters, pelo menos 41 propostas de restrição à construção de data centers foram apresentadas em 38 localidades de dez estados norte-americanos no contexto das eleições. Ohio aparece entre os estados com maior mobilização. Na cidade de Sunbury, uma proposta de limitação da potência dos empreendimentos pode comprometer um projeto da Amazon avaliado em US$ 2 bilhões. PRESSÃO POPULAR ATINGE GOVERNADORES E CANDIDATOS A resistência também alcançou as disputas pelos governos estaduais norte-americanos. Na Pensilvânia, o governador democrata Josh Shapiro passou a defender exigências mais rigorosas para novos empreendimentos, incluindo medidas relacionadas ao consumo de água, aos custos de energia e à aprovação dos projetos pelas administrações municipais. No Texas, o republicano Greg Abbott também passou a enfrentar questionamentos sobre os benefícios fiscais concedidos ao setor e os custos que podem ser transferidos aos consumidores. A pressão mostra que a instalação de data centers, antes apresentada principalmente como oportunidade de investimentos e desenvolvimento econômico, passou a exigir respostas mais amplas sobre seus impactos sociais e ambientais. Apesar da resistência, o setor continua em expansão. De acordo com a consultoria Cushman & Wakefield, a capacidade dos data centers em construção nos Estados Unidos cresceu 48% entre dezembro de 2025 e junho de 2026

artigo.texto: A transitioning Congress finds itself in a pickle on AI data centers Table of Contents As Congress returns to Washington this week, the massive power demands of the AI boom have forced a reckoning over data center infrastructure. The Senate is preparing for a pivotal procedural vote on legislation that would speed approvals for energy projects while requiring large data centers to shoulder more of the costs they impose on the power grid. The bipartisan bill would add much-needed regulations on data centers, but, as some politicians believe, may also encourage more data center construction. Silicon Valley vs. a changed D.C. In the sweeping and history-making midterm elections last week, voters didn't just elect a new generation of Democratic lawmakers. They also sent a pretty unmistakable message to Big Tech, particularly the artificial intelligence industry: Enough with the data centers already. Or, more bluntly, "get out of town." Across the country, local communities are pushing to stop, restrict, or impose conditions on data center development. The election results reinforced that message, making clear that the AI gold rush is facing growing resistance. For the last two years, Silicon Valley has busied itself building more, building bigger and doing it ASAP. If a tech giant wanted to drop a warehouse-sized data center into a community, local governments often offered tax breaks and other incentives, then told residents it was harmless and would mean more jobs. Voters increasingly aren't buying it. Democrats now find themselves in a pickle. Many campaigned on restricting data center development, responding to voters concerned about electricity costs, water consumption, and the impact these enormous facilities have on their communities. Now, the aforementioned pending legislation forces a stark about-face — since, as Reuters reports, some Democrats believe provisions in the proposed bill could encourage the creation of more data centers. If that comes to pass, incoming lawmakers would need to explain why those campaign promises to halt data center construction no longer apply. Can data centers be built responsibly? There's a risk, too, in the new Democratic Congress pushing too forcefully for restrictions on AI, specifically on data centers. My well-seasoned brain believes AI companies will respond to restrictions not simply by complaining about the cost of doing business, but by slowing down the rollout of new technology. Some of that slowdown will be unavoidable. Without enough data centers, electricity, and computing capacity, companies cannot expand indefinitely. But some of it could be strategic. I suspect the message from Silicon Valley will be slightly PR-ish: If you don't want us building data centers, don't expect your ChatGPT, Claude, or Siri to keep getting faster, smarter, and more capable. That "hurry up and now" diagnosis for your sore knee might take a little longer. Picture AI as something other than a magical cloud floating above our heads. Every time you ask an AI assistant to write an email, generate an image, or summarize a document, powerful chips in actual buildings are cranking away, consuming tremendous amounts of electricity and water and pressuring local power grids. And all that power costs mega cash. Utility rates, grid upgrades, and higher electricity bills have turned an abstract technology debate into something much more personal. I don't blame communities for pushing back. Why should residents subsidize a multibillion-dollar technology company's expansion while wondering whether their electric bills will keep climbing? They're already fed up with rising gas and grocery prices and the cost of a new home. But there's another side to this costly coin that Democrats shouldn't ignore. Data centers can bring economic benefits, too, provided technology companies invest in the communities that host them. While data centers rarely employ local, low-skill workers directly, AI companies can bridge this gap by funding local infrastructure projects that immediately put the existing workforce to work. Furthermore, the resulting influx of permanent, high-salaried technicians injects new tax revenue into the community, triggering a powerful economic ripple effect for local restaurants and shops. Communities shouldn't have to choose between protecting residents and benefiting from technological investment. Companies that want to build in these towns should contribute meaningfully to their economic well-being. The risks of slowing down the AI gold rush Government intervention, even when well-intentioned, can also produce unintended consequences that ultimately hurt consumers. Just look at Europe. In 2024, Apple said it would hold back Apple Intelligence and other new features from EU customers, citing "regulatory uncertainties" tied to the Digital Markets Act. Regulators were trying to rein in Big Tech and protect competition. Whether you buy Apple's explanation or see it as a pressure tactic, European customers were left waiting while others got the shiny new toys. This doesn't mean all regulation is bad. It's a reminder that lawmakers cannot promise to put a tight leash on an industry without potentially creating bottlenecks in the products and services it provides. That's precisely the dilemma Democrats now face. If they make it too difficult or expensive to build data centers, AI companies will have fewer places to house the computing power necessary to expand their products. New features could take longer to arrive. More sophisticated applications could cost more. And I wouldn't be surprised if the industry makes sure consumers understand exactly who's responsible. artigo.texto: O Conselho Gestor do Fundo para o Desenvolvimento Tecnológico das Telecomunicações (Funttel) aprovou a destinação de R$ 46,3 milhões para o desenvolvimento de uma plataforma inteligente de gerenciamento de data centers. O projeto batizado de Prisma terá duração de 36 meses e será executado pelo CPQD A iniciativa terá como base um convênio de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação com a Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep), entidade responsável pela administração dos recursos. Em linhas gerais, a intenção do projeto é usar Inteligência Artificial (IA) para identificar onde e como os dados devem ser processados em operações com diferentes infraestruturas computacionais, de modo a tornar os data centers mais eficientes, seguros e sustentáveis. Segundo o Ministério das Comunicações (MCom), a expectativa é de que a tecnologia também reduza o consumo de energia e a pegada de carbono, aumente a resiliência contra falhas no fornecimento de energia, eleve a proteção contra ataques cibernéticos, diminua os custos operacionais, acelere o acesso à informação e aumente a proteção de dados estratégicos. "Investir em tecnologia nacional é garantir que o Brasil tenha mais autonomia para proteger suas informações e desenvolver soluções para os desafios do futuro. Com o apoio do Funttel, estamos fortalecendo a inovação brasileira e criando condições para uma infraestrutura digital mais moderna, segura e sustentável, reduzindo nossa dependência de tecnologias desenvolvidas no exterior", afirmou o ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho, em nota. Data centers de borda O Prisma também deve estimular a expansão de data centers de borda (também chamados de minidata centers) pelo território nacional, com o objetivo de levar o processamento de dados para mais perto de onde são gerados e utilizados, o que reduz o tempo de resposta dos sistemas e melhora o desempenho de serviços digitais. A tecnologia deve beneficiar, sobretudo, setores como saúde, defesa, segurança pública, educação e telecomunicações. "Além de tornar mais rápidos o processamento e o acesso às informações, essa arquitetura permite maior controle sobre o dado que está na borda", destaca o diretor de Tecnologia e Inovação do CPQD, Gustavo Correa Lima.
