artigo.texto: On Monday, the Senate voted to advance a bipartisan bill aimed at easing the construction of new energy infrastructure. The bill, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), has a broad base of support, including from labor leaders who contend it will produce thousands of jobs and clean energy proponents who believe it could unlock wind and solar. Its sponsors are hoping to pass the bill before the current Congress ends in January. But the bill has also received vehement blowback from a growing coalition of anti-data center critics, who argue that it would accelerate the buildout of an industry that Americans resoundingly voted against in the midterm elections. BAAJA does address affordability concerns by forcing data centers to pay the full cost of the upgrades they trigger, and contains transmission reforms designed to modernize the grid. But it also strips back environmental protections and could lead to more data centers powered by gas and built on public lands. Hundreds of local and national organizations have signed letters urging Congress not to pass the bill as written, including the Sierra Club and the Natural Resources Defense Council. Conversely, many industry trade groups have been supportive of the bill, despite the fact that it would likely make building more expensive. On Sunday, Donald Trump urged the Senate to pass the bill on Truth Social, writing that “China will take any Data Center that we don’t want.” The bill represents the first major test for Democrats post-election, as they contend with how to deliver on affordability and many other issues in their sprawling coalition at the same time. “Everything about BAAJA goes against the spirit of voters this midterms, in which we saw voters turn out for candidates who directly oppose data centers,” says Allie Rosenbluth, U.S. campaigns manager at the environmental nonprofit Oil Change International. “This bill is a massive giveaway to the data center industry—and creates a backdoor for fossil fuels to enter the grid through data centers.” Read More: How AI Backlash Shaped the 2026 Midterms Gas and Fossil Fuels America’s data center boom has also been a gas boom. In the scramble to bring AI data centers online as fast as possible, many developers have built their own gas power plants instead of waiting to connect to the grid. Global Energy Monitor data reported by Wired show that U.S. gas projects powering data centers increased from roughly 4 gigawatts in early 2024 to 189 gigawatts in development by mid-2026. In some cases, these gas plants have worsened local pollution and exacerbated health issues like asthma, scientific researchers contend. BAAJA incentivizes a wide range of energy sources to come online faster, including solar and wind. Many experts are hopeful that the bill will accelerate the buildout of transmission lines that are essential for bringing clean energy online. But environmentalists worry that the first and foremost beneficiary of the bill won’t be clean energy sources but rather gas-powered data centers, because there is already a massive pipeline of proposed projects waiting for various approvals. Rosenbluth points to several gas-powered data centers that are currently plodding through the permitting process, including the Ports-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio and the STAK Energy Campus in Alaska. If BAAJA were to pass, she says, key environmental permits they are trying to obtain could be fast-tracked, potentially allowing them to come online much more quickly. Holly Bender, chief program officer of the Sierra Club, says that "based on their need for speed to power, the data center industry is driving a historic and alarming investment in gas and fossil fuels. There’s a lot in this bill that will make it easier and faster to build gas pipelines, while making it harder for communities to have a say.” Public and Tribal lands Another major concern from critics is that the bill will lead to many more data centers getting built on federally-owned land. The Trump administration has embraced this idea, and signed an executive order in July 2025 directing the Interior and Energy departments to make federal sites available for data centers and to streamline their environmental reviews. “We’re going to ‘mine, baby, mine’ so we can ‘build, baby, build’ because we’ve got to build AI data centers,” Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said in 2025. There are at least 17 active applications connected to data center campuses on public land, covering thousands of acres in Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, and other states, one recent study found. BAAJA’s permitting provisions could make those projects easier to advance and harder to stop, including limiting judges’ ability to halt construction due to environmental review. Additionally, some Tribal organizations and leaders have spoken out forcefully against the bill, with a coalition of Tribal leaders writing on Saturday that the bill would “gut the ability of Tribal Nations and the American public to identify and protect historic and cultural places threatened by federally connected projects—including data centers.” Potential benefits However, the bill’s advocates argue that it addresses several of the public’s most pressing data center concerns. The first is around affordability: The bill contains ratepayer protections which would require developers to pay for the added cost of transmission. One study estimates that data centers would pay approximately $55 billion in transmission charges over ten years—about $35 billion more than under current policy. The bill establishes protections to prevent households and businesses from being left with the bill for failed projects. “The day of data center freeloading ends when this bill passes,” Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, one of the bill’s Democratic sponsors, said last week. artigo.texto: LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI have each won an Innovation Award at the world's largest electronics and IT exhibition, "CES 2027." LG Energy Solution was recognized for a software technology that shortens the diagnostic time of used batteries to within 10 minutes, while Samsung SDI was acknowledged for its uninterruptible power supply (UPS) battery solution for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. According to the battery industry on the 10th, LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI have been named among the companies selected for the "CES 2027 Innovation Award" by the Consumer Technology Association (CTA). LG Energy Solution received the award in the Advanced Mobility category, while Samsung SDI won in the Enterprise Tech category. LG Energy Solution's winning entry is its software-based used battery diagnostic solution, "Re.Pulse." The technology involves applying specific current pulses to a battery to measure voltage changes and analyzing them with an AI-based proprietary model to evaluate the battery's state of health (SoH) and residual performance. Its most notable feature is reducing the battery diagnostic time from over seven hours to within 10 minutes. It also enables precise diagnosis down to the cell level within a battery pack, allowing for the repair or replacement of only the degraded parts. Another characteristic is its ability to link with existing battery charge/discharge testers or electric vehicle chargers without requiring separate dedicated equipment. Because it can perform diagnostics without removing the battery from the vehicle, it can be utilized in used battery energy storage systems (ESS) and electric vehicle maintenance and inspection centers. Based on diagnostic results, it can also contribute to increasing resource utilization and reducing carbon emissions by classifying batteries suitable for reuse, remanufacturing, or recycling. Following its award last year for the battery life enhancement technology "Better.Re," LG Energy Solution has won the CES Innovation Award with pure software technology for two consecutive years. Lee Sang-hoon, an official at LG Energy Solution, stated, "This award is a result of recognition for the distinctiveness of our battery diagnostic technology and software competitiveness." He added, "We will continue to advance our diagnostic and management technologies to enhance the utilization value of used batteries and strive to build a sustainable battery circular ecosystem." Samsung SDI made the Innovation Award list with its prismatic battery solution for UPS, "SDI U8A3-UPS." A UPS is a system that supplies emergency power to critical facilities such as data centers when unexpected power outages occur. Recently, it has gained attention as essential equipment for stable power supply as power demand at AI data centers surges. The SDI U8A3-UPS is a product featuring prismatic battery cells made of lithium manganate (LMO) material. It achieves ultra-high output and high energy density, improving space efficiency by 33% compared to existing products. Stable power supply is possible with fewer batteries. It also has the advantage of supplying auxiliary power when power demand spikes during AI computing processes, preventing server failures or data damage. Recently, it demonstrated fire safety by becoming the first in the world to meet all evaluation criteria in a large-scale indoor fire test conducted by UL Solutions, a global safety certification body. With this, Samsung SDI has set a record of winning awards for three consecutive years since its initial participation in CES 2025. Last year, its ultra-high output cylindrical battery "SDI 25U-Power" won the Best of Innovation Award, and its thermal runaway blocking technology "No TP" received an Innovation Award. A Samsung SDI official said, "This is a result of recognition for the innovativeness of core power solutions in the AI era." He added, "We will continue to lead the market with products that combine the performance and safety required by customers."

artigo.texto: Revolve Renewable Power signs CAD$1.5 million deal to acquire 6 MW battery storage portfolio in Ontario Revolve Renewable Power Corp. signed a definitive agreement on October 30, 2026, to acquire Logan Energy Storage ULC — a battery energy storage portfolio in Ontario — for CAD$1.5 million, paid entirely from cash on hand. The portfolio totals 6 MW / 11.7 MWh of capacity spread across three sites in the province. Revolve signs deal to acquire Logan Energy Storage portfolio The equity purchase agreement, executed October 30, 2026, covers all issued and outstanding shares of Logan Energy Storage ULC. Through it, Revolve — trading on the Canadian Securities Exchange as REVV and on the OTCQB as REVVF — picks up a three-project BESS portfolio across Ontario. The CAD$1.5 million price comes entirely from Revolve’s existing cash. No external financing involved. The seller operates at arm’s length to Revolve, and the deal still needs to clear customary closing conditions and applicable regulatory approvals, though no specific closing date has been set. A successful close on Logan marks a concrete expansion of the company’s contracted asset base and a real-world demonstration of its stated strategy in action. Acquisition builds on earlier Trillium Storage purchase This deal didn’t come out of nowhere. Just two months earlier, in August 2026, Revolve wrapped up the acquisition of the Trillium Storage portfolio — six projects totaling 14.2 MW / 24.3 MWh, also in Ontario, funded from the balance sheet. That earlier transaction set a recognizable pattern: disciplined, bolt-on acquisitions with no outside capital required. CEO Myke Clark framed Logan as a natural next step. “The Logan acquisition is another important step for Revolve as we continue to build our storage platform in Ontario,” he said in the announcement, adding that the deal is expected to increase the company’s battery storage capacity in the province and deepen its presence there. Revolve’s stated strategy pairs targeted acquisitions with a greenfield development pipeline — both tracks running in parallel, buying operating or near-operating assets while building new ones from scratch. Closing expected to lift Ontario storage capacity to 20.2 MW Once Logan closes, Revolve expects its total Ontario battery storage capacity to reach approximately 20.2 MW / 36.0 MWh across nine projects. That’s a significant jump from where things stood before the Trillium deal even closed. The company describes the transaction as accretive to revenue. The portfolio is meant to contribute contracted, cash-generating assets that support long-term recurring income — the kind of stable base storage operators rely on when projects are tied to grid service agreements or similar arrangements. No specific timeline has been given beyond the standard reference to closing conditions and regulatory approvals, and projections around capacity additions and revenue accretion carry the usual execution risks. Revolve’s broader role in North American energy storage Revolve Renewable Power Corp. is headquartered in Vancouver, BC, and describes itself as an owner, operator, and developer of power generation and digital infrastructure projects across North America. Its dual listing — CSE: REVV and OTCQB: REVVF — reflects a cross-border investor base. Ontario is an increasingly active market for grid-scale battery storage. The province has been working to balance a growing share of renewable generation with grid reliability needs, and wind and solar output fluctuates in ways that create real operational pressure. Storage assets help manage that variability by absorbing surplus electricity and releasing it when demand peaks. For Revolve, Ontario’s direction makes it a logical place to concentrate its storage platform. What the Logan deal means for Revolve’s Ontario platform Together, the Trillium and Logan acquisitions have moved Revolve from a standing start to a nine-project, 20.2 MW / 36.0 MWh storage portfolio in Ontario — in a matter of months. Both deals were funded from cash on hand, both involved arm’s-length sellers, and both fit the acquisition-plus-development strategy the company has laid out publicly. Logan adds 6 MW / 11.7 MWh to that base at a purchase price of CAD$1.5 million. That’s a relatively modest outlay for a company building scale in a capital-intensive sector. Whether it closes on schedule depends on regulatory approvals and customary conditions, but the structure mirrors what Revolve already pulled off with Trillium — same playbook, different site. If you’re tracking Revolve’s growth in Ontario, the number to watch is 20.2 MW. A successful close on Logan marks a concrete expansion of the company’s contracted asset base and a real-world demonstration of its stated strategy in action. artigo.texto: Elon Musk e data centers: o que muda após eleições nos EUA Eleitores americanos barraram projetos de data centers em diversas localidades. A onda democrata pressiona big techs e pode redesenhar a infraestrutura de IA nos próximos anos. As eleições legislativas de meio de mandato nos Estados Unidos trouxeram uma vitória histórica para o Partido Democrata. Mas o resultado das urnas não se limitou a disputas partidárias tradicionais. Em dezenas de votações locais espalhadas pelo país, eleitores rejeitaram projetos de construção de data centers ou aprovaram medidas que impõem restrições e moratórias à expansão dessas instalações. O recado é claro: a infraestrutura que sustenta a corrida por inteligência artificial virou um problema político. E quem mais sente o impacto é justamente quem mais apostou no lado oposto da mesa. O custo político de meio bilhão de dólares Elon Musk destinou cerca de meio bilhão de dólares em doações ao Partido Republicano neste ciclo eleitoral. O retorno, até agora, foi próximo de zero. O empresário, que transferiu a sede de suas principais empresas para o Texas, agora opera em um estado que elegeu a democrata Gina Hinojosa como governadora, derrotando Greg Abbott. Hinojosa fez da restrição a data centers uma bandeira de campanha. Para Musk, que é um dos maiores construtores de infraestrutura de computação do mundo por meio da xAI e de seus projetos ligados à Tesla, o cenário se tornou significativamente mais hostil. A ironia é difícil de ignorar: suas empresas agora respondem a um governo estadual eleito com a promessa de limitar exatamente o tipo de operação que ele pretende expandir. O caso de Musk é emblemático, mas não isolado. Como discutimos na cobertura de tecnologia do portal, a relação entre big techs e governos locais nos EUA vem se deteriorando há meses. A diferença é que agora essa tensão tem tradução eleitoral concreta. Por que data centers viraram alvo de eleitores A rejeição aos data centers não é um fenômeno exclusivamente partidário. Republicanos, independentes e democratas votaram contra esses projetos por razões que vão além de ideologia. O problema é operacional e ambiental. Grandes empresas de tecnologia adotaram uma postura de sigilo extremo para aprovar projetos. Em muitos casos, exigiram que autoridades eleitas assinassem acordos de confidencialidade (NDAs) antes de conhecer os detalhes das propostas. Informações sobre o tamanho real das instalações e o impacto ambiental foram omitidas, mesmo em regiões do sudoeste americano onde a escassez de água já é crítica. Essa estratégia de opacidade transformou o que poderia ser uma questão técnica em uma causa popular. Movimentos de base, sem coordenação nacional centralizada, se organizaram em diversas comunidades para barrar ou ao menos condicionar a aprovação desses empreendimentos. O sentimento anti-data center se mostrou um motor eleitoral eficiente, especialmente quando canalizado por candidatos democratas. O paralelo com o Brasil é relevante. Como analisamos em matéria sobre o impacto da IA generativa na demanda por infraestrutura, o consumo energético e hídrico dessas instalações é uma preocupação global, não apenas americana. OpenAI já mudou de postura A resposta do mercado foi rápida. A OpenAI divulgou o que chamou de “compute campus policy blueprint”, um conjunto de diretrizes para seus futuros projetos de infraestrutura. Entre as mudanças anunciadas: fim da exigência de NDAs para autoridades públicas, maior transparência sobre a escala dos projetos e compartilhamento antecipado de planos com comunidades locais. A manobra inclui um detalhe revelador. A empresa evitou o termo “data center” em seu documento, preferindo “compute campus”. A tentativa de rebranding é uma admissão de que a expressão “data center” se tornou politicamente tóxica. Se a nova nomenclatura vai pegar, é outra história. Mas o movimento mostra que a pressão regulatória funciona. Esse padrão é conhecido em outros setores. Quando há sinalização clara de que o ambiente regulatório vai endurecer, empresas se antecipam com concessões voluntárias para evitar restrições mais severas. A questão é se essas mudanças são substantivas ou cosméticas. O que vem pela frente para a infraestrutura de IA Os próximos dois anos prometem ser mais difíceis para hyperscalers e construtores de data centers nos Estados Unidos. Com democratas no controle de governos estaduais estratégicos e um sentimento popular contrário à expansão desenfreada, o ritmo de aprovação de novos projetos tende a desacelerar. O impacto não se limita ao ciclo eleitoral atual. A resistência a data centers pode se consolidar como tema permanente, presente também nas eleições de 2028. Para empresas como Microsoft, Google, Amazon e Meta, que planejam investir centenas de bilhões de dólares em infraestrutura de IA nos próximos anos, isso significa custos mais altos, prazos mais longos e maior incerteza jurídica. Para investidores que acompanham o setor, o dado mais relevante é este: a escassez de capacidade computacional, que já era um gargalo técnico, agora é também um gargalo político. Como abordamos em nossa análise sobre IA e investimentos, o preço da computação é cada vez mais determinado por fatores que vão além de silício e energia. A lição para o mercado de tecnologia O caso Musk é instrutivo por várias razões. A primeira é que dinheiro político tem retorno incerto, especialmente quando a causa que você financia entra em conflito com preocupações locais de eleitores. A segunda é que a infraestrutura física da revolução de IA não pode ser tratada como um detalhe logístico. Ela é, cada vez mais, um tema de política pública. Empresas que entenderem isso cedo, como a OpenAI parece estar tentando fazer, terão mais chances de navegar o novo ambiente. As que insistirem na estratégia de sigilo e lobby pesado podem descobrir que o custo político é tão real quanto o custo de capital. artigo.texto: Lexus ES EV Takes Aim at South Korea's approximately $50,000 Segment — With a CATL Battery Again Toyota's premium brand Lexus has introduced electrified versions of its upper-midsize ES sedan in South Korea, rapidly reshaping the competitive landscape of the roughly 70 million won (approximately $52,000) EV market. This price band is the last stretch where automakers can maintain a luxury brand image while still qualifying for government subsidies, making it the segment where imported carmakers are racing to concentrate their new models. The catch: many of the leading EVs in this bracket run on batteries from China's CATL, leaving South Korea's three battery makers with even less room to maneuver. Lexus unveiled the fully redesigned eighth-generation ES in the South Korean market on the 13th of last month. Three powertrains were introduced together: the pure-electric ES350e and ES500e, and the hybrid ES350h. Since its global debut in 1989, the ES had been sold only with combustion and hybrid powertrains; the eighth generation marks the first time it has a pure-electric lineup. Lexus has discontinued combustion-engine models entirely for this generation. The pricing drew market attention. The entry-level Premium trim of the ES350e was set at 71.6 million won (approximately $53,000) — 1.3 million won (approximately $970) below the equivalent hybrid, the ES350h Premium at 72.9 million won (approximately $54,000). EVs typically cost more than combustion or hybrid models of the same class because of their expensive batteries, so this reversal is read as an intent to lift market share through price competitiveness. The ES500e Premium, a dual-motor all-wheel-drive variant, was priced in the 77 million won (approximately $57,000) range. Performance splits the two models' characters. The ES350e is a single-motor front-wheel-drive model with 478 km of range per charge and 227 horsepower. The ES500e is dual-motor all-wheel drive; range drops to 435 km but output rises to 347 horsepower. Note: Prices are for the South Korean market. With a lower-than-expected starting price, orders moved quickly. According to industry sources, cumulative orders for the new ES stand at about 5,000 units, including pre-orders taken over the past month. The electric ES350e and ES500e are said to account for roughly half. There is no shortage of rivals battling in the 70 million won band. Volvo's upper-midsize sedan ES90, Polestar's upper-midsize SUV Polestar 3 and BMW's midsize SUV iX3 all sit in the same range. Tesla's Model Y, which dominates South Korea's EV market, starts at 49.99 million won (approximately $37,000) for the rear-wheel-drive Premium, while the all-wheel-drive Model Y L Premium sells for 72.99 million won (approximately $54,000). Behind the rush of import brands into this price range is a restructuring of the subsidy system. EVs under 85 million won (approximately $63,000) currently qualify for subsidies, but the South Korean government plans to lower the threshold to under 80 million won (approximately $59,000) starting next year. Vehicles priced at 80 million won or more must carry green license plates when purchased as corporate cars. Drop below the 60 million won (approximately $45,000) range and the premium image fades; climb into the 80 million won range and you take on both the loss of subsidies and the license-plate regulation. That is why the 70 million won band — where brand value and practical benefits can be secured together — has emerged as effectively the only safe zone. The problem is that the heart of EVs in this segment is Chinese. The Lexus ES350e and ES500e, Volvo ES90 and Polestar 3 all carry CATL's LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries. The Model Y also uses LG Energy Solution's NCM (nickel cobalt manganese) batteries in its Long Range and Performance trims, but the cheaper rear-wheel-drive trim is fitted with CATL's LFP battery. The BMW iX3 runs on batteries from China's EVE Energy. CATL held the top spot in the global EV battery market with a 39.1% share in the January-September period this year. The reason automakers choose Chinese batteries is simple. The NCM batteries that South Korean companies focus on have high energy density and long range, but contain expensive raw materials such as cobalt and nickel. LFP batteries, by contrast, are based on iron and phosphorus, keeping procurement costs low. For automakers that must hold prices in the 70 million won range while preserving a premium image, cost reduction is a structural necessity. The sense of crisis in South Korea's battery industry goes further. The high-priced premium EV market has limited room to expand, and with Hyundai and Kia's EV sales stagnating, Chinese companies are encroaching on the South Korean market. "To make matters worse, Chinese EV makers such as BYD, followed by Zeekr and Xpeng, are entering South Korea one after another, further narrowing the ground for Hyundai and Kia," a battery industry official said. "The reason South Korean battery makers have recently been putting effort into the energy storage system (ESS) market is also the judgment that it will be difficult to reclaim leadership in the EV segment from Chinese companies for the time being." The implications for South Korea's three battery makers are significant. For LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI and SK On — which have been expanding their LFP lineups — the situation now requires head-on competition with Chinese companies in entry-level and mid-priced EVs where price competitiveness is decisive. If the Lexus ES EV proves a hit, the 70 million won market is expected to grow further, and battery makers that fail to secure an LFP supply chain in this segment may fall behind in the race for volume. Conversely, automakers are expected to further strengthen their 70 million won lineups starting next year, when the subsidy threshold drops below 80 million won, setting the stage for an even fiercer battle for battery orders in this price range.

artigo.texto: Data centers viram alvo político nos EUA e ameaçam planos da big tech Resultados das eleições legislativas nos EUA revelam onda antidata center que já obriga empresas como OpenAI a rever políticas de transparência. As eleições legislativas americanas de 2025 entregaram mais do que uma virada política. Entregaram um recado direto para a indústria de tecnologia: a expansão desenfreada de data centers encontrou um limite concreto na resistência popular. Em dezenas de votações locais espalhadas pelo país, eleitores rejeitaram medidas que facilitariam a construção de novos centros de dados. E onde o tema não estava diretamente na cédula, os candidatos eleitos fizeram campanha prometendo restringir essas instalações. O caso mais emblemático é o do Texas, onde a governadora eleita Gina Hinojosa derrotou Greg Abbott com uma plataforma que incluía limitar a expansão de data centers no estado. O movimento não é trivial. O Texas é hoje um dos principais polos de infraestrutura digital dos Estados Unidos e abriga operações centrais de várias empresas de Elon Musk, que agora se vê em uma posição desconfortável. Meio bilhão de dólares e nenhum retorno político Musk doou cerca de meio bilhão de dólares para o Partido Republicano neste ciclo eleitoral. O resultado prático foi próximo de zero. Seus candidatos perderam em disputas-chave, e o Texas, estado onde concentrou suas operações empresariais, virou democrata pela primeira vez em décadas. É um cenário inédito. O maior doador republicano e um dos maiores construtores de infraestrutura de data centers do mundo opera agora sob um governo estadual que promete dificultar exatamente esse tipo de projeto. A ironia não escapou aos analistas do setor. Mas o problema de Musk é apenas a ponta mais visível de uma tendência mais ampla. A rejeição a data centers virou um fenômeno bipartidário, como já abordamos ao analisar os impactos da inteligência artificial na infraestrutura global. Republicanos, democratas e independentes em diversas regiões se uniram contra projetos que consideravam opacos e prejudiciais ao meio ambiente. Por que eleitores estão contra os data centers A resposta passa por três fatores que se acumularam nos últimos anos. Primeiro, o sigilo excessivo. Grandes empresas de tecnologia, as chamadas hyperscalers, frequentemente exigiam acordos de confidencialidade até de autoridades eleitas antes de compartilhar detalhes de seus projetos. Em muitos casos, a escala real das instalações só ficava clara após a aprovação. Segundo, o impacto ambiental. Data centers consomem volumes enormes de água para resfriamento. No sudoeste americano, onde a escassez hídrica já é uma crise, isso se tornou um ponto de atrito real. Uma única instalação de grande porte pode consumir milhões de litros de água por dia, competindo diretamente com o abastecimento residencial e agrícola. Terceiro, o consumo energético. Em um momento em que a demanda por energia dispara por conta da expansão acelerada da inteligência artificial, comunidades locais começaram a perceber que data centers pressionam as redes elétricas e, em alguns casos, elevam o custo da energia para os moradores. Essa combinação transformou o tema em uma questão genuinamente popular. Não foi uma pauta imposta de cima para baixo, mas algo que emergiu de comunidades que sentiram os efeitos no dia a dia. OpenAI já mudou de postura O mais revelador dos desdobramentos veio rápido. A OpenAI, uma das empresas que mais investem em infraestrutura de computação no mundo, publicou o que chamou de “política de campus de computação”. O documento traz mudanças relevantes: fim da exigência de NDAs para autoridades locais, compromisso de compartilhar planos com as comunidades e promessa de operar com mais transparência. O rebranding também chama atenção. A OpenAI evita deliberadamente o termo “data center” e adota “campus de computação”, uma tentativa clara de se distanciar de uma expressão que se tornou tóxica no debate público americano. É difícil imaginar que a troca de nomenclatura, por si só, mude a percepção popular. Mas as mudanças operacionais que a acompanham são concretas. O episódio ilustra uma dinâmica que investidores e analistas de mercado deveriam observar com atenção: quando o ambiente regulatório sinaliza restrições, as empresas se adaptam. Quando não há pressão, elas operam no limite do que é permitido. O que isso significa para o setor de tecnologia Os próximos dois anos serão mais difíceis para a expansão de infraestrutura digital nos Estados Unidos. E o problema pode se estender para 2028 e além, dependendo de como o sentimento popular evoluir. Para as big techs, o impacto é direto. A corrida pela inteligência artificial depende fundamentalmente de capacidade computacional, e capacidade computacional depende de data centers. Se a construção dessas instalações desacelerar, o ritmo de desenvolvimento de modelos de IA também pode ser afetado. Isso não significa que a expansão vai parar. Significa que vai custar mais, demorar mais e exigir negociações mais complexas com comunidades e governos locais. Empresas que anteciparam essa mudança e construíram relações transparentes com as comunidades terão vantagem. As que operaram no sigilo vão pagar o preço político. Para o mercado como um todo, o recado das urnas americanas é um lembrete de que infraestrutura tecnológica não existe no vácuo. Ela ocupa espaço físico, consome recursos naturais e afeta pessoas reais. Ignorar isso deixou de ser apenas uma falha ética. Agora é um risco de negócio mensurável. A questão que fica para os próximos trimestres é se esse movimento americano vai inspirar restrições semelhantes em outros países. Na Europa, onde a regulação de tecnologia já é mais rígida, a tendência pode se acelerar. No Brasil, onde a discussão sobre data centers ainda é incipiente, a experiência americana serve como antecipação do debate que inevitavelmente chegará. artigo.texto: Revolve Renewable Power agrees to acquire 6 MW Ontario battery storage portfolio for CAD $1.5 million Revolve Renewable Power Corp. (CSE: REVV; OTCQB: REVVF) signed a definitive agreement on October 30, 2026, to acquire Logan Energy Storage ULC and its three-project battery energy storage portfolio in Ontario. The deal is valued at CAD $1.5 million and covers a combined capacity of 6 MW / 11.7 MWh. Deal terms and structure Revolve executed the definitive equity purchase agreements on October 30, 2026, through a subsidiary. The structure is clean: Revolve is buying all issued and outstanding shares of Logan Energy Storage ULC, which holds the three Ontario BESS projects. The total purchase price is CAD $1,500,000, funded entirely from cash already on the balance sheet — no new debt, no equity financing required to close. The seller is at arm’s length to Revolve, so there are no related-party considerations. The transaction still needs to clear customary closing conditions and applicable regulatory approvals before it’s final, and Revolve hasn’t put a target closing date out there publicly. Once the Logan acquisition closes, Revolve expects its Ontario battery storage capacity to reach approximately 20.2 MW / 36.0 MWh across nine projects. Why Revolve is acquiring the Logan portfolio The Logan deal isn’t a one-off move. It fits squarely into Revolve’s stated strategy of building a battery storage platform in Ontario while simultaneously advancing a greenfield development pipeline in the province. Ontario’s energy storage market has become a deliberate focus for the company. Revolve completed its first major step in that direction back in August 2026, when it closed the acquisition of the Trillium Storage portfolio — six projects totaling 14.2 MW / 24.3 MWh. Logan is the follow-on, adding three more projects to that growing base. CEO Myke Clark described the transaction as part of the company’s “disciplined acquisition and development strategy.” That language signals Revolve is selecting assets that fit a defined platform-building approach in a market it’s already committed to — not chasing deals opportunistically. Expected impact on Revolve’s Ontario storage capacity Once the Logan acquisition closes, Revolve expects its Ontario battery storage capacity to reach approximately 20.2 MW / 36.0 MWh across nine projects. That’s a meaningful jump from where it stood before Trillium, when the company had zero operating storage assets in the province. The math is straightforward. Six Trillium projects contributed 14.2 MW / 24.3 MWh. Logan’s three projects add 6 MW / 11.7 MWh on top of that, bringing the combined total to nine projects across the two acquisitions. Clark emphasized that the Logan deal is expected to further establish Revolve’s presence in Ontario — and beyond the capacity numbers, the company is targeting contracted, cash-generating assets that produce recurring revenue rather than depending on merchant power prices alone. Worth noting: these are forward-looking expectations. Revolve has flagged that actual results could differ depending on regulatory approvals, operational performance, and whether the portfolio performs in line with management’s assumptions. Background: Revolve’s growth in Canadian energy storage Revolve Renewable Power Corp. is headquartered in Vancouver, BC. The company owns, operates, and develops power generation and digital infrastructure projects across North America, trading on the Canadian Securities Exchange under REVV and on the OTCQB under REVVF. Battery energy storage systems — BESS — store electricity and discharge it back to the grid when it’s needed. They play an increasingly important role in supporting grid stability and integrating variable renewable sources like wind and solar. Ontario, with its evolving energy mix and ongoing grid modernization efforts, has become an active market for exactly this kind of infrastructure. Revolve’s entry into Ontario battery storage is relatively recent; the Trillium acquisition in August 2026 was its first major transaction in this space, and management has indicated it expects to keep building through further acquisitions and development activity. What this deal means for Revolve going forward Taken together, the Trillium and Logan acquisitions give Revolve a nine-project, 20.2 MW / 36.0 MWh battery storage footprint in Ontario — assembled in roughly three months. For a company that had no Ontario storage assets before mid-2026, that’s a notable pace of portfolio construction. The Logan deal’s modest price tag — CAD $1.5 million funded from existing cash — also reflects a capital-efficient approach. Revolve isn’t stretching its balance sheet to make this happen, which leaves room for continued deal-making if the right opportunities come up. What happens next depends on closing. Once customary conditions and regulatory approvals are satisfied, Revolve will hold a nine-project Ontario storage portfolio that it describes as a foundation for longer-term growth, both through additional acquisitions and through its greenfield development pipeline in the province. artigo.texto: Is this the only U.S. town to vote 'yes' on data centers? On Election Day, voters approved more than 40 measures to slow or ban data center growth. But not all Americans decided against data centers. The majority of voters in Harwood, North Dakota, said "no" to a ballot measure calling for additional steps when the town evaluates, approves, and administers developments like that of data centers, Tech Insider reported. In a town of 845 people, 430 voted, and around 75 percent voted against added restrictions. (As Tech Insider notes, however, that documentation on small towns could be varied — The Washington Post reports that Harwood's population is 845, while other outlets report 940.) The best tech deal this week Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission. The big project in question is a $3 billion, 1.8-million-square-foot data center right outside Harwood, the Washington Post reports. Data center developer Applied Digital is behind the project. You May Also Like The vote caused the Post to claim that Harwood is "the only town in the U.S. that said yes to data centers." While the building of a data center itself wasn't on the ballot, Harwood residents indeed voted against further bureaucracy towards them. Harwood breaks the trend of what happened on Election Day, which Mashable's Rebecca Ruiz said was a clear message: "The AI reckoning is here." Backlash to both AI and data centers had been mounting in 2026, and voters were able to express their discontent last Tuesday. The list of U.S. states that ban data centers could grow in 2027. artigo.texto: A Eletronet anunciou nesta segunda-feira, 9, um investimento de R$ 25 milhões para construção de um novo data center em São Paulo. Com obras já iniciadas, a previsão é de que a unidade entre em operação no primeiro trimestre de 2027. Segundo a empresa especializada em infraestrutura de telecomunicações, o complexo denominado ELET1 terá aproximadamente 350 m², capacidade para cerca de 90 racks e potência inicial de 0,5 megawatt (MW), podendo chegar a 1 MW em uma futura expansão. A Eletronet informou que o novo centro de dados deve fortalecer a oferta de serviços de colocation, conectividade e interconexão, além de ampliar a escala ao atendimento de provedores de nuvem, operadoras de telecom, provedores de serviços de Internet (ISPs) e hyperscalers. "O ELET1 representa um passo estratégico para fortalecer nossa atuação no segmento de data centers. Estamos ampliando nossa estrutura para atender às necessidades dos clientes que já utilizam nossos serviços e abrir novas oportunidades de negócios, em um contexto no qual a hiperconectividade e a disponibilidade se tornam cada vez mais essenciais", afirma Rogerio Garchet, CEO da Eletronet, em nota. Região estratégica De acordo com a Eletronet, o complexo será instalado em uma localização com elevada concentração de redes de telecomunicações e provedores de conteúdo. Desse modo, estará preparado para atender à crescente demanda por serviços de data center para os segmentos de nuvem, streaming e telecom. A unidade também vai abrigar o ponto de interconexão (PIX) da Eletronet no IX.br São Paulo, um dos maiores pontos de troca de tráfego de Internet do mundo. O PIX da empresa, inclusive, tem se destacado no volume de tráfego de download na infraestrutura paulista. O objetivo desse movimento, segundo a empresa, é aumentar as possibilidades de conexão dos clientes com diferentes redes e provedores de serviços digitais. A Eletronet ainda ressaltou que o ELET1 integra a sua estratégia no segmento de data centers e de expansão da sua rede nacional de fibra óptica. Quando o centro de dados estiver em plena operação, a empresa planeja migrar a infraestrutura do data center atualmente em operação em São Paulo para o novo ambiente. Sustentabilidade Em comunicado, a Eletronet salientou que o ELET1 será construído levando em conta as melhores práticas globais de infraestrutura, incluindo soluções de proteção física e lógica, seguindo as diretrizes da norma ISO 27001. Além disso, o data center terá aplicações modernas de gestão ambiental e energética, com base nos padrões ISO 14001, ISO 50001 e LEED. A unidade ainda deve contar com dois geradores redundantes de 500 kVa, dupla entrada de rede, backbone DWDM protegido, sistema de gerenciamento predical (BMS) atualizado, monitoramento contínuo e um Centro de Operações de Rede (NOC) de contingência.

artigo.texto: BYD may soon have a new electric SUV in its India lineup. The BYD Atto 2 EV has once again been spotted testing on Indian roads, but this time the SUV has been seen without camouflage. This latest spotting has revealed its exterior design, side profile and rear styling more clearly than before. Join Our Youtube Channel to stay updated with daily Indian car & bike news instantly! Earlier, a heavily camouflaged test mule of the Atto 2 was also spotted in India, in which only some details of the front design could be seen. Now the undisguised appearance is another indication that BYD is preparing to expand its electric SUV range in the Indian market. The launch timeline and India-specific specifications have not yet been officially announced. In the international market, the Atto 2 is a relatively accessible model in BYD’s electric SUV range. Upon launch in India, it could be positioned below the Atto 3 and serve as the company’s entry-level electric SUV. Also Read: BYD Sealion 7 Festive Edition Costs Rs. 50.60 Lakh, But What Do Buyers Actually Get? BYD Atto 2 EV Spotted: What’s seen in the latest spy shots? The SUV seen in the latest spy shots is the all-electric version, with EV badging on the tailgate. In international markets, the Atto 2 is also available with a plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrain, but the test vehicle spotted in India is the electric version. On the side profile, the SUV gets black and silver body cladding that covers the wheel arches and door sills. It features electric-release door handles, sporty dual-tone alloy wheels, and a charging port on the front fender. The overall design is that of a compact midsize SUV, likely targeting urban buyers. The rear section features connected LED tail-lamps, a roof-mounted spoiler, and a dual-tone bumper. The bumper also gets integrated reflectors and subtle silver accents. The latest spotting gives a much clearer picture of the Atto 2’s overall design compared to the earlier camouflaged test vehicle. BYD Atto 2 EV: Battery, Range and Performance International-spec BYD Atto 2 EV is available with two battery pack options – 45.1kWh and 64.8kWh. Both versions get a front-axle-mounted electric motor, but the output battery varies depending on the variant. According to BYD’s international specifications, the BYD Atto 2 EV has a 0-100kph acceleration time of 7.9 seconds, while the claimed top speed is 170kph. The company claims a WLTP-certified range of up to 430km for the larger battery version. For charging, the SUV offers 11kW AC charging support and up to 155kW DC fast-charging capability. Confirmation of which battery pack and charging specification will be offered in India is expected closer to launch. Also Read: BYD Denza Z9 GT Coming to India With 1000hp+ Power: What We Know So Far Cabin Features: 12.8-inch Rotatable Touchscreen and Panoramic Sunroof The cabin of the international-spec BYD Atto 2 EV comes with a minimalist dashboard layout. It features a 12.8-inch rotatable touchscreen infotainment system, which takes center stage, similar to BYD’s larger Atto 3. It also features an 8.8-inch digital driver display. The feature list includes a panoramic sunroof, a 6-speaker audio system, a 50W wireless phone charger, and a 360-degree camera. The SUV also features a Vehicle-to-Load (V2L) function, which allows compatible external devices to be powered by the vehicle’s battery. Front and rear parking sensors are also part of the international model. It is not yet clear which of these features will be standard or available in selected variants in the India-spec model. Local specifications and equipment list should not be taken as confirmed details. Which electric SUVs will it compete with in India? The potential arrival of the BYD Atto 2 EV in India could make the competition in the midsize electric SUV segment more interesting. This category already includes models like the Maruti Suzuki e Vitara, Toyota Urban Cruiser Ebella, MG ZS EV, VinFast VF6, and Hyundai Creta Electric. The upcoming Tata Sierra EV, Mahindra BE 6, and Tata Curvv EV also expand buyers’ options in this competitive space. The Atto 2’s positioning and final pricing will determine how strong an alternative it can be against these models. If BYD introduces a more accessible electric SUV below the Atto 3 in India, it could give the company a chance to reach a wider customer base. But its success will depend on battery options, real-world range, charging performance, and pricing. Auto India Daily Verdict Undisguised spotting has certainly piqued interest in the BYD Atto 2 EV. A 64.8kWh battery, up to 430km claimed WLTP range, 155kW DC charging, and a feature-rich cabin make it a promising electric SUV, as per international specifications. Pricing will be the most important factor in India. If BYD launches it at a noticeably more affordable price point than the Atto 3, the Atto 2 could become an important volume-oriented model for the company. Official confirmation of the India launch date, battery options, and pricing is currently awaited. artigo.texto: How We Found Eight Data Center Community Benefit Agreements and Why It Matters These days, data centers are the hot-button topic in policy circles everywhere. Between the explosion of AI and the sheer scale of some of these facilities, it seems like people cannot go a single day without hearing them come up in some capacity. Communities weighing a data center project are considering real opportunities: construction jobs, new tax revenue, and the promise of economic development that comes with a major capital investment landing in town. But they are also considering real costs. Data centers bring elevated noise, especially for homes sitting close to a facility; they also can consume significant amounts of water and energy, affecting rates and the energy grid. And the tax breaks that some of the data centers receive could outweigh any financial benefits the community gets in return. Local governments face a surmounting number of questions, with best practices not readily available. The policy decisions we make today will affect much of the work that comes tomorrow and the decades after that. Beginning in early 2026, FAS began interviewing experts in the field, as well as searching for executed agreements on data center developments that were difficult to find. This included tracking local government ordinances as well as finding Community Benefit Agreements (CBAs). Many times, the negotiations between data center developers and officials from the municipality or county are conducted behind closed doors, protected by non-disclosure agreements (NDAs). As a result, community members have significantly fewer opportunities to influence the terms by which the data center should abide by as a fixture in the community. In the spirit of increased transparency, FAS wants to share our experience of “flipping over rocks” and discovering the hard-to-find contract. This is how we discovered eight community benefit agreements and why it matters. Local Policy Levers: The Ordinance and The Contract Generally, local governments have two enforceable levers to create policies around data centers. First, an ordinance considers issues such as zoning, land use requirements, and other permitting features – ultimately providing a pathway to allowable activities (and specific limitations). The ordinance process includes a public comment period, and it applies to all projects that qualify under the definition of a “data center.” A CBA involves the power of contract law, crafting and entering into binding bilateral (or sometimes multilateral) agreements that dictate the expectations of each party. CBAs are helpful in cases where existing zoning and permitting do not specifically identify “data centers” as a specific type of property to regulate (this is most frequent as the proliferation of data centers is so new). However, CBAs can be negotiated with fewer public comment opportunities, and they are required on a case-by-case basis. CBAs are not a new legal concept, and they have been used for large scale projects before on major development projects, like airports or energy generation infrastructure. They very recently started to be used in the context of data centers, after the explosion in usage of AI. Thus, FAS went searching for every agreement that fit the CBA model. As of the time of this writing, only one fully executed and publicly posted CBA exists that pertains to data centers: The Lancaster AI Hub agreement entered into by the City of Lancaster, Pennsylvania and the developers of two large data center campuses in the city. Lancaster’s CBA contains many terms and conditions that are beneficial to a data center agreement with the host community. It covers community transparency, water use, energy, noise restrictions, funding for public works, decommissioning, and many more. However, this agreement appears to leave much of the substance to be decided later on. Oftentimes, it requires the parties to submit separate plans to the city which detail the specifics of how the developers will conduct themselves. Finding Agreements: Discovering CBAs Finding executed CBAs took expertise, a concentrated effort, and follow-up. To expand beyond the Lancaster CBA, FAS first turned to blog posts that mentioned CBAs from sources like the Brookings Institution and Columbia University to see if there were any stories about localities that are negotiating terms with data center developers, or that have already done so. Initially, that is how FAS found Cedar Rapids, IA, St. Louis, MO, and El Paso, TX. Then, we looked for news articles referencing data center construction in these cities to see if they mentioned anything about an agreement between the city and the developers. If the terms of the agreement, or even discussion about its existence, were covered in these articles, that was where we knew we had to dig deeper. While the majority of agreements found were publicly available, the only way to obtain some of them was through a public records request. Thankfully, most states did not have such broad prohibitions on what can be public record, allowing FAS to uncover more contracts to serve as references. Over the summer of 2026, seven other agreements were uncovered besides the one in Lancaster between cities, counties, and data center developers that mention community benefits: During the search for more agreements, FAS was making note of the trends in each one, and comparing trends among the different agreements. Many of these agreements contain a heavy focus on money and taxes. Tax abatements, exemptions, and Payment in Lieu of Taxes (PILOT) schemes served as incentives for the data centers to be built in various communities. In total, we found the following policy areas considered across multiple CBAs: FAS’ Forthcoming Analysis + Next Steps By putting a light on the language of multiple CBAs, we can start to understand what is commonplace, what sections need to be tailored to local needs, and where there is a need to cons

artigo.texto: GREENFIELD — Planning Director Ella Wise will have a full plate over the next few months as she leads the Planning Board through changes in permitting for clean energy facilities, as well as carrying out plans to create zoning ordinances regulating battery energy storage systems and data centers in Greenfield. She told the board on Thursday that her work pertaining to changing regulations in technology will start with training city staff on new Massachusetts laws for consolidated permitting for clean energy projects. In 2024, the state Legislature signed a new climate law to speed up permitting for clean energy infrastructure, including solar, wind, anaerobic digestion and battery energy storage facilities. Wise said the law took effect on Oct. 1, allowing developers to opt into a new permitting process in which all departments review projects for approval at the same time, rather than the previous system in which applicants filed with each department individually. “They need to conduct a certain amount of public outreach and meet with city staff, and if all those conditions are met, they have 12 months for us to give them a ‘yes’ or a ‘no’ on their permit,” Wise said. “And that ‘yes’ or ‘no’ has to include the Planning Board and [the Zoning Board of Appeals’] decision, as well as the Conservation Commission’s decision and the Board of Health.” She added that municipalities also have the option of having the state’s Energy Facilities Siting Board assist with or oversee the review. Wise said the city does not need to change any of its zoning codes and regulations because of the state change, but she recommended that the Planning Board review the codes for clean energy facilities. Throughout the rest of the year, Wise said she plans to work with the Franklin Regional Council of Governments on a battery energy storage system ordinance, and come 2027, she will turn her attention to developing data center regulations before City Council’s one-year moratorium expires. The council adopted the moratorium in September. Battery energy storage systems While Greenfield has regulations in place for solar systems and other energy production facilities, Wise told the Planning Board that the city does not have any for battery energy storage systems, and it would be prudent to develop some. “We do have solar zoning. You don’t have any zoning for batteries,” Wise said. “So I think we need to start that process.” Wise said she has drafted an ordinance for battery energy storage systems based on a model state bylaw, and she plans to spend the next few months revising it, with technical assistance from FRCOG. She hopes that by February 2027, the draft will be ready for Planning Board and City Council approval. The draft, which was included in the board’s packet, defines a battery energy storage system as “a system consisting of one or more battery modules for storing electrical energy, any equipment needed to support the safe and proper function or usage of the battery modules, and one or more physical containers providing secondary containment to any of the above. It may be a primary or accessory use to a solar generating facility, power generation facility or other similar uses.” The draft ordinance states that small Tier 1 facilities would be allowed by right in all districts. Larger Tier 2 and 3 facilities would be allowed by right in the General Industrial (GI) and Planned Industry (PI) zoning districts, but would require special permits in the Rural Residential (RC), Suburban Residential (RB), General Commercial (GC) and Office (O) zoning districts. Battery energy storage systems would be prohibited in all other districts. Wise said that while her draft does outline examples of what the different size tiers could be and where they could be allowed, ultimately, the Planning Board would need to make policy decisions on whether battery energy storage systems should be allowed by right or by special permit, what the setback requirements should be and if there should be any required mitigation of environmental impacts. Data centers Wise said she expects a model data center bylaw to be published by the state next month, which would provide the Planning Board with a jumping-off point from which to start drafting its own regulations. “I don’t think I can work on a BESS bylaw while working on a data center one,” Wise said. “It just feels like so much to juggle. … So what I’m proposing is to focus our energy on BESS over the next few months, trying to get it done at the end of winter so that we have spring and summer to really have a robust process around data centers.” She expects that throughout the first few months of 2027, the Planning Board will research best practices and review other municipalities’ regulations. From March to May, the board will deliberate on what Greenfield’s version should look like and conduct public outreach, finalizing the ordinance in June or July. The city’s one-year moratorium on the construction of data centers is set to expire in September 2027. Planning Board member Thomas Bledsoe said he attended some trainings on data centers recently, and that noise was one of the largest concerns among the potential impacts, which the board should look to address with its regulations. “I really do think noise is a key issue here, and since it’s a 24-hour service, when we have to think hard about it, I would love to have some specific noise parameters in our code,” Bledsoe said. As the board moves forward, he said it should plan to work with other departments, particularly the Board of Health, and other communities.

artigo.texto: SoftBank reported a fiscal second-quarter net loss of 1.12 trillion yen ($7 billion) on Tuesday, as losses tied to U.S. AI data center equipment procurement and Intel share declines weighed on earnings. The Japanese investment giant also recorded a 597.2 billion ($3.7 billion) yen loss in the six months ending on Sept. 30 due to changes in procurement plans for power generation equipment for AI data center projects in the U.S. SoftBank said it had made advance investments to secure power generation equipment for its AI data center projects in the U.S. amid concerns over potential shortages and long procurement lead times. Power is increasingly becoming a key constraint for the AI data center buildout as power grids become overwhelmed with applications from large energy users like data centers. Cumulative payments for power-generation equipment for U.S. AI data center projects, like the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Pike County, Ohio, totaled $9.48 billion as of the end of September. "We made bridge investments in advance to secure power generation equipment in anticipation of shortage," a SoftBank executive said during the company's earnings call. Here's how SoftBank fared in the fiscal second quarter: - Net loss of 1.12 trillion yen in the quarter compared with a net profit of 2.5 trillion yen a year earlier. - Revenue stood at 2.22 trillion yen in the quarter, compared with LSEG estimates of 2.02 trillion yen. Revenue rose 13.3% in the six months ended Sept. 30, supported by growth in telecommunications and AI computing businesses. The company said its SoftBank segment recorded higher sales across all businesses, while revenue at its AI computing segment increased. The company's Vision Fund segment swung to a loss of 81.58 billion yen in the fiscal second quarter, compared with a profit of 2.38 trillion yen a year earlier. Vision Fund 1 recorded an investment loss of $20 million in the quarter, despite a $1.3 billion gain on ByteDance, as shares of publicly traded portfolio companies, including Coupang and Grab, declined. The Vision Funds segment recorded investment gains of 85.45 billion yen, down sharply from 2.81 trillion yen in the year-earlier period. Vision Fund 2 posted investment gains of 89.26 billion yen, while Vision Fund 1 recorded a loss of 3.86 billion yen on its investments. As of the end of September, SoftBank's cumulative investment in OpenAI stood at $54.6 billion, with a fair value of $99.6 billion and a cumulative investment gain of $45 billion, according to the company. SoftBank said a potential increase in OpenAI's valuation following a new funding round had not yet been reflected in its results, pending an official announcement. The updated valuation could be reflected in the fiscal third quarter, potentially boosting its net asset value and improving its loan-to-value ratio, the company said. "ChatGPT has been continuously a weapon of OpenAI, especially for consumers," the SoftBank esecutive said during the company's earnings call, highlighting the chatbot's growing user base. AI worries hit stocks Shares of the Japanese investment giant closed 13.9% higher on Tuesday. The gains came as Asian technology stocks, including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, rose following an overnight rebound on Wall Street. On its AI infrastructure investments, SoftBank highlighted a 20-year lease agreement with OpenAI for eight gigawatts of IT capacity at a data center project in Ohio. Addressing concerns of water consumption at its planned data center in Texas, SoftBank said it was taking steps to reduce water use through a closed-loop, air-cooled system. The company also pointed to plans to hire and source locally. Ahead of its earnings release, SoftBank Group announced on Monday plans with Grab and Malaysia's PETROS to commit a combined $1.85 billion in initial capital to develop AI infrastructure in Malaysia, with a long-term target of at least five gigawatts of AI computing capacity.

artigo.texto: Anchor Energy launches €75m BESS fund Danish investment platform Anchor Energy Partners has launched a fund with a €75m target that aims to invest in flexibility assets across Europe. Anchor Fund I will acquire and operate derisked, ready-to-build flexibility and storage assets, eventually expanding into renewable colocation and industrial energy. The fund’s initial close was backed by founding investor and co-owner 2degrees, a 50:50 joint venture between Macquarie Asset Management and Aware Super. Financial details were not disclosed. The founding partners are Fabian Siegel, Lasse Helstrup, Alejandra Huerta, Abhi Chirimar and Ludvig Holsteinborg. Their experience spans investing and asset management at Orsted, Danske Commodities, AIP, Icecreek Energy and Boston Consulting Group. The team managed €30bn in funds, including two IPOs, and more than 120MWh of operational BESS in Germany and Finland. Copenhagen-based Anchor said using BESS is the fastest way to add flexibility to Europe’s energy system. The continent has less than 80GWh of BESS capacity against a 1.2GWh requirement by 2050.

artigo.texto: Riot Platforms Inc (Riot), a digital infrastructure and Bitcoin mining company has signed a 15 year lease with an unnamed Frontier AI Lab for its entire Corsicana data center campus in Texas, covering 910 MW of critical IT capacity and representing approximately US$ 28 billion in contracted revenue with AI safety and research company Antropic as the first tenant. According to a press release, the triple net powered land lease covers a contiguous 332 acre site and is expected to generate approximately US$ 1.8 billion in average annual rent over the initial term. Riot estimates a net operating income (NOI) margin of approximately 99 percent. The contract value could reach US$ 54 billion if the tenant exercises both five year extension options. The project will be delivered in three phases, 400 MW in September 2027, 200 MW in January 2028 and the remaining 310 MW in July 2028. Rent for each phase will begin no later than 60 days after delivery of its powered pads and will be payable on the full contracted capacity regardless of utilization. “Today, we are excited to announce the largest lease in Riot’s history: a 15-year triple-net powered land lease with a leading Frontier AI Lab for the entirety of our Corsicana campus, representing 910 megawatts of critical IT capacity and approximately $28 billion of contracted revenue over the initial term,” said Jason Les, CEO, Riot Platforms. “Together with our AMD contract and the lease signed with the same Frontier AI Lab at Rockdale earlier this year, Riot has contracted 1,151 megawatts and approximately US$ 38 billion of data center revenue, which we expect will generate more than US$ 2 billion of average annual net operating income at full deployment, firmly establishing Riot as a leading developer of large-scale digital infrastructure.” Riot estimates total capital costs of US$ 5.5 billion, or approximately US$ 6 million per IT MW, the company will contribute US$ 2 million per MW toward site work and electrical infrastructure. While the remaining US$ 4 million per MW will be reimbursed by the tenant in stages after each phase is delivered and begins generating rent. The reimbursements are expected to be financed through non-recourse project debt backed by contracted rental income. If financing on comparable market terms is unavailable, the tenant will fund the reimbursements directly and recover the amounts through credits against rent over the remaining lease term. Riot expects to fund its share from existing liquidity and does not currently anticipate issuing equity for the project.

artigo.texto: Americans were unequivocal at the ballot box this week as they expressed disdain for tech billionaires and mistrust of artificial intelligence. With that backdrop, Anthropic is about to try to go public. The AI company is gearing up for a potentially historic IPO, likely targeting mid-November for its Nasdaq debut. CNBC reported on Friday that Anthropic investors see the company aiming for a valuation of $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion, down from a target of $2 trillion that had been floated in recent months. From Wall Street to Main Street, it's becoming a tougher environment for Anthropic. The Nasdaq on Thursday suffered its steepest drop in 19 months, and it's down to start November after October marked its worst month since March 2025. Chipmakers and neoclouds, the companies most closely tied to the AI buildout, are getting hit the hardest. Voters rebuked AI in Tuesday's midterm elections, while sending Democrats to sweeping congressional victories across the country. Candidates who advocated for more stringent AI regulation won handily in states like Michigan, Ohio, Texas and Georgia, which will all now have Democratic governors, and local communities opposed data center-related ballot measures in 40 out of 41 cases. More than half of voters said AI data centers were a "crucial" or "major factor" in who they supported for Congress, according to an exit poll from NBC News. "People don't want a data center going near them if it's just going to house AI that's going to help a big tech company profit," Maura Austin, a behavioral scientist at the University of Virginia, told CNBC. "What Anthropic is doing when they're going public with such a high valuation is they're really leaning into that big tech, billionaire kind of caricature. I expect that's not going to go well with the public." Anthropic has long tried to position itself as a safety-conscious company that takes AI's potential risks and benefits seriously. CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company alongside a handful of researchers who defected from OpenAI, now its chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude, and it primarily sells its products and services to other businesses. The company's enterprise focus has helped it avoid becoming the public face of AI, leaving that distinction to OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman. But with Anthropic poised to become the first pure-play AI company to hit the public market, minting a number of new billionaires and many more millionaires in the process, a heightened level of scrutiny is coming. "Being a public company, just that by itself pushes you in the limelight," Reena Aggarwal, a professor of finance at Georgetown University, said in an interview. "And then AI is such a hot-button issue that Anthropic will be in the limelight even more." Matt Kennedy, a senior IPO market strategist at Renaissance Capital, said that's not necessarily a bad thing for Anthropic. Public markets force greater transparency, he said, and the company could attract new users through its debut. And since AI has become such a mainstream conversation topic, several private companies are already household names. "I would say that a public company does not deserve more criticisms than a comparable private company," Kennedy said. "So Anthropic should not be put in a harsher public spotlight than OpenAI just because it's public." Anthropic declined to comment. Data center blowback AI backlash accelerated over the summer after a series of high-profile safety and security incidents rattled the public. As concerns mounted, the debate over data centers intensified, while tech's hyperscalers simultaneously boosted their forecasts for capital expenditures, each reaching into the hundreds of billions of dollars. Anthropic and OpenAI depend on state-of-the-art data centers to train models and serve customers, and they're trying to build out capacity as quickly as possible to meet demand. Anthropic said in an amended IPO prospectus this week that it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure." Americans grappling with inflation and stubbornly high gas prices have grown worried that the facilities could exacerbate environmental harms, raise utility bills and contribute to job loss. For many, a proposed data center in their backyard became the physical manifestation of the widespread antipathy toward AI. In the risk factors section of its prospectus, Anthropic said opposition to data center development has become more organized across jurisdictions, and that the company's public profile could draw particular scrutiny to projects associated with it. Nicole Greene, an analyst at Gartner, said she expects that Anthropic's executives have long been prepared to contend with AI backlash, especially given the disruptive nature of the technology. "There's going to be big emotions," Greene told CNBC. "With big emotions and feelings — fear and excitement — comes heightened scrutiny." Amodei acknowledged the souring sentiment around AI in a post on X in August. He said it's the result of a "crisis of trust," and that people believe companies, the government and the tech industry are always "cooking up some new way to screw them over." Rebuilding public confidence is going to be an uphill battle as the company begins providing quarterly financial updates. The University of Southern California published a survey on Monday that found that 71% of respondents don't trust big tech companies to act in society's best interest "at all" around data center development. "Once you've lost trust, it's hard to gain it back," Wändi Bruine de Bruin, a professor at the University of Southern California's Schaeffer Institute, said in an interview. "The numbers are not good." WATCH: Alex Kantrowitz: Anthropic doesn’t have a lot of flexibility on timing of its IPO

artigo.texto: South Korean scientists have just unveiled a new liquid-crystal polymer separator, which, when tested in a lithium-metal battery, retained 94 percent of its capacity after 100 charge-discharge cycles at a 4C charging rate. The separator was built by the a research team at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST). It could reportedly improve battery stability and charging speed, meaning drivers could charge their EVs in just 15 minutes. The study was led by Dong Ki Yoon, PhD, and Hye Ryung Byon, PhD, professors at KAIST’s Department of Chemistry. “Lithium metal batteries can store more energy than conventional batteries,” they stated. “However, during charging, lithium can accumulate in sharp, branch-like structures known as ‘dendrites.'” For the separator, the researchers used liquid-crystalline polymers to control how the lithium ions move inside lithium-metal batteries. Both Yoon and Byon believe that their find could address slow ion transport and dendrite formation. A highway for lithium ions Lithium-metal batteries can store more energy than conventional ones. However, during charging, lithium can accumulate on the electrode surface and, as a result, form dendrites. These tiny needle-like metallic crystals grow on the anodes, and they can damage the separator between the electrodes, which could cause short circuits and increase the risk of fires. More from Energy See All To address this problem, the team created a porous separator made from liquid-crystalline polymers, which have an ordered structure like solids. They also share some properties with liquids. For the project, the team incorporated polyethylene glycol (PEG) chains into the material to facilitate lithium-ion transport. The scientists then monitored the alignment of the liquid-crystal molecules and arranged them either vertically or horizontally to examine how their orientation affected ion movement. The vertically aligned separator created direct pathways for lithium ions to travel toward the electrodes. In contrast to the horizontally aligned separator, it reduced the tortuosity (winding nature), of the ion transport pathways by about 2.5 times. This allowed the lithium ions to move faster and more uniformly. What’s more, it suppressed the dendrite formation and improved the battery stability. Longer battery life Ultimately, the researchers tested the separator in a working lithium-metal battery to evaluate its performance. To their massive surprise, the cell retained 94 percent of its initial capacity after 100 charge-discharge cycles at 4C. In simple terms, a 4C charging rate means a battery can fully recharge in 15 minutes. According to the team, controlling how molecules are arranged could potentially make batteries charge faster and last longer without compromising safety. Yoon emphasized the significance of this finding for future battery development. He said that molecular alignment plays a key role in battery performance. “We expect this approach to contribute to the development of high-energy-density next-generation battery technologies, for which long driving ranges and rapid charging are essential,” he concluded in a press release. The scientists believe the approach could contribute to the development of high-energy-density batteries for future EVs, where rapid charging and longer driving ranges are essential. Further tests will, however, show whether it works in larger batteries as well. The study has been published in the journal ACS Nano.

artigo.texto: - CATL chairman said sodium-ion batteries offer sufficient range for daily urban travel, while more swap stations can ease concerns about longer trips. - The company's swap stations now cover about 200 Chinese cities, with a target of more than 3,000 passenger car stations by year-end. CATL (HKEX: 3750) said its rapidly expanding battery-swapping network in China will help accelerate sodium-ion battery adoption by easing consumer concerns about driving range. The battery maker's chairman Robin Zeng made the remarks at a Benchmark Mineral Intelligence event in Shanghai, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday. Sodium-ion batteries offer sufficient range for daily urban travel, while an expanding swap network can ease concerns among drivers looking to make longer trips on weekends, Zeng said. "We are building battery-swapping stations on our own, leasing batteries to the consumers," Zeng said. "We need to build more swapping stations on the highways and in the cities." About 200 Chinese cities already have CATL swap stations, he said. The company aims to have more than 3,000 passenger car swap stations across China by the end of this year. Battery swapping allows drivers to replace depleted packs with fully charged ones within minutes, offering an alternative to conventional charging. CATL is promoting sodium-ion batteries as an alternative to traditional lithium-ion batteries in vehicles. The technology offers advantages in cold weather and is seen as potentially improving safety and reducing costs. However, energy density remains a key concern for sodium-ion battery adoption. CATL previously said it expects 10,000 to 20,000 electric vehicles to use its sodium-ion batteries this year. The company also views the technology as a risk management strategy to reduce its exposure to sharp swings in lithium prices. The company launched its Naxtra sodium-ion battery brand in April 2025 and jointly unveiled a passenger vehicle equipped with the battery with Changan Automobile in February this year. CATL said at the time that the vehicle's cells have an energy density of up to 175 Wh/kg and enable a driving range of more than 400 kilometers (249 miles), demonstrating the technology's ability to meet daily travel needs. Cold-weather performance is another key selling point. According to information CATL released in February, the battery retains more than 90% of its capacity at minus 40 degrees Celsius (minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit). The swap network provides supporting infrastructure for broader sodium-ion battery adoption. CATL announced in December 2025 that it had built 1,020 Choco-Swap stations across 45 cities. Its subsidiary Contemporary Amperex Energy Service Technology (CAES) said at the time that it planned to deploy sodium-ion batteries based on Naxtra technology at scale across its swap network starting in 2026.
