artigo.texto: Nas aldeias da minoria étnica Thai, o conceito de floresta está passando por mudanças positivas. Enquanto no passado as pessoas rezavam aos espíritos da floresta para amenizar a raiva ao colher madeira para a construção de casas, agora suas orações expressam alegria e o desejo de que a floresta floresça ainda mais. As mudanças climáticas deixaram de ser uma ameaça futura e se tornaram uma realidade manifestada por meio de eventos climáticos extremos cada vez mais severos. Sob essa pressão, espera-se que a 31ª Conferência das Partes da Convenção-Quadro das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (COP31), que começa na Turquia, promova compromissos mais firmes no enfrentamento das mudanças climáticas, especialmente na implementação de soluções de adaptação e na transição energética. Para o Vietname, a COP31 representa uma oportunidade para promover a cooperação internacional e reafirmar os esforços na proteção ambiental e na resposta às alterações climáticas. Em particular, o desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono florestal de alta qualidade é uma das direções importantes, contribuindo para reforçar a posição do Vietname no mercado internacional de carbono. Com uma maior conscientização sobre o valor das florestas, as pessoas estão participando cada vez mais ativamente da proteção desse recurso. Além da receita gerada pelos contratos de proteção florestal, os créditos de carbono estão abrindo novas oportunidades para a criação de meios de subsistência e o aumento da renda das comunidades. Contudo, a implementação prática do primeiro acordo de crédito de carbono revelou uma importante lição: a necessidade de uma implementação em larga escala, evitando a fragmentação. Cada projeto precisa abranger pelo menos 100.000 hectares, enquanto as áreas florestais destinadas às famílias são frequentemente dispersas e pequenas. Portanto, a formação de um órgão central de coordenação para conectar e organizar a implementação é um requisito essencial. O Sr. Nguyen Tien An, Diretor do Fundo Provincial de Proteção e Desenvolvimento Florestal de Nghe An , afirmou que o fundo atuará como um ponto focal para apoiar as comunidades participantes. Ao mesmo tempo, o fundo poderá coordenar ou autorizar organizações com plena capacidade jurídica a executar tarefas relacionadas. Além de estabelecer um órgão central de coordenação, também foi dada ênfase à consulta pública e à melhoria da capacidade de medição, relato e avaliação. Muitas localidades, incluindo províncias que se preparam para novos acordos, pesquisaram e prepararam proativamente as condições para participar do mercado interno de carbono e implementar projetos inter-regionais de grande escala. Na província de Lam Dong , as autoridades locais também estão se dedicando a preparar o conhecimento e a capacidade para a implementação de créditos de carbono florestal. O Sr. Le Dinh Viet, vice-chefe do Departamento Provincial de Proteção Florestal de Lam Dong, afirmou que a província organizou uma conferência com a participação de especialistas em carbono do governo central para trocar experiências, disseminar conteúdo e fornecer orientações sobre a implementação de tarefas relacionadas no próximo período. Além dos esforços proativos das autoridades locais, o quadro político para a gestão e o desenvolvimento florestal também está sendo gradualmente aprimorado. Após o decreto sobre o mecanismo piloto de pagamento, o Vietnã emitiu um novo decreto sobre investimento e apoio ao investimento na gestão, proteção, uso e desenvolvimento de florestas. Segundo o Sr. Pham Hong Luong, Diretor Adjunto do Departamento de Silvicultura e Proteção Florestal, a nova política é de grande importância para promover os pontos fortes internos dos proprietários florestais, ao mesmo tempo que cria condições para que parceiros e investidores internacionais participem no apoio ao desenvolvimento de projetos de grande escala a nível regional e inter-regional. Desde o compromisso assumido na COP26 de alcançar emissões líquidas zero até 2050 até o primeiro acordo de crédito de carbono florestal com o Banco Mundial , nos últimos cinco anos, o Vietnã construiu gradualmente as bases para o desenvolvimento de um mercado de carbono florestal de alta qualidade. O aprimoramento contínuo das políticas, o fortalecimento da capacidade organizacional e a garantia da participação da comunidade serão fatores cruciais para maximizar o valor dos recursos florestais e contribuir de forma prática para a mitigação das mudanças climáticas.

artigo.texto: Fortunes are diverging lately for Korean and Chinese companies competing in the global battery market. Expectations are rising that domestic manufacturers including LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI will keep improving results on stronger demand in the U.S. energy storage system (ESS) market. Chinese companies, by contrast, face a red light as oversupply worries and U.S. restrictions on Chinese-made products cloud growth. ◇ China's CATL grows in size, but profitability flashes warning signs According to the battery industry on the 9th, China's CATL, the world's largest battery maker, posted third-quarter revenue of 165.221 billion yuan (about 33.3 trillion won), up 58.9% from a year earlier. Net profit rose 14.5% to 21.246 billion yuan (about 4.3 trillion won). Despite double-digit increases in both revenue and net profit from a year earlier, the results fell well short of market expectations. London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG) had projected CATL's third-quarter revenue growth rate at 60.2% and net profit growth rate at 41.2%, respectively. The underwhelming results were immediately reflected in the share price. On the 20th of last month, when the third-quarter results were released, CATL's stock on the Hong Kong market fell 6.6% from the previous day. Global investment bank JPMorgan also cut its rating on CATL shares listed in Hong Kong to Neutral from Overweight. Chinese battery makers including CATL continue to expand in scale. In particular, Chinese products have increased their share of the electric-vehicle market this year. Market researcher SNE Research said that from January through September, Chinese companies—seven suppliers including CATL—accounted for a 73% share of batteries installed in electric vehicles (EVs), plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) and hybrids (HEVs) worldwide, up 3.5 percentage points from a year earlier. Korea's big three—LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI and SK On—had a 12.6% share, down 4.1 percentage points. The problem is profitability is slipping relative to topline growth. With domestic competition saturated, China has been pushing large volumes overseas at low prices. Automakers struggling amid cutthroat competition are also diversifying supply chains to smaller battery vendors that sell cheaply to cut costs, a trend seen as squeezing margins at major manufacturers including CATL. According to the South China Morning Post (SCMP), Chinese EV makers Xiaomi and Li Auto said they will team up with battery manufacturers such as CALB and EVE Energy to reduce battery procurement costs. CALB and EVE Energy are classified one tier below giants like CATL and BYD in China. ◇ Korean battery makers spread their wings on rising U.S. ESS demand Korean battery makers, by contrast, are beating market forecasts with improving results. They have struggled in EV batteries against a flood of cheap Chinese products, but demand for ESS batteries has surged in the United States, benefiting domestic suppliers. Samsung SDI posted third-quarter revenue of 4.6856 trillion won and operating profit of 407.8 billion won. Revenue rose 52.6% from a year earlier, and operating profit swung to a surplus from a 591.3 billion won loss. Operating profit, in particular, was twice the previous quarter's 203.8 billion won and the highest in 12 quarters since the third quarter of 2023. Samsung SDI's operating profit far beat the market consensus—an average forecast—of 235.4 billion won, an earnings surprise that stood in contrast to CATL. LG Energy Solution also saw revenue jump 59% in the same period to 9.6434 trillion won, while operating profit rose 25.7% to 756 billion won. Both were record highs on a quarterly basis. Its third-quarter operating profit was more than double the 320 billion won market consensus. Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution said soaring demand for ESS used in U.S. artificial intelligence (AI) data centers drove the improvement. A gradual recovery in Europe's EV market, which lifted EV battery sales, was also a tailwind. ◇ U.S. midterms: Democrats win by a landslide; ESS demand seen rising, China curbs to continue Industry officials expect the U.S. ESS market to grow quickly, likely extending domestic makers' run of stronger results. Many also see the Democrats' landslide in the U.S. midterms held on the 3rd—on a platform of expanding energy infrastructure including ESS—as a boon for Korean companies. Voice of America (VOA) reported on the 9th that although counting was not yet complete, the Democrats had already secured 252 of the 435 House seats, far more than a majority and beating the Republicans' 161. They also won 52 Senate seats to the Republicans' 44. In gubernatorial races, Democrats won in 28 states, ahead of Republicans who won in 20. The Democrats announced in May an energy agenda that included plans to expand investment in the national power grid and energy storage systems (ESS). While they take a dim view of regulating AI data center construction, they intend to keep growing the ESS market as part of grid expansion. Hyundai Motor Securities said in a pre-midterm report, "If Democrats control both chambers, they will push to restore renewable energy tax credits and expand ESS investment," adding, "Both parties have previously toughened tariff policy on Chinese batteries, so the post-election direction will likely remain to block China's supply chain." Some, however, see a chance for a rebound by Chinese battery makers. China is also ramping up ESS investment, and once plants under construction in Europe start up, they could further encroach on Europe's EV battery market. The European Union (EU) is currently imposing high tariffs on Chinese EVs. It is also finalizing details of the Industrial Acceleration Act (IAA), pursued to counter China and protect domestic industry, ahead of its entry into force. artigo.texto: - Australian Vanadium awarded $15 million from Investment Attraction Fund (IAF) to establish vanadium electrolyte manufacturing facility - IAF supporting a diversified economy and unlocking private sector investment - Funds will support large-scale battery installations as well as increasing local content in the vanadium flow battery supply chain The Cook Labor Government has awarded $15 million through the Investment Attraction Fund (IAF) New Energies Industries Round 2 to Australian Vanadium Limited (AVL) to establish a high-capacity, relocatable vanadium electrolyte manufacturing facility in Western Australia. The project will expand AVL's capacity to produce vanadium electrolyte to support large-scale battery installations as well as increasing local content in the vanadium flow battery supply chain. Vanadium flow batteries use liquid vanadium electrolyte solutions in separate tanks to both store and release electricity. Skilled employment and training opportunities in advanced manufacturing, chemical processing, engineering, construction, commissioning, and plant operations will be created, while its modular and relocatable design enables deployment across regional and industrial centres throughout the State. The project presents an opportunity for the State to further invest in energy transition initiatives by supporting grid-scale energy storage, strengthening critical minerals supply chains, and help to build local industries required for a low-carbon future. The IAF funding will also support the development of grid-scale vanadium flow batteries and long-duration energy storage infrastructure in the State. The IAF has supported 47 projects since first launching in 2022 with over $215.2 million in funding awarded, generating 290 direct jobs and 1,479 contractors engaged. To date, more than $4 in spending is generated from every $1 distributed through the fund. For more information on the IAF, see: Investment Attraction Fund As stated by State Development and Economic Diversification Minister David Michael: "The Investment Attraction Fund continues to play a critical role in attracting projects that strengthen Western Australia's industrial capabilities and support our energy transition. "By supporting AVL's electrolyte manufacturing capability, we're creating new opportunities in advanced manufacturing while helping position WA at the forefront of long-duration energy storage technologies. "The development of a high-capacity vanadium electrolyte facility will support local jobs, strengthen our manufacturing capability, and provide the foundations for future grid-scale battery projects across the State." As stated by Energy and Decarbonisation and Manufacturing Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson: "The Cook Labor Government wants to see more things made right here in WA. "Our Made in WA plan is working, with new data showing manufacturing jobs have risen 13 per cent over the past year. "This is another great example of the Cook Labor Government backing innovative Western Australian manufacturing projects."

artigo.texto: On November 9, a Dutch new energy delegation led by KURT WU, Founder and General Manager of EverGreen Sustainability, visited Shanghai Metals Market (SMM) for an exchange. The SMM team, including Cherry Li, Key Account Manager, Alissa Peng, Account Manager, and Daniel Huang, Senior Energy Storage Analyst, warmly received the delegation and extended a sincere welcome to the guests from afar. This is a professional and diverse delegation, with members covering the entire industry chain, including project developers, EPCs, system integrators, energy asset owners, EMS technology enterprises, distributors, and industry platforms. The delegation includes: - THEO GROEN, CEO of Groen Energy in the Netherlands; - JAN SCHUT, CEO of Envitron; - ERIK BRINK, CEO of Nettion; - GERARD SCHEPER, Founder and CEO of European Solar & Storage; - RINIE EVERTSE, Founder of Evertse Solar Control; - BEREND PASTOOR, Chairman of Groen Zonenergie; - HENRICO VAN DEN BOOMEN, CEO of Eigenenergie.net B.V.; - PAUL DAANEN, Technical Director, Eigenenergie.net B.V.; - ROBERT MEIJER, CEO of AG Solar; - JOOP POLDERMANS, Senior Energy Project Manager at JOOP POLDERMANS; - WIDJAI JIPAT, CEO of EPTA Energy; - GERBEN DRAGT, CEO of GD Solar; - HASHIM FATMI, COO of EnergyPlanet Global; - REMCO VAN DER HORST, Founder of Greenproc B.V.； - Floriske Deutma, Board Member of Netherlands-China Business Council - KURT WU, Founder and General Manager of EverGreen Sustainability During the exchange, the SMM team first introduced SMM's development history and data service capabilities. Founded in 1999, SMM started with traditional non-ferrous metals business and gradually expanded into the new energy sector. Headquartered in Shanghai, its business covers Asia, Europe, and Africa, and it set up offices in India and Australia this year. The company currently has more than 500 employees, half of whom are analysts, each specializing in specific metals and new energy sub-sectors. Next, the SMM team conducted a special workshop to share market research findings and analytical capabilities across the ESS industry chain: global energy storage demand grew 74% from 2025 to 2026, with growth expected to pull back to 22% in 2027. Regional market divergence is pronounced, with China remaining the world's largest market, North America's share continuing to rise driven by AI data center power demand, Europe constrained by localisation policies, and Australia's residential demand strengthening on the back of subsidies. Daniel Huang also highlighted that the lead time from battery cell shipment to grid connection and commissioning takes only 3–6 months in China, compared with 7–14 months in Europe, where large projects commonly involve 10% advance stockpiling. This difference in delivery cycles profoundly influences the global supply pace. The SMM team further examined price movements in the ESS Stack market, attributing the upward shift in the battery cabinet price center to the combined effects of raw material costs, exchange rate fluctuations, export tax rebate policy adjustments, and the competitive landscape. Scenario analyses were conducted on the transmission path of rebate reductions, margin impacts across different markets, and the trajectory of mid-term FOB prices in Europe amid the iteration toward large-format battery cells. At the battery cell level, the discussion drew on changes in industry operating rates and concentration, as well as the trend of top-tier players tilting production schedules toward large-format cells, to illustrate that growth in shipment volume does not equate to cost breakthroughs. Yield, capacity utilisation rate, and expansion discipline are the true variables for cost reduction. This was further extended to assessments of the medium and long-term share and cost convergence of lithium battery cathode routes and sodium-ion batteries. Finally, returning to upstream lithium carbonate, the meeting reviewed price trends and phase-specific drivers, emphasising that the risk lies not in nominal capacity but in whether supply can be delivered on schedule. Variables such as mine production resumptions, ex-China ore export policies, and midstream settlement terms collectively determine actual available supply and the price pace, thereby providing industry chain clients with a systematic reference for decision-making on pricing, procurement, and project scheduling. After the presentation, the delegation members raised a stream of pertinent questions based on their own businesses, covering the potential impact of EU cybersecurity regulations on the market share of Chinese enterprises, the layout trends of Chinese producers building factories in Indonesia, the selection of lithium price indices in European procurement contracts, the market space for battery recycling, and the independence and release mechanism of SMM data. The SMM analyst team responded one by one and introduced the product system, including databases, built-in AI queries, monthly reports and free spot prices. This visit and exchange has built a bridge for direct dialogue between enterprises in the PV+ESS industry chains of the Netherlands and China. Both sides will take this exchange as a starting point to continuously deepen cooperation in data services and market insights, jointly supporting the energy transition in Europe and globally.

artigo.texto: Diferentemente dos sistemas de alimentação ininterrupta (UPS) convencionais, o BESS (Sistema de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias) é um sistema de armazenamento de energia em larga escala conectado diretamente à rede elétrica. O sistema pode carregar e armazenar eletricidade em momentos apropriados e devolvê-la à rede quando necessário. O BESS pode ser concebido como uma "instalação de armazenamento de energia" capaz de operar em duas direções: quando o sistema está em estado de flutuação, o BESS recebe eletricidade para armazenamento; quando há necessidade de suporte, o sistema gera eletricidade de volta para a rede. Dessa forma, o BESS pode contribuir para suavizar a curva de demanda, reduzir a pressão durante os horários de pico e aumentar a flexibilidade da operação do sistema elétrico. Com a crescente demanda por eletricidade e as significativas flutuações de carga dependendo do clima e da hora do dia, a melhoria da capacidade operacional do sistema elétrico de Hanói exige não apenas investimentos em fontes de energia e redes, mas também em novas soluções tecnológicas. Antecipando a tendência da tecnologia de armazenamento de energia, a EVNHANOI concluiu a instalação, energização e operação piloto de cinco sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) nas subestações de 110 kV de Bac Thang Long, Quang Minh, Sai Dong 2, Phung Xa e Thanh Oai. Cada sistema possui capacidade de armazenamento de 10 MW/20 MWh, elevando a capacidade total de armazenamento para 50 MW/100 MWh. Esta é a primeira vez que a tecnologia de armazenamento de energia em larga escala é aplicada à rede elétrica de Hanói, representando um novo passo na modernização da infraestrutura de energia e no desenvolvimento de uma rede inteligente. A seleção das subestações para o projeto piloto baseou-se nas características de carga e nos requisitos operacionais da rede elétrica de Hanói. O sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) é uma tecnologia completamente nova na rede elétrica da capital. Desde a instalação, testes e energização até a operação oficial, as unidades da EVNHANOI trabalharam em estreita coordenação para garantir que o sistema atendesse plenamente aos requisitos técnicos e operasse de forma estável e segura. Durante a operação, a equipe técnica monitora continuamente o status das baterias, a capacidade de carga e descarga, a temperatura, os sistemas de proteção e os alertas técnicos. Cada turno de inspeção é realizado de acordo com procedimentos rigorosos, com coordenação entre a equipe de despacho, a unidade de gestão técnica e a equipe diretamente na subestação para garantir que todos os parâmetros permaneçam dentro dos limites de segurança. O processo de operação prática também proporciona à EVNHANOI a oportunidade de acumular dados, aprimorar os procedimentos técnicos, avaliar a confiabilidade dos equipamentos e adquirir experiência em gestão para uma tecnologia ainda muito recente no Vietnã. Segundo o Sr. Pham Huu Manh, Diretor Adjunto do Conselho de Gestão do Projeto de Desenvolvimento de Energia de Hanói, a implementação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) não visa substituir as fontes de energia existentes, mas sim adicionar uma ferramenta técnica que ajude o sistema elétrico a ser mais proativo na resposta às flutuações de carga, além de criar uma base para a pesquisa de modelos modernos de operação da rede no futuro. Quando combinado com sistemas de coleta de dados, monitoramento, controle e gestão de energia, automação da rede e tecnologias digitais , o BESS deixa de ser apenas um sistema de armazenamento de energia e se torna um elo na estrutura de uma rede inteligente. No próximo período, a EVNHANOI continuará monitorando e avaliando a eficiência operacional, aprimorando os procedimentos técnicos e pesquisando soluções de aplicação adequadas. Isso servirá de base para a construção gradual de uma rede elétrica mais inteligente, flexível, segura e moderna na capital, atendendo às necessidades do desenvolvimento socioeconômico e melhorando a qualidade do fornecimento de energia elétrica para a população de Hanói.

artigo.texto: When using electric vehicles or smartphones, users often experience inconvenience from long charging times and gradually shortening battery life. To increase charging speed and extend usage time, next-generation batteries with high energy density are essential. However, fast charging has had limitations because deposits can accumulate inside batteries, degrading performance and even increasing the risk of fire. A Korean research team has developed a new foundational technology to address this problem by creating a "highway" through which lithium ions can move rapidly inside a battery. KAIST (President Choongsik Bae) announced on November 9 that a joint research team led by Professors Dong Ki Yoon and Hye Ryung Byon from the Department of Chemistry developed a next-generation battery separator technology that precisely controls lithium-ion transport pathways by regulating the molecular alignment of liquid-crystalline polymers. Lithium metal batteries can store more energy than conventional batteries. However, during charging, lithium can accumulate in sharp, branch-like structures known as "dendrites." This phenomenon has been a major cause of reduced battery life and can damage the internal separator, potentially leading to explosions. The research team sought to solve this problem using liquid crystal materials, which combine the ordered characteristics of solids with the fluidity of liquids. Because the orientation of liquid crystal molecules can be altered through surface treatment and other methods, the researchers used this property to regularly align the pathways through which lithium ions travel. Based on this liquid-crystal alignment control technology, the team also created a porous liquid-crystalline polymer separator containing nanoscale pores. Polyethylene glycol (PEG) chains, which facilitate lithium-ion transport, were incorporated into the separator. In particular, the researchers freely controlled the alignment direction of the liquid-crystal molecules either vertically or horizontally and compared the resulting lithium-ion transport characteristics. The results showed that the liquid-crystalline polymer separator with vertically aligned molecules formed a kind of "highway" that allowed lithium ions to move directly toward the electrodes. Compared with a horizontally aligned separator, it reduced the tortuosity of the ion transport pathway by approximately 2.5-fold, enabling lithium ions to move much faster and more uniformly. This effectively suppressed dendrite formation and significantly improved stability. The research team applied the newly developed separator to an actual lithium metal battery and verified its fast-charging performance. Even under demanding fast-charging conditions at a high charging rate of 4 C*, the battery retained 94% of its initial capacity after 100 charge-discharge cycles. This demonstrates that controlling the molecular alignment of liquid-crystalline polymers can be a highly effective strategy for improving both the charging speed and lifespan of next-generation batteries. *4C charging rate: A rate at which a battery can theoretically be fully charged in approximately 15 minutes based on its rated capacity. C is a unit indicating the charging and discharging rate of a battery: 1C corresponds to 1 hour, 2C to 30 minutes, and 4C to 15 minutes. Professor Dong Ki Yoon said, "This study demonstrates that controlling the molecular alignment of liquid-crystalline polymers can be used to efficiently design lithium-ion transport pathways and thereby improve battery performance and stability," adding, "We expect this approach to contribute to the development of high-energy-density next-generation battery technologies, for which long driving ranges and rapid charging are essential." Geunjung Lee, a Ph.D. student at KAIST, and Dr. Rak Hyeon Choi participated in the study as co-first authors, while Professors Hye Ryung Byon and Dong Ki Yoon participated as co-corresponding authors. The research was published in the international journal ACS Nano in September 2026. Paper title: Directional Li+ Flux Control via Liquid-Crystalline Polymer Separators for Fast-Charging Lithium Metal Batteries, DOI: https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.6c09591 Author information: Geunjung Lee†, Rak Hyeon Choi†, Geonhyeong Park, Juri Kim, Younwoo Kim, Hye Ryung Byon*, Dong Ki Yoon*; † co-first authors, * corresponding authors. This research was supported by the Mid-Career Researcher Program of the Ministry of Science and ICT and the National Research Foundation of Korea, as well as the GIST InnoCORE Program.

artigo.texto: *This content was translated by AI.View Original A next-generation battery free from fire concerns is just one step away from commercialization. TNP Solution, a specialist in next-generation secondary batteries, has successfully completed a field demonstration of an energy storage system (ESS) linked to solar power in a multi-housing complex using aqueous zinc-ion batteries, and is accelerating its push toward commercialization. The company announced that it completed the "Demonstration of High-Safety Energy Storage System Based on Aqueous Zinc Batteries Linked to Solar Power" as the lead organization for the "2025 Climate Change Response Innovative Technology Demonstration Project," which is being promoted by Seoul City and managed by the Seoul Research Institute. Professor Kim Chan-hoon's research team at Hanyang University participated as a technology cooperation partner, while the Seoul Housing and Communities Corporation (SH) served as the demonstration site operator. This demonstration is significant because it involved operating an aqueous zinc-ion battery-based ESS linked to solar power generation equipment in an actual multi-housing complex where residents live, rather than in a laboratory setting. The company explained that through the process of storing generated solar power in batteries and supplying it when needed, it verified the feasibility of charge/discharge control, integration with power conversion devices, and system operation. For batteries to be installed in living spaces inside and outside buildings, verification is required not only for cell-level performance but also for safety, system control, and operational reliability. TNP Solution plans to utilize the operational experience gained from this demonstration in the product development of future urban-type ESS and building energy storage systems. Kang Seong-gu, CEO of TNP Solution Co., Ltd., stated confidently during a phone interview with this outlet, "The safety of batteries is a value that cannot be compromised in spaces where actual citizens carry out their daily lives." He added, "This demonstration marks a turning point proving that aqueous zinc batteries are high-safety energy solutions immediately applicable in real-life environments, going beyond the laboratory level. We will actively pioneer the urban power market, which absolutely requires safety and reliability, differentiating ourselves from markets focused on high density." Meanwhile, the "aqueous zinc-ion battery" is a secondary battery that has recently attracted attention. As the adoption of solar power and distributed power sources expands, total costs—including energy density, fire safety, installation costs, and maintenance fees—are becoming increasingly important in domestic and international ESS markets. In particular, in spaces where people reside or essential facilities are located, such as multi-housing complexes, hospitals, data centers, and telecommunications facilities, battery safety is a core condition for adoption. An aqueous zinc-ion battery is a secondary battery that utilizes a water-based electrolyte and a zinc metal anode. By using a non-flammable aqueous electrolyte, it can minimize the risk of ignition from the electrolyte itself. Additionally, by utilizing relatively abundant zinc, it possesses competitiveness in terms of raw material and manufacturing costs. Although it may have lower energy density than lithium-ion batteries, it is gaining attention as an alternative or complementary technology for stationary ESS, UPS, emergency power for telecommunications facilities, and industrial applications where safety and economic efficiency are prioritized. *This content was translated by AI.View Original

artigo.texto: Following her reelection Tuesday, Nov. 3, Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek’s priorities for the next four years include installing a universal statewide preschool program, passing new regulations on data centers and increasing the amount of time Oregon students spend in school. Kotek shared her goals at a Friday, Nov. 6, news conference in Portland following her victory this week over state Sen. Christine Drazan, a Republican from Canby. Drazan late Friday afternoon officially conceded the race and said in a news release she wished Kotek well. “I sincerely hope she recognizes that the challenges facing our state demand a different approach than what we’ve seen over the last four years,” she said in a statement. Going into the election, Kotek was polling as one of the least popular governors in the nation, but her campaign benefitted from nationwide dissatisfaction with Republican President Donald Trump and Republicans in Washington, D.C. Kotek said she’d be engaging with people from across the state differently in her second term to reach voters who were on the fence about her, and she indicated she’d use social media more to communicate her decisions and to have conversations. Kotek during her campaign availed herself to supportive online influencers, inviting them to several events where she eschewed invites to news outlets. She visited every county during her first year in office, though carefully choreographed tour stops meant she met primarily with select elected leaders, nonprofit service agencies and business owners. On Friday, Kotek said she’d also be doing more to assert her power over the Oregon Legislature when the six-month 2027 session begins at the end of January. After presiding over the House for nine years as speaker, she spent her first term as governor largely deferring to lawmakers instead of participating in negotiations, most notably on a large-scale transportation funding package lawmakers failed to pass in 2025. “I am not going to stand back and wait for the Legislature to figure it out. I need to see progress in the first month, the second month, the third month,” she said. “People voted Democrats in because they want stuff to happen, and I need the Legislature to do that. I’m going to be in the building. I’m going to be on top of them every day, saying we got to get stuff done.” Her legislative advocacy for the next session will start with her Dec. 1 recommended budget, which she said will include no additional funding for the Oregon Department of Transportation. Debates over funding for the beleaguered agency with a nine-figure budget deficit consumed the bulk of the last two legislative sessions and culminated in voters resoundingly rejecting a 6-cent gas tax increase and other proposed fee increases in May. “That’s trade-offs, because that means taking money away from highway projects and other things to pay for basic ops and maintenance. But that’s what you’ll see in my budget,” she said. “If legislators want to do something different, we’re going to have to come to the table and talk about it.” Data Canters Kotek said she wants regulations for, and state oversight of, data center development solidified in the first 60 days of the session. She said it should include clear standards and transparency around data center energy and water use, how energy is being obtained, and what agreements data center companies have made with local communities hosting them. Kotek’s data center advisory panel, convened earlier this year, will share with her recommendations that will inform her policy proposal for the Legislature, and she the group would also inform legislation to “take on large corporations who are using artificial intelligence on a regular basis to figure out how they can make more money and charge people more.” Universal preschool Kotek promised universal statewide childcare by the end of her second term. She did an about-face on criticisms of Portland’s Preschool for All program at an event in October, saying she’d find a way to make sure all Oregonians had access to free preschool. She said it’s part of her long-term education goals, which also include increasing the amount of time Oregon kids spend in school (the state has among the shortest school years in the nation) and improving attendance. She said she’d continue to push for funding for her early literacy initiative to improve Oregon kids’ proficiency in reading, which is among the lowest in the nation. “In terms of how to pay for things, I’ve made no commitments,” Kotek said about potential revenue proposals from progressive groups and candidates, including a new wealth tax. State agency reform Kotek said she’d be implementing some of the recommendations from her Prosperity Council’s June report that advocated cutting taxes, climate programs and investing state funds in business infrastructure and development. Among the first will be next week, when Kotek rolls out a fast-track program for statewide permitting, requiring state agencies to approve or deny applications within clear timelines. She said she’d also reorganize Oregon’s economic development agency Business Oregon into a more hands-on Department of Commerce working directly with businesses and industry in the state. And in December, Kotek will also go to the Legislative Emergency Board to ask for $10 million for the Bend-La Pine School District and the city of Bend to help pay for services and support needed in the aftermath of the Oct. 15 school shooting at Silver Rail Elementary that left five people dead including the gunman. artigo.texto: Voters just told pollsters, loudly, that they do not want a data center down the road. An NBC News exit poll reported that 76% of voters opposed building a new data center in their community, and the Associated Press reported the same roughly three-quarters share. Yet the AI industry still needs the buildings, the chips and the power that those facilities concentrate in one place. That tension is the political story of November 2026, and it sits at the center of where AI model development goes next. The ballot results backed up the polling. According to The Detroit News, voters in at least 29 jurisdictions passed data-center bans or restrictions on November 3, 2026. The New York Times counted 40 of 41 local ballot initiatives going against the industry. We tracked the early returns in our report on 41 data center votes putting the AI boom on notice, and this piece takes the next step: what the backlash means for the people who build and fund AI models. A caution on the framing first. Headlines this week say voters “hate” data centers, and that phrase is not what the polling shows. The numbers confirm opposition to proposed facilities in voters’ own communities. They do not confirm a blanket rejection of every data center, and they do not confirm that voters understand how much of the AI stack depends on them. The gap between those two readings is where the next two years of policy will be fought. For wider context on the models themselves, see our AI and machine learning coverage. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What the NBC Exit Poll Actually Measured The headline number from NBC News is the 76% share of voters who opposed building a new data center in their community. That is a question about a specific, local, physical thing. It asks whether a respondent wants a building, its noise, its traffic and its power draw near their home. Voters answer that kind of question differently from an abstract one about whether AI is good for the country. The same poll then asked how much data centers mattered to the congressional vote. NBC reported that 23% of voters called them “crucial” to their choice, and 33% called them a “major” factor. Add those two groups together and you reach 56%, which matches a separate report summarizing the NBC findings as showing that 56% of voters viewed AI and data centers as a crucial or major factor in their vote. The Associated Press framed the same finding more narrowly, reporting that about one-quarter of voters called AI data centers crucial to their vote for Congress. Those figures deserve a careful read. A voter who ranks an issue as “major” has not necessarily switched parties over it. Nothing in the reported results tells us how many votes actually moved, or in which direction. What the numbers do establish is salience. A topic that barely registered in national polling a few years ago now shows up as a top-tier concern for more than half the electorate, according to the NBC exit poll as summarized in that separate report. We covered the salience angle in more detail in our piece on how midterms put AI on trial. The short version is that the industry can no longer treat local siting fights as isolated zoning disputes. They now function as a national referendum, fought one county at a time. 29 Jurisdictions and 40 of 41 Local Measures Two outlets counted the local results in slightly different ways, and both counts point the same direction. The Detroit News reported that voters in at least 29 jurisdictions passed data-center bans or restrictions on November 3. The New York Times reported that in 40 of 41 local ballot initiatives, voters chose to limit or prevent data-center development. The two figures measure different universes, so they should not be added together or treated as a contradiction. A 40-to-1 split is rare in American politics. Most ballot measures on contested land use come out closer, because developers can usually point to jobs and tax revenue. That the industry lost nearly every contest suggests the usual promises of local economic benefit failed to persuade. The reported results do not tell us why in each case, and we have no verified breakdown of turnout or margins for individual measures, so we will not guess at them. It is also worth separating what a ban or restriction does from what it prevents. A local measure can block a new facility without touching existing ones. It can also set conditions, such as approval requirements, that slow construction without stopping it. The reporting we have confirms that voters chose to limit or prevent development. It does not give a uniform definition of the rules that now apply across those jurisdictions, and readers should treat each measure as its own legal text. Ohio Sits at the Center of the Backlash The New York Times reported that more than half of those 40 successful initiatives were in Ohio. That concentration matters. It means the national count owes a large share of its weight to a single state where organized opposition, local politics and a heavy pipeline of proposed facilities collided at once. The statewide race pointed the same way. According to The Detroit News, Amy Acton was reported as winning election as Ohio’s next governor, and the report said she favored a moratorium and tougher regulations on the industry. We should be precise here. The report describes her policy preference. It does not tell us what legislation she will propose, whether the legislature will go along, or how a state-level moratorium would interact with the local measures already passed. For AI companies planning capacity, Ohio is a warning about concentration risk. A region can look like an ideal site on paper, with land, fiber and power access, and still turn hostile once several projects arrive close together. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no COP31 começa nesta segunda (9) na Turquia com Brasil no centro do debate climático e data centers na agenda Publicado 08/11/2026 • 19:44 | Atualizado há 11 horas KEY POINTS A 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (COP31) começa nesta segunda-feira (9), em Antalya, na Turquia, com o Brasil no centro das discussões sobre a continuidade dos compromissos assumidos na COP30, em Belém, e uma nova frente de debates sobre o impacto ambiental dos data centers. Até 20 de novembro, representantes de governos, empresas e organizações internacionais discutirão como ampliar o financiamento climático, acelerar a transição energética e abastecer a expansão da inteligência artificial com eletricidade de fontes renováveis. A COP é o principal fórum multilateral de decisões climáticas vinculado à Convenção-Quadro das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima. As negociações buscam transformar os objetivos do Acordo de Paris em medidas de redução de emissões, adaptação aos eventos extremos e apoio financeiro e tecnológico aos países mais vulneráveis. A conferência será presidida pela Turquia, com o ministro Murat Kurum indicado para comandar a COP31. O australiano Chris Bowen terá a função de presidente das negociações, em um arranjo que divide as responsabilidades políticas e diplomáticas do encontro. Leia também: COP30 termina com aprovação do Pacote de Belém e foco em implementação climática Entre os temas centrais estão a passagem dos compromissos climáticos para a execução, a ampliação dos investimentos em energia limpa e a redução da dependência de combustíveis fósseis. Os governos também discutirão medidas de adaptação, como proteção contra secas, enchentes e ondas de calor. O financiamento climático será outro ponto decisivo: países em desenvolvimento cobram recursos mais acessíveis para reduzir emissões e enfrentar perdas e danos associados a eventos extremos. Também entram no debate mercados de carbono, proteção de florestas e infraestrutura resiliente. A COP31 marca ainda o início do segundo balanço global do Acordo de Paris, processo destinado a avaliar coletivamente o avanço dos países e identificar onde é necessário acelerar a ação climática. Leia também: Presidência da COP30 propõe cronograma global para abandonar combustíveis fósseis até 2033 A expansão dos data centers, instalações que sustentam serviços digitais e sistemas de inteligência artificial, terá espaço específico na programação paralela da conferência. Na terça-feira (10), o Pavilhão da Itália receberá um encontro sobre soluções para abastecer essas estruturas com energia limpa e avaliar seus benefícios climáticos. O evento reunirá especialistas em planejamento energético e infraestrutura digital. Na segunda-feira (16), a Agência Internacional de Energias Renováveis (Irena) e a Global Renewables Alliance organizarão uma discussão sobre data centers verdes, consumo de eletricidade e integração com as redes elétricas. Entre os pontos previstos estão o uso de energia renovável, a transparência das informações de consumo e formas de evitar que a demanda da inteligência artificial amplie a geração baseada em combustíveis fósseis. A programação de Ação Digital Verde também inclui o Compromisso de Antalya sobre Inteligência Artificial, iniciativa da presidência da COP31 para incentivar práticas digitais alinhadas às metas climáticas. No mesmo dia 16, o Pavilhão Brasil receberá o lançamento do AI Climate Institute. Esses eventos integram a agenda de debates e iniciativas da conferência, sem representar, por si só, um acordo obrigatório entre os países. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC A Cúpula de Líderes ocorrerá na quarta-feira (11) e na quinta-feira (12). O presidente turco Recep Tayyip Erdoğan e o secretário-geral da ONU, António Guterres, estão previstos na abertura. O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva também participará, conforme confirmação do governo brasileiro. Entre os nomes esperados estão ainda o primeiro-ministro britânico Andy Burnham e outras autoridades nacionais. A programação de alto nível prevê discursos, encontros bilaterais e mesas sobre eletrificação, indústria verde, financiamento, adaptação urbana e proteção das florestas. Além dos chefes de Estado, terão papéis importantes Murat Kurum, na presidência da conferência, Chris Bowen, na condução das negociações, e representantes de organizações internacionais, do setor privado e de comunidades afetadas pela mudança do clima. Leia também: Lula participará da COP31 na Turquia O Brasil chega à COP31 depois de sediar a COP30, em Belém, e pretende manter protagonismo nas negociações. Lula participará da cúpula de 11 e 12 de novembro e deverá defender medidas concretas de transição energética, combate ao desmatamento e financiamento da proteção florestal. A presidência brasileira da COP30 levará à conferência propostas de mapas do caminho para o afastamento dos combustíveis fósseis e para a reversão do desmatamento. O governo também pretende ampliar o apoio ao Fundo Florestas Tropicais para Sempre (TFFF) e apresentar resultados de políticas ambientais brasileiras. O Pavilhão Brasil será o principal espaço nacional na Zona Azul, área reservada às negociações oficiais. Organizado pelo Ministério do Meio Ambiente e Mudança do Clima, pela presidência da COP30 e pela ApexBrasil, reunirá governos, povos indígenas, comunidades tradicionais, empresas, universidades e organizações sociais. A programação inclui debates sobre energia eólica, combustíveis sustentáveis, financiamento verde, mercados de carbono, agroecologia, cidades resilientes, proteção indígena e uso de tecnologia na política climática. A inauguração do pavilhão está prevista para segunda-feira (9). Leia também: Governo aprova 18 diretrizes para reduzir dependência de combustíveis fósseis O resultado da COP31 dependerá de acordos entre países com interesses e capacidades econômicas

artigo.texto: NVIDIA has just come through a sharp pullback, with the stock down over the past month and year after a very large multiyear rise. This leaves a straightforward question for you as an investor: Are today's cash flows, and the ones buyers expect over time, enough to support the current share price after this reset? - Over the past 5 years, NVIDIA has returned roughly 5x. This means a lot of future cash generation is already embedded in expectations and needs to be weighed carefully against the recent slump. - Fresh scrutiny over AI data center regulation, export controls and the CEO misconduct probe can influence how quickly data center demand translates into cash inflows and how much capital NVIDIA may need to commit to maintain its position. - What if you looked at NVIDIA through its earnings instead? See what NVIDIA's 23.4x P/E says about the price. For investors, the debate is whether NVIDIA's recent price, after the sell off and rebound attempts, is adequately supported by the cash it produces and is expected to produce in the years ahead. If you want to test the same cash flow question you are asking of NVIDIA across a wider set of AI infrastructure plays, take a look at 53 AI infrastructure stocks. Is NVIDIA Still Cheap on Cash Flow? The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model here focuses on the cash Nvidia can return to shareholders over time. On the latest twelve month view, Nvidia generated roughly $126.7b of free cash flow, and the model assumes those cash flows keep growing rather than shrinking from that base. Projected free cash flows step up materially into the early 2030s, then slow into a more measured second stage as the business matures in the model. That path helps explain why the DCF outcome sits substantially above the current share price of $186.64, even after the recent pullback. The Democratic midterm sweep, and the renewed focus on AI data center regulation it triggered, helps explain why the market price can still sit below what these cash flow projections support. Find out what NVIDIA could be worth using our Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) estimate. The NVIDIA Narrative: What Would Justify Today's Price? NVIDIA's valuation puzzle only really comes into focus once you spell out the futures that might justify it. Simply Wall St Narratives on the Community page do that explicitly by linking different views of NVIDIA's potential on growth, profitability and earnings to what the stock could be worth under each path, and each one anchors its number to a clear view of where expansion, margins and key risks might go next so you can revisit the logic as fresh information turns up.

artigo.texto: BYD Yangwang Altior Debuts as Ultra-Luxury Flagship Sedan – 1,000 km Range, 5.6-Metre Length and Limited Production BYD's premium Yangwang brand has unveiled the Altior in Abu Dhabi, challenging established luxury carmakers with an imposing executive sedan featuring coach doors, a lavish four-seat cabin and next-generation battery technology. Chinese automotive giant BYD has taken another significant step into the global ultra-luxury automobile market with the unveiling of the Yangwang Altior, a flagship executive sedan designed to compete with some of the world's most prestigious luxury cars. Unveiled in Abu Dhabi on November 7, 2026, the Altior represents Yangwang's latest attempt to establish itself as an alternative to established European luxury manufacturers, particularly Mercedes-Maybach, Bentley and Rolls-Royce. Measuring an imposing 5.6 metres in length, the new sedan combines an executive-focused interior, distinctive coach doors and BYD's latest battery technology. The manufacturer is initially accepting pre-orders for an exclusive four-seat limited edition, with production restricted to just 399 examples worldwide. The limited-edition model is expected to cost approximately 2.08 million yuan (around ₹2.8 crore, indicative), although the final selling price has not been confirmed. Yangwang Altior – Key Highlights Exterior Design – A 5.6-Metre Luxury Limousine The Altior's styling reflects Yangwang's ambition to move beyond conventional premium vehicles and compete in the chauffeur-driven luxury segment. Its imposing front fascia incorporates a gemstone-inspired grille, drawing design inspiration from traditional Chinese ceremonial vessels. The sedan also features an elaborate two-tone exterior finish, enclosed alloy-wheel styling and floating wheel-centre emblems. One of the most distinctive elements is its rear-hinged coach doors. Opening to almost 90 degrees, these doors are designed to provide more convenient access to the rear passenger compartment. Integrated umbrella storage adds another traditional luxury-car touch. The Altior's 3,500 mm wheelbase is particularly noteworthy. Rather than prioritising compact exterior dimensions, Yangwang has designed the vehicle around maximising passenger space and creating a commanding road presence. Its substantial width of 2,030 mm further reinforces its positioning as a full-size executive limousine. Interior – Four-Seat Executive Lounge Inside, the Altior takes a passenger-first approach, with its initial four-seat configuration emphasising rear-seat luxury rather than maximum seating capacity. Two individual rear seats are separated by an elaborate centre console, creating a private executive environment. The seats incorporate leg rests, while champagne-glass holders, rear-seat controls and electrically operated privacy sunshades further enhance the chauffeur-driven experience. The interior combines quilted upholstery with decorative wood and metallic trim. Yangwang has also incorporated Chinese design influences to differentiate the Altior from its European competitors. The first special edition, named Shanhe Dingyun, features an exclusive brown-and-white colour scheme with details including jade-decorated air vents, gold-finished speaker grilles and unique commemorative badges. A conventional five-seat configuration is planned for a later stage, potentially broadening the car's appeal beyond customers seeking a dedicated executive limousine. Battery Technology – Over 1,000 km Claimed Range Despite its emphasis on luxury, the Altior also serves as a showcase for BYD's battery development. The sedan incorporates the company's second-generation Blade Battery technology alongside its latest Flash Charging system. Yangwang has quoted a driving range exceeding 1,000 km under China's CLTC testing cycle. However, it is important to distinguish the claimed test-cycle figure from real-world driving performance. Actual range will depend on driving conditions, speed, climate control usage and other factors. Yangwang has not yet fully clarified the model's production powertrain configuration. Detailed specifications covering battery capacity, motor output and charging duration also remain to be officially established. Limited Edition – Just 399 Units Worldwide Yangwang has opened pre-orders in China for the four-seat Shanhe Dingyun limited edition, with customers required to pay a deposit of 300,000 yuan. Only 399 examples of this edition will be offered globally, giving it an exclusivity-driven positioning from the outset. The anticipated price of 2.08 million yuan would place the Altior considerably above mainstream luxury sedans, signalling that BYD intends to compete on exclusivity, technology and craftsmanship rather than affordability. artigo.texto: Minneapolis set to pass sweeping data center regulations MINNEAPOLIS (FOX 9) - Minneapolis leaders appear close to a compromise on data centers as the city's temporary pause on construction nears its Nov. 21 end. What the proposed Minneapolis rules would do What we know: The proposal discussed at a Minneapolis City Council Committee of the Whole meeting would allow data centers only downtown or in the North Loop. They could only go into existing buildings, with minimal modifications allowed. In an attempt to address the potential for noise pollution, computers will have to be 20 feet away from exterior building walls. Local perspective: The plan would cap data centers at 150,000 square feet. Cities cannot place a limit on energy or water use, but under these new regulations companies would have to disclose that information to the city. "This is nothing other than keeping control for governing these data centers within us rather than farming it out to the state of Minnesota," said Councilmember Michael Rainville. By the numbers: The city says downtown has eight data centers serving tech companies right now. Many more data centers serving onsite computing needs of existing businesses exist around the city, according to city staff. Council members said they heard from Xcel Energy that there is interest in up to eight more data center projects downtown. Why the council remains sharply divided Why you should care: The council is split in half, with one side pushing for a full ban and the other pointing to downtown's high vacancy rate and seeing data centers as part of the solution. City staff said 30 percent of Downtown Minneapolis stands empty, which leaves residents to carry a disproportionate amount of the city’s property tax burden. The other side: "A complete ban on data centers is tone deaf. Tone deaf to the benefit to our labor – skilled labor. Tone deaf to our residents increased property tax burden. And tone deaf to the revenue problem that we have right here in our city," said Council member Elizabeth Schaffer. "What's tone deaf is saying that people want data centers," said Council member Soren Stevenson. "No data center in Minneapolis. That's easy. That's the easiest vote I ever had." Big picture view: Some council members who want a ban said the midterms were largely a referendum on data centers. "What we're talking about is actually the tone deaf proposal," said Council member Robin Wonsley. "It is very clear that our residents do not want to see this in their neighborhoods, in their community and in our city." What happens before the moratorium ends The council passed a six-month moratorium in May. That moratorium expires Nov. 21. Data centers could again move in with little oversight if the new rules do not pass. What's next: On Thursday, Nov. 12, the council will vote on the proposal. If council members stick with the plan discussed Monday, Nov. 9, the mayor's spokesperson tells FOX 9 Mayor Frey will support it. The Source: FOX 9 report from Emily Pofahl and Minneapolis City Council discussion.

artigo.texto: Google compra data center da Crusoe no Wyoming por US$ 17 bi Crusoe vendeu projeto problemático no Wyoming ao Google após falhas de custo e prazo. O caso expõe os limites das startups de data centers na era da IA. A Crusoe, desenvolvedora de data centers sediada em Denver e avaliada em US$ 30,9 bilhões, confirmou a venda de um projeto inacabado no sudeste do Wyoming para o Google. A gigante de Mountain View, que ironicamente havia sido cortejada pela Crusoe como cliente para essa mesma instalação sem sucesso, agora assume o desenvolvimento com planos de investir US$ 17 bilhões no campus. O valor exato pago pela aquisição não foi divulgado. Mas o contexto da negociação diz muito sobre o momento do mercado de infraestrutura para inteligência artificial: mesmo empresas bilionárias estão esbarrando nos limites físicos e logísticos de construir na velocidade que a demanda por computação exige. O que deu errado no projeto da Crusoe no Wyoming A Crusoe havia anunciado o projeto no ano passado em parceria com a Tallgrass, empresa de infraestrutura apoiada pela Blackstone. O plano original era ambicioso: escalar a instalação até 10 gigawatts de capacidade energética. Para dimensionar esse número, a maioria dos grandes data centers em operação hoje trabalha com capacidades muito inferiores. O Google, segundo relatos, levantou preocupações sobre o custo e o cronograma de construção sob a gestão da Crusoe. Garantir equipamentos, assegurar fornecimento de energia e lidar com a crescente oposição de comunidades locais tornaram a entrega dentro do prazo e do orçamento uma tarefa que a startup não conseguiu cumprir sozinha. É um padrão que se repete no setor. Desenvolvedoras independentes de data centers enfrentam gargalos que vão da cadeia de suprimentos de transformadores e geradores até disputas regulatórias com prefeituras e concessionárias de energia. O caso da Crusoe no Wyoming é emblemático, mas está longe de ser isolado. Por que o Google decidiu assumir em vez de abandonar A decisão do Google de comprar o projeto, em vez de simplesmente buscar alternativas, revela uma dinâmica central do mercado de infraestrutura de IA: terrenos com acesso a energia em escala são ativos escassos. Encontrar um novo local, negociar conexões com a rede elétrica e obter licenças ambientais pode levar anos. Assumir um projeto já em andamento, mesmo que problemático, encurta esse caminho. Os US$ 17 bilhões que o Google pretende investir no campus do Wyoming se somam a uma ofensiva global da empresa em infraestrutura. A corrida por capacidade computacional para treinar e rodar modelos de IA transformou data centers no ativo mais disputado do setor de tecnologia. Apesar do revés no Wyoming, a relação entre Google e Crusoe não foi encerrada. A startup continua desenvolvendo um outro data center para o Google próximo a Amarillo, no Texas. Isso sugere que a questão não era de confiança na empresa como um todo, mas de capacidade de execução naquele projeto específico. Crusoe: da mineração de Bitcoin aos maiores contratos de IA A trajetória da Crusoe é, por si só, um retrato das transformações do setor de tecnologia nos últimos anos. Fundada por Chase Lochmiller e Cully Cavness, a empresa começou como um negócio de mineração de criptomoedas alimentado por gás natural que seria queimado e desperdiçado. O modelo de aproveitar energia residual para minerar Bitcoin era engenhoso, mas o verdadeiro salto veio com a migração para infraestrutura de IA. Hoje, a Crusoe opera em uma escala completamente diferente. Seu campus em Abilene, no Texas, está sendo construído em fases para Oracle e OpenAI. Um segundo campus de 900 megawatts na mesma região atende a Microsoft, com o primeiro prédio previsto para entrar em operação em meados de 2027. A Meta também é cliente. E, segundo informações de mercado, a firma de trading Jane Street assinou um contrato de US$ 13 bilhões por cinco anos para serviços de nuvem com a Crusoe. Em setembro, a empresa levantou uma rodada de US$ 3,9 bilhões, mesmo com o problema do Wyoming já público. Entre os novos membros do conselho está JB Straubel, cofundador da Tesla e fundador da Redwood Materials, que havia investido na Crusoe em 2021. A Crusoe se tornou, inclusive, a primeira cliente do negócio de armazenamento de energia de Straubel. O que isso significa para o mercado de data centers O episódio Crusoe-Google ilustra uma tensão estrutural. A demanda por computação para IA cresce em ritmo exponencial, mas a construção de infraestrutura física segue presa a limitações do mundo real: tempo de construção, disponibilidade de energia, capacidade de fabricação de equipamentos e aceitação comunitária. Grandes empresas como Google, Microsoft e Amazon têm balanço para absorver atrasos e estouros de orçamento. Startups, mesmo aquelas avaliadas em dezenas de bilhões, operam com margens de erro muito menores. O modelo de negócio da Crusoe, que gera receita alugando espaço em data centers, cedendo suas próprias GPUs e vendendo poder computacional para inferência de modelos de IA, é sólido em tese. Mas a execução de projetos na escala de 10 gigawatts exige um nível de maturidade operacional que poucos players independentes possuem. Para o investidor que acompanha o setor de tecnologia, o recado é claro. A infraestrutura de IA é o novo petróleo em termos de demanda, mas os custos e riscos de construção são reais e frequentemente subestimados. Empresas que conseguem entregar projetos no prazo e no orçamento terão vantagem competitiva duradoura. As que não conseguem acabam vendendo ativos para quem pode. O Wyoming da Crusoe agora é o Wyoming do Google. E os US$ 17 bilhões que vêm a seguir mostram que, nessa corrida, capital não é o problema. Execução é. Este conteúdo é informativo e educacional e não constitui recomendação de investimento. Rentabilidade passada não é garantia de resultados futuros.

artigo.texto: 1 in 4 data centers sits in a water-stressed area — here’s what that means for nearby communities When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission. AI has become integrated into our lives whether we like it or not. Despite big tech forcing schools to choose and lawsuits highlighting its dangers, the controversial technology is here to stay. New research published in Environmental Science & Technology puts specific AI concerns on a global map, highlighting 9,347 identified data centers, with roughly a quarter located in areas where water demand would exceed available supply for at least one month a year. The water has to come from somewhere Data centers use water to remove heat from their equipment. In evaporative cooling systems, some of that water evaporates rather than returning to the local water system. Electricity generation and hardware manufacturing add an indirect water footprint, too, according to the Pacific Institute. Where and when that consumption happens matters. The institute warns that data center water demand peaks during hot, dry periods, when supplies may be constrained, and other users also need more. Meeting those peaks can require additional utility infrastructure and spending. "They are landing on top of the water supply of cities and farms," study lead author Lorenzo Rosa said in an American Chemical Society release. That makes data center construction relevant to people who may never pay for an AI subscription. Before approving a facility, a community needs to understand whether its water system can accommodate a large new customer during a dry summer. Cities and municipalities are the largest water users, accounting for nearly 41% of the facilities studied, while agriculture is the primary user, accounting for another 28%, according to the American Chemical Society. A yearly average can miss the pressure The Potomac River basin offers a useful example. An analysis by the Interstate Commission on the Potomac River Basin describes current average data center water consumption in the Washington metropolitan area as relatively small. Its estimated 2025 average was about 4 million gallons a day, with peak-day consumption of approximately 15 million gallons. Cooling choices help explain the variation. Around 40% of facilities in the analysis rely exclusively on air cooling, while many others take advantage of cooler winter weather to reduce cooling demands. The commission cautions that approaches using less water often require more energy. For residents, an annual consumption figure only answers part of the question. They also need to know how much water a facility could require during the hottest days, when local supplies may already be under pressure. What communities deserve to know The same global study also examined existing data center locations under a scenario of 3°C of global warming relative to around 1900. The share exposed to water shortages rose to roughly a third. That projection applies future climate conditions to the facilities identified in the study; it doesn't account for where additional data centers might be built. Better disclosure would make proposed projects easier to assess. The Pacific Institute identifies a lack of standardized reporting on data center size, location and water use as an obstacle for communities and water managers. Residents deserve clear answers about a proposed facility's water source, expected summer demand and plans for drought. They also deserve to know who would pay for any necessary infrastructure upgrades. What communities can do now If a data center is proposed near your home, get answers now. Start with your local planning board or water utility and ask where its cooling water would come from, how much it could use on the hottest days, and what would happen during a drought. Be direct and ask who would pay for any water-system upgrades, too, and whether the operator would be required to make its water use public. Those details can help residents assess a project before approval. To learn more about the infrastructure behind AI, start with Google's data center water reporting or Microsoft's local environmental fact sheets. These disclosures can help you understand water use where facilities operate, though they won't tell you the footprint of your individual chats.

artigo.texto: Chinese battery giant CATL is reportedly exploring a new type of air-breathing battery known as a lithium-air battery, which could, in theory, deliver over 1,243 miles (2,000 km) of range for electric vehicles (EVs). What’s more, these so-called lithium-air batteries could deliver at least five times the energy density of solid-state batteries. All this without adding extra weight to the technology and, critically, the EV. However, it is not all gravy. It turns out that lithium-air batteries are exceptionally good at storing energy (at least on paper). But, it turns out, they are very difficult to make rechargeable, durable, and practical. For the uninitiated, the simplest way to understand it is to think of a lithium-air battery as a rechargeable battery that works a little like a combustion engine. It draws oxygen from the atmosphere to help release energy, rather than carrying all its reactive materials internally. Batteries that breathe By contrast, a conventional lithium-ion battery has two electrodes containing materials that store and release energy. Everything it needs is essentially contained within the battery. A lithium-air battery, on the other hand, does something very different. They essentially use oxygen from the surrounding atmosphere as one of its reactants. During discharge, lithium metal reacts electrochemically with oxygen in the air to produce lithium peroxide (Li₂O₂) and release electrical energy. More from Energy See All This provides the free electrons to power the EV’s motors and systems during operation. When charging, electrical energy forces the reaction to reverse, breaking down the lithium peroxide, releasing oxygen and restoring the lithium metal. The big advantage of this is that you don’t have to carry the oxygen reactant around inside the battery from the start. And that’s where the technology’s enormous energy density of 3,505 watt-hours per kilogram (Wh/kg) figure comes from. Critically, that’s a theoretical figure based on its chemistry and oxygen mass. It doesn’t necessarily translate into the battery’s actual performance. To put that into context, a typical conventional lithium-ion cell has an energy density of around 200–300 Wh/kg. Advanced solid-state batteries come in at 350–500 Wh/kg. Still experimental, CATL explains So, quite an improvement, at least in theory. One major problem with it is that the technology has a tendency to “clog itself up.” The produced lithium peroxide is a solid substance that accumulates within the battery’s porous electrode. You can liken it to a sponge that gradually fills with a solid deposit. Eventually, oxygen struggles to penetrate the electrode, reactions become more difficult, and usable capacity falls. This is supposed to be reversed during charging, but the process isn’t 100 percent effective. Another issue is that air isn’t just pure oxygen; it contains other gases like water and carbon dioxide. Both of these can interfere with the battery chemistry, producing “contaminant” products that are hard to remove. So, to work at peak efficiency over time, such a battery would likely need some form of air filtration system built in too. CATL isn’t claiming the new technology will revolutionize the industry just yet. It remains, at present, a long-term exploratory research project. In other words, CATL is interested enough to research it, but it hasn’t established that the technology can be commercialized. At least, not yet.

artigo.texto: As opposition to building artificial intelligence (AI) data centers spreads across the United States, struggling small towns are betting their survival on luring those facilities. Major U.S. cities are tightening rules on data centers over heavy power consumption, noise, and environmental concerns. By contrast, rural towns where manufacturing has collapsed and populations are shrinking—unlike affluent suburbs—see data centers as the only tax base left to keep schools and roads running. The Washington Post (WP) reported on the 8th (local time) that the midterm elections held on the 3rd featured 41 local ballot measures across 10 states that could restrict data center development. Of those, 40 measures, or 97.6%, produced outcomes favorable to limiting data center construction. In network exit polls, 76% among respondents said they opposed building a new data center where they live. Fifty-seven percent said AI will do more harm than good to society. In Piqua, Ohio, residents banned a large data center that Meta planned to build for $1 billion (about 1.3566 trillion won) and recalled officials who had backed the project. In Texas, where data centers have clustered, Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa, who campaigned on a moratorium on new construction, was elected governor. Even amid nationwide pushback, the tiny city of Harwood, North Dakota, with a population of 845, chose the opposite path. On the 3rd, Harwood residents voted down a ballot measure that would have required independent reviews and public hearings for large industrial projects, with 105 votes in favor and 325 against. It is seen as 75.6% of voters rejecting additional rules that could slow data center development. Residents backed the project on the calculation that once the data center is completed, the city's property tax revenue would grow to six times the 2024 level. Harwood's population is 845—about one-twenty-fourth the size of a Korean eup (20,000 people). The town has little industrial base beyond a few bars and grain elevators. Most residents commute to Fargo, North Dakota's largest city nearby. On Harwood's outskirts, Texas-based developer Applied Digital is building a data center of about 167,000 square meters with a $3 billion (about 4.09 trillion won) investment. Harwood Mayor Blake Henke has sparred with neighboring Fargo over annexing the data center site since the project began. He concluded that even if Harwood refused, the center could go up on land under Fargo's jurisdiction right next door. In that case, Harwood would bear the noise and traffic while Fargo collected the taxes. "If the data center is going to end up in essentially the same spot anyway, we'd rather receive the tax breaks and the revenue," Henke told WP. The city estimated annual property taxes from the completed facility at $1.65 million (about 2.2 billion won), roughly six times Harwood's 2024 property tax take. Applied Digital has also pledged more than 200 full-time jobs. It has already contributed funds to the city fire department and a park warming shelter. Across U.S. small towns hollowed out by industrial decline, data centers are seen as relief pitchers that can stave off extinction. Ellendale, a rural town of about 1,100 in the same state of North Dakota, embraced Applied Digital before Harwood did. The company is now expanding a data center campus there with a $5 billion (about 6.82 trillion won) investment. Mayor Don Flaherty said that if the campus grows to three buildings with up to 530 megawatts (MW), the number of full-time jobs will rise to 300 to 350—close to one-third of the current population. Ellendale's assessed value stood at $3.5 million (about 4.7 billion won) at the end of 2025, and the city projected that figure would more than double within a few years. "By 2028–2029, Applied Digital will pay more than $25 million (about 3.39 billion won) a year in property taxes and become North Dakota's largest property taxpayer," Flaherty said. There are also cases where attracting data centers has transformed public infrastructure. Quincy, an agricultural city about 240 kilometers east of Seattle in the northwest, used to grow potatoes. But over the past 20 years, more than 30 tech firms followed Microsoft in seeking cheap land and abundant power, completely changing the city's finances. An analysis by local outlet the Spokesman-Review of the city's audit reports found that Quincy's annual total revenue jumped from $6 million (about 810 million won) in 2006 to $47 million (about 6.4 billion won) in 2024. The population also grew from about 5,300 two decades ago to about 8,200. Data centers now account for 57% of Quincy's total local government tax revenue. With the expanded funds, the city built a new hospital, high school, fire station, and library. In rural Mecklenburg County, Virginia, a former correctional site that once produced no tax revenue became the highest-taxed property after Microsoft arrived in 2010. Data centers now support about 45% of the county's general fund. In Richland Parish, a rural area in northeastern Louisiana considered one of the poorest parts of the United States, data centers are shaking up the local economy. According to the New York Times (NYT), Meta announced in 2024 that it would build the $10 billion Hyperion data center there. In July this year, it raised the investment to more than $50 billion (about 67.83 trillion won). As construction ramped up, Richland collected $38.7 million (about 5.25 billion won) in sales taxes just in the first quarter this year from materials and equipment purchases. With tax revenue surging, annual bonuses for teachers in Richland jumped more than fivefold from about $10,000 last year to more than $50,000 (about 68 million won) this year. Still, attracting data centers does not yield only rosy outcomes. Communities face internal rifts, and rising incomes bring side effects.
