artigo.texto: Engine manufacturer Cummins (NYSE:CMI) fell short of the market's revenue expectations in Q3 2026, but sales rose 13.5% year on year to $9.44 billion. Its non-GAAP profit of $8.25 per share was 0.7% above analysts' consensus estimates. Is now the time to buy CMI? Find out in our full research report (it's free). Cummins (CMI) Q3 2026 highlights: - Revenue $9.44 billion vs S&P analysts' estimates of $9.96 billion (13.5% year-on-year growth, 5.2% miss) - Adjusted EPS $8.25 vs S&P analysts' estimates of $8.20 (0.7% beat) - Adjusted EBITDA $1.82 billion vs analyst estimates of $1.86 billion (19.3% margin, 2.4% miss) - Operating margin 15.3%, up from 10.2% in the same quarter last year - Market capitalization $61.75 billion StockStory's take Cummins delivered third quarter results that disappointed Wall Street's revenue expectations, triggering a negative market reaction. Management attributed the shortfall to a combination of ongoing supply chain constraints in its Power Systems segment and weaker-than-anticipated demand for North American pickup truck engines. CEO Jennifer Rumsey highlighted that robust demand for data center power solutions and heavy-duty truck engines partially offset these headwinds, stating, "order intake in the third quarter exceeded what we thought it would be," but bottlenecks limited shipments, especially in Power Systems and Distribution. Looking forward, management's guidance is built on continued strength in power generation—especially driven by data center customers in North America, China, and Asia-Pacific. The company expects to recover most delayed shipments in the next quarter and is expanding manufacturing capacity for future demand. However, CEO Jennifer Rumsey cautioned that uncertainty around EPA regulations and elevated diesel prices could moderate pickup truck engine sales, while CFO Mark Smith flagged that supply chain and regulatory factors will impact the pace of new product transitions. Key insights from management's remarks Management pointed to strong data center-related orders, supply chain challenges, and evolving regulatory dynamics as key themes shaping the quarter's performance and their updated outlook. - Data center power demand: Cummins saw exceptionally strong demand for power generation equipment from data center operators, with multi-year orders extending into 2028. This trend is global, with accelerated growth in China and the Asia-Pacific region, not just North America. - Supply chain bottlenecks: Delays from a key supplier in Power Systems constrained shipments, resulting in lower-than-anticipated revenues in that segment and Distribution. Management expects these issues to be largely resolved in the next quarter, allowing delayed deliveries to catch up. - North American truck uncertainty: Weaker-than-expected demand for pickup truck engines was attributed to elevated diesel prices and interest rates, as well as regulatory uncertainty surrounding upcoming EPA emissions rules. Customers are delaying some purchases as they await clarity on Non-Conformance Penalties (NCPs) and the phased transition to 2027-compliant products. - Product launches and feedback: Cummins completed the "Forever Rising Tour," showcasing its upcoming X15, X10, and natural gas X15N engines to customers. Feedback was positive, particularly regarding reliability and drivability, supporting confidence in the 2027 product launch schedule. - Investment in capacity and new technologies: The company opened a new manufacturing facility for cooling systems and is expanding production to meet rising demand, especially for smaller generator sets. This includes investment in battery energy storage systems (BESS) for data centers, marking Cummins' largest deployment to date.

artigo.texto: MEMPHIS, TN — Elon Musk says two additional data centers tied to SpaceXAI’s expanding artificial intelligence operation in the Memphis area are expected to begin operating before the end of the year. The announcement comes as the rapid growth of the facilities faces increasing scrutiny from residents and city officials concerned about the effects of large-scale data center development. The two sites, known as Gun Range and Spam, are part of the company’s Colossus 2 computing complex. Musk said Gun Range is expected to become operational by the end of November, with Spam scheduled to follow in December. Those dates are projections from Musk and have not been independently confirmed. The names reflect the properties’ previous uses. Gun Range was formerly a police and fire training facility, while Spam was a warehouse that stored products made by Hormel Foods. Both properties are in Southaven, Mississippi, across the state line from Memphis. Together, the two facilities are expected to house approximately 420,000 Nvidia GB300 graphics processing units. Musk indicated that Gun Range would contain about 220,000 chips configured to train artificial intelligence models. Spam is expected to house approximately 200,000 chips designed to handle inference, the process of responding to requests from users and running already-trained AI systems. The new buildings will expand Colossus 2, which already includes facilities known as Macrohard, Macroharder and Minihard. Musk has said the broader Colossus 2 complex is expected to contain approximately 1.2 million Nvidia Blackwell chips by the end of 2026. The company uses the computing infrastructure to support its Grok artificial intelligence platform. The expansion follows the launch of the original Colossus supercomputer in 2024 at a former Electrolux manufacturing facility in South Memphis. The company later expanded its operations into the Whitehaven area and Southaven. Musk has also said he has been spending several days a week in Memphis overseeing construction. The projects have drawn opposition from nearby residents who have raised concerns about pollution, noise, electricity demand and water use. In April, the NAACP filed a federal lawsuit against xAI and subsidiary MZX Tech, alleging that the companies operated methane gas turbines without required permits at the Southaven site. A federal judge recently rejected the companies’ request to dismiss the lawsuit, allowing the case to proceed. Meanwhile, the Memphis City Council approved a 135-day pause on new data center permitting after rejecting a proposed yearlong moratorium. The measure is intended to give city officials time to develop land-use and siting rules addressing neighborhood protections, infrastructure and environmental concerns. It does not stop existing facilities from operating or automatically halt projects with protected approvals. The latest expansion highlights the challenge facing communities across the Mid-South as technology companies move quickly to build the infrastructure needed for artificial intelligence while residents and local governments seek greater oversight of the projects. Há dois anos, escrevi nesta coluna sobre a pegada de carbono das baterias de íons de lítio. O título Pegada de carbono das baterias – parte 1: do 8 ao 80 era uma provocação para mostrar como diferentes estudos podiam chegar a resultados muito diferentes para uma mesma tecnologia, dependendo das premissas adotadas e, principalmente, dos dados utilizados. Naquele momento, um dos pontos que mais me chamou a atenção estava no grafite utilizado nas baterias. Quem acompanha as discussões sobre veículos elétricos provavelmente já se acostumou a ouvir que a bateria é o grande vilão ambiental do carro elétrico. A afirmação é simplista e há uma questão interessante por trás dela. Quanto realmente sabemos sobre as emissões associadas à fabricação das baterias? A resposta depende muito da qualidade dos inventários utilizados nas avaliações de ciclo de vida. Em 2024, esta coluna já havia destacado diferenças expressivas nos dados disponíveis para a produção de grafite. Um dos problemas estava relacionado à produção de grafite sintético em rotas industriais amplamente utilizadas na China, entre elas o processo Acheson. A produção exige temperaturas muito elevadas e grande consumo de eletricidade. Além disso, os cadinhos de grafite utilizados no processo sofrem desgaste e precisam ser substituídos. Quando esse material não é corretamente contabilizado, uma parcela relevante das emissões simplesmente desaparece do cálculo. Naquele artigo, mostrei que algumas bases de dados utilizadas em avaliações de ciclo de vida apresentavam valores de emissões para o grafite muito inferiores aos encontrados quando o processo industrial era representado de maneira mais completa. Era uma questão metodológica, mas com consequências práticas. Se o inventário de um dos principais materiais da bateria está errado, a pegada de carbono atribuída à bateria também estará. Na época, era razoável tratar o assunto como uma hipótese que precisava de melhores dados. Agora, esses dados começam a surgir e permitem avaliar com mais segurança o peso do grafite na pegada de carbono das baterias. Um estudo publicado por pesquisadores alemães no Journal of Energy Storage (PUSHPENDRA et al, 2026) utilizou dados industriais primários, revisitando justamente o problema do grafite. O resultado é relevante porque mostra que a escolha do inventário utilizado na avaliação pode alterar significativamente a pegada de carbono atribuída à bateria. Em uma célula NMC622 analisada pelos pesquisadores, composta por níquel, manganês e cobalto na proporção 6:2:2, a pegada de carbono passou de aproximadamente 58 para 93 kgCO₂e/kWh quando os dados de grafite foram atualizados com dados industriais primários. Um aumento de cerca de 60%. Embora o estudo tenha sido conduzido com uma célula do tipo níquel-manganês-cobalto, suas conclusões são relevantes também para as baterias LFP (lítio-ferro-fosfato), hoje amplamente utilizadas em veículos elétricos e sistemas de armazenamento estacionário. Isso porque ambas as tecnologias utilizam predominantemente grafite no ânodo. Em outras palavras, mesmo quando se eliminam metais críticos como níquel e cobalto do cátodo, a origem e o processo produtivo do grafite continuam exercendo influência decisiva sobre a pegada de carbono da bateria. Observe ainda que não se trata de uma diferença marginal. É o tipo de alteração que pode mudar a conclusão de uma análise de ciclo de vida. O resultado também não apareceu do nada. Um estudo publicado por CARRÈRE et al. (2024) no mesmo periódico já havia identificado forte subestimação nos dados disponíveis para o grafite sintético de grau-bateria. Outros trabalhos publicados nos últimos anos chegaram a conclusões semelhantes, apontando que os inventários utilizados em muitas avaliações ainda dependem de dados antigos, secundários ou que não representam adequadamente as rotas industriais atuais. O que isso tudo significa? Frequentemente, vemos números sobre “uma bateria emite determinada quantidade de CO₂ por kWh”, “um veículo elétrico compensa sua fabricação depois de tantos quilômetros” ou “determinado modelo apresenta determinada vantagem sobre um veículo a combustão”. Nada disso é tão simples. O grafite é um bom exemplo de como uma variável aparentemente secundária pode alterar o resultado final. Por isso, quando se pretende calcular a pegada de carbono de uma bateria, escolher um número médio da literatura e simplesmente multiplicá-lo pela capacidade em kWh pode produzir uma falsa sensação de precisão. Uma bateria de 50 kWh não carrega consigo uma etiqueta dizendo quantas toneladas de CO₂ foram emitidas para fabricá-la. Esse número precisa ser construído a partir da cadeia de produção. Se queremos comparar tecnologias de propulsão, precisamos comparar sistemas completos. O veículo elétrico tem emissões associadas à mineração, ao processamento de materiais, à fabricação da bateria, à geração de eletricidade e ao uso. O veículo a combustão tem sua própria cadeia de petróleo, refino, distribuição e combustão. Quando utiliza biocombustíveis, entram também na conta as emissões e remoções associadas à produção de biomassa, ao processamento industrial e à logística envolvida. Híbridos acrescentam uma combinação adicional de componentes, combustíveis e fontes de energia. A pergunta relevante não é qual tecnologia parece mais limpa. É qual delas apresenta menor impacto quando colocamos todas as etapas na conta. E, para responder, precisamos de bons dados. Meu artigo de 2024 não pretendia dizer que todas as baterias tinham uma determinada pegada de carbono. A questão era justamente a incerteza. artigo.texto: Microsoft President Brad Smith talks data centers, Millionaires Tax WASHINGTON STATE — Microsoft President Brad Smith acknowledged tech companies will need to brace for further legislation to limit data centers, amid a growing wave of pushback against the facilities. In his first comments since Election Day, Smith addressed the fact that 40 of 41 local ballot measures across the country were approved to limit data centers. “We are going to see more legislation. We're going to see state legislation across the country. We're going to see federal legislation across the country. I don't know how many of those bills will pass, but I think at some level, the best thing for our industry to recognize is usually to give people confidence that things will be done in a responsible way,” Smith said in an interview on the Microsoft campus in Redmond on Monday morning. “Everyone who wants to build a data center has to do it responsibly. I think that's the message.” Smith says the company’s internal polling suggests 15% of the public wants to build data centers, another 15% don’t want them built at all, and 70% say they want them built responsibly. Smith points to the story in Quincy, Washington, where Microsoft broke ground on a new data center and tax revenue in Grant County skyrocketed, leading to the construction of a new school, hospital, police station and fire station. “The poverty rate’s been cut in half. The property taxes that people pay have fallen, but property tax revenue has grown 12-fold, basically because of data centers,” he said. “When we started 20 years ago, Quincy, Washington, had one traffic light. Now it has two. There are ways to do this.” Smith and Microsoft also dipped their toes into the state elections, funding a political action committee called “Washington Needs to Compete." Smith had sounded alarm bells prior to the vote, suggesting a payroll tax in the future would be like “waving a flag” asking businesses to move jobs out of state. The PAC aired ads during Seahawks games but stopped short of taking a position on the Millionaires Tax, and Gov. Bob Ferguson was reportedly upset about it all. On Monday, Smith said, “The public has voted, it's offered its point of view, and that tax has been upheld, and barring a change from the Supreme Court, we should all assume it's going to become part of Washington state law as we go forward.” “I think everybody in the state worries about affordability. We do. Our employees do. Everybody does. We also need to recognize that when taxes rise on businesses, businesses inevitably pass those costs on to consumers, and so ongoing tax increases are making the state less affordable,” he added. As for his relationship with Ferguson, Smith said, “We have long worked with Bob Ferguson. We work with him as attorney general. We work with him as governor. I think the state is fortunate to have him as a governor. I look forward to working to support him. I especially look forward to working with him and our leaders in Olympia. Let's go forward in a way that really focuses on budget stability, affordability for our people, the creation of new businesses and jobs for our economy.” Ferguson, along with Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, has indicated the payroll tax is off the table with the approval of the Millionaires Tax.

artigo.texto: Normally this newsletter is dedicated to local San Diego issues. But allow me, for a moment, to fixate on members of Congress. They’re actually doing something – though how good it will be, on the whole, is up for debate. A contingent of Democrats and Republicans just wrote the country’s biggest set of permitting reforms in years, and they’re trying to pass it before Democrats take over, following the “blue wave” midterm elections. The reforms would accelerate permitting for energy and transmission projects while also limiting environmental review, and put the onus on data center developers to pay for all their own energy costs. The Senate got enough votes Monday to limit debate on the so-called BAAJA or Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act and move it forward for a final vote. The bill could have big implications for the data center proposed on U.S. Navy land near downtown San Diego. This 400-plus-page law would force data centers, rather than taxpayers, to pay for all their costs – both the power and the upgrades to the local power grid to keep it running. While California lawmakers passed similar laws on data centers this last session, they don’t apply to San Diego’s proposed project. The state doesn’t have jurisdiction over land owned by the U.S. Navy. For that reason, among others, San Diego Rep. Scott Peters, along with clean energy proponents and developers and labor leaders, urged fellow Democrats to support the bill generated by the currently Republican-controlled Congress. “Democrats say they want to lower utility costs and combat climate change. Research shows the bipartisan permitting package would do both,” Peters told Politico recently. If you’d like to go deeper, David Roberts, a clean energy journalist and host of the Volts podcast, spent two hours unpacking its main reforms, chief among them allowing both electric transmission lines (the biggest powerlines carrying energy across state lines) and natural gas pipelines to be built much faster. Electricity demand by Americans had been stagnant until the recent business of building data centers to fuel artificial intelligence coupled with electrification of cars and buildings exploded. But it takes 10 to 15 years to actually build a new transmission line, the highways of the power grid that can carry power from state to state. Whole regions of the country are beginning to hit their limit in terms of how much power they can get to customers during heat waves, for example. The culprit? Many backers of the bill say it’s long, arduous permitting processes making it difficult to expand energy grid infrastructure. Without transmission lines, it’s a lot harder to bring new clean energy projects online, dispatch their power to places that need it and really transition the grid off of fossil fuels. The kicker is, BAAJA also makes it easier to build things like natural gas pipelines which are not good for the climate. (That’s because natural gas is a fossil fuel burning as almost pure methane, a huge climate heater-upper). But that’s how lawmakers were able to make this a bipartisan deal. In any good compromise, neither side is happy. The bet, as Roberts put it, is that both energy sources (Republicans favoring fossil fuels and Democrats favoring clean energy) would be on more equal footing to compete for energy proliferation. To speed up their permitting, both would get to bypass, in large part, the National Environmental Protection Act, which requires an analysis of a project’s environmental impacts. (Projects would still be subject to laws like the Clean Water Act, however.) Environmental groups like the Center for Biological Diversity have decried this law for that reason. Daniel Palken, Roberts’ guest who works for the oil-exec-owned Arnold Ventures, says that if this bill passes, it would allow a fair amount more drilling for oil and gas especially on federal land. The Rhodium Group, an independent research think tank based in New York City, did a bunch of modeling on what the outcome of the bill reforms might be – and the conclusion was to take some bad with the good. The researchers’ paper said that the bill would allow for up to 249 gigawatts of clean resources to be built through 2040 – a 50 percent increase to average U.S. electricity demand now. Liquified natural gas production, mainly to be exported outside the U.S., would increase by up to 15 percent. They estimate that tradeoff, in the best case scenario for the climate, would reduce economy-wide greenhouse gas emissions by 149 million metric tons by 2040. That’s like taking 32 million cars off the road for one year. But it’s not as astounding as it sounds. Humanity as a whole needs to reduce greenhouse gas emission by 1,350 billion metric tons to have a 50 percent shot at reducing global warming by 2 degrees Celsius – a level of warming the United Nations predicts will still cause near total destruction of the world’s coral reefs and intensify drought, sea level rise and extreme heat on millions. The two-way squeeze of cost pressure and order losses below cost is reshaping the industry's competitive landscape. 1. However, it is worth noting that if lithium carbonate prices continue to weaken, December market conditions may fall short of November—some clients' new orders have already shown losses below cost, and downstream willingness to take orders has clearly declined. From the perspective of enterprise operations, the trend of orders concentrating toward top-tier players is becoming increasingly evident: industry leaders have orders on hand exceeding 1 kt, while their in-house monthly capacity is only several hundred mt and cannot fully cover demand, requiring a dual-line approach of "in-house production + toll processing" to ensure delivery. 3. artigo.texto: Trump '100%' backs bill to make data centers pay more, potentially lowering electricity costs President Trump says the White House is "100% behind" a bipartisan bill that could reduce electricity bills by requiring data centers to pay more for energy infrastructure. Trump '100%' backs bill to make data centers pay more, potentially lowering electricity costs President Trump says the White House is "100% behind" a bipartisan bill that could reduce electricity bills by requiring data centers to pay more for energy infrastructure. President Donald Trump said Monday he is fully behind bipartisan legislation that could lower Americans' electricity bills by requiring large data centers to shoulder more of the costs of expanding the nation's electrical grid. "We are behind it 100%," Trump told reporters when asked about the legislation. Congress is considering the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act as electricity demand grows rapidly across the country, driven in part by the explosion of artificial intelligence and data centers. The legislation would speed up federal approval of energy infrastructure projects while requiring large data centers to contribute more toward the costs of expanding the electrical grid. An analysis by Grid Strategies estimates that, under the legislation, data centers would pay an additional $35 billion toward transmission infrastructure over the next decade, compared with what they would otherwise pay under current policies. A separate analysis from Rhodium Group estimates the bill could save the average American household between $50 and $78 a year on electricity by 2040, compared with what households would otherwise pay without the legislation. Both analyses examined an earlier version of the bill, before lawmakers released amendments Saturday. The savings are projections, not guaranteed reductions from today's electricity bills. "This bill has specific provisions related to data centers where they pay more. In fact, they pay more than their fair share. Intentionally to enable them to pay for more of the grid and then other rate payers, you and me. And homes and businesses. We would all pay relatively less," said Rob Gramlich, president of Grid Strategies. How the legislation would work Energy experts say the country faces an infrastructure bottleneck as electricity demand grows. Building the power plants and transmission lines needed to keep up can take years, with federal permitting among the obstacles. The legislation aims to speed up that process by setting stricter deadlines for environmental reviews and making it easier to approve new transmission lines. It would also give states additional options to require data centers to pay more than the cost of serving them and use the additional revenue to reduce electricity costs for other customers. States including Virginia, Ohio and Florida have already approved special electricity rate structures designed to make large power users shoulder more of the infrastructure costs associated with serving them. Why the bill faces opposition The legislation would also make it easier to approve fossil fuel projects, drawing opposition from environmental groups. Critics warn it could weaken federal safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge new projects. The bill was negotiated by four senators: Republicans Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah, and Democrats Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island. The four lawmakers released amendments Saturday aimed at addressing some of those concerns, including strengthening consultation with Native American tribes and giving states more opportunities to weigh in on proposed projects. Major industry groups representing renewable energy developers and oil and gas companies support the legislation. The bill also includes a provision that Whitehouse says would prevent the Trump administration from continuing to pay offshore wind developers to abandon their projects. The administration has spent nearly $4 billion on such settlements, according to the Associated Press. Despite endorsing the legislation, Trump continued criticizing wind energy Monday, telling reporters that "wind turbines are a major loser." Will Congress pass it? The bill's future remains uncertain despite bipartisan support and the president's endorsement. Some Democrats helped write the legislation and want it passed now, while others, including House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, are pushing for changes. Jeffries' office said last week that the legislation "falls short" in several areas. The debate comes just days after Democrats won control of Congress, giving them more leverage to negotiate energy legislation when the new Congress takes office in January. The Senate scheduled a procedural vote for Monday evening on whether to advance a legislative vehicle for the permitting proposal. The vote requires 60 senators to move forward and would not constitute final passage of the legislation.

artigo.texto: Letter: Hearing on Proposed Data Center Ban Nov. 12 I am writing to make residents aware of two important opportunities to make their voice heard in the next week. Ban Data Centers – Hearing on Thursday, November 12th at 7:00 p.m. Zoom Link At our Town Council meeting on Oct 5, we voted to refer a zoning bylaw amendment to the Planning Board and the Council’s Community Resources Committee that would ban data centers in all zones in Amherst. This zoning amendment had a total of nine council sponsors (over half of the council, myself included) because we recognize the harmful impacts of data centers on host communities. Please see this document compiled by Amherst for the People for more information, including information specifically relevant to the Amherst context. At the Planning Board/CRC hearing held on Oct. 22, members of the Planning Board and CRC discussed the possibility of recommending that this amendment be converted into a moratorium on data centers, which would allow the town time to study and create regulations around data centers. If you are against data centers in Amherst, please attend the next hearing at the Planning Board/CRC to let them know that we want a ban only. Here are some key points: - We don’t need to waste town staff time on studying how to regulate data centers, because we don’t want them in our community. - The measure that was brought to the Planning Board and CRC to study was a ban – and it was supported by over half of the council because the people we represent also don’t want data centers in our community. FY28 Budget Hearing – Monday, Nov. 16, 6:30 p.m. (Town Hall or Zoom) On Monday, November 16th, the Town Council will hold a public forum on the budget for next year. It is essential that residents weigh in on their priorities now, because the Finance Committee is working on budget guidelines that the Council will vote on in early December. The Finance Committee and Town Manager always increase each department’s budget by the same percentage, which has led to major budget cuts in our schools and the chronic underfunding of CRESS, our civilian responders – among other issues. Please attend the budget hearing to make your voice heard. Equality is not the same as equity. The finance committee and the council should carefully consider the needs of each department when creating the budget guidelines. It’s really important to understand that if residents don’t speak out and impact the budget guidelines now, it will be very hard if not impossible to make any changes next year – even if the percent increase voted for the schools and other key departments lead to cuts. If you have any questions or concerns, please feel free to contact me directly at canomartina@amherstma.gov Amber Cano-Martin Amber Cano-Martin is an Amherst Town Councilor representing District 2.

artigo.texto: Analog chipmaker Microchip Technology (NASDAQ:MCHP) beat Wall Street's revenue expectations in calendar Q3 2026 (fiscal Q2 2027), with sales up 42.2% year on year to $1.62 billion. On the other hand, next quarter's revenue guidance of $1.61 billion was less impressive, coming in 1.4% below analysts' estimates. Its non-GAAP profit of $0.97 per share was 3.4% above analysts' consensus estimates. Revenue $1.62 billion vs S&P analysts' estimates of $1.61 billion (42.2% year-on-year growth, 0.8% beat) Adjusted EPS $0.97 vs S&P analysts' estimates of $0.94 (3.4% beat) Adjusted operating income $639.9 million vs analyst estimates of $628.9 million (39.5% margin, 1.8% beat) Revenue guidance $1.61 billion at the midpoint for Q4 CY2026, below analyst estimates of $1.63 billion Adjusted EPS guidance $0.91 at the midpoint for Q4 CY2026, below analyst estimates of $0.95 Operating margin 28.6%, up from 7.8% in the same quarter last year Inventory days outstanding 184, up from 175 in the previous quarter Market capitalization $35.21 billion StockStory's take Microchip Technology's latest quarter saw sales climb on robust demand in industrial and data center end markets, with management attributing growth to new design wins and strength across key verticals. However, the market reacted negatively to the results, reflecting concerns over the sustainability of these gains. CEO Steve Sanghi noted that several non-recurring items, including licensing revenue and a distribution price adjustment, boosted reported sales. He emphasized, "Industrial and data center end markets were the two biggest drivers of our growth." The company also faced rising inventory levels as it prepared for future customer needs. Looking ahead, Microchip Technology's guidance reflects cautious optimism tempered by supply chain constraints and seasonal factors. Management highlighted that some high-margin orders in advanced products cannot be fulfilled this quarter due to extended lead times at foundries and outsourced assembly and test (OSAT) suppliers. Sanghi explained, "Our net sales guidance is lower than what we would have expected a quarter ago," citing both the absence of last quarter's one-time items and supply limitations. The company expects incremental capacity additions and a gradual improvement in fulfillment, but does not anticipate a swift normalization of gross margins given ongoing supplier price increases and operational bottlenecks. Key insights from management's remarks Management credited broad-based design win momentum, particularly in data center and industrial applications, for the quarter's growth. Non-recurring revenue items and evolving supply chain dynamics contributed to deviations from consensus expectations. Industrial and data center momentum: Management pointed to strong demand and recent design wins in industrial automation, robotics, and data center infrastructure, with the data center segment now representing nearly 17% of sales. The company is ramping next-generation PCIe Gen 6 switch and retimer products, highlighting 24 design wins that will scale revenue over the next year. Impact of non-recurring items: The quarter benefited from approximately $53 million in one-time revenue from licensing, pricing changes on channel inventory, and a customer contract. CFO Eric Bjornholt clarified these items carried 100% gross margin but are not expected to repeat, creating a less favorable comparison for the coming quarter. Supply chain bottlenecks: CEO Steve Sanghi described persistent constraints at both internal fabrication sites and external OSAT partners, with the AI sector crowding out capacity for legacy and analog products. Lead times for many core products have lengthened from 4-8 weeks to as long as 32 weeks, affecting the timing of high-margin shipments. Inventory management and production shifts: Inventory days outstanding increased as Microchip received high-value wafers in anticipation of demand and shifted some production internally to offset external bottlenecks. The company is qualifying new OSAT partners and rebalancing its internal versus external manufacturing strategy but expects these transitions to take several quarters. Acquisitions and portfolio expansion: Microchip completed the acquisitions of Hailo (AI edge computing) and VORAGO (aerospace and defense), integrating these into existing business units. While these deals will add to operating expenses in the short term, management expects them to accelerate the roadmap in AI and provide high-margin opportunities in aerospace and defense. Drivers of future performance Microchip's forward outlook is shaped by ongoing supply constraints, pricing pressures from suppliers, and the need to balance capacity with persistent demand across end markets. Supply chain and capacity expansion: Management stressed that lead times remain extended due to capacity constraints at foundries and OSAT partners, impacting fulfillment of high-margin products. While incremental internal and external capacity additions are planned for the coming quarters, the timing of improvements remains uncertain, and some backlog will spill into future periods. Supplier price increases and margin headwinds: Sanghi acknowledged that further price hikes from foundry and OSAT suppliers starting in January will pressure gross margins. While Microchip is reluctant to push another immediate price increase to customers, the company will need to assess whether these costs can be absorbed or passed on, with a long-term gross margin target of 65%. Diversified end-market demand: Despite concerns about an overheated data center market, management highlighted steady momentum in industrial, aerospace and defense, automotive, and communication segments. The company's relatively modest exposure to data center revenue, compared to peers, leaves it less vulnerable to a slowdown in that sector, while broad-based design wins are expected to support growth. artigo.texto: South Korean defense and technology giant Hanwha Ocean plans to advance the power and control system for its Floating Data Center (FDC). The company announced on Friday that it has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with ABB, a transnational corporation specializing in electrification and automation, for this purpose. Hanwha Ocean introduced the FDC at the Gastech Exhibition & Conference 2026 in September. The solution is designed to operate offshore, generating its own power and using seawater-based cooling systems to improve energy efficiency. Now, under the new deal with ABB, Hanwha Ocean will lead the basic design and power system configuration, establish design criteria for LNG engine-based power generation, and assess equipment layouts and suitability for offshore conditions. ABB, in turn, will analyze power system reliability and power quality based on Hanwha Ocean’s design and conduct technical reviews to improve efficiency amid fluctuating demand in the offshore environment. “AI data centers can experience rapid fluctuations in power demand during computing operations. Together, we will develop technologies to adjust LNG engine output in response to these changes and maintain stable operation of power equipment,” Hanwha Ocean shared on social media. Through this collaboration, Hanwha Ocean aims to extend its offshore engineering and construction capabilities into digital infrastructure and continue strengthening the core technologies behind FDCs.

artigo.texto: Cabinet tackles grid congestion with large-scale energy storage The Dutch government wants to expand energy storage to ease pressure on the country’s overloaded electricity grid. Published on November 9, 2026 According to the government, more energy storage is needed to ensure that renewable electricity remains available when there is little wind or solar power being generated. It therefore aims to increase battery storage capacity in the Netherlands to 110 gigawatt-hours (GWh) by 2040, more than 50 times the level at the end of 2025. The expansion should also help reduce pressure on the electricity grid. Climate and Energy Minister Stientje van Veldhoven and State Secretary Jo-Annes de Bat announced the plans in a letter to the Dutch House of Representatives. To make the expansion possible, the government has reached agreements with grid operators, industry association Energy Storage NL, regional and local authorities, and the Authority for Consumers and Markets (ACM). These agreements are set out in a joint Energy Storage Policy Agenda. Batteries to ease pressure on the grid The expansion is intended, among other things, to reduce pressure on the electricity grid. In many parts of the Netherlands, the grid is so congested that businesses and households have to wait for a new or upgraded connection. This is also holding back the construction of new homes. By storing electricity when demand is low and making it available during peak periods, batteries can help relieve pressure on the grid. According to the government, grid-friendly energy storage could also reduce the need for investments in expanding the electricity grid. Faster permitting The 25 action points include measures to speed up the permitting process for large-scale battery projects. Grid operators, the energy storage sector and regional authorities will need to work more closely together to achieve this. The parties are also working on agreements concerning the conditions and compensation for energy storage. One example is the use of flexible grid contracts, under which large batteries are connected subject to conditions that take into account the available capacity on the electricity grid. Compensation for households Large-scale batteries are not the only way to help stabilise the electricity grid. Households can also receive compensation if they help manage peak demand using their home batteries, heat pumps or electric vehicle chargers. Since November 1, households in the provinces of Gelderland, Utrecht, Flevoland and North Brabant have been able to participate in the scheme through a number of energy suppliers. The scheme is expected to be extended to the rest of the Netherlands in 2027.

artigo.texto: UK has no plans to slow down AI data center construction The country’s growth minister said the data centers will continue as “essential infrastructure” projects. As the US deals with the fallout associated with the ongoing demand for data centers, the UK is looking to capitalize on it instead, according to one of the country's ministers. Dan Tomlinson, the UK's minister for growth, told the The Financial Times that data center construction will continue as "essential infrastructure." Tomlinson told FT that AI is becoming more widely used throughout the UK's economy, meaning the country will need more data centers to support that growth. However, the minister added that data center construction in the UK will have to invest in local communities and create jobs to receive government support. Tomlinson also told FT that the UK government has taken away some lessons from the "free-for-all in parts of the US" with data center construction and that the country would take a more nuanced approach with better oversight. According to the UK Compute Roadmap, a policy paper detailing how the country can meet AI's growing power demands, the UK needs to have at least a computing capacity of 6GW from data centers by 2030. The UK previously made it easier for data centers to earn approvals, thanks to the "AI Growth Zones" initiative introduced by former prime minister Keir Starmer in 2025. However, UK residents have taken to protesting on sites of planned data center construction. Across the Atlantic, a majority of American voters said they're in favor of restricting the rapid pace of data center construction in local ballot results.

artigo.texto: Invinity Energy Systems plc (AIM: IES), a leading global producer of vanadium flow batteries operating in the UK and Canada, has unveiled a major upgrade to its Endurium vanadium flow battery platform, now available for general purchase. The upgraded Endurium module offers a 50% rise in energy capacity and a 33% enhancement in peak power output, along with several engineering advancements. This upgrade supports further product cost reductions and enhances project economics for customers, marking a key milestone in the company’s ongoing cost reduction initiative. Key Points - Invinity Energy Systems plc (AIM: IES) is a top global manufacturer of vanadium flow batteries with facilities in the UK and Canada. - The new Endurium module is now commercially available, delivering 50% more energy capacity and 33% higher peak power output. - Enhancements include increased electrolyte volume, upgraded electrical and power distribution systems, and refined fluid management and control algorithms. - Investors should monitor upcoming product roadmap milestones and progress on the company’s cost reduction and margin enhancement goals. Endurium’s 50% Energy Capacity Increase Driven by Multiple Engineering Enhancements The improved performance of the upgraded Endurium module results from a series of engineering modifications rather than a single change. Invinity highlights the expansion of electrolyte capacity, enhancements to electrical and power distribution subsystems, and advancements in fluid management and control system algorithms as key factors. Collectively, these improvements significantly boost power and energy density, reducing the number of modules needed to deliver the same electrical output as before. The upgraded Endurium is now available for customers seeking large-scale, long-duration energy storage solutions. Reduced Module Count Lowers Installation and Lifecycle Expenses for Clients A major commercial benefit of the upgrade is that fewer Endurium modules are required to meet specific energy storage needs, cutting equipment and space demands. Invinity notes this leads to decreased installation and lifecycle costs, enhancing project economics. The Endurium platform is designed for heavy-duty, high-throughput use and built to last 30 years or more without degradation or fire risk—advantages over lithium-ion alternatives. These features are particularly valuable for customers in renewable energy and grid infrastructure sectors seeking durable, long-lasting storage assets. Upgrade Advances Company’s Cost Reduction Program Reaffirmed to Shareholders Invinity links the Endurium upgrade directly to its ongoing product cost reduction program, recently reaffirmed to shareholders. The development was achieved by Invinity’s internal product development and R&D teams. CEO Jonathan Marren called the upgrade "another milestone" and noted further enhancements remain on the product roadmap, with continued emphasis on cost reduction, margin improvement, and strengthening Endurium’s market position as the company grows. The announcement did not disclose specific financial details, cost savings, or margin targets.

artigo.texto: Eletronet investe R$ 25 milhões em novo data center em São Paulo Com obras iniciadas, ELET1 terá 90 racks e potência inicial de 0,5 MW; lançamento está previsto para o primeiro trimestre de 2027. A Eletronet, empresa da Axia Energia (antiga Eletrobras), anunciou investimento de R$ 25 milhões na construção de um novo data center em São Paulo. Batizada de ELET1, a unidade terá 350 m², capacidade para cerca de 90 racks e potência inicial de 0,5 MW. As obras já começaram, e o lançamento está previsto para o primeiro trimestre de 2027. O projeto prevê uma segunda fase de expansão, na qual a potência poderá chegar a 1 MW, cujo prazo de entrega ainda não foi definido. A instalação ampliará a oferta de serviços de colocation, conectividade e interconexão, com atendimento a provedores de nuvem, operadoras de telecomunicações, provedores de internet (ISPs) e hyperscalers. Interconexão e migração da infraestrutura O ELET1 abrigará o ponto de interconexão (PIX) da Eletronet no IX.br São Paulo. Segundo a empresa, a unidade ficará em uma região com concentração de redes de telecomunicações e provedores de conteúdo. O projeto também contempla a migração da infraestrutura instalada no atual data center da companhia em São Paulo. A Eletronet afirma que a transferência será planejada para preservar a continuidade dos serviços. “Estamos ampliando nossa estrutura para atender às necessidades dos clientes que já utilizam nossos serviços e abrir novas oportunidades de negócios, em um contexto no qual a hiperconectividade e a disponibilidade se tornam cada vez mais essenciais”, afirma Rogerio Garchet, CEO da Eletronet (na foto acima). Segundo o executivo, o investimento acompanha o avanço de aplicações em nuvem, inteligência artificial, streaming e serviços digitais, que demandam suporte a volumes crescentes de dados. Energia e redundância Entre os recursos previstos para o ELET1 estão dois geradores redundantes de 500 kVA, dupla entrada de rede, backbone DWDM protegido, sistema de gerenciamento predial (BMS) e monitoramento contínuo. A unidade também contará com um Centro de Operações de Rede (NOC) de contingência. “Mais capacidade precisa vir acompanhada de eficiência, resiliência e previsibilidade operacional. Por isso, o ELET1 foi concebido com uma arquitetura que otimiza o uso dos recursos e oferece mais flexibilidade à operação”, afirma Emerson Hioki, diretor de tecnologia da Eletronet. (Com assessoria de imprensa)

artigo.texto: A COP31 começa na segunda-feira (09/11), na Turquia, com novas regras para o Brasil negociar resultados de redução de emissões no exterior. A decisão, aprovada pelo governo federal na sexta-feira (06/11), estabelece limites para transferências internacionais de carbono e pode atrair investimentos para projetos ambientais. Entretanto, a abertura dessas oportunidades dependerá de autorizações, compradores e comprovação dos resultados. O Comitê Interministerial sobre Mudança do Clima aprovou a medida com base no Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris, que permite a cooperação internacional para o cumprimento de metas climáticas. Assim, o país passa a contar com parâmetros para autorizar operações que envolvem resultados de mitigação transferidos internacionalmente, conhecidos como ITMOs. Créditos de carbono na COP31 terão limites para negociação internacional O Brasil poderá autorizar transferências de até 50 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ equivalente entre 2026 e 2030. Para o período de 2031 a 2035, o limite previsto sobe para 100 milhões de toneladas, com possibilidade de revisão. As regras priorizam atividades capazes de remover carbono da atmosfera, como a restauração florestal, além de projetos que reduzam emissões de metano em aterros sanitários. Há, porém, uma diferença importante: os ITMOs são resultados de mitigação autorizados para transferência internacional e não se confundem automaticamente com créditos comercializados no mercado voluntário. Além disso, a regulamentação estabelece condições distintas para projetos florestais. Em regra, metade dos resultados de restauração poderá ser transferida. Já iniciativas dentro ou no entorno de unidades de conservação poderão comercializar a totalidade dos créditos, observadas as exigências aplicáveis. Como as novas regras podem atrair investimentos? Para empresas e investidores, a definição dos limites permite avaliar projetos com maior previsibilidade regulatória. Isso pode favorecer iniciativas de recuperação ambiental e aproveitamento de metano, cujas receitas dependem da capacidade de demonstrar reduções ou remoções de emissões. O interesse por esse mercado já aparece nos projetos de créditos de carbono florestal na Amazônia, que atraíram propostas de restauração ambiental. Contudo, o volume autorizado não representa créditos vendidos nem receita garantida. Cada operação dependerá de requisitos técnicos, validação dos resultados e condições comerciais negociadas com compradores internacionais, observando as regras aprovadas pelo governo federal. A decisão integra a agenda brasileira que será apresentada na COP31, em Antália, de 9 a 20 de novembro. O governo também aprovou diretrizes para o mercado regulado nacional, previsto na Lei nº 15.042/2024, mas esse sistema possui regras próprias. Para os projetos brasileiros, a próxima etapa será demonstrar viabilidade financeira. A autorização internacional amplia as possibilidades de negociação, mas o retorno dependerá do preço obtido pelos resultados ambientais e dos custos para gerá-los, comprová-los e transferi-los.

artigo.texto: Confira o resumo que a OESTE.IA, a IA da Revista Oeste, fez pra você A Noruega decidiu suspender temporariamente novas reservas de conexão de data centers à rede elétrica para avaliar a crescente demanda de energia dessas instalações, impulsionada pela expansão da inteligência artificial. A medida foi anunciada pela operadora do sistema elétrico, Statnett, nesta segunda-feira, 9, e deve durar até, no máximo, 1º de agosto de 2027. A Noruega vai suspender temporariamente novas reservas de conexão de data centers à rede elétrica. A decisão busca avaliar como o país vai lidar com a demanda de energia dessas instalações, que vem crescendo com a expansão da inteligência artificial (IA). A operadora do sistema elétrico norueguês, Statnett, anunciou a medida nesta segunda-feira, 9, em comunicado. A previsão é que a suspensão termine, no máximo, em 1º de agosto de 2027. Receba nossas atualizações Leia também: “Nvidia investiga suspeita de espionagem envolvendo CEO“ A construção de data centers avança em diversos países. Empresas de tecnologia investem centenas de bilhões de dólares em estruturas destinadas à operação e ao treinamento de sistemas de inteligência artificial. A expansão, contudo, também provoca resistência de comunidades nos Estados Unidos e na Europa, principalmente por causa da demanda por terrenos e eletricidade e do possível aumento das tarifas de energia. O ministro da Digitalização da Noruega, Torgeir Micaelsen, defendeu o controle sobre a expansão dessas instalações. “Queremos data centers na Noruega, mas não podemos aceitar todos os tipos de data centers”, afirmou a jornalistas nesta segunda-feira. “Portanto, precisamos controlar o crescimento e garantir que a Noruega receba os data centers de que realmente necessita, aqueles que proporcionam os maiores benefícios para a sociedade.” Demanda supera o consumo máximo do país Segundo dados da Statnett, os data centers já conectados à rede norueguesa somam 800 megawatts (MW) de capacidade. Outros 4.200 MW têm reserva de conexão, enquanto 9.100 MW aguardam na fila por capacidade. Além desses pedidos, empresas solicitaram conexão para mais 18 mil MW. Com isso, a demanda total à espera de acesso chega a 27.100 MW. O volume supera o consumo máximo de energia da Noruega, que fica pouco acima de 25 mil MW. Os números ajudam a dimensionar a pressão que os novos empreendimentos podem exercer sobre o sistema elétrico do país. Um relatório recente do Conselho Norueguês de Tecnologia também questionou os benefícios econômicos dessas instalações. Segundo o documento, os data centers geram poucos empregos permanentes depois da conclusão das obras. O conselho informou ainda que 90% dessas estruturas pertencem a empresas estrangeiras. + Entenda mais de Mundo em Oeste

artigo.texto: As Toyota's luxury brand Lexus rolls out electric versions of its midsize-plus ES sedan, competition is heating up in Korea's 70 million won EV segment. The 70 million won range is expected to see fast-growing demand because it preserves a premium image while still qualifying for subsidies. But most of the key models at this price point, including the ES EVs, are equipped with batteries from China's CATL, leaving Korean battery makers on the sidelines. According to the auto industry on the 10th, Lexus on the 13th of last month launched the all-electric ES350e and ES500e and the hybrid ES350h as part of the new eighth-generation ES in the Korean market. The ES is a core Lexus model that made its global debut in 1989. The new ES is the fully redesigned eighth generation, the first full change in eight years since 2018. Until now, the ES was sold only with internal-combustion and hybrid powertrains, but starting with this eighth generation Lexus has dropped the combustion-engine model and added an EV. The entry-level Premium trim of the ES350e is priced at 71.6 million won. That is 1.3 million won cheaper than the ES350h Premium trim at 72.9 million won. Because EVs carry costly batteries, they are often pricier than comparable combustion or hybrid models. Lexus appears to have set the EV's starting price below the hybrid to quickly gain share on price competitiveness. Lexus also priced the higher-spec ES500e Premium in the 77 million won range. The ES350e is a front-wheel-drive model with a single motor, while the ES500e is all-wheel drive with dual motors. The ES500e's range is 435 km per charge, shorter than the ES350e's 478 km, but it outmuscles the ES350e with 347 horsepower versus 227 horsepower. After Lexus priced the new ES EVs in the lower-than-expected 70 million won range, domestic consumer interest surged. Industry sources say total orders for the new ES, including one month of preorders, have reached about 5,000 units. EVs—the ES350e and ES500e—account for roughly half. Rivals starting in the 70 million won range include Volvo's midsize-plus ES90 sedan, Polestar's midsize-plus SUV Polestar 3, and BMW's midsize SUV iX3. Tesla's midsize SUV Model Y, which dominates the Korean market, starts at 49.99 million won for the base rear-wheel-drive Premium, while the all-wheel-drive Model Y L Premium sells for 72.99 million won. Automakers are clustering new models in the 70 million won bracket because policy changes on subsidies are seen as boosting demand at this price point. Currently, EVs priced under 85 million won qualify for subsidies, but the government plans to lower the threshold to under 80 million won starting next year. In addition, vehicles priced 80 million won or more must carry green license plates if purchased as corporate cars. Price a car in the 60 million won range or lower and its premium image fades; move into the 80 million won range and you risk losing subsidies and being required to use green plates, among other drawbacks. As a result, import brands are concentrating on the 70 million won segment to protect brand value while reaping multiple practical benefits. The problem is that batteries in EVs priced in the 70 million won range are effectively dominated by China's CATL. CATL is the world's No. 1 supplier, with a 39.1% cumulative share of the global EV battery market from January through September this year. The Lexus ES350e and ES500e, Volvo ES90, and Polestar 3 all use CATL's LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries. For the Model Y, the Long Range and Performance trims use LG Energy Solution's NCM batteries, but the cheaper rear-wheel-drive trim also uses CATL's LFP battery. The BMW iX3 is equipped with batteries from China's EVE Energy. Automakers are largely sourcing batteries from CATL and other Chinese makers because they are relatively inexpensive. NCM batteries, the mainstay of Korean suppliers such as LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI, offer higher energy density and longer range but cost more due to pricey cobalt and nickel. LFP batteries, by contrast, use iron and phosphorus as main materials and can be procured at lower cost. Battery industry officials worry that LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI, and SK On—the three Korean players—will keep losing share at home to Chinese batteries. The high-end premium EV segment has limited room to expand, and domestic automakers such as Hyundai Motor are struggling to grow EV sales. "To make matters worse, after BYD, Chinese EV makers such as Zeekr and Xpeng are entering Korea one after another, further squeezing Hyundai Motor and Kia," a battery industry source said. "Korean battery makers' recent focus on the energy storage system (ESS) market also reflects their judgment that it will be hard to win back EV leadership from Chinese companies anytime soon."

artigo.texto: Bloom Energy (NYSE:BE) turned up in two big data center announcements on Nov. 5. NTT DATA said it had agreed to deploy 900 megawatts of the fuel cell maker's onsite power across data center projects around the world. And Alphabet's Google said Bloom would build the fuel cells for a 702-megawatt plant powering its first data center in Wyoming, a $17 billion project. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » The stock had a bad day anyway. Shares ended at $167.52, off around 16%, amid worries that rising opposition to new data centers after the Nov. 3 midterms might slow the build-out of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. The growth stock is still up over 90% this year. But it now sits about 52% below the $345.85 record close it set on June 22. How much new business did Bloom win on Nov. 5? Less than the headlines may suggest, because just one of the two deals is new. I think the other still matters, though, and the stock looks much more reasonably priced than it did in October. Image source: The Motley Fool. Google's fuel cells were ordered in January Google won't buy the fuel cells itself. American Electric Power plans to invest around $4 billion in the 702-megawatt project near Cheyenne, Wyoming, the utility said on Oct. 14. It'll sell the plant's output to Google under a 20-year power purchase agreement, and it expects the plant to be fully running by late 2028. The fuel cell order came months earlier. In January, an AEP subsidiary agreed to buy solid oxide fuel cells for around $2.65 billion for a plant near Cheyenne. The purchase used most of an option for 900 extra megawatts under AEP's 2024 supply deal with Bloom. For a sense of scale, that one order is worth over half of Bloom's full-year revenue forecast of $4.4 billion to $4.6 billion for 2026. So, Google's news didn't add to Bloom's orders. The fuel cells were bought in January, and AEP had already named Google as the plant's customer in October. That still means something, I think. A fuel cell order backed by a 20-year power contract with Google looks more likely to become revenue on time than one linked to an unnamed buyer. NTT DATA is the new business NTT DATA's deal is the new business, and the companies called it Bloom's biggest international project so far. NTT's data center arm plans to use the fuel cells as its main power source, with the relationship meant to reach gigawatt scale across its global portfolio. What the release didn't say matters, too. It gave no dollar value, no project locations, and no timeline beyond first shipments starting in 2027. This deal shouldn't show up in Bloom's 2026 revenue, and Bloom hasn't said how much of it falls in 2027 or later. But 900 megawatts is a lot of fuel cells -- nearly a full year of output at the 1 gigawatt of annual production capacity Bloom's Fremont, California, plant had going into 2026. The company planned to double that capacity by year-end. Bloom needs deals like this, because its quarter-to-quarter growth slowed sharply in the third quarter. Second-quarter revenue of $1.07 billion was 42% above the first quarter's $751 million. Third-quarter revenue then climbed 16% sequentially to $1.24 billion, up 138% year over year. And October's raised outlook (management's third raise this year) implies a sequential gain of 9% to 25% in the fourth quarter. That's still strong growth. Keeping it up into 2027 and 2028, though, depends on deals like NTT DATA's moving from announcement to shipment. Is the price finally reasonable? Based on the midpoint of management's adjusted earnings forecast for 2026 ($3.10 to $3.40 a share), Bloom stock cost around 52 times earnings at its Nov. 5 close. The same forecast had it at around 67 times earnings at the $217.77 close on Oct. 22. On next year's expected earnings, shares now trade at around 31 times earnings. Still, 52 times earnings is a premium price. It assumes Bloom keeps growing quickly well past this year. But Bloom landed a big new deal on Nov. 5 as its shares got much cheaper. Of course, a slower U.S. data center build-out might delay some deliveries. And October's weak spot hasn't gone away. Bloom's operations burned $27 million in cash in the third quarter, mostly because it booked revenue faster than it could bill customers for it. Is Bloom stock worth buying after a 16% one-day drop? I'd consider buying some shares at this price, a few at a time. And I'd maybe add more when billing catches up with revenue. Should you buy stock in Bloom Energy right now? artigo.texto: Three separate threads on X this week converged on the same conclusion: Tesla's Cybercab is better positioned than its critics admit. Fresh ride-hailing data dismantles the most common knock on the two-seat design, a closer look at the vehicle's conversational AI reveals something closer to a co-pilot than a voice assistant, and an IRA credit breakdown suggests the battery economics are more aggressive than most analysts have modeled. 1. The two-seat design is backed by actual trip data — not assumptions The loudest skepticism around the Cybercab has always been its passenger capacity: two seats, no more. Critics argue that consumers buying four- and five-seat vehicles signals demand for that space. Sawyer Merritt pushed back hard on that framing this week, citing a Federal Highway Administration study showing that roughly 85% of private ride-hailing trips involve just one or two passengers — with 64.2% of trips carrying a single rider. The distinction matters. What people buy for personal ownership — where occasional family trips, cargo capacity, and optionality all factor in — is a poor proxy for what a robotaxi fleet actually needs to serve. A vehicle optimized for the 85% use case isn't a compromise; it's a deliberate product decision. According to background research, Tesla also targets an operating cost below $0.30 per mile for the Cybercab, a figure that only works at scale with a purpose-built, stripped-down platform. Carrying two seats instead of five is part of how that number gets achieved. 2. The conversational AI goes well beyond voice commands Whole Mars Catalog described the Cybercab's passenger interaction this way: you'll be able to talk to the car like a cab driver — ask it to do whatever you want, as long as it's legal and won't hurt anyone. That framing is more meaningful than it sounds. Most in-car voice systems today are command-and-response: say a specific phrase, get a specific action. What's being described here is a conversational agent — one that can handle open-ended requests, route changes mid-trip, music preferences, and presumably questions about the ride itself. According to background research, the Cybercab's on-board voice interface is powered by a specialized version of ChatGPT, functioning as a multimodal agent capable of anticipating road behavior and interacting vocally with passengers. The system is designed to react to unexpected situations and navigate complex intersections — meaning the AI isn't just listening to passengers, it's also processing the environment in real time. For riders accustomed to awkward, keyword-dependent car interfaces, this represents a meaningful step change in what a driverless ride actually feels like. 3. IRA battery credits could push the pack cost under $3,000 The third data point is the one with the most direct financial implication. Whole Mars Catalog flagged that with the IRA battery production credit factored in, the cost of a full Cybercab battery pack could come in under $3,000. Here's the math behind it. The Cybercab carries a 47.6 kWh usable battery pack built on 4680 cells. The IRA provides a production credit of $35 per kWh for battery cells and $10 per kWh for battery modules — up to $45 per kWh if both apply. On a 47.6 kWh pack, that's a potential credit of roughly $2,142. When stacked against Tesla's already-aggressive 4680 cell cost targets and a stated build cost goal of under $30,000 for the full vehicle, the battery pack becomes one of the cheapest line items on the bill of materials for a vehicle of this capability. A sub-$3,000 pack cost isn't just a talking point — it's the kind of structural cost advantage that makes a $0.30/mile operating target credible rather than aspirational. Taken together, these three threads sketch a Cybercab that is more defensible on design, more capable on software, and more competitive on economics than the skeptic narrative suggests. The real test remains deployment scale — but the underlying numbers are holding up. 🚕 Following the Robotaxi rollout? Quadrilhas organizadas estão interceptando caminhões para roubar cargas valiosas de componentes para data centers, como servidores, cabos de cobre e chips de memória. Com ataques altamente planejados antes dos veículos deixarem os depósitos, os prejuízos com os roubos já somam US$ 110,6 milhões desde junho, registrando perdas que variam entre US$ 2 milhões e US$ 38 milhões por ocorrência. A corrida do ouro da inteligência artificial está recriando uma espécie de "Velho Oeste do século XXI", reunindo todos os elementos de um faroeste clássico. De um lado, estão as minas de ouro — os data centers — e investidores com bolsos cheios, dispostos a comprar as pás e todo o material necessário para extrair o metal precioso, que agora assume a forma de dados. Faltavam apenas os saqueadores de estradas para completar o cenário, mas eles acabaram de chegar. Desta vez, a diligência é um caminhão semirreboque carregado de peças para equipar data centers. Conforme revelou a emissora norte-americana NBC News, a nova carga cobiçada reúne servidores, cabos de cobre para instalações e chips de memória. E as quadrilhas não improvisam: escolhem a carga de maneira calculada muito antes de o veículo deixar o depósito e o interceptam antes que chegue ao destino final. Prejuízos passam de US$ 100 milhões desde junho Estima-se que, desde 3 de junho, os roubos registrados de cargas de tecnologia somaram **US$ 110,6 milhões**. Segundo levantamento da FreightWaves com Scott Cornell, presidente da Associação para a Proteção de Ativos Transportados (TAPA Americas) e executivo especialista em crimes de transporte na SPG Cargo & Logistics, os prejuízos em cada ataque variam entre **US$ 2 milhões e US$ 38 milhões**. artigo.texto: Hyperscale Data, Inc. Announces Intent to Launch Exchange Offer to Acquire Up to $50,000,000 of Outstanding Shares for Cash and New Preferred Shares Company Moves to Address Significant Gap Between Market Value and Balance Sheet Strength LAS VEGAS , Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Hyperscale Data, Inc. (NYSE American: GPUS), an artificial intelligence ("AI") data center company ("Hyperscale Data" or the "Company"), today announced that it intends to commence an exchange offer to purchase up to 192,307,692 shares of its Class A Common Stock, $0.001 par value per share ("Common Stock") in exchange for units (the "Units") consisting of (a) $2.00 in cash and (b) one share of preferred stock with a stated value of $24.00 per share (the "Preferred Stock"), per 100 shares of Common Stock. The Preferred Stock will be entitled to receive an annual dividend of 12.00%. Stockholders will be able to exchange blocks of 100 shares of Common Stock for one Unit consisting of (a) $2.00 in cash and (b) one share of Preferred Stock which values the Common Stock at $0.26 per share and represents an 82% premium to the November 6, 2026, closing price of $0.1429. The exchange offer will require that a minimum of 100 million shares of Common Stock be tendered by common stockholders. The Company will seek to list the Preferred Stock on the NYSE American. If the application to list the Preferred Stock is approved by the NYSE American, trading in the Preferred Stock is expected to commence within a 30-day period after the approval of listing. The Company expects to formally launch the proposed exchange offer around November 17, 2026, subject to board approval, regulatory approval and customary closing conditions. The proposed exchange offer reflects Hyperscale's view that its current market valuation does not accurately reflect the strength of its balance sheet, including its holdings of cash and Bitcoin. Milton "Todd" Ault III, Executive Chairman of Hyperscale Data, stated: "We believe there is a material disconnect between the intrinsic value of Hyperscale and where our Common Stock is currently trading. "The exchange offer is intended to provide shareholders with an opportunity for liquidity and an instrument that will allow stockholders to participate in the long-term growth of the Company while receiving a fixed payment. artigo.texto: Anthropic has spent billions developing Claude, one of the world's leading artificial intelligence models. Now it's preparing to spend a staggering amount of money to make sure Claude has somewhere to run. In its recent IPO filing, Anthropic disclosed approximately $895.4 billion in purchase commitments and lease agreements, substantially all related to computing and infrastructure. About $447.5 billion of those commitments are expected to come due by the end of 2030. But Anthropic isn't simply buying computing capacity from Amazon and Alphabet anymore. It's also pursuing dedicated data center infrastructure, including arrangements in which third parties develop facilities that Anthropic leases and operates through specialized partners. Anthropic isn't necessarily constructing or owning the buildings itself. And its filing doesn't identify most of the companies that will build and equip those facilities. Still, some interesting publicly traded companies do this type of work and offer investors exposure to data center construction. Sterling Infrastructure: Preparing the ground Before installing a server, someone has to prepare the site. My pick in this realm is Sterling Infrastructure (STRL +14.97%), which provides site development services for large industrial projects, including data centers and semiconductor manufacturing facilities. Sterling performs excavation and grading at construction sites and prepares infrastructure to support large buildings. Its electrical contracting business adds another source of revenue from complex construction projects. Business is booming. In the third quarter, Sterling's E-Infrastructure Solutions segment generated $1.30 billion in revenue, an increase of 212% from a year earlier. That segment accounted for 83% of the company's total quarterly revenue. Sterling also reported $4.14 billion in signed backlog and another $2 billion in unsigned awards. Management says its broader pipeline of identified work, including future project phases, approaches $8 billion. STRL Sterling Infrastructure NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/09/26 Quanta Services: Delivering the electricity Data centers need power, and a lot of it. Quanta Services (PWR +9.35%) provides transmission lines, substations, and other infrastructure to connect data centers to the power grid. AI data centers aren't the only customers demanding more electricity. Utilities are investing in grid modernization, while industrial facilities and other large electricity users need additional capacity. That gives Quanta a much broader opportunity than any single AI company's expansion plans. Revenue in the third quarter was $12.01 billion, up 57% from a year ago. Its Electric segment generated $9.80 billion, accounting for nearly 82% of total revenue. Meanwhile, Quanta's total backlog reached a record $63.7 billion, providing substantial visibility into future work. PWR Quanta Services NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/09/26 Vertiv: Keeping the chips cool AI chips and servers generate a lot of heat as they work together on AI tasks. And without a way to cool off, they won't work for long. Vertiv Holdings (VRT +9.63%) makes liquid cooling systems that help solve that problem, as well as power equipment and related infrastructure for data centers. The company's Q3 revenue was $4.31 billion, up an impressive 61% from a year ago. Organic orders more than doubled, and adjusted operating margin increased 290 basis points to 25.2%. The company's deferred revenue also reached $4.12 billion at the end of September, compared with $1.81 billion at the end of 2025. That reflects payments received for products and services that haven't yet been recognized as revenue. Converting that demand into completed deliveries remains important. VRT Vertiv NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/09/26 Three stocks to buy to invest in AI infrastructure Anthropic's filing makes clear that expanding computing capacity involves considerably more than purchasing advanced chips. It requires land, construction, electricity, cooling equipment, and specialized contractors. Sterling, Quanta, and Vertiv each participate in a different part of that process. While none is identified as an Anthropic contractor in the filing, all three serve customers beyond Anthropic. That's why they're worth examining.

artigo.texto: Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has defended the anti-data center movement. He argues that slower compute growth would buy time to harden the world against AI-driven cyber and bio risks. The timing matters for markets. AI chip stocks and Bitcoin miners that now rent power to AI labs depend on a fast data center buildout. Why Buterin Isn't Worried About the Anti-Data Center Movement Buterin said in an X post on Nov. 8 that he disagrees with the strong emotional reaction to anti-data center groups. His case rests on algorithmic progress. By his estimate, whatever bigger data centers could do in two years, today's will manage in four, or sooner. Even extreme success for the anti-data center movement would therefore cause nothing close to a disaster, the Ethereum co-founder argued. Cybersecurity problems are already visible, he noted, and bio risks may follow soon. The world needs every bit of time to prepare. He added that science faces many bottlenecks besides AI. As a result, delaying AI by one year would slow research by far less. Buterin stressed that his view needs no doomer claims about recursive self-improvement (RSI), where AI systems upgrade themselves. The post fits his recent warnings. At Devcon 8, he said AI could crack crypto by finding shortcuts through its cryptography. Who Pays if the AI Buildout Slows? The anti-data center movement has spread from protests to policy. Sen. Bernie Sanders has called for a national data center moratorium after Democrats won Congress. In Europe, several hundred activists occupied a Microsoft construction site in Amsterdam on Nov. 6, Al Jazeera reported. Police detained 150 to 200 people. However, not everyone agrees with Buterin. BlackRock CEO Larry Fink has warned that halting data center construction would push the US into recession. Bitcoin miners carry their own exposure. Riot Platforms sold most of its Bitcoin to fund Texas AI data centers. The state's governor-elect has pledged a permit freeze. Still, Buterin said that even if the anti-data center movement's success proved net-bad, it would be no worse than many other political fights. For AI-linked assets, the debate is shifting from whether the buildout continues to how fast.
