artigo.texto: All eyes were on Texas during the midterms, and artificial intelligence (AI) stocks, especially the neoclouds, took a beating when a Democrat governor won the state. The main fear is that increased AI regulations will make it harder to build data centers in the future, and existing projects may get delayed. It's a legitimate concern, and Texas isn't the only state that was affected. Ohio, Georgia, and Arizona also saw Democratic victories, and they have been instrumental states for the AI boom. Bears will argue that Democratic victories can turn into a major bottleneck for AI as construction projects are delayed or canceled. Here's what investors should consider. Governors still answer to the House and Senate While governor victories capture headlines, each governor must still answer to their state's House and Senate. Those two political arms introduce more variety that can result in gridlock instead of sweeping AI regulations. Here's how it varies for the four states that have played a vital role in artificial intelligence: - Texas: Republicans lost the House but have the Senate. - Ohio: Republicans maintained the House and the Senate. - Georgia: Republicans lost the House but have the Senate. - Arizona: Democrats won the House and the Senate. Ohio has the best political profile for tech companies. A gridlock essentially lets existing data center projects continue. Texas and Georgia can still create a gridlock due to Republicans controlling the Senate, but their political leverage isn't as good as Ohio's. Data centers in Arizona won't face the same political gridlock since Democrats have secured the House and the Senate. Arizona Democrats are in the best position to act swiftly. Job cuts are a real risk Although activism and protests toward data centers have gotten louder in recent months, delaying and canceling these projects comes with downsides that extend beyond lost innovation. While an anti-big tech stance may cause people to look the other way when hyperscalers face roadblocks, those same data center delays and cancellations have a real impact on jobs. Politicians on both sides of the aisle love to tout job growth. For instance, former President Biden was enthusiastic about a $3.3 billion data center in Wisconsin since it could create 2,000 permanent jobs once built. If many data centers are delayed or canceled, it can lead to thousands of people losing their jobs. While regulation may become stricter, kneecapping the industry also translates into lost jobs. Democrats may not care as much about GDP during this cycle since Trump is still the president, but slowing down AI infrastructure can result in negative GDP growth, since it's the main catalyst powering the economy. A negative GDP growth reading won't be a good look. The Democrats can introduce measures that make their voters happy without uprooting the entire AI trade. Local engagement will become more valuable Good PR will be incredibly valuable for neoclouds as the Democrats gain more control of the government in January. Investors can expect to see companies take more steps to financially support local communities beyond new jobs. These initiatives can help them win over residents and provide tangible benefits to the entire community. Part of that may mean reduced tax breaks, a point of contention that was gaining steam before the midterm results. Some tech companies are also acquiring old infrastructure and converting it into AI data centers. For instance, Terawulf is turning a retired coal plant into an AI data center. Those types of changes are less disruptive and let AI data center developers focus on job creation. If more neoclouds and colocation developers take this approach, it will be harder for Democrats to issue sweeping changes that stall out the industry. Investors should pay attention to how data center developers are enhancing local communities, because winning over locals will reduce uncertainty with their gigawatt pipelines.

artigo.texto: The dust from the midterms had hardly settled Wednesday when OpenAI leaders began reckoning with an urgent question: would the outcome make it harder to secure the vast amounts of computing power the company needs to keep growing? During a Q&A with employees, OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman fielded questions about data centers and public sentiment on AI, according to people familiar with the matter. A day earlier, a wave of data-center opposition had helped candidates promising to freeze development win statehouses in Texas, Georgia, Ohio and Michigan—all major states for data-center sites. Altman acknowledged that the public is concerned about water use and said that whatever the reason, he understood why people might not want to live near data centers, the people said. At one point, he mused that the company should perhaps look to build data centers in the desert. Meanwhile, senior leaders were busy discussing whether the company would need to reset expectations for its data-center capacity next year, The Wall Street Journal previously reported. And employees involved in OpenAI’s data-center development were exchanging intelligence on newly elected Democratic politicians in key states and discussing how best to engage with them, according to messages viewed by the Journal. Across Silicon Valley, similar scenes played out as tech companies that have committed hundreds of billions of dollars to the artificial-intelligence race, and carefully cultivated relationships with AI-friendly officials at all levels of government, rushed to plan for a changed reality. Overnight, they found themselves facing the prospect of blanket moratoriums, tighter environmental regulations and longer review timelines, along with potential new AI-safety regulations that could further bog them down. The tech investor Brad Gerstner said on the “All-In” podcast that as much as 35% of the U.S. data-center construction planned for next year is now at risk. Executives in charge of government relations for so-called hyperscaler companies moved quickly to open lines of communication with incoming governors and their transition teams, seeking an understanding of how their campaign-trail rhetoric would translate into policy actions. Dina Powell McCormick, who as president of Meta Platforms oversees its AI-infrastructure operations, said at the WSJ Tech conference Wednesday night that the company had already found one incoming governor prepared to parley. “We did have a governor that won last night who did make data centers a big part of their platform say, ‘As soon as we get past the inauguration, let’s meet, because we don’t want to lose this investment in our town. We don’t want these jobs to go elsewhere,’ ” she said. But on the whole, Powell McCormick said, Meta assumes that building data centers in the U.S. is “going to be harder” and getting new ones done from scratch will be “very challenging.” She said Meta and other tech companies are increasingly considering building new data centers outside the U.S. as one way around the new hurdles. Another avenue, she said, is to scale up existing data centers, where surrounding communities that have seen benefits in the form of job creation and tax revenue don’t require as much persuasion. To have any hope of winning over the public, Powell McCormick said, the AI industry will have to get much better at talking about its product and the potential societal benefits. “I think we have to double and triple down on telling the story,” she said. OpenAI President Greg Brockman , also speaking at the conference, echoed that point, saying, “We need to do a better job of really communicating to local communities about why data centers are something that can be beneficial to them.” On Thursday, OpenAI became the latest AI giant to unveil a broad commitment governing how it approaches building new data centers. The company said it would not require public officials to sign nondisclosure agreements to engage in data-center negotiations and that it would solicit community input and provide clear public information about the energy, water and noise impacts of its infrastructure investments. Anthropic, in an S-1 filing last week for a planned initial public offering, previewed for investors the risk that local and state governments might adopt data-center moratoriums. “Such moratoriums, or similar actions, could delay or prevent the construction or expansion of facilities on which we depend for compute,” the filing said. Anthropic said it was pursuing projects in several “non-U.S. jurisdictions” as part of a plan to “reduce concentration risks associated with operating a significant portion of our compute infrastructure in the United States.” The S-1 detailed approximately $895.4 billion of AI computing and infrastructure commitments through 2045. The company has separately announced plans to build data centers in Texas and New York, with sites coming online this year. artigo.texto: Byhmgard signs loan agreement with Signet Bank for the financing of the SW Power battery storage plant in Rīga, 15 MW / 30 MWh Byhmgard AB (publ) ("Byhmgard" or the "Company") announces that its wholly owned project company SW Power SIA (the "Project Company") has signed a loan agreement with Signet Bank AS for a project loan of just over EUR 3.0 million, corresponding to 50 percent of the financing of the Company's battery storage plant at Ata iela in Rīga, Latvia (the "Plant"). The total financing requirement for the Plant amounts to approximately EUR 6.1 million (approximately SEK 67 million). The remaining 50 percent is intended to be financed largely through the Company's wholly owned subsidiary Byhmgard Invest AB, which in turn owns all shares in the Project Company, acquiring battery systems on a payment plan and contributing them to the Project Company as a contribution in kind. This credit is guaranteed with support from the financing agreement with Middelborg AS and Gimle Invest AS announced by the Company on 11 March 2026. The loan from Signet Bank is sized to be serviced by the group's revenue from energy arbitrage, which the Company estimates at approximately EUR 20 million over 20 years, with a further potential of approximately EUR 33 million from balancing and capacity services to the state-owned transmission system operator Augstsprieguma tīkls (AST). As previously announced, commercial operation is planned for the second quarter of 2027. Financing The financing requirement of approximately EUR 6.1 million is financed half by a project loan from Signet Bank AS, Rīga, secured on the Plant and the Project Company. The loan is disbursed against costs incurred during construction and is repaid monthly from autumn 2027. The other half is intended to be financed through the Company's subsidiary Byhmgard Invest AB, which in turn owns all shares in the Project Company, acquiring battery systems on credit and contributing them to the Project Company as a contribution in kind. The battery systems make up most of the portion of financing provided by Byhmgard Invest AB, and the balance, approximately 30 percent, is contributed in cash by Byhmgard Invest AB. The credit for Byhmgard Invest AB's acquisition of the battery systems is supported by guarantees from Middelborg AS and Gimle Invest AS in accordance with the financing agreement announced on 11 March 2026, under which these parties undertake to cover the part of the project cost not financed by bank debt. The financing of the Company's second plant in Rīga, SW Battery SIA, is being finalised and is intended to follow the same structure. Revenue calculation The loan from Signet Bank is sized on estimated revenue from energy arbitrage, that is trading on the Nord Pool day-ahead and intraday markets. According to the Company's revenue analysis, the Plant is estimated to generate revenue of approximately EUR 20 million over the period 2027 to 2047, which meets the bank's coverage requirement for interest and repayments. The Company's revenue analysis is based on historical price spreads on the Nord Pool day-ahead market for Latvia, one full charging cycle per day, assumptions on efficiency, degradation and availability, and an assumed price development over the period. Once the Plant has been approved for balancing and capacity services with the state-owned transmission system operator in Latvia (AST), further revenue of approximately EUR 33 million is estimated based on external market assessments that Byhmgard has requested from local third-party market participants. These calculations indicate total revenue of approximately EUR 53 million for the period 2027 to 2047 in the electricity, balancing and capacity markets. Any revenue from balancing and capacity services is, however, not necessary for the payment of interest and repayments on the loan. Estimated revenue varies with price spreads in the electricity market and in the balancing and capacity markets, and the actual outcome is expected to fall within the range of EUR 20 million to EUR 53 million. All amounts are estimated revenue before operating costs. The plant and timeline The Project Company is wholly owned by Byhmgard through its subsidiary Byhmgard Invest AB. The Plant has a grid connection of 14.99 MW and consists of six liquid-cooled lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery containers with two hours of storage, approximately 30 MWh. Land rights and the environmental decision have been obtained, and the grid connection agreement has been entered into. As previously announced, the Project Company has signed an EPC agreement with Latvijas Energoceltnieks (LEC) and an operation and maintenance agreement with Alstra Energy AB. LEC will only commence its work under the EPC agreement after Byhmgard issues a notice to proceed. Notice to proceed to LEC is issued when the building permit is registered with the relevant authority in Rīga. The building permit is expected to be obtained in mid-November 2026. Costs for LEC's work, approximately EUR 0.6 million, begin to accrue when the notice to proceed is issued and are included in the total investment of approximately EUR 6.1 million. Costs for Alstra Energy AB's work, approximately EUR 70 thousand per year, begin to accrue once operation has commenced and are included in the Plant's operating costs. Delivery of the battery systems to Rīga is expected in spring 2027 and commercial operation in the second quarter of 2027. An application for approval for ancillary services is planned to be submitted thereafter. CEO comment "The loan agreement is a decisive step in the financing of our first own plant, and we are closer to our goal of moving from delivering battery systems to owning and operating them. The loan is sized on estimated revenue from energy arbitrage, which gives a robust base, while potential ancillary services to AST may provide a substantial upside. artigo.texto: State clean energy programs and the communities they’re meant to serve want the same thing. Both want more resilient, more affordable, cleaner power. And yet, across solar and storage programs throughout the U.S. Northeast, projects stall, applications bounce back and forth, and entire counties opt out of battery storage altogether. This is not because anyone disagrees on the goal, but because the two sides are speaking different languages about cost, risk, and timeline. COMMENTARY The disconnect is a translation and timing problem, and underneath it, a fluency problem: clean energy is still young enough as an industry that we haven’t built a shared, baseline understanding of how it works, which is exactly the vacuum fear and misinformation grow fastest in. The technical, financial, and safety information communities need almost always exists somewhere; it just doesn’t arrive in a form, on a timeline, or in a language that matches the person who has to act on it. The Technical Handoff Gap Consider a state clean energy incentive program that requires applications to meet a minimum technical requirement, such as a shading threshold verified through third-party modeling software. Programs like this are purposely built to require licensed contractors, rather than homeowners, to submit on a project’s behalf. In practice, though, the person doing the actual submitting inside that contractor’s office is often administrative staff, handling documentation and portal logistics rather than the shading analysis itself. The friction shows up when an application gets flagged for revision. If a shading model overestimated sun exposure, if a battery specification sheet vaguely says it’s UL listed, or if a site location on a drawing is off, the fix requires looping back to whoever built the original technical analysis, understanding what needs to change, and resubmitting. For an administrative submitter without training to read these types of documents, it could be a multi-week round trip, and every round trip pushes a project’s timeline further from the one the applicant was promised. The review requirement is holding a consistent technical bar as intended, but it is colliding with an industry that hasn’t yet agreed on what baseline fluency should look like. As the technology moves from niche to standard, programs need to better explain their requirements, and applicants and communities need to get better at asking questions. The Bandwidth and Fit Gap Some states have built entire portfolios of clean energy incentive programs, including production-based solar incentives, demand-reduction standards that reward market participation, dedicated resilience programs, and more. We’ve worked directly on application reviews and feasibility studies for programs like these, as well as supported the people weighing whether to pursue them, including town officials, church administrators, and facility managers. Across nearly every one of those conversations, we found real interest and need, but simply not enough bandwidth to figure out which program actually solves their problem. These aren’t organizations with dedicated energy staff. Most of the people making these decisions have the same relationship to electricity most people do: they know what it costs, not how it works. They know their power went out last summer, or that heating bills wiped out half their annual budget, but they don’t have a working sense of peak demand, energy arbitrage, or how a given program lines up with either problem. For example, many states have built resilience-specific tracks alongside their standard incentive programs. Local leaders recognize that a community hub (Figure 1) worried about outages needs a different program than a homeowner just trying to lower a bill. But the program simply existing isn’t the same as someone knowing it’s the right fit. The real work is helping someone who’s never had to think about kilowatts vs. kilowatt-hours figure out which program they need. The Trust and Visibility Gap A string of BESS fires, layered on top of a wave of unrelated lithium-ion fires involving e-bikes and scooters, has created a perception problem for the industry. The largely negative image of battery storage that many community members hold is hard for any single conversation to undo, especially in dense urban areas or in smaller communities served by volunteer fire departments. Faced with that uncertainty, it was faster and safer for many municipalities to pass a moratorium than to build out permitting and zoning frameworks on their own, and the result was close to a domino effect, with moratoria spreading across counties and towns statewide. The irony is that most states had already responded substantively, not just rhetorically. They published model laws, a customizable zoning and permitting template local governments could adopt directly. These outlines stood up to a peer review program that puts technical experts in front of every project above a size threshold, reviewing design drawings, vetting proposed equipment, confirming fire suppression systems are in place, and checking third-party test reports, emergency response plans, and hazard mitigation analyses. Projects receiving state incentive awards go through this layer of scrutiny as a condition of funding. Very few communities living near these proposed projects seem to know that layer exists, which means a state-level solution and a community-level fear are running in parallel, as if unaware of each other. Information and trust broke down because nobody built a shared understanding before it was urgently needed. Developers typically don’t live in the communities where they’re proposing projects, which raises a fair question on both sides: How does that engagement avoid feeling staged, and how is a community supposed to know what to ask for or how to respond? What is Required There’s a version of developer-community engagement that gets this sequencing right from the start

artigo.texto: Washington County to consider yearlong pause on data centers The Washington County Quorum Court held a County Services Committee meeting on Monday. One of the issues discussed at Monday's meeting was a proposed yearlong moratorium on data centers in Washington County. The committee debated the item and discussed amendments that would be made to the original draft. The item was passed by the committee and will move to quorum court for a formal discussion and potential vote. The next Washington County Quorum Court meeting is scheduled for Thursday, Nov. 19. Evelyn Rios Stafford, the Justice of the Peace for District 12, is one of the supporters of the moratorium. She said that the proposed moratorium would allow time for the quorum court to look over planning and zoning rules. "We've heard a lot of concerns over the last year from residents of our county. They see data centers opening up in other places. And they are concerned about the amount of electricity they use, the amount of water. Is it going to raise people's utility bills? Are they going to create noise if they come into our county? And so I think we need to take the time and take a pause in order to see what we need to do to protect our residents," Rios Stafford said. According to Rios Stafford, there are currently no plans for data centers in Washington County.

artigo.texto: North Dakota Town Bucks Backlash, Welcomes Data Center In a year when voters across the country largely tried to slam the brakes on new data centers, one tiny North Dakota town hit the gas, the Washington Post reports. Residents of Harwood, population 845, rejected a ballot measure that would have forced independent reviews and public hearings for big industrial projects, effectively clearing the way for a $3 billion, 1.8-million-square-foot data center on the edge of town. The measure failed by roughly 3-to-1, Fortune reports, even as national exit polls showed 76% of voters opposed to new data centers in their communities and most skeptical of AI's impact. Harwood's mayor argued the project was inevitable—if not in Harwood, it would likely still have ended up nearby—that the town should be the one to capture its projected $1.65 million in annual property taxes and 200 or so new jobs. Opponents warned of environmental risks, noise, and future cleanup costs—but were decisively outvoted. artigo.texto: Geraldo Campos Jr., Marisa Wanzeller e Lais Carregosa, da Agência iNFRA As negociações dentro do governo em torno do Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter) avançaram, segundo relataram interlocutores à Agência iNFRA. No entanto, há alguns aspectos relacionados ao setor elétrico que ainda precisam ser pacificados, dentre eles, a possível exigência de aquisição de energia nova para abastecimento dos data centers. A expectativa é que o decreto seja publicado ainda em novembro, após a participação do presidente Lula na COP31, na Turquia. O setor aguarda o governo definir se será necessário que os empreendimentos comprem energia de usinas novas, construídas para o seu abastecimento, ou recém-construídas, conforme o conceito de “adicionalidade energética”. O tema divide agentes no setor. Outra negociação ainda na mesa é quanto à cobrança de encargos dos data centers. Segundo interlocutores, os investidores querem ser isentos do pagamento da CDE (Conta de Desenvolvimento Energético) por meio da celebração de contratos de autoprodução por equiparação. Também é esperada a lista de fontes de geração que serão aceitas, com expectativas do segmento de gás natural para que a molécula seja incluída. Adicionalidade A exigência de novas usinas para atender os data centers não é um consenso. De um lado, há empresas que veem na adicionalidade uma possibilidade de expansão dos negócios. Do outro, há geradores com usinas que ficarão descontratadas que miram esse mercado e avaliam que erguer novas plantas de geração tiraria a competitividade dos projetos e acarretaria custos para o sistema elétrico. Na última sexta-feira (6), o presidente Lula falou sobre o tema e defendeu que os empreendimentos de data centers construam suas usinas. O presidente disse que os centros consomem muita energia e que “quem vier investir [que] construa a sua própria energia”. Ele continuou: “Não vai ser a energia do povo que vai ser usada para data center”. A preocupação está em linha com o que se observa em países onde o desenvolvimento de data centers já está mais avançado, como os Estados Unidos. Lá, a população viu a conta de energia aumentar em algumas regiões. Autoprodução Também circula nos bastidores que o Ministério da Fazenda levou à mesa de discussão uma proposta para que os empreendimentos sejam enquadrados como autoprodutores de energia. Dessa forma, os data centers ficariam isentos do pagamento da CDE – a conta que reúne os custos dos subsídios do setor elétrico. Com a possibilidade aventada, os técnicos do MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) fazem agora o cálculo dos impactos dessa renúncia. Eles analisam se é possível “reduzir os danos”, disseram fontes. Na autoprodução por equiparação, o consumidor da energia se torna acionista da SPE (Sociedade de Propósito Específico) da usina. Dessa forma, é equiparado ao autoprodutor “clássico” – que investiu em geração própria para atender ao empreendimento consumidor. Gás natural Quanto às fontes de suprimento, a resistência de parte do governo federal à inclusão do gás natural está menor, segundo pessoas a par das tratativas. Agora, a tendência é que o decreto contemple o insumo, ainda que com condicionantes, como compensação pelas emissões de carbono. Os secretários-executivos dos ministérios de Minas e Energia, da Fazenda, da Indústria e Comércio e da Casa Civil reuniram-se na última semana, ocasião em que o MME defendeu o gás natural. Interlocutores afirmam que a Fazenda – que vinha travando a entrada do gás – passou a admitir a possibilidade de incluir a fonte. Falta, agora, fechar o modelo das condicionantes. No MME, a intenção é que as compensações de carbono mantenham os projetos de gás viáveis. No setor, no entanto, os agentes estão preocupados com os termos, que podem onerar os investimentos e acabar restringindo, na prática, a implementação de térmicas a gás para abastecer os data centers. Algumas possíveis formas de compensação aventadas nos bastidores são o uso de tecnologia de CCUS (Captura, Utilização e Armazenamento de Carbono, na sigla em inglês) ou a aquisição de créditos de carbono. Riscos Agentes ligados ao segmento de gás natural vinham demonstrando temor com a possibilidade de o gás ficar totalmente fora da regulamentação do Redata. Agora, admitem que esse risco é menor, mas ainda agem com cautela e dizem que será preciso ver os termos impostos pelo governo nas condicionantes. Uma regulamentação restritiva por causa das condicionantes, segundo um executivo, pode afastar investimentos em térmicas colocalizadas com data centers e pressionar as tarifas de energia. Isso porque os centros de dados poderiam ter de usar energia da rede nos horários com escassez de energia renovável, aumentando a demanda por potência. Caso o decreto vete ou restrinja o gás, o setor cogita buscar alterar os termos da regulamentação via Congresso. Isso poderia ser feito por meio de um PDL (Projeto de Decreto Legislativo). “Ficou claro que o Legislativo, ao aprovar o Redata, não quis restringir nenhum combustível de baixa emissão, como o gás natural”, comentou um agente termelétrico. Por outro lado, os geradores renováveis apontam que as termelétricas a gás natural emitem mais carbono do que os limites estabelecidos internacionalmente, de aproximadamente 0,10 tonelada de gás carbônico por MWh (megawatt-hora). Dessa forma, essas usinas não se enquadrariam na exigência da lei. Atraso O diretor de Relações Institucionais e Governamentais da Brasscom (Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação e de Tecnologias Digitais do Brasil), Sergio Sgobbi, diz que a demora na regulamentação tem afastado os investidores, que estão buscando outras alternativas. Ele aponta que é essencial a publicação das regras de habilitação e coabilitação dos empreendimentos, e a lista de equipamentos que terão os tributos federais desonerados para aquisição. “Enquanto a regulamentação não vier a público, tudo é incerto e, diante da incerteza, o investimento não

artigo.texto: A new database of local government meeting records puts a hard number on something planners have heard in hearing rooms all year. Prophecy Gov, a San Francisco AI startup, operates a tool called American Sentiment, and it classified 90.5% of 10,202 public comments about data centers as negative, according to TechRadar’s coverage of the report. The comments came from 906 public meetings held by 417 local governments across 48 states during 2026. Headline writers boiled that down to “America hates data centers.” That phrase is headline wording, not an on-record statement from a named person, and the data does not say 90.5% of Americans oppose data centers. It says that when residents speak at the microphone, they mostly speak against. The finding arrives in a year when siting fights have moved from zoning footnotes to front-page politics. Our earlier look at the 41 data center ballot measures that put the AI boom on notice covered the voting side. This story covers the hearing-room side, and for anyone who buys or builds cloud capacity, it matters just as much. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What American Sentiment Actually Measured American Sentiment is a database, not a survey. Prophecy Gov collected public comments made at local government meetings, then classified each one by tone. The comments were not solicited, weighted, or balanced against a population sample. Residents chose to speak, and the tool recorded what they said. That design has real strengths. Public comment is where land-use decisions get shaped, and local boards often cite what they hear from residents when they vote on rezoning, tax abatements, or utility agreements. A dataset of 10,202 comments across 48 states gives researchers something they rarely had before: a searchable record of the arguments people actually make in the room. The classification split is stark. Beyond the 90.5% negative share, 7% of comments expressed support for a potential nearby data center, and 2.5% asked questions. Those three buckets account for the whole dataset. In other words, almost nobody in these meetings arrived undecided and left with a neutral note on the record. TechRadar framed the result with the “America hates data centers” headline, and other outlets echoed the sentiment. The underlying dataset is more careful than the headline. It measures comment tone at 2026 meetings, nothing more. Keep that boundary in mind through the rest of this analysis, because the gap between “comments” and “public opinion” is where most of the debate will happen. The Numbers at a Glance The table below collects every figure reported so far from the American Sentiment database. No price data, technical specifications, or named speaker quotes have surfaced in the coverage, so this is the full quantitative picture as of November 09, 2026. Two details deserve a second look. First, the 73% figure describes meetings, not comments, so it measures how often a hearing featured zero supporters. Second, water is named as the top concern, but the reports available so far do not give a percentage for it. Anyone citing a specific water share is guessing. Why 90.5% Is Not a National Poll The most important caveat is also the simplest. The dataset measures the comments collected, and those comments are not a representative national opinion poll. A poll draws a sample that mirrors the population. A public comment period draws whoever shows up, and showing up takes time, motivation, and often a personal stake. Who shows up at the microphone People who live next to a proposed site have the strongest reason to attend. They worry about noise, traffic, property values, and power lines. People who might benefit from a data center, such as future employees, local suppliers, or residents who like lower property tax rates, have a diffuse stake and little reason to give up an evening. That asymmetry is old, and planners know it well. The self-selection problem cuts both ways Self-selection inflates opposition in the raw numbers, but it does not make the opposition fake. Local boards act on what they hear. If 9 in 10 speakers oppose a project, elected officials feel that pressure whether or not a silent majority would have voted differently. For developers, the comment record matters as a political force even if it fails as a statistical sample. The sensible reading: American Sentiment tells us what local decision-makers are hearing, not what the country thinks. Those are different questions, and only the first one drives permit votes. The 7% Support Gap and the 73% of Empty Support Benches Seven percent of comments backed a nearby data center. That sounds small, and in raw terms it is. Using the reported shares, it works out to roughly 714 supportive comments out of 10,202. The more telling number is the meeting-level one: 73% of tracked meetings had no supporters at all. Run the arithmetic and the picture sharpens. About 661 of the 906 meetings featured no one speaking in favor, which leaves roughly 245 meetings with at least one supportive voice. In those 245 hearings, supporters were still outnumbered overall, since the 90.5% negative share holds across the whole dataset. total_comments = 10202 meetings = 906 negative = total_comments * 0.905 # ~9,233 support = total_comments * 0.07 # ~714 questions = total_comments * 0.025 # ~255 mention_ai = total_comments * 0.21 # ~2,142 no_support_meetings = meetings * 0.73 # ~661 with_support = meetings - no_support_meetings # ~245 comments_per_meeting = total_comments / meetings # ~11.3 These counts are our own rounding of the reported percentages, so treat them as approximations rather than figures published by Prophecy Gov. artigo.texto: KINGSTON, N.Y. — The city is seeking city residents to apply to serve on its new Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Task Force. Mayor Steve Noble’s office said task force members will review the city Zoning Working Group’s proposal and “offer their perspectives to ensure the city’s form-based code adequately addresses land-use, environmental, and thermal runaway safety challenges associated with commercial battery arrays.” The BESS Task Force will consist of 10 members, including two City Council members, City staff, representatives from the Conservation Advisory Council and Climate Smart Action Committee, and two City residents appointed by Common Council President Andrea Shaut. City residents interested in applying can complete a short application https://www.surveymonkey.com/r/CWZCNB9. The application deadline is Monday, Nov. 16. In October, the city’s Common Council voted unanimously to create the task force with a goal of drafting zoning regulations for utility-scale battery energy storage systems after proposals for such facilities have caused controversy in neighboring communities. Such facilities consist of lithium-iron-phosphate battery cells packaged into modules, about the size of oversized briefcases, which are then put into racks and stored in containers resembling shipping containers. The facilities require proximity to a utility’s substation. The five proposals in Ulster County — three in the town of Ulster, one in Saugerties and one in New Paltz — are all proposed near a Central Hudson substation. So far, no utility-scale battery energy storage systems have been proposed within city limits, and lawmakers have even questioned the feasibility of locating such a facility within city limits. Proposed lithium-ion battery energy storage projects, including the three projects proposed in the neighboring town of Ulster, have met with controversy across the county. Two of those projects, on Hurley Avenue in the town of Ulster, are close to the city line Mission Clean Energy has proposed a 120-megawatt lithium-ion battery facility on a 7.3-acre site at 463-465 Hurley Ave. That project is about 500 feet west of the controversial Terra-Gen site at the former John A. Coleman Catholic High School, where the Town Board is being asked to approve a 250-megawatt lithium-ion facility on 15 acres. In the town of Ulster, board members are also reviewing a proposal from BayWa r.e. for a 150-megawatt lithium-ion battery facility on Frank Sottile Boulevard. It would be on about 10.4 acres adjacent to the former town landfill, with a new substation constructed on the other side of the road. It would be adjacent to a residential neighborhood and the 164-unit Ulster Gardens apartment complex. In the town of Saugerties, Key Capture Energy has proposed a 100-megawatt facility on Tomson’s Road near a Central Hudson substation that has met with opposition from residents and calls from Saugerties village officials for a moratorium on such projects and most recently led to sparring between members of the public and a Saugerties Town Board member at an October Town Board meeting. For questions about the Kingston BESS Task Force, email Shaut at ashaut@kingston-ny.gov.

artigo.texto: CATL and Dongfeng reportedly signed a group-level agreement on ultra-fast charging and battery swapping on October 29, 2026. Separate talks over Shenxing III’s first vehicle launch were reported as unsettled on November 3, so the agreement and the battery’s potential debut are distinct developments. China EV Signal reported the agreement’s scope, while CarNewsChina reported the status of the launch talks. A charging time is useful only when you know the starting and ending charge levels. What the CATL-Dongfeng agreement covers The reported agreement concerns cooperation on ultra-fast charging and battery swapping. The separate negotiations concern first-launch rights for Shenxing III, CATL’s lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery. CarNewsChina said those talks had begun in the second quarter of 2026 and were still unsettled in its November 3 report. How CATL explains Shenxing III’s design In a technical presentation, CATL compares Shenxing III cells measuring 300 millimeters with “common” 400-millimeter cells. Its presenter says shortening a cell by 100 millimeters cuts heat generation by 20%. A separate report attributed another figure to CATL: a 20% improvement in thermal efficiency from its cooling system. Thermal efficiency and heat generation are different measures. In the presentation, CATL also puts the cells’ internal resistance at 0.25 milliohms and claims they retain more than 90% of their capacity after 1,000 ultra-fast charging cycles. What CATL’s charging times say CATL claims Shenxing III can charge from 10% to 35% in one minute and from 10% to 80% in 3 minutes 44 seconds. The company also claims a 10C equivalent charging rate, with peaks of 15C. Just Auto reported these figures. The 6-minute-27-second result has two reported endpoints: Just Auto and Híbridos y Eléctricos give 10% to 98%, while InsideEVs reports 10% to 90%. CATL’s separate cold-weather claim is a charge from 20% to 98% in about nine minutes at −30°C, as reported by Just Auto.

That kind of check focuses attention on who supplies the heavy equipment and grid muscle behind the hype. This piece walks through three stocks exposed to that same story, and how this AI power grab might shape their risk and reward. The stocks highlighted below are just a sample. The full screen surfaces 26 more power infrastructure suppliers whose data center and AI stories are not covered here but follow a similar theme. To identify and analyze those potential opportunities in more detail, head straight into the Power Infrastructure Suppliers to Data Center and AI Growth screener. ERock (EROC) ERock gives the screener a pure play on dedicated power for energy hungry data centers, with modular gas units aimed at operators that want their own generation capacity rather than waiting in long utility queues. ERock, Inc. designs and operates modular distributed power systems for U.S. commercial and industrial users, closely aligned with data centers and utilities that want dedicated on site generation. The business generated about $162 million from electric equipment and has a market value near $1.9 billion. "Longer gas turbine lead times and multi year interconnection queues are pushing customers toward modular, quicker to deploy options like RockBlock. This can support utilization of the Hyperion facility and potentially improve gross margins as assembly volumes rise." What happens to ERock's earnings path if a single assumption around that growing pool of long-term AI power projects shifts direction? If that pivot point matters to your thesis, read the full narrative for ERock to see how competing AI power contracts, capital needs and policy shifts could reshape ERock's trajectory. Generac Holdings (GNRC) Generac Holdings is one of the clearest plays on the screener's theme, supplying the heavy backup and prime power gear that keeps large data centers and AI campuses online when the grid cannot. It is a global energy technology group with most revenue coming from the U.S. at about US$3.8b and roughly US$900 million from international markets, and the stock is valued at about US$10.4b. For data center investors, Generac Holdings is where the power problem turns into a concrete product story, with heavy equipment, long contracts and a growing role in keeping AI servers running when the grid is stretched. "Accelerating AI driven build outs of hyperscale and colocated data centers are now supported by Generac Holdings having about US$450m of expected 2026 data center revenue, a US$1.6b dedicated backlog, and multiple multiyear hyperscale agreements including an Amazon deal projected at about US$2.4b of deliveries in 2027 to 2028."

artigo.texto: Editor’s note: This month, we offer views from the left and right on issues around artificial intelligence. To our columnists: What’s your take on the growing use of AI in our society and how it will likely impact our region? Do local communities have a responsibility to oppose or support the data centers that power AI? by Carl Mumpower and Bill Branyon On the right Carl Mumpower: Let’s answer the last question first. Support for local AI data centers? Not an issue. We’re too expensive. Poor counties will win that lottery. But there could be an upside to being neighborly. When the Terminators start showing up, it’ll give antifa a productive mission. On the rest, with one exclusion, we’re stuck with speculation. The exception? Western North Carolina is blessed to exist on a self-correcting planet. Anything coming from man will thus (1) contain built-in limitations and (2) hide opportunities amid the miseries. In other words, AI is going to bring our region good and bad, dependably countered by the law of unintended consequences. Some of the AI good will include: complex, lightning-speed answers to questions; extraordinary efficiency potential for business, industry and government; unprecedented information access and research simplification; vastly expanded automated manufacturing capacity; hyperefficient bookkeeping, record and data keeping; reduced costs and better patient care through dramatically expanded medical best-practice protocols; crime reduction through universally shared antisocial-behavior tracking and accountability enforcement; and personalization abilities that will find AI behaving more pleasantly than most humans. The bad? Autonomy, liberty and anonymity will be at increased risk; our capacity to militarily kill one another will be gravely expanded; a good number of people — through job obsolescence — will have to become mechanics, plumbers, nurses or something else useful that AI can’t do; without care, education will become less about learning and more about figuring out how to disguise the use of AI to shortcut assignments; surveillance will expand far beyond our imagination in all urban settings; and socialism and the Chinese Communist governance model will be unleashed, while democracy will have to struggle mightily toward self-preservation. Things to remember as we construct our anticipatory anxiety script? AOL’s anticipated internet dominance; premature assertions about the demise of paper; Y2K disaster presumptions; catastrophic climate change forecasts; COVID-19 protocol assurances; hysterical MAGA outcome predictions; the end of decayed dinosaur carcasses as a source of petroleum; and the notion that LED light bulbs would last 20 years. Further considerations? Watch out — it turns out that AI is lazy. It digs down as few layers as necessary to produce a “satisfactory” answer to most questions and service requests. Birthed out of the hands of man, we should’ve seen this one coming. Back in the ’80s, John Naisbitt’s book Megatrends: Ten New Directions Transforming Our Lives was all the rage. Among his suggestions was that the future would find us living in a high-tech, high-touch world. He got the first part right. AI — crafted toward an appealing personality — may finally add a softer texture to our heretofore increasingly low-touch crabbiness. There’s one more little teeny-weeny problem. AI is also sociopathic. Various dictionaries define the term as lacking a sense of morality, conscience and/or social accountability. Considering the international cast of characters crafting AI’s springboard, should we be concerned with HAL’s sociopathic potentials? You bet. It is my pleasure to gift you with this human intelligence-generated chew toy. “With artificial intelligence we are summoning the demon.” — Elon Musk On the left Bill Branyon: “I’m sorry, Dave. I’m afraid I can’t do that,” said HAL the computer as it refused to save Dave the astronaut in 2001: A Space Odyssey. Then came Star Trek’s relentless Borg, Matrix movies, I Robot’s endless hordes and scores of other such movies to get us in the habit of fearing AI. Then Bill Gates piggybacked on this cinematic dread by insisting, “We have to acknowledge that AI is almost uniquely dangerous because it’s unbounded in how good it will get.” Elon “USAID murderer” Musk added that AI is a “fundamental risk to the existence of human civilization.” Then Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger made the misanthropic statement that there’s a greater than 10% chance that “AI could kill all humans … within the next decade.” What bonkers bravado it takes for those tech bros to claim they can dominate in a few years what evolution took 3.8 billion years to create: humanity. On the other hand, what could be a better sales pitch than blaring that AI is so powerful it’ll destroy everyone? The snake-oil bros are either consciously or unconsciously hustling us. AI is probably about 10% amazing substance and 90% hubristic hype. Perhaps that’s why there’s such a rush to attach some concrete substance to it in the form of building thousands of gigantic data centers? A Michigan Advance article republished in The Washington Post says yes to that question, contending that the scurry to build data centers will make tech bro CEOs even more billions. Yet, as Martin Kushler notes in the article, when you Google data-center products, “you frankly get a bunch of nebulous buzzwords like ‘cloud computing’ … ‘high-performance computing’ and ‘edge services.’” So “for the small investors at the bottom, one has to wonder whether this is a 21st-century ‘tulip mania’” — a reference to the 1634-37 Dutch frenzy for new colors of tulips that inspired the first speculative bubble in history. Now, even AI-obsessed Jeff Bezos contends AI “is a kind of industrial bubble.” How many millions of people will it financially destroy when it pops? artigo.texto: BYD planeja investir R$ 1 bi em nova fábrica no Brasil Nova unidade da montadora chinesa produzirá vans elétricas e caminhões; empreendimento deve criar 2.000 empregos A montadora chinesa BYD planeja investir R$ 1 bilhão na instalação de uma nova fábrica de vans elétricas e caminhões no Brasil. O empreendimento deve criar 2.000 empregos, de 2028 a 2029. As informações foram divulgadas pela CNN Brasil nesta 2ª feira (9.nov.2026). Minas Gerais, São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro disputam a instalação da unidade. A fabricante ainda não definiu a localização e considera os incentivos oferecidos pelos governos estaduais para decidir onde realizará o investimento. Os modelos que serão fabricados no novo complexo também não foram anunciados. A BYD, no entanto, apresentará os caminhões elétricos eT35 e eT75 na Fenatran, feira do setor de transportes que começa nesta 2ª feira (9.nov), em São Paulo. A montadora levará ainda uma versão do eT23 adaptada para o transporte de bebidas. BYD NO BRASIL O projeto faz parte da expansão industrial da BYD no país, iniciada com a abertura do complexo automotivo de Camaçari, na Bahia. Com a nova unidade, a empresa pretende ampliar a atuação no mercado de veículos comerciais e competir com fabricantes tradicionais de vans movidas a diesel. Com investimento anunciado de R$ 11,3 bilhões, o complexo de Camaçari é responsável pela produção dos modelos de carros Dolphin Mini, King, Song Pro e Atto 2. A BYD pretende ampliar a capacidade anual da unidade para 300.000 veículos na próxima etapa de expansão da empresa no país. Em balanço divulgado em 5 de novembro, a montadora informou que a fábrica baiana já ultrapassou a marca de 150 mil veículos produzidos e conta com 9.500 empregos diretos desde a inauguração, em outubro de 2025.

artigo.texto: Trending BOARDMAN -- Don't be quick to dismiss data centers. There's room for talk, understanding and opportunity. That’s the message from an organization of business, union and educational leaders that emerged Monday to promote data center development in the Mahoning Valley. The co-founders of Mahoning Valley Coalition for a 21st Century Economy -- the Youngstown/Warren Regional Chamber and the Western Reserve Building Trades -- said at a news conference that education and conversation are needed to understand how the high-tech facilities can benefit the region and its economy. Their effort is backed by 29 entities -- from Youngstown State University and Brilex Industries to the Cafaro Company and SoftBank Group. "We now have an opportunity, if we do this right, to reverse decades of brain drain, create a 21st century economy that helps us retain our best and brightest, and be the destination for other people's best and brightest," said Guy Coviello, president and CEO of the Regional Chamber. The group's initiative comes as some Valley communities have rejected data center development. Moratoriums have been enacted in Niles, McDonald, Girard, Warren, Newton Falls, Vienna, Howland, Braceville, Boardman, Cortland and Ellsworth Township. Voters in Hubbard voted to ban data centers in last week’s general election. "Come to mutual agreements without moratoriums," Coviello said. "The indirect impact of moratoriums on the data center industry is it sends a message out to all industries that one slight thing and you might slap a moratorium on my industry or my business. "When you say no to data centers, you say no to Hynes Industries. You say no to Wheatland Tube. You say no to Foxconn." The Ohio Supreme Court recently backed the village of Lordstown in a zoning issue involving a data center developer. During her campaign, Gov.-elect Amy Acton said she supported a conditional moratorium on data centers. She set six standards a developer must meet before coming into the state. "As we start talking about bans and moratoriums and different things like that, that’s not the right way to go," said Marty Loney, president of the Western Reserve Building Trades. "What we don’t understand, or what we don’t have, is then an avenue to be able to sit down with these companies and make those community benefit agreements where it works for everybody." Loney said the monetary benefits to the Valley are considerable. "Everybody talks about temporary jobs, right?" he said. "An average-sized data center is about 1,700 construction jobs over a several-year period. That to me doesn’t sound temporary. That sounds like community benefits for our tax base. "It’s a great way for young folks to have a great future here in the Valley." He said the new coalition is designed to deliver accurate information to the public and to dispel fears. "What we can’t lose sight of, though, is that people have legitimate concerns. ... We can't allow a small group of critics to dictate what's best for our local area." Rick Organ, CEO of Austintown-based Hynes Industries, told the audience that the century-old steel company has evolved and grown. Data centers have played a role. "It has profoundly impacted our business in a positive way," he said. "Over the course of the past two years, we have invested over $30 million in our business. We’ve doubled down to produce components and parts into the data center marketplace. "We’ve been in it for a number of years. It represented about 10% of our business as recently as two years ago. Today, it represents 40% of our business." Besides Hynes Industries, supporting the initiative are BBM Railway Equipment; Brilex Industries; Cafaro Company; Discover Global; Edge City; Foxconn; HBK CPAs & Consultants; HSH Contractor; Humtown Products; McDonald Industrial Development; Methodica Capital; North Jackson Commerce Park; Ohio Business Roundtable; Oppidan; Platz Realty Group; QUICKmed; Roemer Industries Inc.; Sharon Tube; SoftBank Group; Sunbelt Solomon; Taylor-Winfield Technologies; Top Property Holdings; Warren Area Chamber of Commerce Economic Development Foundation; Warren Area Chamber of Commerce Education, Civic and Cultural Foundation; Western Reserve Port Authority; Wheatland Tube; Youngstown State University; and Zekelman Industries. Covielli said he and Loney have already met with Boardman Township's zoning commission and the Trumbull County Council of Governments. "We want to continue to offer ourselves to be available to come and speak to any public body that wants to receive our information, our handouts and also to ask us questions directly," he said. That includes trips to communities opposed to data centers. "We’ll certainly go everywhere that we are welcome to go and meet with folks."

artigo.texto: Feds ask for proposals for industrial use of Hanford land. Data centers possible The Department of Energy issued a request for industry proposals Friday to use up to 3,700 acres of unneeded Hanford nuclear site land in Eastern Washington for industrial projects. The uses to be considered could include data centers or other computing capabilities, new energy generation, advanced manufacturing or development of critical materials. The land under consideration includes 1,876 acres of federal land along Route 4 South to the south of Energy Northwest’s commercial nuclear power plant, but on the other side of Route 4. It is immediately north of former Hanford land transferred by DOE to the Tri-Cities community in 2015 for industrial development through the efforts of the Tri-City Development Council. That acreage is listed by DOE as “available” and the remaining 1,249 acres is to the west of that tract and is listed by DOE as potentially available. DOE could enter into one or more long-term realty agreements at those sites, with all funding for work to come from those holding the new agreements. “With our Hanford team delivering historic cleanup progress, now is the time to invest in a community that has shouldered the burden of the past for far too long,” said Tim Walsh, DOE assistant secretary for environmental management. “At a site where too many see only challenges, I see opportunities for revitalization and new generational and life-changing jobs as we clean the legacy of the past to power a future built on affordable American energy, high-paying jobs, innovation and enduring economic vitality,” he said. Under the American Energy Hubs initiative, DOE is repurposing land once needed for wartime use, including developing nuclear weapons during World War II and the Cold War, for industrial use. The Hanford nuclear site adjacent to Richland was used from World War II through the Cold War to produce almost two-thirds of the plutonium for the nation’s nuclear weapons program. Hanford industrial land use plan The Tri-City Development Council sees the request for industry proposals, which DOE calls a “Request for Offer,” as closely aligning with the community’s vision for using some Hanford land for industrial development of base-load energy generation, such as new nuclear energy. The Comprehensive Land Use Plan for the Hanford site calls for most of the DOE land to be used for preservation and conservation. A limited portion, about 10%, is designated for industrial development to help replace Hanford jobs as environmental cleanup is completed. Now environmental cleanup is underway on radioactive and hazardous chemical waste and contamination at places around the site, with much of the site’s land never used for plutonium production or waste disposal. Most of the remaining Hanford cleanup is north of the area being considered for industrial development. TRIDEC sees the types of projects that could be considered, including nuclear energy projects, advanced manufacturing, data centers or related industries, as a good fit, especially for nearby Richland, said David Reeploeg, TRIDEC vice president of federal programs. “They have the potential to create a lot of additional good-paying jobs (and) further grow and diversity our economy,” he said. “We’re really excited about DOE now taking the next step into making this a reality.” As any plans proceed, TRIDEC wants to work closely with tribes, which have cultural resources they want to protect and treaty rights at Hanford, Reeploeg said. “We look forward to working collaboratively with the Tri-Cities community and the best of private industry as we accelerate cleanup and explore the art of the possible,” said Ray Geimer, the DOE manager for Hanford. “Exploring these opportunities is the next logical step for a site that is advancing cleanup and for a community that has always been all in on the all-of-the above American energy and innovation.” Protecting Richland power Proposals for the industrial land will be evaluated for technological readiness, financial viability and detailed plans to complete regulatory and permitting requirements. Consideration also will be given to compatibility with existing local redevelopment plans and potential partnerships with tribal and local businesses, according to DOE. Responses from interested businesses are due Jan. 29. Applicants who are selected will be responsible for building, operating and decommissioning each project and must secure utility interconnection agreements, according to DOE. Applicants may propose projects on all or a portion of available land, and DOE may consider multiple projects. It also says that project owners must adhere to President Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, which is designed to protect local power users as data centers are built. Companies would be responsible for new power generation resources and the cost of all power delivery infrastructure. The Hanford site is positioned to attract major private development because of its skilled trade workforce, DOE’s Pacific Northwest National Laboratory in Richland, its economic development leaders and community attitudes, according to DOE. Nuclear power center “We feel like there’s the potential for any number of different types of development on this land,” Reeploeg said. “We’re especially excited about the potential for new nuclear, whether it’s expanding what Energy Northwest is already planning on doing or other potential new nuclear opportunities.” Energy Northwest is working with Amazon to deploy an X-energy reactor, a small advanced nuclear reactor, on the land it leases near Richland. New energy generation could be combined with energy-intensive industries, whether that is data centers or advanced manufacturing, he said. DOE’s request for proposals give an opportunity to create a master plan for the development for best use of industrial resources, he said. artigo.texto: Bolivar city council discusses possible data center moratorium BOLIVAR, Tenn. (WBBJ) - Bolivar City Council members discussed a possible moratorium related to data centers as they consider how such a facility could affect the community. Mayor Julian McTizic said an inquiry was made about a potential data center at the city’s industrial complex, but it did not lead to a property sale. “The council just decided not to take any action but also make sure we do some studies on what it will look like for a data center to be in our community,” McTizic said. McTizic said multiple people have expressed interest in coming to the community, although he has not recruited data centers. Some community members have raised questions about the potential financial and environmental effects of a data center. Bolivar sits along the Hatchie River, which Councilwoman Caroline Miller described as an important local resource. “We are here on the Hatchie River. That’s one of our greatest resources,” Miller said. “We have water and, you know, we want to maintain that. We want to honor that.” City leaders said they want to stay ahead of the issue, be transparent and keep the community informed as they consider potential interest in a data center before property is purchased. Members of the public were given an opportunity to address the council during the meeting, but no one spoke. Copyright 2026 WBBJ. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: A corrida pelo avanço dos modelos de inteligência artificial provocou um salto dramático na demanda por recursos hídricos ao redor do mundo. Empreendimentos de grande porte chegam a retirar 5 milhões de galões de água por dia para evitar o superaquecimento de servidores, sobrecarregando o abastecimento público em regiões castigadas pela estiagem. Por que os chips de inteligência artificial exigem tanta água? O processamento ininterrupto de redes neurais profundas exige milhares de placas de processamento gráfico operando em capacidade máxima. Essa densidade de circuitos concentrada em gabinetes fechados gera um volume de calor residual que inviabiliza o uso exclusivo de ventiladores convencionais de ar. Para resfriar essa infraestrutura com baixo custo financeiro, a indústria adota torres de arrefecimento evaporativo. Nesse processo, o calor das máquinas é transferido para a água líquida, que evapora na atmosfera e impede o derretimento dos semicondutores durante as operações de cálculo. Quanto representa o consumo diário de 5 milhões de galões na prática? A retirada contínua de água potável por um único galpão tecnológico altera de forma profunda a disponibilidade hídrica dos municípios vizinhos às centrais de dados. Para mensurar a proporção desse impacto frente ao uso humano e urbano tradicional, examine o comparativo volumétrico estruturado na tabela a seguir: Como a evaporação nas torres sobrecarrega bacias e lençóis freáticos? Ao contrário do uso doméstico, em que a água consumida retorna à rede coletora como esgoto para ser tratado, o resfriamento de computadores consome a água de forma consuntiva definitiva. Cerca de 80% do volume captado se transforma em vapor e se dissipa com as correntes de vento, sem recarregar o rio ou aquífero de origem. Esse esvaziamento silencioso dos mananciais foi detalhado pelo Environmental and Energy Study Institute ao analisar o impacto hídrico de servidores. Em regiões agrícolas de clima semiárido, a captação maciça rebaixa o nível dos poços artesianos e compromete a irrigação de lavouras vizinhas durante o verão. Conflito pelo Acesso à Água A instalação de polos tecnológicos em áreas com risco de seca gera disputas administrativas por outorgas públicas, obrigando prefeituras a escolher entre a atração de investimentos e a segurança de abastecimento da população. Leia também: A ilha brasileira que existe há 435 anos e conquista quem procura uma vida mais tranquila perto do mar Quais alternativas de engenharia reduzem o gasto de água nas instalações? Para mitigar a dependência de reservatórios potáveis e responder a novas exigências regulatórias, projetistas desenvolvem métodos térmicos que operam em circuito fechado ou aproveitam fontes residuais. Entre as principais tecnologias disponíveis para substituir as torres evaporativas convencionais, destacam-se as seguintes frentes: - ❄️ Sistemas em circuito fechado: Radiadores que recirculam o mesmo líquido em tubulações seladas, impedindo a perda de vapor para o ar. - 🔬 Imersão direta em fluido dielétrico: Servidores submersos em óleo mineral sintético que conduz o calor sem contato com água líquida. - 🚰 Água de reuso industrial: Utilização de efluentes sanitários tratados de estações municipais no lugar de água potável encanada. Quais são as principais dúvidas sobre o uso de água na inteligência artificial? O consumo oculto gerado pelo uso de ferramentas digitais no dia a dia levanta questionamentos sobre a pegada ecológica dos servidores. Veja os esclarecimentos a seguir: Perguntas Frequentes Esclareça o impacto ambiental dos centros de dados A expansão da infraestrutura digital global depende da superação do desperdício de água potável no resfriamento mecânico. A adoção de circuitos fechados e o uso de águas residuais tratadas são os caminhos necessários para viabilizar a tecnologia sem esgotar bacias essenciais à sobrevivência das cidades.

artigo.texto: Google Adds TPU 8tx, 8i Max for Enterprise AI Google Cloud is expanding its TPU lineup with one chip for secure AI workloads and another for higher-capacity inference with large context windows. To meet growing demand for AI inference, Google Cloud on Monday beefed up its Tensor Processing Unit family with two new chips: a more secure version of its TPU 8t accelerator and a higher-capacity version of its TPU 8i inference chip. The new processors are designed to address two emerging enterprise requirements: stronger protection for sensitive AI workloads and better performance for agentic AI applications with large context windows, said Mark Lohmeyer, vice president and general manager of AI and computing infrastructure at Google Cloud. The announcements build on Google Cloud’s eighth-generation TPU chips introduced in April. At that time, the company launched TPU 8t for training, which it said delivers up to 2.7 times better training performance than the prior generation, and TPU 8i for inference, which it said offers 80% better inference price-performance. TPU 8tx Adds Security; TPU 8i Max Boosts Capacity One of the new accelerators, TPU 8tx, is built on the same silicon as TPU 8t and adds hardware-level encryption for secure inference and small-scale training. The chip is paired with custom AMD CPU hosts to help protect and isolate sensitive data and model weights, even while inference is actively running, Lohmeyer said during a media briefing. Google Cloud also introduced TPU 8i Max, a variant aimed at enterprises running increasingly agentic workloads with large context windows. Lohmeyer said the chip is intended to address memory constraints by effectively “adding more lanes to the highway.” To create TPU 8i Max, Google Cloud combined two TPU 8i chips into a single package, doubling compute, SRAM, and HBM bandwidth compared with TPU 8i, the company said. TPU 8i Max delivers 384 GB of high-bandwidth memory, Lohmeyer said. “We’re just seeing tremendous demand for the TPU platform and systems,” Lohmeyer said during the briefing. He added that Google Cloud is also seeing a broadening of AI use cases, including demand for confidential computing and for agentic inference with very large context windows while maintaining strong performance. Custom TPUs Could Sharpen Google Cloud’s Edge Dave McCarthy, group vice president at IDC, said Google Cloud’s move toward more specialized custom AI chips could help it further differentiate itself from rival cloud providers. “The fact that Google was able to launch the 8i and 8t earlier this year, and now they’re coming out with these new ones within the same calendar year, is just showing the pace of innovation,” McCarthy said. “They’re showing their commitment to R&D to build this stuff. And if what they’re saying is true – twice the bandwidth, all these new features – that’s showing they’re potentially outpacing the competition in terms of new product releases.” McCarthy described confidential computing as an emerging requirement for AI workloads. Cloud providers have traditionally focused on protecting data in transit and at rest, he said, whereas confidential computing is intended to protect data in use. “If Google can come out with a strong confidential compute story, it kind of gives them a little bit of an edge,” said McCarthy, adding that Nvidia is still developing its strategy in this area. Google Cloud also said TPU 8i Max allows more silicon to fit within an existing rack footprint, enabling significantly more computing power per square foot and per watt in its data centers. That could help Google Cloud increase capacity without adding more racks or building more data centers, at least in the near term, potentially easing some of the capacity pressures facing the industry, McCarthy said. More broadly, McCarthy said Google Cloud’s strategy of continually enhancing its silicon and making TPUs available through other providers could expand the company’s market reach while creating an additional revenue stream. Oracle recently announced it would make TPU chips available to customers of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. During the media briefing, Lohmeyer also said Google Cloud would allow select customers to deploy the TPU 8tx in their own data centers.

artigo.texto: TIM vai conectar fábrica e carros da BYD TIM Brasil vai conectar fábricas e carros da BYD A TIM Brasil e a BYD fecharam acordo que permitirá à montadora chinesa ampliar a disponibilidade e a gama de serviços digitais em seus veículos, além de conectar a infraestrutura de seu complexo industrial em Camaçari (BA) com tecnologia 4G e 5G. A parceria prevê a instalação de uma rede celular privativa - exclusiva para a BYD - cobrindo as linhas de produção da montadora na Bahia. As empresas não divulgaram o valor a ser investido. “Nós estamos falando de máquinas, equipamentos, sistemas, controles, acessos, pessoas, carros. É um ecossistema geral. [...] É uma infraestrutura ‘outdoor’ [externa] e uma ‘indoor’ [interna] que ela [TIM] terá essa responsabilidade de tocar: a fábrica e essa interação com todos os sistemas de operação, de industrialização, de controles”, explicou Alexandre Baldy, vice-presidente sênior da BYD do Brasil, em entrevista ao Valor. A expectativa é de que a rede privativa contribua para aumentar a eficiência da cadeia de suprimentos, além de conectar os trabalhadores espalhados pelo complexo industrial, já em atividade, que deverá ter 2,2 milhões de metros quadrados de área construída, num terreno de 4,6 milhões de metros quadrados. “Temos atualmente 9.520 colaboradores, [...] mas hoje, durante as 24 horas de um dia, você tem ali 14 mil, 15 mil pessoas transitando dentro do nosso parque industrial”, contabiliza Baldy. Para além do nicho de redes privativas, a parceria com a montadora marca também a mais recente investida da TIM no chamado mercado de serviços B2B2C, aqueles em que uma empresa presta serviço a outra companhia, que por sua vez atende o consumidor final. A operadora conecta mais de 630 mil veículos à internet, como parte de um acordo anunciado em 2020 com a Fiat Chrysler Automóveis (FCA), que posteriormente incorporou o grupo PSA, transformando-se na Stellantis. “Hoje já estamos emplacando, essencialmente, 60% das vendas de carros conectados”, diz Alberto Griselli, diretor-presidente da TIM Brasil. A frota de carros eletrificados (elétricos e híbridos) da BYD que circula no país soma quase 400 mil veículos, segundo estimativa da própria montadora. A partir do acordo com a TIM Brasil, cuja cobertura 4G abrange 100% dos municípios brasileiros e a 5G alcança 1.171 cidades, toda essa base de veículos será beneficiada, afirma Baldy. Serviços disponíveis via smartphone para clientes da BYD - como controle do ar-condicionado, abertura e fechamento das portas, aquecimento dos bancos e localização do veículo - terão sua área de cobertura ampliada. Além disso, haverá novas opções de interatividade. A cobrança pelos serviços de conectividade não será feita do usuário final, mas da montadora, como parte de um modelo de negócios B2B2C. Dentro da estratégia da TIM para o mercado corporativo, a Internet dos Veículos (IoV) - uma variante da Internet das Coisas (IoT) - é uma forma de a operadora monetizar seu investimento na cobertura móvel de rodovias. Ao fim do segundo trimestre, a TIM contabilizava mais de 13,7 mil quilômetros em rodovias cobertas. Uma alternativa natural para ampliar essa cobertura seria recorrer a uma parceria com uma operadora de satélites, o que permitiria alcançar regiões remotas do país onde não chegam as redes terrestres de telecomunicações. “Estamos negociando [uma parceria], sim, pois essa tecnologia é complementar à nossa”, adianta Griselli. A operadora recebeu em 22 de outubro autorização da Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) para testes e aplicações comerciais de sistemas D2D - que permitem a conexão direta entre celulares e satélites - dentro do ambiente regulatório experimental (“sandbox”) criado pela agência, com vigência prevista até 22 de abril de 2029, explica Rafael Pistono Vitalino, sócio especialista em regulação do escritório PDK Advogados.
