artigo.texto: Google has taken over an unfinished data-center project in southeastern Wyoming from Crusoe, according to The Hans India, which ran the story under a headline that calls Crusoe a $30.9 billion AI startup. Crusoe confirmed the sale on Friday, November 6, 2026. Google announced plans to invest $17 billion in the Wyoming campus. Neither side has disclosed what Google paid for the site. That last point trips up a lot of coverage. The $17 billion is Google’s planned investment in the campus, not the purchase price, and the price itself stays private. Our first report on the Google Crusoe Wyoming data center deal laid out the basic facts on the day. This analysis asks a different question: what does the handover say about who controls AI compute, and why did a developer that did the early work on the site end up passing it to a company it had reportedly pitched as a customer? We separate what Crusoe and Google confirmed from what reports attribute to people familiar with the matter. Two tables below sort the numbers and the open claims. The later sections cover the AI-model angle (why new model generations push big buyers toward owning sites), a comparison of the ways a hyperscaler can secure capacity, the market impact, and five predictions. Every figure comes from the November 6 reporting. Where a detail is missing, we say so instead of filling the gap. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What Crusoe Confirmed on November 6 The confirmed core is short. Crusoe, an eight-year-old, Denver-based AI-infrastructure company, sold its unfinished southeastern Wyoming data-center project to Google. The company confirmed the sale on Friday, November 6, 2026. Google announced it will invest $17 billion in the campus. The acquisition price was not disclosed. Crusoe’s contribution before the sale is also on the record. Its pre-development work covered site selection, government approvals, and a power strategy. Those three items matter more than they sound. A large AI campus needs land, regulatory sign-off, and a credible answer to where the electricity comes from. Developers who hold all three can sell a site to a buyer with deeper pockets, and that is the position Crusoe held on Friday. Headlines framed the deal in different ways. TechCrunch titled its piece “Crusoe sells troubled Wyoming data center project to Google”, which signals a project in difficulty. Bloomberg went with “Google Takes Over Wyoming Data Center That Crusoe Had Pitched”, which points to the customer relationship. Yahoo Finance chose “Google buys Wyoming data center site as hyperscalers move to own AI capacity”, a trend framing. Each headline emphasizes a different reading of one transaction, and none of them replaces a statement from the companies on why the deal happened. Treat the word “troubled” as TechCrunch’s characterization. The reasons behind the takeover remain unconfirmed, a point we return to below. Related guides: Readers who want something to keep after this story can start with npm audit for Node.js projects, one of our guides in the same area, and the Shattered guides hub groups the rest by task, with the comparisons that explain the trade-offs behind each recommendation. The Numbers That Get Mixed Up Four dollar figures circulate around this story, and they measure four different things. Readers who skim headlines often merge them into one imagined price. The table separates them. A little arithmetic puts the scale in view. Google’s planned $17 billion equals roughly 55 percent of Crusoe’s $30.9 billion valuation. The September $3.9 billion round equals about 12.6 percent of that valuation. Those ratios compare a spending plan with a company’s worth, so they illustrate size and do not describe the economics of the deal. As NewsBytes put it in its headline, the price stayed undisclosed, and any estimate of Crusoe’s gain or loss on the site is guesswork. The Markets Insider write-up of the deal called it a $17 billion expansion, which is accurate for Google’s side. It does not mean Google wrote a $17 billion check to Crusoe. Most of that money, if Google follows through, goes to construction, equipment, and power infrastructure over the life of the build. Why “AI Startup” Is the Wrong Label for Crusoe The headline on The Hans India story calls Crusoe an AI startup. The reporting itself describes something narrower. Crusoe develops AI infrastructure and data centers. Its work in Wyoming involved land, permits, and power, not models, chatbots, or software products. The label matters because it changes how readers judge the news. An AI-software startup that loses a contract tells you about demand for its product. An infrastructure developer that hands a site to a customer tells you about construction cost, delivery schedules, and who carries risk. Those are different businesses with different yardsticks. Infrastructure firms get measured in megawatts delivered and dates met, and software firms get measured in users and benchmark scores. It also changes the valuation story. A $30.9 billion price tag on a software company would rest on revenue multiples. A $30.9 billion valuation on a developer of AI campuses rests on the market’s belief that contracted capacity will get built and filled. Losing one project does not break that belief, but delays and cost overruns at any single site test it. Readers who see “startup” may picture a fragile newcomer. The reports describe an eight-year-old company that raised $3.9 billion in a single round only two months ago. The Unconfirmed Reasons Behind the Takeover Two explanations dominate the reporting, and neither comes from an identified on-record Google statement. artigo.texto: A resistência à instalação de novos data centers, uma infraestrutura que cria poucos empregos e consome energia e água em volumes gigantescos, está a aumentar em todo o mundo. O exemplo mais recente ocorreu na semana passada nas eleições intercalares nos EUA, onde os candidatos com posições contrárias à instalação de data centers somaram vitórias. Nas sondagens realizadas nesse dia, o eleitorado confirmou que a questão foi determinante para o seu sentido de voto. Além dos danos ambientais, as populações queixam-se do aumento dos preços da eletricidade nas zonas onde foram instalados os centros de dados. Nas dezenas de referendos locais realizados no mesmo dia nos EUA, apenas num caso os eleitores deram a vitória à posição da indústria. Estes megacentros de dados são usados para alimentar modelos de inteligência artificial das grandes empresas tecnológicas. A oposição à construção dos grandes data centers alastra à Europa e o governo norueguês deu o exemplo ao anunciar esta segunda-feira a suspensão de novos pedidos de ligação à rede elétrica por parte destes data centers. A Noruega produz hoje mais energia do que a que consome, mas as estimativas apontam para um défice futuro por causa dos data centers, com a consequente subida do preço da eletricidade. O total de pedidos de ligação feitos este ano ascende aos 26 mil megawatts de nova capacidade, o que é mais do que a capacidade instalada na Noruega, com os data centers a representarem 75% dos pedidos, afirmou o ministro da Energia Terje Aasland, citado pela Reuters. A decisão do Governo, anunciada pelo operador da rede elétrica Statnett, foi justificada pelo ministro da Digitalização Torgeir Micaelsen com o objetivo de “obter um maior controlo sobre o crescimento dos centros de dados e garantir que dispomos dos centros de dados de que realmente precisamos”. Ficam assim suspensos temporariamente os novos pedidos de ligação e o futuro regime de licenças irá favorecer data centers que prestem serviços às áreas da defesa, da polícia e da preparação para emergências, aos serviços de saúde e a outras infraestruturas críticas, tais como a rede móvel e o sistema financeiro, afirmou Micaelsen. De fora ou com restrições acrescidas no acesso a terrenos e eletricidade ficarão as grandes empresas que operam as clouds e também as empresas de criptomoedas. E os novos data centers terão de pagar os custos da rede, podendo ser obrigados a construir centrais elétricas a gás, incluindo sistemas de captura e armazenamento de carbono, para produzirem a sua própria eletricidade, afirmou o governo. Também a Dinamarca aprovou no mês passado no Parlamento uma lei que empurra os data centers para o fim da fila de prioridades no que toca ao acesso à rede elétrica, atrás dos serviços de saúde e segurança, da rede de carregamento de carros elétricos e das habitações.

artigo.texto: Iniciativa transforma benefícios ambientais da reciclagem em créditos de carbono e gera renda para cooperativas de catadores; projeto será apresentado em painéis sobre sustentabilidade e justiça climática na Turquia O Ministério Público de Mato Grosso do Sul (MPMS) levará à 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas (COP31) uma experiência que une reciclagem, geração de créditos de carbono e inclusão social. O Projeto Reciclarbono, apoiado pela instituição e finalista dos Prêmios CNMP 2026 e J.Ex., estará entre as iniciativas brasileiras apresentadas nos debates sobre soluções ambientais. A conferência será realizada em Antália, na Turquia. O MPMS será representado pelo promotor de Justiça Luciano Furtado Loubet, integrante do Núcleo Ambiental da instituição e presidente da Associação Brasileira dos Membros do Ministério Público de Meio Ambiente (Abrampa). Loubet foi convidado a compartilhar experiências desenvolvidas no Brasil em painéis sobre gestão de resíduos, economia circular, cidades sustentáveis e justiça climática. Entre os destaques está o debate internacional “The Informal Sector Enabling Climate Action”, promovido pela Zero Waste Foundation e pelo Climate High-Level Champions’ Office. A Abrampa participará como palestrante na Zona Azul da COP31, área destinada às negociações e aos eventos oficiais da conferência. Projeto transforma reciclagem em créditos de carbono Desenvolvido em parceria com instituições públicas e acadêmicas, o Reciclarbono transforma os benefícios ambientais gerados pela reciclagem em créditos de carbono. O valor obtido é convertido em renda para cooperativas e associações de catadores. A iniciativa busca associar a redução dos impactos ambientais à valorização dos trabalhadores da reciclagem, aproximando a economia circular das estratégias de enfrentamento às mudanças climáticas. Debates incluem gestão de resíduos e cidades sustentáveis A programação da COP31 também prevê discussões sobre encerramento de lixões, combate à poluição marinha, economia circular de baixo carbono e gestão de resíduos sólidos. Os painéis incluem ainda experiências municipais para a construção de cidades sustentáveis e temas relacionados à segurança jurídica de políticas climáticas. A participação do MPMS e da Abrampa amplia a presença de experiências brasileiras nos debates internacionais sobre sustentabilidade, inclusão social e políticas públicas ambientais, levando iniciativas acompanhadas em Mato Grosso do Sul para a discussão global sobre mudanças climáticas. artigo.texto: CATL is researching a 'super' battery that will allow electric vehicles to travel 2,000km on a single charge. CATL's lithium-air battery technology is attracting attention as it is said to have a theoretical energy density of up to 3,505 Wh/kg, opening up the prospect of enabling electric cars to travel up to 2,000km on a single charge. A recent report by the Chinese tech website IT Home , cited by Car News China, has fueled expectations for lithium-air batteries. This type of battery, which uses oxygen from the environment to participate in an electrochemical reaction to generate energy, is being developed by CATL. According to theoretical calculations, this technology could achieve a specific energy of approximately 3,505 Wh/kg, significantly higher than the lithium-ion batteries commonly used in electric vehicles. Some even suggest that lithium-air batteries have the potential to achieve five times the energy density of solid-state batteries, thereby enabling electric vehicles to achieve a range of up to 2,000km per charge. However, that's only in theory. The figure of 3,505 Wh/kg reflects the specific energy of the chemical reaction, not the parameter of a complete battery pack that can be installed in a car. When accounting for electrodes, electrolyte, protection systems, and auxiliary equipment, the weight and volume of the battery pack will increase significantly. Information about CATL's interest in this technology comes from a statement by Wu Kai, the company's Chief Engineer, at the Equipment Powerhouse Forum 2026. He identified lithium-air batteries as one of the Chinese battery manufacturer's long-term research directions. Nevertheless, in its battery technology development roadmap, CATL still prioritizes solutions with closer commercialization prospects, including sodium-ion batteries and all-solid-state batteries. Lithium-air batteries are still in the long-term research phase. The company has not announced a target of bringing electric vehicles with a 2,000km range to market, nor has it given a timeframe for commercialization of this type of battery. How do lithium-air batteries work? The biggest difference between lithium-air batteries and conventional lithium-ion batteries lies in the way the reactants are involved. With lithium-ion batteries widely used in electric vehicles, lithium is stored in two electrodes. During charging and discharging, lithium ions move back and forth between the anode and cathode through the electrolyte to generate an electric current. Meanwhile, lithium-air batteries use lithium metal as the negative electrode, while oxygen taken directly from the outside air acts as the reactant at the positive electrode. Because they don't have to carry the entire reagent material like conventional batteries, this technology has the potential to achieve very high specific energy. When the battery discharges, lithium reacts with oxygen to form lithium peroxide (Li₂O₂) inside the porous electrode. During charging, the reaction reverses, releasing oxygen and returning the lithium ions to the negative electrode. Utilizing oxygen from the environment instead of storing all the reactants within the electrode structure is what gives lithium-air batteries their inherent energy advantage. However, this very characteristic also makes the technology more complex in practical use, as it is difficult to control humidity and impurities in the air. Notably, the figure of 3,505 Wh/kg commonly cited is the theoretical specific energy of the reaction between lithium and oxygen to form lithium peroxide, taking into account the mass of oxygen involved in the reaction. Some other calculations yield a figure closer to 12,000 Wh/kg, but use different algorithms that do not account for the mass of oxygen. Neither of these energy levels represents the electrical storage capacity of a complete automotive battery pack. In reality, the battery pack must also include electrolyte, electrode layers, shielding, and an air management system. These components significantly increase weight and volume, resulting in a much lower actual energy density than the theoretical figure. You may also like Laboratory studies have recorded some notable advances. In 2024, a research team from Jilin University and the Chinese Academy of Sciences published test results of a pouch-type lithium-air battery configuration using a gel-like polymer electrolyte formed during the manufacturing process. This design achieved a specific energy of 757.5 Wh/kg and demonstrated 241 operating cycles under specific test conditions, with a current density of 500 mA/g and a capacity of 1,000 mAh/g. This is a remarkable result in battery materials research. Another research direction was published in the journal Science in 2023 by scientists from the Illinois Institute of Technology and Argonne National Laboratory (USA). The research team developed a solid-state lithium-air battery structure that uses a four-electron reaction to form lithium oxide (Li₂O) instead of lithium peroxide, as is commonly done. This battery sample has completed at least 1,000 charge-discharge cycles at room temperature. The theoretical energy density is estimated at approximately 1,200 Wh/kg. These results show that lithium-air batteries have made progress beyond initial theoretical calculations. However, differences in chemical composition, operating conditions, and measurement methods mean that the results cannot be directly compared. More importantly, no research has yet produced a lithium-air battery pack that fully meets the requirements for use in passenger cars and mass production. Three obstacles preventing lithium-air batteries from entering cars. In fact, the industry had been researching lithium-air batteries for years before CATL showed interest in the technology. artigo.texto: Woodbury County Zoning Commission hears data center concerns in Salix SALIX, Iowa (KTIV) - Woodbury County Zoning Commission continued their tour of Woodbury County, Monday Nov. 9, this time in Salix for one of their data center town halls. Back in June, the Woodbury County Board of Supervisors passed a 12-month moratorium on all potential data centers in the county. And now, the county’s zoning commission is looking for public input on what requirements or regulations they would like to see added to a county data center ordinance. That ordinance would only affect unincorporated areas in the county not incorporated cities or towns. Monday, the commission heard from residents in Salix. There, people voiced their concerns about data centers affecting the environment, water quality, local roads, and noise pollution. Overall, many asked the commission to take their time to creating regulations. “To my mind, the costs and risks far outweigh the benefits. While we do not want woodbury county closed to business the goal would be to ensure that if a hyper scale data center were to be proposed in this county, its residents would be protected from harm,” said Janet Yanek, a concerned resident. Some residents did acknowledge that they aren’t fully against data centers, they just ask the county to have enough regulations in place so they don’t impact residents. “I don’t think there’s anything wrong with data centers if they are in the right spot. I think that resources are a big thing to look at and keeping the costs on the companies that are building them is also a big thing to look at. But keeping the residents first is the biggest things in my eyes,” said Preston Zemanek, a concerned resident. The zoning commission plans to hold another town hall in Correctionville on January 18th. That location has yet to be determined. If you are a resident of Woodbury County and would like to submit your input, you can email dpriestley@woodburycountyiowa.gov or reach out to the Woodbury County Planning and Zoning at 620 Douglas Street, Sixth Floor, Sioux City, IA 51101. artigo.texto: Eletronet aporta R$ 25 milhões em novo Data Center em SP Nomeado ELET1, o Data Center terá capacidade para cerca de 90 racks e potência de 0,5 MW, podendo ser expandida para 1 MW. Lançamento é previsto para o primeiro trimestre de 2027. A Eletronet, uma empresa Axia Energia, anunciou o ELET1, seu novo Data Center em São Paulo, que ampliará a oferta de serviços de colocation, conectividade e interconexão da companhia e fornecerá mais escala ao atendimento de provedores de nuvem, operadoras de telecomunicações e provedores de Internet (ISPs), e hyperscalers. Com investimento de R$ 25 milhões, o centro terá aproximadamente 350 m², capacidade para cerca de 90 racks e potência inicial de 0,5 MW, podendo chegar a 1 MW na segunda fase de expansão. Com as obras já iniciadas, a previsão de lançamento é para o primeiro trimestre de 2027. O projeto acompanha o aumento da procura de empresas dos segmentos de cloud, streaming e telecomunicações por infraestrutura de Data Center em regiões estratégicas de São Paulo, com alta disponibilidade e acesso a um amplo ecossistema de conteúdo. O ELET1 estará em uma localização com elevada concentração de redes de telecomunicações e provedores de conteúdo. O Data Center também abrigará o PIX (Ponto de Interconexão) da Eletronet no IX.br São Paulo, o maior ponto de troca de tráfego de Internet do mundo, tanto em volume quanto em número de participantes. O PIX da companhia se destaca por liderar o volume de tráfego de download entre as operadoras participantes do IX.br São Paulo. Para os clientes, estar nesse ambiente aumenta as possibilidades de conexão com diferentes redes e provedores de serviços digitais. “O ELET1 representa um passo estratégico para fortalecer nossa atuação no segmento de Data Centers. Estamos ampliando nossa estrutura para atender às necessidades dos clientes que já utilizam nossos serviços e abrir novas oportunidades de negócios, em um contexto no qual a hiperconectividade e a disponibilidade se tornam cada vez mais essenciais”, afirma Rogerio Garchet, CEO da Eletronet. Segundo ele, o projeto acompanha o avanço de aplicações em nuvem, inteligência artificial, streaming e serviços digitais, que exigem suporte para volumes cada vez maiores de dados. “Queremos ir além das necessidades atuais e antecipar os próximos ciclos do mercado, fortalecendo nossa capacidade de conectar clientes, redes e ecossistemas digitais”, diz. Com segurança, tecnologia de última geração e resiliência operacional entre os pilares da iniciativa, o ELET1 seguirá as melhores práticas globais de infraestrutura, com soluções voltadas à proteção física e lógica, alinhadas às diretrizes da norma ISO 27001. O Data Center também contará com aplicações modernas e práticas de gestão ambiental e energética, tendo como referência os padrões ISO 14001, ISO 50001 e LEED, apoiando no melhor desempenho energético e na redução do PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness). Entre os recursos previstos estão dois geradores redundantes de 500 kVA, dupla entrada de rede, backbone DWDM protegido, sistema de gerenciamento predial (BMS) atualizado, monitoramento contínuo e um Centro de Operações de Rede (NOC) de contingência.

artigo.texto: Missoula company CubCloud AI has sued the city of Missoula over a recent zoning change that blocks data center development within the city limits, citing the state’s Right to Compute Act. The company, represented by the Arizona-based Goldwater Institute through the Big Sky Legal Project, argues in the lawsuit filed Nov. 4 that the city’s rules preventing it from expanding its business are not supported by a “compelling governmental interest,” nor are they narrowly tailored as required by the Right to Compute Act. “The City’s new ordinance targets data centers because it considers them the wrong type of business,” said the Goldwater Institute’s Dave Roland in a press release. “The fact that the ordinance’s blanket restrictions sweep in CubCloud shows they are not narrowly tailored toward protecting the public from excessive noise, light, pollution, etc., as the Right to Compute Act requires.” Missoula City Attorney Ryan Sudbury told Montana Free Press that, as of Monday morning, the city had not been served with the lawsuit but that he was aware of the case. Sudbury said city officials had internal discussions about the Right to Compute Act while crafting the zoning amendment and that the city plans to defend the change. “Nobody knows what the law is intended to do or what it means,” Sudbury said. “It has not been tested in court. … If we get served, we will defend the city’s action.” The Montana Legislature passed the Right to Compute Act in 2025. The law links the development of computational resources, such as data centers, to constitutional rights, including property and freedom of expression. As with other constitutional rights, government infringement of the right to compute is limited except when driven by a compelling governmental interest, such as the preservation of public health and safety. While some local governments have argued the law prevents them from regulating data centers, others, including Missoula County, have moved forward with crafting new rules. Large data center proposals have received significant pushback from residents. Missoula County’s recently released data center study found even small-scale operations can have some significant impacts on energy demand, water use and air and water pollution. The city adopted a new zoning code in late 2025 that went into effect earlier this year. While the new code allowed data centers in heavy industrial areas — which are not included on the zoning map — the rules inadvertently permitted data centers citywide if they took up less than 50% of a facility. The amendment approved in October closed that loophole by revising the definition of a data center and regulating the facilities based on how the equipment is used rather than how much floor space it occupies. CubCloud AI was founded about a year ago and has 18 employees, according to the complaint. The business provides private computational resources, remote data processing, server hosting and cloud computing services. CubCloud operates a facility on Kestrel Drive near the Missoula Montana Airport that previously met the city’s requirements because the computational resources occupied about 20% of the floor area, the complaint said. Joshua Rhines, CubCloud CEO, planned to build a new stand-alone building on the site that would house additional computing resources. Under the city’s updated rules, the business could not build similar facilities on its existing site or anywhere else within city limits. The complaint argues the facilities do not generate noise, odors, physical intrusions or other adverse conditions that would constitute a nuisance or unreasonably interfere with neighboring properties. The complaint argues the zoning amendment violates the Right to Compute Act by restricting the company’s ability to own or use computational resources and is not supported by a compelling government interest. Even if a compelling government interest was identified, the rule is not narrowly tailored to fulfill that interest, the complaint states. The Goldwater Institute is a public policy research and litigation organization focused on limited government, individual liberty and free speech, according to its website. The organization has partnered with the Montana-based Frontier Institute, a conservative think tank, on the Big Sky Legal Project to provide free legal services to Montanans “whose rights are being violated by federal, state, or local government.” Missoula City Council Member Kristen Jordan argued last month that the zoning code is insufficient to prevent data center development, which could be approved through a rezoning request. (WFIE) - Warrick County commissioners voted Monday to table a proposed data center ordinance after hearing from residents. Commissioners heard from people on both sides of the issue. Some residents say they appreciate the county’s transparency, but want another six-month moratorium. Commissioners also discussed land in Boonville and the possibility of annexing property there for a data center. Many residents asked for a moratorium to answer the questions. “That all needs to be taken care of before you even consider one of these things ... Why wasn’t there a voter referendum in this last election?” Last week, the Area Plan Commission voted 5-2 to send the proposed ordinance to commissioners with an unfavorable recommendation. CenterPoint also spoke tonight, saying data centers could lower utility rates and support economic growth. Copyright 2026 WFIE. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: The CRU published a decision on the initial procurement of Long Duration Energy Storage (“LDES”): Long Duration Energy Storage Decision Paper. This follows an earlier consultation, which we looked at in our insights blog post: Energy update: Long Duration Energy Storage. The CRU now approves the core framework for the initial procurement of up to 500 MW through a technology-neutral, service-based procurement, progressed through the ECP connection process (for more detail, see our briefing: New Connection Policy for Onshore Generators and Storage). EirGrid proposes a two-stage procurement: qualification followed by a tender phase. Which projects can participate? To qualify, projects must have: - a minimum four hours’ import and export duration on the transmission system, - a 1:1 ratio of maximum export capacity (“MEC”) to maximum import capacity, - a minimum capacity of 20 MW for hybrid projects or 75 MW for standalone projects, - a maximum capacity of 100 MW, and - round-trip efficiency of at least 75%. At qualification stage, projects must hold a connection offer at 110 kV or above. At tender stage, projects must have a connection agreement, planning consent for the facility and grid connection, evidence of land rights for the grid connection, maps and AutoCAD drawings of the grid infrastructure, and a detailed connection programme. Co-located sites must have at least 30 MW of TSO-connected renewable generation, with separate market registration and sub-metering. How will projects be selected? At qualification stage, company and project requirements will be assessed on a pass/fail basis. Company requirements include financial turnover (to be confirmed through further consultation), relevant experience and cyber-security requirements. Qualifying tenders will be scored on cost (50%), impact (30%) and connection method (20%). - Impact scoring evaluates a project’s ability to reduce renewable dispatch down and remain available to provide wider system value, using data from hourly ECP modelling. - Connection method scoring is intended to incentivise efficient use of grid. EirGrid’s proposal is that new standalone transmission connections will receive zero points, while the maximum of 20 points will be given to existing standalone connections at tender closing date or to hybrid connection arrangements (with at least 30 MW of renewable generation). EirGrid does not propose MEC sharing for this initial procurement, considering it infeasible within the required timeframe. We touch on some of the issues in our insights blog post: Energy Update: Sharing Maximum Export Capacity at electricity grid connection points. Highest-ranked projects will progress to a Best and Final Offer stage and a Deliverability Assessment, aspects of which are to be further consulted upon. What revenue support will be available? Service duration will be ten years. The CRU has approved in principle a competitively bid revenue floor, subject to an LCOS-informed bid limit. EirGrid proposes that the floor be set on a pay-as-bid basis and remain fixed over the contract term, subject to indexation, with a true-up payment where eligible market revenues fall below it. The storage asset will retain 70% of revenues above the floor, with 30% shared with consumers. EirGrid proposes returning the consumer share through transmission use-of-system charges. The cost of electricity bought for charging (and therefore the round-trip efficiency losses) will be netted off against gross eligible market revenues, but the asset’s other operating, commercial and financing costs will not be deducted. Open-book accounting will be required. EirGrid proposes quarterly interim settlements and annual reconciliation. Full approval of this framework remains subject to EirGrid demonstrating its effective interaction with other mechanisms, as noted further below. How will assets operate? Contracted assets will retain full SEM market access, subject to Trading Envelope compliance. The CRU supports the Trading Envelope model in principle and has approved initial issuance of dynamic import/export limits at 10:00 on the day before the Trading Day. EirGrid must publish a Trading Envelope methodology in advance of the tender and house the methodology and issuance timing in a protocol document so that any material changes are subject to public consultation and CRU approval. The CRU supports in principle non-compliance charges (for taking positions outside a Trading Envelope) and a Trading Non-Activity Scalar (which would reduce the floor for insufficient participation or cycling). Methodologies remain to be consulted on, including treatment of inactivity caused by TSO instructions or Trading Envelope limits. Next steps Many of the revenue and operational design features are subject to final approval by the CRU following demonstration by EirGrid that these mechanisms operate together as a coherent and financeable package providing effective incentives for assets to operate and deliver system value. Before tenders are invited, EirGrid must consult on and finalise the Trading Envelope methodology, Trading Non-Activity Scalar, Deliverability Assessment methodology, contractual arrangements and governance and change-control provisions. The consultation on contractual arrangements is to include timelines. Before contracts are awarded, EirGrid is required to notify the CRU of the proposed selected portfolio, aggregate volume and expected costs.

NSI sued city hall, asking the court to let it proceed with its plans. The lawsuit also contends city planners approved the project before the moratorium was put in place. Springfield City Council is expected to vote on extending the moratorium at the Nov. 16 council meeting until February. This ruling did not go in NSI’s favor, but in September another judge stopped a moratorium to allow NSI to build in Benton County. That means county commissioners there can’t enforce the moratorium until a final judgment is made. November 10, 2026. By Mrinmoy Dey Tata Power has operationalised 60 MWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS) across Mahalaxmi, Saki and Mankhurd to strengthen Mumbai’s electricity distribution network, which serves over 8 lakh consumers. The installations store electricity during lower-cost solar generation hours and discharge it during evening peak demand, helping optimise power procurement costs, improve energy utilisation and reduce dependence on expensive peak-hour electricity, the company stated. Equipped with fast-response and high ramp-rate capabilities, the systems support dynamic load management and enable the distribution network to respond to fluctuations in demand. Operating at approximately 1–1.5 cycles per day, the installations also support peak load management and power procurement optimisation. The decentralised, grid-connected systems provide localised energy storage and dispatch capabilities, while their black-start functionality supports grid restoration during power system disturbances. The operational capacity forms part of Tata Power’s larger plan to modernise Mumbai’s electricity infrastructure. In April 2025, the company received approval from the Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission (MERC) to deploy 200 MWh of BESS across 10 strategic locations in the city. The larger deployment is aimed at strengthening grid stability, managing peak demand, improving reactive power management and supporting faster restoration of electricity supply to critical infrastructure, including hospitals, Metro services, airports and data centres, the company stated. artigo.texto: Power Where Are the Biggest U.S. BESS Projects Being Built? U.S battery energy storage systems, virtually unknown at a utility-scale only a few years ago, are growing larger, representing construction investments in the U.S. Released Monday, November 09, 2026 Reports related to this article: Written by Eric Funderburk for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary U.S. battery energy storage systems are growing larger, often exceeding hundreds of megawatts in capacity and racking up substantial construction investments. A Big Market The deployment of battery energy storge systems (BESS) across the U.S. has represented a major shift in the U.S. power sector, opening the door to a utility-scale power source that was virtually unknown only a few years ago. And that door has opened in a big way. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) in August reported that nearly 52 gigawatts (GW) of battery energy storage was deployed in the U.S. at the end of June 2026, with 8.3 GW of that coming in the first half of 2026 alone. A previous article from Industrial Info Resources noted that $3.8 billion worth of standalone BESS projects were lined up to break ground in September. In addition to standalone battery facilities, dozens of BESS units are lined up to accompany solar installations, evening out power supply at times when solar power isn't actively being generated. Industrial Info Resources data show more than 1,400 U.S. BESS projects, valued at nearly $642 billion, either underway or on the planning table, although these frequently include solar power and a handful of wind projects accompanying the battery storage. Current construction represents more than $25.5 billion in investments. The Bigger, the Better? So where are the largest BESS projects currently being built in the U.S., and what is driving this $25 billion in current construction? One BESS installation rises to the top of the list: Intersect Power's Darden Clean Energy Project in Fresno, California. This massive 1,150-megawatt (MW) battery installation will be able to match the output of the accompanying 1,150-MW solar power plant at maximum discharge for a period of up to four hours with its 4,600-megawatt-hour discharge rating. The BESS unit plans to employ Tesla's lithium-ion-phosphate (LFP) battery technology and is expected to begin operating in 2028. Subscribers can access details of the project, including construction timelines, key contact details, and equipment and service needs on both the solar BESS components of the project, by clicking here. Battery storage also is a major component of the Steel River Energy Center being built near Osceola, Arkansas, which will feature 720-MW/2,880-MWh of battery capacity at full buildout. Work is underway on the first two phases of construction, which will add 480 MW of battery capacity to accommodate 1,000 MW of solar generation. A third phase of construction to add more solar generation along with an additional 240 MW of battery energy storage capacity is planned to get started at a later date. Work is just getting started on SB Energy's Libra hybrid energy center in which 700 MW of solar capacity is equally matched a 700-MW/2,800-MWh BESS unit. SB Energy has employed SOLV Energy to construct the project on federal lands managed by the U.S. Bureau of Land Management (BLM) near Yerington, Nevada. The project has a targeted in-service of 2028. Oregon a Prime BESS Destination Planned BESS builds are a more slippery target, but a few substantial projects seem to likely to move forward, including an anticipated 1,400 MW of battery storage at an Oregon project backed by Amazon. Ownership of the Sunstone solar/BESS project in northeastern Oregon was transferred to a subsidiary of Amazon earlier this year, but drawing on Amazon's substantial resources and a hard deadline of November 2027 to get moving on construction, the project seems likely to move forward. The first two phases of construction will add a combined 400 MW of BESS capacity, while a projected third phase would add a massive 800 MW of additional battery energy storage, although work on this final phase remains a few years out. Another substantial BESS project is on the books for Sherman County, Oregon, in the form of the Buckley solar/BESS facility, which could begin construction next year. The project planned by Boise, Idaho-based Clenera Renewable Energy would include 1,200 MW of solar and matching 1,200 MW of battery capacity with a four-hour discharge time. Substations, transmission tie-ins and all manner of equipment are part of the project, so an anticipated completion date of early 2029 could prove somewhat optimistic, depending on when construction kicks off and the pace at which is performed. Key Takeaways - BESS capacities are growing larger, often matching the solar generation capacity it frequently accompanies. - Oregon is the destination for two substantial BESS projects, each planned to add 1,200 MW or more of battery capacity. Um projeto de Mato Grosso do Sul que converte os benefícios ambientais da reciclagem em créditos de carbono e repassa o valor a catadores é finalista do Prêmio CNMP 2026. O Reciclarbono foi desenvolvido pelo Ministério Público de Mato Grosso do Sul (MPMS), em parceria com o Ministério Público do Trabalho (MPT-MS), a Universidade Católica Dom Bosco (UCDB) e o Instituto Brasileiro de Pesquisa Aplicada em Resíduos e Clima (Ibraparc). O projeto mede o impacto positivo gerado pelo trabalho de coleta e triagem, como a redução da emissão de gases de efeito estufa, e o transforma em créditos de carbono certificados. O valor obtido vira uma nova fonte de recursos para as organizações participantes. Hoje, o Reciclarbono reúne cooperativas e associações de diferentes municípios do estado. Renda para quem faz a coleta Segundo o MPMS, o diferencial é que o mercado de carbono costuma estar ligado a grandes empreendimentos, e aqui os catadores ficam no centro da solução. Os recursos podem complementar a renda dos trabalhadores e ajudar a financiar equipamentos, infraestrutura e melhores condições de trabalho nas cooperativas e associações. O promotor de Justiça Luciano Furtado Loubet, do Núcleo Ambiental do MPMS, afirmou: “Durante muito tempo, os catadores foram vistos apenas como parte da cadeia da reciclagem. O Reciclarbono ajuda a mostrar que eles são agentes ambientais fundamentais.” Quando sai o resultado A classificação final do Prêmio CNMP 2026, que reconhece iniciativas inovadoras dos Ministérios Públicos do país, será conhecida na cerimônia de 11 de novembro, na sede do Ministério Público do Distrito Federal e Territórios (MPDFT), em Brasília. artigo.texto: Last week, Ohio had more data center-related measures on the ballot than any other state, and voters from Piqua to Grove City, Conneaut to Urbana, overwhelmingly voted to restrict the hyperscale developments. Barry Blankenship started leading a data center resistance group in Trenton in southwest Ohio after two projects were proposed near his home. He says the ballot measure results send a message to local leaders about where residents stand. “That shows when the power of the people comes together, we can beat money and we can beat big tech,” Blankenship said. Note: election results are unofficial until confirmed by each county’s Board of Elections. Find more detailed information about local results below. The Ohio Newsroom’s Erin Gottsacker spoke with WVXU Environment Reporter Isabel Nissley about the types of ballot measures voters considered and what the results say about public sentiment. On why voters favored restricting data center developments Nissley: Data centers really connected to this larger election issue of affordability. The computing facilities require massive amounts of electricity, which is driving up energy costs statewide, and people in several communities told me they're already having to make tough choices with their finances. They're scared for what they'll have to cut next if electricity bills keep climbing up. Other people say they don't want this resource-guzzling big tech infrastructure as a neighbor. They say they're worried about data centers' noise, pollution, water use, a lack of transparency about projects from government officials and more. Those concerns are bipartisan, and they drove Ohioans to the polls to deliver an overwhelming rebuke of data centers last week. Ballot measures to limit the developments passed with a large margin of support statewide, from Sunbury in central Ohio, which passed a ban on large facilities with 79% of the vote, to Perry in Northeast Ohio, which approved restrictions with 87% of voters in favor. On how Ohio election results compared with other parts of the country Nissley: About a dozen other states had data center-related measures on the ballot, and like in Ohio, many passed with large margins of support. What's different here is the number of data centers. There are more than 200 projects planned or under construction in Ohio. That's the fifth highest number in the nation. On the impact on future developments Nissley: Organizers say last week's vote is just the start of getting more restrictions on data centers in Ohio. A statewide coalition made up of lawyers and everyday people worked with the dozen plus communities to draft ballot language. Now, Conserve Ohio says it's looking to expand its efforts in more communities and help more people amend their city charters to ban data centers. The group is also collecting signatures for a statewide petition to amend the Ohio Constitution to prohibit the construction of large-scale data centers. In terms of projects that are permitted or under construction, it looks like they'll largely proceed as planned. But future projects won't have as easy of a path forward if they're allowed to build at all. On the consequences of limiting data center development Nissley: Organizations like the Ohio Chamber of Commerce see data centers as major economic drivers. A Chamber of Commerce Research Foundation study says $40 billion have been and will be invested in data centers around the state through 2030, as well as jobs and state and local tax revenue. With new restrictions on these projects, they say communities will lose out and suffer economically. How ballot measures fared Data center ballot measures ranged from outright bans, to new regulations, to recalls of elected officials who supported data centers. Southwest Ohio City of Trenton: a charter amendment to prohibit the construction of data centers over 25 megawatts within city limits passed with 80% of the vote. City of Piqua: a charter amendment to ban the construction of data centers larger than 25 megawatts of peak power demand passed with 67% of the vote. City of Piqua: recall of commissioners in the city’s 1st, 3rd and 5th wards. All three were recalled with at least 70% of the vote. City of Urbana: a charter amendment to ban the construction of data centers larger than 7.5 megawatts of peak power demand passed with 77% of the vote. City of Urbana: a recall of Mayor Bill Bean passed with 73% of the vote. City of Wilmington: four referendums to reverse the February rezoning of four parcels totaling more than 500 acres near U.S. 68 from “rural residential” to “light industrial” adjacent to proposed data center campus. Each zone change was reversed with support from at least 79% of voters. Monroe Township (Adams County): a resolution establishing a zoning review process for “higher-impact development” passed with 60% of the vote. Sprigg (Adams County): a resolution establishing a zoning review process for “higher-impact development” passed with 53% of the vote. Northeast Ohio City of Hubbard: a blanket ban on all data centers in the city passed with 76% of the vote. City of Conneaut: a charter amendment prohibiting data centers larger than 25 megawatts in the city passed with 64% of the vote. Village of Perry: an ordinance requiring that data center development companies seeking tax incentives provide financial backing to commitments around jobs and tax revenue. Developers must post a bond to back those claims before receiving any incentives. The measure also implements noise requirements. It passed with 87% of the vote. Village of Monroeville: a pro-data center ballot issue FAILED with 87% of the vote. It was an advisory ballot question regarding an ordinance to allow data center development in the village. Because it is advisory, this question does not mandate the village to take any particular action but informs them of community sentiment. artigo.texto: Minneapolis City Council advances data center plan, lays out rules Minneapolis leaders moved a data center ordinance ahead as members remained split over tax relief, oversight and environmental concerns. The Minneapolis City Council moved the ordinance forward Monday, with the city’s moratorium set to end in two weeks. The proposal is headed to a full council vote later this week. There were more than 1,600 public comments as the council debated the rules. The ordinance would require data centers to be downtown, 150,000 square feet or smaller and only in existing office space. Other restrictions included that data centers cannot be the primary use of a building or be on the first two floors. Supporters said the projects could help as downtown property values slump and the tax base falls. “I have heard some say that the economic benefit of these small-scale data centers is wishful thinking; I beg to differ,” Minneapolis City Council Member Elizabeth Shaffer said. “Will small-scale data centers be a cure-all for revenue generation?” Shaffer asked. “I’ve already said no. Is it a step in the right direction for some revenue generation and property tax relief? Yes.” Councilmember Aurin Chowdhury backed an all-out ban, but that effort failed Monday. Chowdhury said residents wanted stronger limits and raised concerns about environmental effects. “What I hear from my constituents is, ‘Don’t sell us out to big tech, don’t sell it out to this industry that oftentimes tries to go around the rules and find loopholes,'” Chowdhury said. “It could have absolutely gone further,” Chowdhury added. “Residents asked for far more.” The council also failed to approve an overlay district that would have required future data center projects to get council approval. Mayor Jacob Frey’s office said he did not support that step but does support the ordinance the full council will take up later this week. His office shared the following: “The Mayor had been in conversation with council members ahead of today’s meeting. He supports the regulatory framework that was approved today.”

artigo.texto: HARRISBURG, PA — Four Chester County lawmakers are backing legislation that would require large Pennsylvania data centers to secure additional electricity capacity, disclose water consumption and commit to substantial local economic benefits, introducing new statewide oversight as communities confront the infrastructure demands of large-scale computing facilities. House Bill 2888, introduced Nov. 4 and referred to the House Energy Committee, would establish energy, environmental, employment and public-reporting requirements for hyperscale data centers. Chester County Democratic Reps. Chris Pielli, Kristine Howard, Melissa Shusterman and Danielle Friel Otten are among its co-sponsors. The legislation would create state-level obligations for qualifying facilities while preserving municipal authority over zoning and land use, a distinction relevant to ongoing data-center development disputes in East Whiteland, East Brandywine and other Chester County municipalities. Under the proposal, operators of new hyperscale data centers would be required to develop plans for obtaining sufficient additional electricity capacity to meet their facilities’ full demand. The legislation also establishes escalating requirements for clean, reliable electricity generation, with alternative compliance payments available under specified circumstances. Operators would have to certify that changes to their energy plans would not impose additional costs on other electricity customers, addressing concerns about how major new power demands could affect the broader electric system. The bill generally defines hyperscale data centers by electricity demand, including facilities requiring at least 20 megawatts of power when served by utilities with peak loads of 2,500 megawatts or more. Affiliated or colocated facilities could be considered together when determining whether the threshold applies. Water consumption would face additional scrutiny. Qualifying operators would have to submit water-management and sustainability plans to state agencies and disclose annual electricity and water consumption. Depending on a project’s location and potential environmental effects, water plans could require hydrogeological studies, baseline monitoring and corrective measures to protect high-quality waterways, public drinking-water sources and nearby tributaries. The legislation would also establish minimum economic commitments for new or expanding facilities. Covered projects would be required to submit community-benefit plans providing for at least $250 million in investment, 200 construction jobs paying prevailing wages and 50 permanent positions paying at least 125% of Pennsylvania’s average statewide wage. Those requirements would apply to qualifying facilities beginning operations, expanding or making new investments after the legislation took effect. Developers would also be required to negotiate in good faith with host municipalities over community impacts, including noise, traffic, lighting, emergency-response demands and visual screening. Negotiations would additionally address local financial contributions and annual reporting, creating a formal process for municipalities to seek commitments from developers beyond existing zoning procedures. The proposed law would not eliminate local zoning authority or independently authorize or prohibit individual data-center projects. Municipal governments would retain their existing responsibilities for land-use decisions. State oversight would instead supplement those local processes through separate operating, environmental and economic-development requirements. The Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection and Department of Community and Economic Development would administer portions of the proposed framework. After a 60-day period to correct violations, regulators could assess civil penalties reaching $25,000 per day for continuing noncompliance. Unresolved false or materially misleading submissions could trigger penalties of up to $50,000 per day. The bill’s reporting requirements would extend to qualifying data centers already operating in Pennsylvania, while its community-benefit obligations would focus on new operations, expansions and investments following enactment. For Chester County, the proposal would add a potential statewide regulatory framework to a development issue already generating local debate over land use, infrastructure capacity and municipal oversight. Its legislative prospects remain uncertain. House Bill 2888 was referred to the House Energy Committee on Nov. 4 and has not received a committee or floor vote. Pennsylvania’s 2025-26 legislative session ends Nov. 30, leaving less than a month for lawmakers to advance the measure. If the bill does not pass before the session concludes, it would need to be reintroduced in the next legislative session to receive further consideration. For now, the proposed energy, water and community-benefit requirements remain legislative proposals rather than enforceable obligations on Pennsylvania data-center operators. artigo.texto: Manifestantes invadem canteiro de obras de data center da Microsoft em Amsterdã: relatório A polícia holandesa disse que deteve de 150 a 200 pessoas por invasão durante o protesto. As autoridades holandesas disseram que detiveram de 150 a 200 pessoas por invasão. Um manifestante disse a uma emissora local que eles estavam tentando impedir a construção do data center, de acordo com uma reportagem da Associated Press na sexta-feira. A reportagem acrescentou que a Microsoft estava ciente da manifestação e respondeu por meio de um porta-voz: “Entendemos que as pessoas se sentem fortemente em relação ao projeto e respeitamos o direito delas de expressar essas opiniões pacificamente”, disseram. “No entanto, não toleramos ações que sejam ilegais ou que coloquem a segurança das pessoas em risco.” Espera-se que um ambiente regulatório mais rigoroso nos EUA se siga às recentes eleições de meio de mandato, que registraram uma onda de democratas prometendo reprimir os data centers, que usam grandes quantidades de eletricidade e água, informou a AP. artigo.texto: Mato Grosso Pivetta vai à COP 31 em busca de certificação para créditos de carbono O governador Otaviano Pivetta embarca para a Turquia nesta segunda-feira para chefiar a comitiva de Mato Grosso na 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas, a COP 31, que ocorre entre 9 e 20 de novembro. A missão do estado é convencer investidores internacionais da confiabilidade dos créditos de carbono gerados a partir da redução do desmatamento em território mato-grossense. A agenda do governador prevê reuniões com investidores da Coalizão Life, grupo que reúne Reino Unido e Noruega e concentra hoje o maior volume de recursos disponíveis para a compra de reduções de carbono no mundo. O grupo permanece na Turquia até o dia 18. Segundo a secretária de Estado de Meio Ambiente, Mauren Lazzaretti, o objetivo é obter a certificação internacional dos créditos acumulados nos últimos anos. A estratégia é demonstrar aos compradores que esses ativos têm credibilidade, de modo que a venda se converta em mais conservação ambiental e inclusão social. REDD+ e a reta final do modelo jurisdicional Durante a conferência, a força-tarefa dos governadores do Consórcio da Amazônia Legal deve apresentar as medidas que os estados vêm adotando para construir o modelo de Redução de Emissões por Desmatamento e Degradação Florestal, o REDD+ Jurisdicional. Em Mato Grosso, o processo está na etapa final. Pivetta enviou à Assembleia Legislativa um projeto de lei que autoriza a criação da Companhia Mato-grossense de Ativos Ambientais S.A. (CMAA), sociedade de economia mista voltada a estruturar, gerir e comercializar créditos de carbono, créditos de biodiversidade e outros ativos ambientais produzidos no estado. A nova empresa deve dar suporte institucional ao compromisso de Mato Grosso de zerar as emissões líquidas de carbono até 2035 e ampliar a capacidade do estado de atrair investimentos nacionais e internacionais ligados à economia de baixo carbono. Outros temas na agenda A comitiva mato-grossense também participa de debates sobre riscos climáticos, combate a incêndios florestais, economia florestal e estratégias de enfrentamento a crimes ambientais.

artigo.texto: Power DTE Boosts Spending Outlook, Eyes Data Center Growth Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $6 billion worth of active and proposed projects from DTE Released Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Reports related to this article: Written by Will Ploch, Assistant Editor-in-Chief for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary DTE Energy is raising its five-year investment plan in an effort to boost lower-carbon resources, including battery storage, and to cater to the U.S. data center market. Leaning into a Changing Economy DTE Energy Company is shifting its focus to some of the most energy-hungry parts of the U.S. economy: The Detroit, Michigan-based power provider announced last week it plans to sell off a non-utility subsidiary for $3 billion, so it can focus more on its regulated electric utility and fund a newly revamped five-year investment plan. Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $6 billion worth of active and proposed projects from DTE. Last week, DTE raised its five-year investment plan, which covers 2027-31, to $44.2 billion. Specifically, the company aims to invest $39 billion at its DTE Electric subsidiary and $5.2 billion in its gas operations; the previous, 2026-30 investment plan totaled $34.5 billion, with $30 billion for DTE Electric and $4.5 billion for gas operations. The DTE Electric investment "includes approximately $23 billion of cleaner generation investment, supporting cleaner and more affordable energy for our customers while meeting demand growth," said Joi Harris, the chief executive officer of DTE, in a quarterly earnings-related conference call. "The plan includes 7.6 gigawatts (GW) of new solar and wind resources, 2.1 GW of new combined-cycle natural gas generation, and 2.7 GW of energy storage." According to Industrial Info Resources data, battery energy-storage system (BESS) projects account for more than $1.8 billion of DTE's active project slate. The two highest-valued projects both are just south of Detroit: the 350-megawatt (MW) Monroe I Energy Center in Monroe and the 200-MW Fermi Energy Center in Newport. Both are set to begin construction in the spring of 2027. Industrial Info Resources offers more information on these BESS developments in its Global Market Intelligence (GMI) Power Project Database, where subscribers can find details--including construction schedules, investment values and necessary equipment--in detailed reports on the Monroe and Newport projects. DTE's energy-storage efforts got a boost earlier this year, when it partnered with LG Energy Solution Vertech to develop Michigan-made BESS units across the Wolverine State. Under the agreement, the two companies will invest $1.6 billion across eight projects, which will deliver 1.5 GW of battery storage over a two-year period. By the Numbers - More than $6 billion: Total investment value of active and proposed projects from DTE - $44.2 billion: Total value of DTE's five-year investment plan, which covers 2027-31 - $470 million: DTE's net income for third-quarter 2026, a 12.2% increase from the same period last year Making Room for New Partnerships Shifting priorities also were seen in DTE's recent decision to sell subsidiary DTE Vantage, which focuses on non-utility operations, to institutional investors advised by J.P. Morgan Asset Management in a deal valued at roughly $3 billion. Harris said the deal, which was announced in the earnings call, is expected to close in the first half of 2027. Industrial Info Resources is tracking activity at eight operational plants owned or co-owned by DTE Vantage. Subscribers can learn more from a detailed list of plant profiles in Industrial Info's GMI Power Plant Database. Last month, the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC) approved special contracts between DTE and Google, in which the utility will provide electricity for Google's planned Belleville Data Center Campus near Van Buren Township, which is about 30 miles southwest of Detroit. DTE Electric will develop, own and operate the data center, which will be paid for by Google, according to the MPSC's website. Under the agreement, Google must finance DTE's development of up to 1.6 GW of renewable energy and 480 MW of battery storage to serve the Belleville complex. The data center, which is expected to begin service by the end of 2027, will be fueled by energy from a variety of power-generation facilities, rather than a single plant. Subscribers can learn more about Google's Belleville project from a plant profile and a detailed list of project reports. "Looking ahead, our data center development pipeline remains robust," Harris said in the earnings call. "We continue to see approximately 5 to 6 GW of additional opportunities, including 2 GW currently in advanced discussions." DTE reported net income of $470 million for third-quarter 2026, a 12.2% increase from the same period last year. Consolidated revenues stood at $2.25 billion, a 12% decrease. The Industrial Info Resources GMI Project and Plant databases offer a full list of detailed reports for projects mentioned in this article, and a full list of related plant profiles. Industrial Info Resources also offers a full list of reports for active and proposed projects from DTE. (NASDAQ: EMPD) (the “Company” or “Empery Digital”) today provided an update on its Midwest data center investment and its share repurchases. The Company and Hunt Properties, Inc. (“Hunt Properties”) continue to advance lease negotiations for the Midwest AI data center facility and expect to execute a lease in the near term. While these negotiations continue to progress, the definitive agreement to purchase the property has been amended and extended to maintain flexibility while lease negotiations continue. Management believes that the Midwest data center facility is ideally positioned to serve hyperscalers due to the immediate availability of 150 megawatts of power with an owned substation and the potential to expand to approximately 300 megawatts of power. Following these repurchases, Empery Digital has 29,372,106 shares outstanding, after giving effect to the potential exercise of 1,653,686 pre-funded warrants, and approximately $49 million remains available under the share repurchase authorization. Empery Digital is committed to transparency, efficiency, and accountability, applying rigorous decision-making to drive sustainable, long-term shareholder value. artigo.texto: Data centers need power – lower income, rural residents pay the price By Caitlin Hayes, Cornell Chronicle As the engines of artificial intelligence, large data centers can consume as much power as medium-sized cities, straining grids and prompting expensive upgrades to U.S. energy infrastructure. New research finds that residents, and especially lower-income and rural residents, are disproportionately bearing the costs. In the study, published Nov. 9 in Nature Energy, Cornell researchers analyzed growth in energy demand and infrastructure projects for four major U.S. power grids from 2020 to 2025 and found that data centers have hiked wholesale energy prices and on average paid only 38% of the infrastructure costs linked to their growth – $3.12 billion of an $8.25 billion bill in 2025. The remaining $5.13 billion, or 62%, fell largely on residents, with the lowest income households seeing extra energy costs up to 28% of their incomes. “We were trying to answer a very simple question: With the booming of data centers, who pays for that expansion and who benefits?” said Fengqi You, the Roxanne E. and Michael J. Zak Professor in Energy Systems Engineering in the Cornell Duffield College of Engineering. “It’s not just a question of generating enough electricity but of whether the rules for paying for the grid are keeping pace with who is driving new demand.” The research is the first multi-region, long-term assessment of how data center development impacts infrastructure growth and how costs are distributed across communities. It comes amidst a boom in data center construction. The researchers found that transmission investment in energy infrastructure projects increased from $2 billion in 2020 to $34 billion in 2025, with data centers driving much of that rise. Debates are ongoing – from local communities to state governments to Congress – about who picks up the bill as growth accelerates; data centers are projected to consume between 8% and 17% of U.S. electricity by 2030, with 70% to 80% of that attributed to AI. With first author and postdoctoral researcher Cheng Feng, You also looked at data centers’ economic benefits, finding that each gigawatt of data center capacity can create 15,000 jobs across the economy, with an average 2,700 jobs directly associated with the data center (although not necessarily all on-site). “In a lot of discussions right now, people take one side or the other, completely yes on data centers or completely no,” said You, director of the Cornell AI for Sustainability Initiative. “But there are benefits and costs, and the key issue in the end is how to balance the trade-offs.” Sharing the cost of power infrastructure The team analyzed data from 4,000 existing and proposed data centers, as well as power-price records, rate filings from utilities, power-line plans, and federal household and job data. The major grids they studied encompass regions with the largest clusters of data centers, including the southern San Francisco Bay area; north Texas around Dallas-Fort Worth; the Midwest; and the mid-Atlantic region, including northern Virginia, where the biggest concentration of data centers has been built to date. State incentives for data centers have provided returns on the investments, if inconsistently, the researchers found. Some states, such as California, reaped $180 in worker income for every dollar spent, while Virginia increased income $2 for every dollar invested. The researchers determined that the presence of an existing, qualified workforce was a stronger indicator of high returns than the amount of incentive spending. Data centers also increased wholesale electricity prices, the amounts utilities pay regional power markets before delivering the electricity to homes. In the most-affected hubs, data center growth raised those prices by nearly 10% or more by 2025. In Virginia, the costs jumped 15% and in California’s southern Bay Area, 20%. In contrast, residents in New York and New England, where data center construction has been limited, have not seen clear price increases due to data center expansion, the researchers found. “I think that means we’re at a good starting point in New York to think about the next steps,” You said. “Economic benefits, job benefits, investment, fairly allocating the costs – these are the dimensions and trade-offs we need to consider.” A key problem is how the costs of new infrastructure projects are currently shared: The allocation is often based on previous patterns of energy consumption. “It’s kind of a chicken-and-egg problem,” You said. “Because if you’re going to build a data center, you need to expand this power infrastructure. Otherwise, there’s no electricity for them to run. But before they build, they’re not using energy. So with this model of relying on past consumption, households end up taking on much of the infrastructure costs.” Many more rural and lower-income residents saw proportionally higher bills; the share of rural families shouldering a high energy burden – spending more than 6% of their incomes on energy – rose 76% more than among urban residents. The authors cite a national survey finding that rural residents are also less likely to use AI tools like ChatGPT than urban residents. The impact on energy bills also has a wide geographical reach. For example, residents in New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Ohio help pay for grid upgrades linked to data center growth in Virginia, the researchers said. “You do not have to live next to a data center to help pay for its power infrastructure,” You said. “The grid connects communities across states, and cost-sharing rules connect them financially.” Using insights from the data, You and Feng recommend changes to cost-sharing rules and strategies to lower burdens. In all four regions, they found that, if data centers cut back power use during 22 of the region’s peak demand hours each year, they would relieve strain on the grid and minimize the need to expand. artigo.texto: Protect Kansas circulating 3-part petition to ban hyperscale data centers TOPEKA, Kan. (WIBW) - Both Topeka and Shawnee County now have a moratorium in place for data centers. Similar to what we just saw happen in Emporia, the group Protect Kansas is collecting signatures to ban hyperscale data centers. Even with moratoriums in Shawnee County and the city of Topeka, Protect Kansas is taking matters into their own hands. “The city can change their moratorium at any time. They’ve let us know that they could vote that in and change that any day,” Colleen Campbell, Protect Kansas co-founder, said. The petition is broken into 3 parts: - No data centers over 25 megawatts - Preventing Topeka from supplying water to data centers outside city limits - “No annexing the data centers from the county into the city,” Campbell said. “So it’s not completely banning data centers. It’s just saying, ‘hey, we don’t want these hyperscale ones that use a lot of resources,’” Campbell said. It’s not just about protecting people in the city. “The county doesn’t have any recourse for a petition or any kind of way for them to have their voices heard,” Campbell said. The petition needs 6,000 signatures that can be verified by the city clerk. “The city council actually has a chance to just accept the petition as is so they can go ahead and make it as law,” Campbell said. If city council doesn’t accept it, the petition could be challenged in court or put it to a public vote. Though the moratoriums are in place, Protect Kansas wants this to go beyond the expiration dates. “This gives us long-term protection, and it’s really mirroring what the moratorium has already done, so we’re just looking for that longer-term, more solid protection,” Campbell said. WIBW reached out to the city for comment on the petition, but the city has not responded. The Shawnee County moratorium expires at the end of Feb. 2027, and the Topeka data center moratorium expires in mid-July 2027. Copyright 2026 WIBW. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: A Crusoe, desenvolvedora de data centers com sede em Denver e avaliada em US$ 30,9 bilhões, confirmou nesta sexta-feira a venda de um projeto inacabado no sudeste do Wyoming para o Google. O Google prevê investir US$ 17 bilhões para concluir o campus, mas não revelou quanto desembolsou pelo ativo. Por que o Google tomou as rédeas do projeto O Google já havia tentado fechar com a Crusoe um contrato como cliente desse mesmo empreendimento, sem sucesso. Agora assume o desenvolvimento depois de, segundo informações divulgadas, demonstrar preocupação com o custo e o cronograma de obra sob a gestão da companhia de Denver. O projeto foi anunciado no ano passado em parceria com a Tallgrass, empresa de infraestrutura apoiada pela Blackstone, com a meta de chegar a 10 gigawatts de potência, unidade que equivale a um bilhão de watts. Os números da operação A venda havia sido antecipada por outro veículo de imprensa em junho. Mesmo assim, o revés no estado não impediu a Crusoe de levantar US$ 3,9 bilhões em setembro. Como a Crusoe ganha dinheiro e quem são seus clientes A receita vem de três frentes: alugar espaço a clientes que levam os próprios chips de IA, alugar as GPUs (unidades de processamento gráfico) da própria empresa e vender capacidade computacional para rodar modelos de IA. Essa última atividade é chamada de inferência, isto é, o uso de um modelo já treinado para responder às consultas dos usuários. Os projetos mais robustos atendem nomes de peso do setor. Em Abilene, no Texas, o campus avança por fases para a Oracle e para a OpenAI, enquanto um complexo separado de 900 megawatts, vizinho ao primeiro, será usado pela Microsoft. A Meta também figura entre os clientes. A companhia nasceu das mãos de Chase Lochmiller, atual CEO, e Cully Cavness, como um negócio de mineração de criptomoedas movido a gás natural que, de outra forma, seria queimado. Em setembro, com a rodada de captação, entraram três conselheiros, entre eles JB Straubel, fundador da Redwood Materials e membro do conselho da Tesla, que já havia investido na Crusoe em 2021. A empresa também foi a primeira cliente do negócio de armazenamento de energia de Straubel. Leitura para o investidor O episódio do Wyoming expõe o principal gargalo da infraestrutura de IA em grande escala: equipamentos, acesso a energia e oposição de comunidades locais podem atrasar obras e encarecer orçamentos. Para desenvolvedores independentes, que dependem de capital externo e de contratos com clientes, um projeto de gigawatts que sai do controle se transforma em risco de difícil absorção. Há duas leituras possíveis. De um lado, a Crusoe segue com avaliação elevada e conseguiu captar recursos após o revés, o que sinaliza apetite do mercado pela carteira da empresa. De outro, a perda do ativo e a não conquista do Google como cliente naquele projeto indicam que a execução pesa tanto quanto a tese de crescimento. A relação, contudo, não foi encerrada: a Crusoe segue desenvolvendo para o Google outro data center, perto de Amarillo, no Texas. O caso reforça que o retorno de campus de IA depende de cronograma, custo e energia, variáveis que nem sempre aparecem nos anúncios de capacidade. Entre os pontos a acompanhar estão o valor da transação, ainda não divulgado, e o andamento das obras nos demais campi.
