artigo.texto: I'm a firm believer in investing in what you know—and what you use. During a recent visit to my parents' New Hampshire property, my brother and I tackled overdue maintenance, and having the right equipment on hand was critical to finish the work in the limited time we had. He and I rented both a compact track loader (CTL, not pictured) and a bulldozer (pictured above) from United Rentals (NYSE: URI) to push through some of the heavier work. For those who may not be familiar with the company, United Rentals can quickly deploy heavy equipment to a remote site. Here's why I believe it sets up well for a defined-risk, moderately bullish options trade. The good news is that United Rentals is currently trading at a below-market forward multiple — both on a Price-to-Earnings (P/E) basis, currently ~17.3x forward estimates of ~$61.10/share, and on an Enterprise Value-to-EBITDA (EV/EBITDA) basis at ~8.8x $9.25 billion in FYE2027 EBITDA. This despite the fact that the company is compounding revenues, earnings, and EBITDA at a noticeably faster clip than the cap-weighted S&P 500. Effectively, one can buy superior, market-beating growth at a discounted market multiple. The recent third-quarter earnings confirmed this trajectory. URI delivered a beat and raise, pointing to robust underlying demand across its end markets, and the sell-side is scrambling to catch up, revising its forward estimates upward. Improving earnings estimates is one of the most reliable, time-tested short-term investment factors. Stocks with positive estimate revisions tend to meaningfully outperform those burdened with declining estimates in the short term. The macro backdrop provides a sturdy foundation for this growth. We are in the midst of a broader nonresidential construction recovery, which has driven an environment of improving and resilient rental rates. Although admittedly a potential slowdown in data center construction could become a future headwind, broader infrastructure demand remains robust. A balanced view requires acknowledging the risks. While URI looks cheap relative to the broader market, it is not exactly cheap relative to its own history. The stock is currently trading roughly 20% to 25% above its five-year average multiple. One could easily argue that the historical multiple was simply too cheap for a business of this quality, scale, and capital efficiency. Still, mean reversion back to historical levels of "cheapness" remains a downside risk. This brings us to the options market. When you have a stock with solid momentum, fundamentals, and positive estimate revisions, but you're hesitant to pay a premium to its historical valuation, outright unhedged equity accumulation isn't always the optimal route. Instead, selling cash-covered puts offers a highly strategic entry mechanism. The trade With URI's implied volatility currently hovering in the 42% to 45% range, the options market is pricing in enough movement to offer a decent premium. By selling a cash-covered put, we acknowledge both the good and the bad. It respects the aggressive growth, market share capture, and the recent beat-and-raise quarter, while appropriately hedging against the risk of that elevated historical multiple. If the stock continues its upward march, the puts expire worthless, and we pocket a high-probability yield that easily beats fixed income. If the stock pulls back—perhaps toward that 5-year average multiple—we are assigned the shares at a lower effective cost basis, which, if it happens, we could lower even further by writing upside covered calls against it. (This approach to entering a stock, then writing covered calls if assigned, is sometimes referred to as "the wheel strategy"). So either we acquire an attractive stock at a price we dictate (the short strike, less the premium collected for selling it) or we simply collect premium for assuming that risk if the stock does not decline. For a company that provides the literal heavy lifting for infrastructure growth, that's a structural advantage worth trading. artigo.texto: CATL's 2,000-Kilometre EV Battery Claim Faces Severe Engineering Reality Check Chinese battery giant CATL is advancing research into lithium-air technology that theoretically promises electric vehicles a range of 2,000 kilometres, but formidable engineering hurdles keep the innovation confined to the laboratory. Chief editor: Ken Kariuki 0701401086 Chinese battery giant CATL is advancing research into lithium-air technology that theoretically promises electric vehicles a range of 2,000 kilometres on a single charge, but material scientists warn that formidable engineering hurdles keep the innovation confined to the laboratory. The prospect of a 2,000-kilometre range relies on the extraordinary theoretical energy density of lithium-air cells, which can reach up to 3,505 watt-hours per kilogramme. While this figure dwarfs the 200 to 300 Wh/kg capacity of current lithium-ion packs, translating the chemistry from a controlled cell environment to a mass-produced, safe, and durable automotive battery pack remains a monumental challenge that experts estimate is at least a decade away from commercial viability. The Chemistry of Air-Breathing Cells Unlike conventional lithium-ion batteries that rely on heavy, expensive transition metals like cobalt, nickel, and manganese for the cathode, lithium-air batteries use oxygen drawn directly from the ambient atmosphere as the cathode reactant. During discharge, lithium ions from the anode combine with oxygen to form lithium peroxide or lithium oxide, releasing energy in the process. This fundamental shift in chemistry eliminates the need for heavy metal oxides, drastically reducing the weight and potentially the raw material cost of the cell. Because the cathode reactant is not stored inside the battery casing but is instead continuously drawn from the environment, the theoretical specific energy of the system approaches that of gasoline, making it the holy grail of electrochemical storage. The 2,000-Kilometre Theoretical Gap Recent industry reports highlighting CATL's research have generated immense excitement, frequently citing the 2,000-kilometre range figure. However, this metric is derived from the theoretical limit of the raw chemical cell under perfect laboratory conditions. In a real-world electric vehicle, the battery cell represents only a fraction of the total system weight. A functional battery pack requires heavy thermal management systems, reinforced casings, complex wiring, and safety buffers. When the 3,505 Wh/kg cell-level figure is adjusted for pack-level integration, the effective energy density drops precipitously. Furthermore, the 2,000-kilometre claim assumes a highly efficient vehicle chassis and optimal driving conditions, ignoring the immense energy demands of highway speeds, climate control, and varying topographies. Furthermore, the immense weight of the required air filtration systems and protective casing means that a pack-level energy density of 1,000 Wh/kg is currently viewed as the absolute maximum achievable ceiling for commercial automotive applications within the next decade. Formidable Engineering Hurdles The transition from theory to reality is blocked by severe material science constraints that have plagued lithium-air research for decades. Engineers must overcome a matrix of chemical and physical limitations: - Moisture and Air Contamination: Lithium metal reacts violently with water. An air-breathing battery requires complex, heavy filtration membranes to let oxygen in while keeping atmospheric moisture and carbon dioxide out, which negates a significant portion of the weight savings. - Dendrite Formation: During the charging cycle, lithium ions tend to form needle-like structures called dendrites on the anode. These microscopic spikes can pierce the internal separator, causing catastrophic short circuits and thermal runaway. - Oxygen Electrode Degradation: The chemical byproducts of the oxygen reduction reaction are highly corrosive. They rapidly degrade the porous carbon cathode and the liquid electrolyte, leading to a severe loss of capacity over time. - Poor Cycle Life: While modern lithium-ion packs easily endure 1,500 to 2,000 charge cycles, practical lithium-air cells currently struggle to maintain stability beyond a few dozen cycles before failing entirely. Industry Timelines and Commercial Reality CATL's dominance in the global EV supply chain means its research directions heavily influence long-term industry pivots. The company is actively exploring various post-lithium-ion chemistries, including solid-state and condensed matter batteries, which offer more immediate, albeit less spectacular, improvements in safety and energy density. For the automotive sector, the lithium-air breakthrough represents a vital horizon for the post-2035 era, rather than an imminent product launch. Consumers waiting for a 2,000-kilometre EV will need to rely on incremental advancements in silicon-anode technology and semi-solid-state architectures for the foreseeable future. Until material scientists can solve the cycle-life and moisture-sensitivity paradoxes, the 2,000-kilometre battery will remain a brilliant theoretical benchmark rather than a driveway reality. Automotive executives remain highly skeptical of near-term integration, noting that the supply chain for specialized lithium metal anodes and solid electrolytes is virtually nonexistent at the scale required for global vehicle production. Consequently, legacy automakers and EV startups alike are focusing their immediate capital expenditure on incremental improvements to high-nickel cathode formulations. How did this story land? artigo.texto: Desenvolve SP e Möbius lançam fundo de R$ 70 milhões para provedores e data centers FIDC terá R$ 50 milhões da agência paulista e R$ 20 milhões da gestora para recebíveis, equipamentos e operações de consolidação. A Desenvolve SP e a Möbius Capital lançaram um Fundo de Investimento em Direitos Creditórios (FIDC) de R$ 70 milhões destinado ao financiamento de infraestrutura digital no Estado de São Paulo. O fundo tem como público provedores regionais de internet e data centers de pequeno porte e poderá financiar a compra de equipamentos, antecipar recebíveis e apoiar operações de fusão e aquisição. A estrutura conta com R$ 50 milhões subscritos pela Desenvolve SP em cotas seniores e R$ 20 milhões pela Möbius Capital em cotas subordinadas. O comunicado não informa quando os recursos estarão disponíveis para contratação nem detalha taxas, prazos ou limites de crédito por empresa. Uma das modalidades previstas é a antecipação de recebíveis dos provedores, originados em contratos com clientes pessoas físicas e jurídicas. O fundo também poderá investir em operações de crédito para a aquisição de equipamentos de infraestrutura tecnológica e para a expansão das empresas, incluindo compras e fusões de negócios do setor. “Temos um histórico de realizar financiamento para aquisições de provedores de internet, operações via mercado de capitais para fomentar o crescimento de empresas do setor, além de dar apoio no avanço da profissionalização e governança dessas companhias”, afirma Roberto Savaris, sócio e fundador da Möbius Capital. Segundo o anúncio, o fundo pretende ampliar o acesso ao crédito em regiões subatendidas, especialmente nas cidades do interior paulista. Entre os objetivos estão a expansão da conectividade em localidades com baixa penetração e a ampliação do acesso à infraestrutura de data centers. Composição de recursos públicos e privados A Desenvolve SP é a agência de fomento do Estado de São Paulo, vinculada à Secretaria de Desenvolvimento Econômico. Seu diretor-presidente, Ricardo Brito, relacionou a participação no fundo à estratégia de combinar recursos públicos e privados. “Nossa meta é ampliar o acesso ao crédito e facilitar recursos para negócios inovadores. Por meio do blended finance, conseguimos atrair investimento privado, potencializar o impacto do recurso público e alcançar mais empreendedores”, afirmou Brito. Os valores anunciados correspondem a recursos subscritos. O material divulgado não esclarece se os R$ 70 milhões já foram integralizados. A Möbius Capital foi uma das gestoras selecionadas na chamada pública da Desenvolve SP para FIDCs e Fundos de Investimento em Participações (FIPs). O processo incluiu a apresentação de uma Carta-Consulta com informações sobre a tese de investimento, estrutura, estratégia, governança, equipe, histórico e valor solicitado. Após a análise de elegibilidade e uma apresentação presencial, a proposta passou pela diligência da gestora e do fundo. Concluída essa etapa, o Comitê de Investimentos da Desenvolve SP aprovou o compromisso de investimento. Na sequência, foram implementados os termos e condições do compromisso, conforme os processos internos da agência. O comunicado não detalha os critérios de acesso ao financiamento pelas empresas interessadas. (Com assessoria de imprensa)

artigo.texto: A data center owner specifies 400 pieces of owner-furnished, contractor-installed equipment. The purchase orders go out. The manufacturers confirm ship dates. The construction schedule is built around those dates. Six months later, a generator arrives at the jobsite with undocumented damage. Nobody knows when it happened. Nobody knows who touched it last. The vendor says it left the factory clean. The carrier has no record of an incident. The site crew is pointing fingers. This is the accountability gap. And it costs the industry more than most owners realize before they've lived through it. The OFCI model creates accountability risk by design Owner-furnished, contractor-installed programs make financial sense. Owners can leverage their purchasing power, standardize equipment across a portfolio, maintain direct relationships with manufacturers, and build a data record that — if captured correctly — can improve how future programs are planned and executed. On paper, it looks like control. In practice, most OFCI programs distribute that equipment across a chain of custody that nobody fully owns. A manufacturer ships to a freight forwarder. The freight forwarder hands off to a carrier. The carrier delivers to a warehouse. The warehouse holds it until the GC is ready. The GC coordinates final delivery. The installation crew takes it from there. At each handoff, responsibility technically transfers. But accountability rarely does. Each party documents what they received, in whatever format their own system requires, and hands the equipment forward. If something is missing, damaged, or mislabeled, the discovery almost always comes late, usually at the point in the project when it causes the most disruption. The data problem underneath the accountability problem Most owners believe their OFCI equipment is being tracked. In many cases, it is; loosely, across multiple systems, with inconsistent standards and no shared source of truth. A manufacturer has a ship date in their ERP. A carrier has a delivery confirmation in their TMS. A warehouse has a receiving record in their WMS. The owner's project team has a schedule in their construction management platform. None of these systems talk to each other. The data lives in silos, and nobody is reconciling it in real time. When the project team needs to know where a piece of critical equipment is, they start making phone calls. When they need to know its condition, they hope someone took photos. When a discrepancy surfaces, they spend days reconstructing a chain of events from fragmented records. That is not visibility. It is archaeology. Research has found that US construction professionals spend an average of 14 hours per week on non-optimal activities such as searching for project data, correcting mistakes, and managing rework. That is 35% of their working hours. For the US construction sector at large, this accounted for over $177 billion in excess costs in 2018. What the gap actually costs The damage is rarely dramatic. It accumulates in the places that are hardest to measure. A generator arrives at the jobsite before the pad is ready. The site team has nowhere to put it, so it sits on the trailer longer than planned. That costs money. When the pad is finally ready, the equipment needs to be repositioned. That costs more money. If it was sitting in an uncontrolled environment, there may be questions about condition. That costs time. A switchgear unit ships with components missing — a configuration issue at the manufacturer that nobody caught on the way out. The project team discovers it during installation. Replacement parts have a 14-week lead time. The schedule absorbs the hit. None of these costs appear on a single line item. But they accumulate, and they all count toward the total cost of ownership for a program that looked predictable on paper. A pallet of equipment arrives at a warehouse and is logged as received. When it is released to the jobsite three months later, three pieces are missing. Nobody knows if they were missing at receipt or left during storage. The warehouse record is a single line item. The investigation goes nowhere. Each of these incidents has a specific cause. But the underlying condition is always the same: nobody owned that equipment at the moment the problem was created. A joint study by PlanGrid and FMI found that roughly 48% of US construction rework is directly attributable to inaccurate, inaccessible, and incompatible project data, costing the industry more than $31.3 billion annually. Chain of custody is a process, not a document The common solution to accountability gaps is paperwork. Bills of lading. Receiving records. Inspection checklists. These create documentation, but documentation is not the same as accountability. A receiving record captures what the warehouse accepted. It does not necessarily capture condition. A bill of lading records that a delivery was made. It does not capture what the driver saw when they opened the trailer. A checklist completed quickly and filed away creates a paper trail that is almost impossible to use as evidence when something goes wrong months later. Research bears this out. Project teams with centralized, easy-to-locate documentation are twice as likely to feel confident proving which party was responsible when a dispute arises. Teams whose documentation lives in email threads, text messages, and phone calls report the lowest confidence. Documentation structure determines whether it can actually be used. Real chain of custody means every touchpoint captures the same data — condition, serial numbers, quantities, photographs — in a format that feeds a single record the owner can actually use. Exceptions get flagged in real time, not discovered months later. And one party owns the continuity of that record across the entire chain, not just their piece of it. artigo.texto: Envision and ju:niz Energy Extend Partnership With 442 MWh Battery Storage in Bavaria The Smareg 13 project in VÃ¶hringen becomes the third joint project for the two groups. According to them, it relies on the Gen 8 platform, four-hour storage and a low-noise design. Envision Energy and ju:niz Energy are expanding their partnership with Smareg 13 (VÃ¶hringen II), a 442 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in Bavaria. According to the two groups' press release, it is their third joint project, bringing the total volume of their collaboration to nearly 600 MWh. Elsewhere in Europe, other players are developing smaller capacities, such as PGE Dystrybucja, which secured a grant for a 4 MW energy storage system in Lutomiersk. Storage also remains in focus across the Rhine on the gas side, where German gas storage is at a record low and the INES organisation is calling for reform. A developer and operator role for ju:niz Energy ju:niz Energy is responsible for the development, financing and realization of Smareg 13. The company will operate the system over the long term. The project forms part of its German BESS portfolio, which the company says is growing. The site is located adjacent to the operational Smareg 12 facility. According to the press release, the project would strengthen storage capacity in Bavaria and provide greater flexibility and balancing capability as Germany integrates a growing share of renewable energy. Envision's Gen 8 platform at the core of the project Smareg 13 will deploy Envision's Gen 8 BESS platform, which combines four-hour energy storage, advanced battery technology and grid-forming capabilities. The two companies say its low-noise design allows deployment in acoustically sensitive environments. According to the press release, this feature addresses one of the key site challenges. Henry Peng, Senior Vice President of Envision Energy and President of the EU and LATAM regions, says the group is moving forward with a significantly larger project before its first two projects have completed delivery. He sees this as evidence of Envision's role as a long-term technology partner. According to him, the company is also expanding its local capabilities in Germany. Vural Oezcan, chief operating officer (COO) at ju:niz Energy, says the project combines a very advanced development status with four-hour storage technology. He expects Smareg 13 to contribute to flexibility and system stability. He adds that Envision has proven to be a strong technology partner in the existing cooperation. artigo.texto: - Utah House Speaker Mike Schultz criticizes MIDA's role in data center decisions. - Schultz cites public concerns and process flaws in the Stratos Project's approval. - Reforms may include giving local governments more authority over data center approvals. SALT LAKE CITY — Utah House Speaker Mike Schultz agrees that the general public had "fair concerns" regarding the Stratos Project as the massive data center project, led by celebrity businessman Kevin O'Leary, was going through the state approval process. That's why he bemoans how those concerns and the whole process were handled. "You have Kevin O'Leary saying, China this and China that and whatever else, and I wanted to bang my head against the wall as that was happening. ... I've never been more frustrated than that," said Schultz, R-Hooper, recalling the drama during a joint Deseret News/KSL editorial board meeting on Monday. O'Leary worked out a framework for the data center proposal in a remote area of Box Elder County with the Military Installation Development Authority, a board made up of government appointees. It seeks to bolster the U.S. military's access to artificial intelligence and cloud-computing capabilities. Box Elder County leaders carried out additional votes to move it forward. One of the leaders who voted in favor said they felt pressured to accept it to avoid costly lawsuits. They could have rejected it and "the project area would not exist," MIDA executive director Dan Hemmert said last month. Project officials recently filed a new water application, which states the facility would include 11 data center building clusters along with a 7.5-gigawatt generation facility comprised of 15 500-megawatt combined-cycle natural gas power plants. It plans to use a little more than 1,700 acre-feet annually from Salt Wells Spring Stream. Meanwhile, multiple Utah residents who opposed the project have sued O'Leary and Fox News in recent months, claiming that the billionaire defamed them by falsely claiming they were agents of the Chinese government during interviews with the network for objecting to the plan. While O'Leary has sought a dismissal in at least one of the suits, the whole series of events was difficult to watch and proved that process adjustments are needed for data centers, Schultz said. "The thing that broke down on that was the process. That's where it went awry," he said. "Really getting back to fundamentally following the process on these controversial issues will help alleviate those concerns." A 'huge mistake' Data center reform may be one of the priorities during the 2027 legislative session, which is expected to be different following a drastic change in the Utah Legislature, said Schultz and Senate President-elect Evan Vickers, R-Cedar City. Senate President Stuart Adams, who serves as the MIDA board chair, was ousted in the Republican primary. Republicans also lost a supermajority in the House of Representatives for the first time in decades, the Associated Press projected on Monday. It's unclear how much of that was tied to data centers, but top state leaders acknowledged that it may have factored in lost public trust. Reforms to data center policy may start with giving local governments a greater say when it comes to approving data centers. Utah stepped up to oversee data centers when it became clear that they could overwhelm the state's energy grid without coordination between local governments, Schultz explained. However, he believes the recent backlash shows that the current process is broken. "MIDA should never be doing data centers," he said. "That was a huge mistake. ... I think it's important to know that and recognize that and make sure that doesn't happen again." Data centers can bring short-term property tax relief for Utahns and drastically improve local property tax bases in rural counties, the University of Utah Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute noted in August, which could help affordability challenges — likely another key subject next year. If you can go through this process and check those boxes, it really comes down to a local decision. Do you want it or don't you? –Utah Senate President-elect Evan Vickers But the institute warns that they can create future tax increases and "greater volatility" in some areas. That's on top of environmental concerns, which typically include urban heat, water consumption, and strains on electricity grids, the Yale School of Environment points out. The state, Vickers said, has already passed requirements tied to utility rates and water consumption. Modern facilities might be able to offset additional concerns, but the debate over pros and cons should be taken up on a local level. It's something that might require local entities to break down each request to see if it's the right fit. "If you can go through this process and check those boxes, it really comes down to a local decision," he said. "Do you want it or don't you?" Other adjustments? Utah may also examine other concerns, such as the rate of tax increments handed out for projects, Schultz noted. He and Vickers spoke on the issue weeks after fellow state lawmakers grilled Hemmert on the Stratos Project during interim meetings at the Utah Capitol. Some wondered if MIDA provided adequate notice about the project to the public or questioned whether local officials are facing pressure when considering MIDA partnerships. Others worried that public trust in MIDA was waning. Gov. Spencer Cox also called for major reforms to MIDA in August, largely over concerns tied to the Stratos Project. It's unclear how that will factor into future legislation, but Schultz said he prefers a future system where the state sets coordination guidelines and local governments decide on future projects. artigo.texto: Romulus City Council voted to temporarily ban data centers, discuss Flock cameras ROMULUS, Mich. (FOX 2) - The City of Romulus is getting ahead of the data center debate before it even begins, as they are temporarily banned before they even open. Data Centers and Flock, oh my! Big picture view: Data Centers and Flock cameras were the hot topic of discussion at Romulus City Hall on Monday. Residents joined the meeting expressing a number of environmental concerns and that they do not need one in their neighborhood. Meanwhile, the city council stressed that nothing has been proposed. A six-month moratorium would prevent them from even looking at proposals or applications, so the city council voted unanimously for the moratorium. Besides Data Centers, Flock cameras became another topic of discussion. The city has twenty up and running with thirty more scheduled to go up. Residents at the meeting questioned how they are being funded. Residents asked: Is it paid for by the city's Tax Increment Finance Authority, also known as ‘TIFA Board?’ Or was it the police department? Some say the original contract with Flock was for $47,500 but allege a short time later it was $90,000. What they're saying: When FOX 2 asked Mayor Robert McCraight about this discrepancy in October, he said it was a "typo by a clerical person." "It’s just a way to clean it up. We want to make sure everybody’s on board and on the same page," he said. "The TIFA Board knew what they were voting on to support and help alleviate some of that drain or general fun which is public safety dollars. But Romulus is a different community. We housed DTW. We talked about it before with 30-million travelers. That’s more than Disneyland and the Magic Kingdom. "So when you talk about 60–70 percent of the violent crime in Romulus is committed by people who don’t live here, we need to use tools to push that number down and our accredited police department is doing such. But we’re always going to look at one's venues. Is that the best technology that we have right now? It seems like. Can we get better? Absolutely." Watch FOX 2 Detroit LIVE The Source: FOX 2 attended the Romulus City Council meeting for details in this report.

artigo.texto: As manifestações na Europa movimentaram participantes em mais de sete cidades na região. Em Dublin, cerca de 2 mil pessoas marcharam pelas ruas da capital irlandesa, segundo a emissora pública RTE. Já em Helsinque, aproximadamente 1,3 mil manifestantes se reuniram no centro da cidade, além de atos registrados em municípios menores do interior da Finlândia, conforme informou a emissora estatal YLE. Representantes da coalizão Stop Dirty Data Centres, que reúne organizações comunitárias e de defesa do clima, declararam que o objetivo das manifestações é “frear a expansão descontrolada de data centers voltados para inteligência artificial e impedir que a democracia se torne refém dos interesses da indústria de big tech”. Movimentos civis da Escócia à Espanha e da França à Dinamarca aderiram à mobilização, exigindo uma moratória para paralisar novas obras “até que a sociedade decida democraticamente o que é necessário para garantir que a IA e os data centers sirvam às pessoas e ao planeta, e não à ganância privada”. Os atos deste sábado ocorrem na esteira de uma manifestação realizada na sexta-feira (6) em Amsterdã, na Holanda, onde centenas de ativistas entraram em confronto com as forças policiais em frente a um data center da Microsoft, resultando em uma prisão. A corrida global para a construção dessas instalações acelerou fortemente nos últimos meses, impulsionada por aportes de centenas de bilhões de dólares de gigantes da tecnologia em infraestrutura para treinar e operar modelos de inteligência artificial. O ritmo dessa expansão alarmou comunidades locais, preocupadas com a ocupação do solo, a disparada no consumo de eletricidade, o encarecimento das tarifas de energia e a falta de retorno econômico tangível para os cidadãos. A Irlanda tornou-se um dos principais polos de data centers da Europa ao atrair investimentos maciços de gigantes norte-americanas como Microsoft, Amazon e Google (controlada pela Alphabet). Em 2025, os data centers responderam por 23% de todo o consumo medido de energia elétrica no país, segundo dados do órgão oficial de estatísticas da Irlanda. Na Finlândia, manifestantes marcharam em direção aos escritórios do Google e seguiram até o Parlamento, em Helsinque. Em setembro, a multinacional anunciou seu maior investimento da história em território europeu: um pacote de € 13 bilhões (cerca de US$ 14,5 bilhões) para expandir um data center já existente e construir outras duas unidades no país. Ao todo, projetos de fazendas de servidores que somam cerca de € 80 bilhões tramitam em diferentes etapas de planejamento e execução na Finlândia, segundo estimativas da Confederação das Indústrias do país. A insatisfação popular entre os finlandeses aumentou após revelações de que representantes ligados ao Google desmataram áreas florestais, removeram a cobertura vegetal e abriram estradas em um dos terrenos antes da conclusão do relatório de impacto ambiental. A empresa responsável pela execução da obra é alvo de um inquérito criminal, enquanto o governo finlandês discute projetos de lei para impor limites à expansão das estruturas de IA.

artigo.texto: Harrisburg data center offers insight into technology and community concerns A Harrisburg data center operated by Alerify provides a closer look at the technology behind the cloud, as concerns grow over the development of larger hyperscale data centers in Pennsylvania. Video above: Top news stories from News 8 at 5 p.m. Inside a smaller data center "This data center here isn’t one of those large AI hyperscale data centers. It's actually only 2,500 square feet. And it fits in this commercial building right behind me," said Andy Kochanowski, CEO of Alerify, during a tour of the facility. Kochanowski explained that customers trust the center with their data and equipment, emphasizing the importance of security. "Customers trust us with their data and their equipment, and they don’t want anybody, you know, getting into it," Kochanowski said. Inside the facility, the hum of machines and air conditioning systems is constant. "That noise, is that all of the machines and everything?" asked News 8's Maegan Summers during the tour. "That noise is at some of the machines, but mainly it's the air conditioning systems to keep the equipment cool," Kochanowski said. The center houses computer servers and data storage rented by various customers, essentially serving as the physical form of the cloud. "It's almost like your personal belongings when you put them in storage. But we're doing it for computer equipment. So that's called co-location," Kochanowski said. "Virtual server hosting is basically, instead of owning equipment, you want to create a private server up in the cloud. This is the cloud," he added. Cooling and power demands The facility operates at about 50% capacity, with aisles of equipment rotated between hot and cold zones to regulate temperatures. "It's comfortable in here. It’s probably like 71 or 69. Yeah. So it's reasonable. But if you come in here, it’s probably going to feel like a temperature difference," Kochanowski said. Between cooling the building and powering the machines, the data center uses 40,000 to 80,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity per month. Despite its relatively small size — about 2,500 square feet, comparable to a tennis court — larger hyperscale data centers can span hundreds of thousands of square feet. One such center being built in Lancaster is 850 times larger than the Harrisburg facility. "We've seen more of these hyperscale data centers start to come up. Do you think that they're necessary?" Summers asked. "They need to go somewhere. You know, obviously I'm a consumer. I have a home. I don't want to see my electric rates go up either. And I don't want to deal with the noise. But they do need to go somewhere," Kochanowski said. Community concerns about hyperscale centers The rapid development of hyperscale data centers has sparked concerns among community groups like Lancaster Stands Up. Taylor Enterline, a member of the group, outlined their worries about the environmental and community impact. "The electric grid. What happens when there's a blackout? If there's a blackout, the data center is going to keep running. They have all these backup generators. But where does the help come from? For our neighbors, our biggest one is water. Our beautiful Susquehanna, down the road, is sacred. It's beautiful. How are we protecting our water?" Enterline said. Enterline suggested state-level regulations on hyperscale data centers and artificial intelligence, as well as community benefit agreements to hold developers accountable. "Testing and control. Right. We're not just like testing beforehand. We're testing during and we're testing afterwards. And if they are not following through on that, who is holding them accountable? Who knows if these large, you know, monstrosities of AI hyperscale data centers are going to be needed in five to 10 years? Who's responsible for shutting those down, cleaning them up? It should not be on the community who didn’t want them in the first place," Enterline said. Exploring more efficient practices As a smaller data center owner, Kochanowski shared his perspective on environmentally friendly practices, including partnering with Penn State students to develop more efficient air conditioning systems. "There are a lot of dilapidated, old foundries and steel mills that already have the power into those places but are just barren. We have to redo something like that versus starting brand new. We also need to be very conscientious of the noise, especially in communities. And the power draw, you know, to the extent they can produce their own power, that's great," Kochanowski said. He also highlighted the benefits of closed-loop cooling systems for water conservation. "I think that’s the best way to go, honestly. I mean, to the extent you can recirculate that water through that computer equipment and not have to continue to tap the challenges making that water cool itself down before it cycles back through," Kochanowski said. The future of data centers Looking ahead, Kochanowski predicted continued growth in the data center industry but noted that advancements in equipment could reduce the need for large facilities. "I think it's going to continue to grow. The question becomes whether or not the equipment needed shrinks. Then it may not be as big an issue in the future as what it is today," Kochanowski said.

artigo.texto: Community Corner ‘Nobody Here Asked For This’: Protestors Rally Against South Brunswick Data Center Advocates want the DEP to reject the air permit for the 341,000-square-foot AI data center in South Brunswick. SOUTH BRUNSWICK, NJ — More than 150 people packed Christ Congregation in Princeton on Friday to push back against a 341,000-square-foot AI data center going up on Route 1 in South Brunswick. The town hall came three days before the state’s deadline for public comment on the project’s air permit. Residents from South Brunswick, Princeton, Franklin and other nearby towns attended. Advocates were on hand to help them file comments with the state Department of Environmental Protection. Sentinel Data Centers, the developer, has applied to the DEP for an air permit to run 12 diesel generators at the site, which is on the former Princeton Nurseries property. Organizers said 20 generators are planned in total once the facility is fully running. Find out what's happening in South Brunswickfor free with the latest updates from Patch. The public comment period closes Monday. “A lot of people are still in shock that their local officials could approve something like this. They’re mad, and they’re ready to fight back. No one wants to breathe in toxic fumes from a data center,” said Ben Dziobek, executive director of Climate Revolution Action Network. Find out what's happening in South Brunswickfor free with the latest updates from Patch. “Nobody here asked for this facility, and nobody here is going to benefit from it,” Dziobek said. “If Governor Mikie Sherrill and Commissioner Ed Potosnak approve these diesel generators, they’re going to do it over the objections of thousands of people who will have to live with the consequences.” Charlie Kratovil, senior organizer at Food & Water Watch New Jersey, called on the state to reject the application. “The Bloomberg data center’s application for permission to pollute using a dozen dirty diesel generators is an immediate threat to our air, water, and climate,” Kratovil said. “We need Governor Sherrill to protect New Jersey by denying this permit and issuing a strong moratorium on data center construction.” Steven Donziger, an environmental and human rights attorney, talked about possible legal challenges to the project. “I’ve spent decades taking on some of the most powerful corporations in the world, and one thing I’ve learned is that no corporation is above the law,” Donziger said. “Bloomberg and Sentinel Data Centers should not be allowed to put corporate profits ahead of the health and safety of New Jersey families. Residents have every right to challenge this project, demand accountability, and pursue every legal avenue available to protect their communities.” The DEP held a public hearing on Sentinel’s application in late September. The department later extended the comment period after state Sen. Andrew Zwicker asked for more time for residents to weigh in. The final decision rests with DEP Commissioner Ed Potosnak. Before Sherrill appointed him to lead the department, Potosnak served on the Franklin Township Council and led the New Jersey League of Conservation Voters. The project has drawn opposition from residents, U.S. Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, D-12th District, and Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, D-12th District. The Princeton Mayor and Council and students at Princeton University have also come out against it. High school and college students planned a protest for 1 p.m. Saturday, outside the South Brunswick Municipal Building at 540 Ridge Road, less than 24 hours after the town hall. Climate Revolution Action Network organized the protest with the South Brunswick High School Democrats, New Jersey High School Democrats, Union County High School Democrats, College Democrats of New Jersey and TCNJ Democrats. Residents who want to comment before Monday’s deadline can use Climate Revolution Action Network’s template letter at climaterevolutionnj.org/sbdc. artigo.texto: Com bilhões de dólares injetados em novos data centers nos Estados Unidos, as comunidades locais questionam o retorno real desses investimentos bilionários em infraestrutura de energia, terrenos e equipamentos. O impacto real no mercado de trabalho Embora exijam aportes massivos, essas instalações costumam empregar apenas algumas dezenas de profissionais diretamente, como engenheiros, técnicos de TI e seguranças. Essa baixa contratação direta tem alimentado o ceticismo e gerado oposição comunitária em estados como Texas e Ohio, resultando em atrasos ou cancelamentos de US$ 156 bilhões em projetos apenas no ano de 2025. Uma pesquisa realizada por especialistas em economia urbana e mercado imobiliário analisou 1.584 data centers inaugurados entre 2000 e 2023 para entender se essas estruturas realmente fomentam postos de trabalho na região. A análise cruzou dados de localização, capacidade de consumo de energia e registros federais de emprego, comparando os municípios beneficiados com localidades semelhantes que não receberam os centros. Como e quando os empregos surgem Os dados indicam que, em média, de 1.000 a 1.300 postos de trabalho indiretos são criados nos municípios entre três e cinco anos após a abertura do primeiro centro. Nos dois primeiros anos, o cenário no mercado de trabalho permanece praticamente inalterado, excluindo o setor de construção civil. O estudo aponta que cada megawatt adicional de capacidade está associado a cerca de 7,4 empregos locais extras após cinco anos. Considerando expansões futuras, a estimativa cai para aproximadamente 2,7 postos de trabalho fora da construção por megawatt de capacidade final. Onde os novos postos se concentram Diferente do esperado, o crescimento das vagas não se reflete no comércio varejista ou em restaurantes. A expansão está fortemente concentrada nos setores imobiliário, de serviços profissionais e técnicos, além de transporte e armazenagem. Apesar de gerarem empregos indiretos, os pesquisadores ressaltam que os impactos ambientais e estruturais, como o consumo elevado de água e energia, além dos incentivos fiscais recebidos, mantêm o debate aberto sobre a viabilidade dessas instalações para as cidades.

artigo.texto: The Aurora City Council moved forward with a ban on giving tax incentives to data center developers on Monday. The ordinance, proposed by Aurora Mayor Mike Coffman, was approved unanimously by the council in a study session and will go to a future regular meeting for an official vote. Recommended Stories Aurora’s city code allows the city to use retail tax revenue and construction material use tax revenue generated by qualifying development projects to help finance public improvements and attract businesses. It also allows the city to waive sales or use taxes for certain developers. The ordinance, if passed at a future regular meeting, would prohibit data center incentives entirely. “There is an unprecedented amount of money behind data centers largely driven by AI and they do not need our tax dollars,” Coffman said about his proposed ordinance Monday. No councilmembers opposed the ordinance, but several brought up concerns or alternative proposals. The council already has the ability to vote on every sales and use tax incentive, including those for data centers, Councilmember Alison Coombs said, adding that if the council does not want to give incentives to a data center, it can vote against them. If the council wants to have a broader conversation about whether its oversight procedures work well, that conversation should go to a policy committee, Coombs said. Coffman countered that the process, which happens in executive sessions, is not transparent to the public. “I don’t think it’s wise to bind the hand of future councils,” Councilmember Curtis Gardner said, adding that creating a sweeping rule for one industry “is not a good way to do governance.” Four tax incentives have been issued for data centers totaling $83 million. As of earlier this year, about $9 million had been paid out against that potential, City Manager Jason Batchelor said. After some debate, the mayor stood firm on his proposal, saying he was putting it forward for a recorded vote as-is. “If somebody else wants to have a discussion on process and procedure, you’re welcome to do that, but you will vote on this issue,” Coffman said. None of the councilmembers present opposed the ordinance. Data centers have been a major topic of discussion in recent council meetings, during which the council has passed several data center regulations but twice denied a data center moratorium. Dozens of residents have attended recent meetings to oppose data centers in Aurora, specifically the Trident Data Center from Vantage Data Centers, which was planned for an area near Green Valley Ranch communities.

artigo.texto: Rivian and Redwood Materials Expand Partnership to Span the Lifecycle of the Battery Redwood will now recycle Rivian’s battery scrap and end-of-life packs as well as provide energy storage for its manufacturing plant IRVINE, Calif.–(BUSINESS WIRE)–American automaker Rivian (NASDAQ: RIVN) and energy technology company Redwood Materials today announced a major expansion of their partnership, establishing Redwood as one of Rivian’s key partners to enabling end-to-end energy solutions—recycling Rivian’s production scrap and end-of-life EV batteries, as well as providing stationary battery storage at its manufacturing plant in Normal, Illinois. Through the partnership, Redwood collects Rivian EV battery packs through Rivian’s nationwide network of service centers when they are no longer suitable for in-vehicle use. Redwood then evaluates each battery pack to determine whether to repurpose it for energy storage—deployed directly at Rivian’s manufacturing facilities or at other locations—or to recycle it. Redwood will now also recycle battery scrap generated at Rivian’s manufacturing operations. This new scope of the partnership builds on the existing work, announced in April 2026, that is deploying 10 megawatt-hours (MWh) of battery energy storage from repurposed Rivian battery packs at the automaker’s manufacturing plant in Normal, Illinois. RJ Scaringe, Rivian Founder and CEO, said: Giving Rivian battery packs a second life in stationary storage is a massive unlock for the energy transition, “By partnering with JB and the Redwood team, we’re turning retired EV batteries into a powerful tool to make the grid more reliable and lower energy costs for everyone.” JB Straubel, Redwood Materials Founder and CEO, said: Every Rivian battery pack that comes back to us is a potential source of domestic grid energy storage in addition to critical materials, “Redwood’s unique ability to integrate and redeploy Rivian batteries with our technology is an opportunity to enable fast, flexible and more cost-efficient energy storage. As the demand and cost for energy keeps rising, working with companies like Rivian is how we help meet these challenges.” When EV batteries reach the end of their useful lives in vehicles, they often still have substantial useful energy capacity for second-life applications, such as stationary storage. Energy storage applications with repurposed batteries can ease stress on the grid during periods of high electricity demand, improving grid reliability while reducing energy costs for the user, as well as the grid at large. During periods of low demand or when low-cost renewable energy is most productive, these packs can store electricity for easy dispatch during periods of higher demand. When paired with Rivian—and other—EV battery packs, Redwood’s proprietary technology architecture offers an integrated system that can respond intelligently to the needs of the facility it is serving. Once batteries are no longer useful in energy storage applications, or where scrap is generated during manufacturing, they can be recycled. Redwood’s advanced process is capable of recycling and recovering critical minerals like lithium, nickel, cobalt, and copper at rates exceeding 95 percent, encouraging the development of a circular, domestic supply chain for battery materials in the United States. This expanded partnership reflects a broader shift underway in how American manufacturers source power. As grid connections take years to secure and conventional infrastructure remains supply-constrained, companies increasingly need partners who can solve more than one piece of the problem—recovering materials, managing recycling, and deploying storage as a single system rather than separate vendors. Rivian’s work with Redwood is a model for that approach: one partnership spanning the full lifecycle of a battery, built to move faster than the grid alone can. artigo.texto: Jefferson County residents weigh extending data center moratorium at public meeting MONTICELLO, Fla. -- Jefferson County residents and leaders gathered for a public workshop to weigh the potential impacts of data centers and to discuss whether the county’s one-year moratorium should continue. County leaders said the workshop was intended to give both commissioners and the public a clearer understanding of how data centers could affect the area, including electricity and water consumption, runoff and noise. The meeting was also framed as an educational session, not a vote on any specific project. “You should always be concerned about anything that we are not very sure about. That’s the reason for this workshop, Tonight their not voting on anything the board of county commissioners is just educating themselves as well as the public so that they can make an informed decision once the moratorium expires in June of 2027,” said Doug Baber, county manager for Jefferson County. Some residents voiced skepticism about whether data centers would be a good fit for the community, including concerns about who would ultimately pay for the infrastructure and utility demands associated with large facilities. “People in the community were paying for the data centers utility usage and I need to know..My light bills are high enough, I don’t need to pay for a billionaires data center,” said Mary Harris, a Jefferson County resident. Jefferson County leaders agreed on June 18 to a one-year moratorium on data centers to allow time to consider their impact. Baber said the technology and the public perception around it can shift quickly. “Data centers change every day, through the good on some things, the bad on other things and a lot of times their the boogie man. So the things that you don’t know and you don’t respect often you think the worst of,” Baber said. During the workshop, electricity usage and the size of potential facilities were among the sticking points discussed. The forum also gave county commissioners and residents a chance to consider possible guardrails for data centers moving forward, as environmental concerns continue to be raised statewide about the pros and cons of data centers locating near neighborhoods.

The battery would work with the barn's existing solar array. UL certification, permitting and procurement have to happen first. The city has not released a power rating or a run-time target. Issaquah's order of work, heat pumps in 2025, solar in 2026, battery next, gives other cities a phased model for turning a busy public building into an outage shelter. No demo required, no credit card. Emerald Battery Labs, a Seattle-based sodium-ion battery manufacturer, announced on October 29 that it will develop a 60 kWh battery system for Pickering Barn in Issaquah, Washington. The plan pairs that storage with the 64.9 kW-DC solar array already on site, so the city's resilience hub can eventually carry critical loads when the grid goes down. A $671,000 grant from TransAlta Centralia Generation LLC supports part of the work. The city's October council calendar lists Agenda Bill 9256 for the TransAlta grant and the Pickering Barn battery storage. As Microgrid Media points out, that official record backs up the municipal project and the grant action, while Emerald's release supplies the vendor, the chemistry and the 60 kWh design. For now the battery exists as a design. Certification, permitting, procurement, installation, controls integration and commissioning all come before it can carry a single critical load. Issaquah still has to answer the questions every facilities director and emergency manager will face on their own site: how much power, for how long, and for which loads. A busy barn, upgraded in phases Pickering Barn belongs to Issaquah's Resilience Hub Initiative, which picks public facilities that can deliver essential services and community support during emergencies. The city's Solar + Storage Microgrid Feasibility Study flagged the barn as a priority site for a community resilience microgrid. The rest of the year it works as a gathering place, home to a weekly farmers market from May through October. Pickering Barn on an ordinary year Microgrid Knowledge; City of Issaquah via Microgrid Media The city installed heat pumps at the facility in 2025 and added the solar array earlier in 2026, which counted as the project's first phase. Storage is the second phase. According to Microgrid Knowledge, the upgrades are meant to work together: cut energy costs, use more renewable energy and give other public buildings a working example of how they can support community resilience. Issaquah has some history here: in 2023 it became the first city in Washington to earn LEED Gold certification from the U.S. Green Building Council. The battery is the piece that would let the barn disconnect, or island, from the grid and run critical loads on stored solar energy. The array on the roof does not make the barn a microgrid on its own. As Microgrid Media lays out, separating from the utility grid takes an islanding strategy, inverters and controls set up for it, protection, switching and a defined set of critical loads. Emerald's job description fits that list: battery integration with the city's existing solar and electrical hardware, energy management, battery management system communications and system-level safety validation. For operators who already have a rooftop array, that scope suggests a battery retrofit reopens the electrical design around the panels. It is more than adding a cabinet next to them. How long 60 kWh actually lasts Sixty kilowatt-hours is a tank size, and a tank size alone can't tell an emergency manager how many hours a warming center stays open. Run time depends on the battery's usable capacity, the inverter's power rating, the state-of-charge reserve held back, how much the solar produces, conversion losses, and the size and priority of whatever stays energized. The city and Emerald have not released a power rating or a verified outage-duration target. Kilowatt-hours (kWh) measure stored energy: how much is in the tank. Kilowatts (kW) measure power: how much load the system can carry at any one moment. A battery can have plenty of energy and still be unable to start a large load if its power rating is too low. The city's own solar estimate helps with scale, but only up to a point. Issaquah describes the array as a 65 kW project expected to generate 53.74 MWh a year and cut municipal electricity costs by more than $6,000 a year. Spread evenly over 365 days, that works out to roughly 147 kWh a day. On paper, an average day produces more than twice what the battery can hold. Averages are where the comfort ends. An annual figure smooths out the seasons and says nothing about cloudy stretches or the demand from a crowded building. Those gaps matter for anyone judging how far a 60 kWh battery could stretch during an outage. The savings figure tests something else: it reflects the array paying its way on normal days while connected to the grid. Outage service depends on what the battery and controls can deliver once the barn is islanded. The load list is what turns the tank size into a service promise. The city intends the barn to work as a warming and cooling center, and the resilience-hub idea also covers device charging and other support. artigo.texto: Mercado global de etiquetas para fios: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Mercado de etiquetas para fios até 2035: demanda por cabeamento de data centers impulsiona o crescimento Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de Etiquetas para Fios, o mercado entra em 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compras mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de suprimento mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de etiquetas para fios é um componente essencial, ainda que muitas vezes negligenciado, do setor mais amplo de soluções de identificação elétrica e industrial. No período de análise de 2026, o mercado se caracteriza por demanda estável, sustentada por exigências obrigatórias de segurança, conformidade e eficiência operacional nos setores de infraestrutura, manufatura e tecnologia. Este relatório oferece uma avaliação abrangente do estado atual do mercado, de suas cadeias de suprimento complexas e da dinâmica competitiva entre fornecedores globais de materiais e fabricantes especializados. As trajetórias de crescimento estão fundamentalmente atreladas ao investimento global em eletrificação, expansão de data centers, automação industrial e infraestrutura de energia renovável. O mercado não é monolítico: segmenta-se por tipo de material, tecnologia de impressão e indústria de uso final, cada qual com drivers de demanda e cenários competitivos próprios. Embora a sensibilidade a preço continue sendo um fator, a proposta de valor das etiquetas para fios está cada vez mais ligada à durabilidade, à legibilidade e à integração com sistemas digitais de gestão de ativos. O período de análise até 2035 prevê um mercado em evolução, respondendo à integração tecnológica e às pressões por sustentabilidade. Este relatório oferece uma base granular e orientada por dados para que as partes interessadas compreendam os fluxos de volume e valor, identifiquem oportunidades estratégicas e naveguem pelos desafios logísticos e competitivos que definirão o desenvolvimento do mercado na próxima década. O cenário-base para o mercado mundial de etiquetas para fios até 2035 pressupõe expansão contínua em ritmo moderado, com valor e volume globais crescendo de forma constante a partir da base de 2025. A demanda é ancorada por exigências obrigatórias de identificação em instalações elétricas, cablagem de dados e telecomunicações e painéis de controle industrial, nos quais as etiquetas apoiam a conformidade com normas de segurança, a eficiência da manutenção e a rastreabilidade. O driver concreto mais forte é a rápida expansão de data centers e de infraestrutura de cablagem de alta densidade, que exige grandes volumes de marcadores de fios duráveis e legíveis para instalação, comissionamento e manutenção contínua. A automação industrial e a fabricação de painéis de controle acrescentam demanda, à medida que montadores de painéis e integradores de sistemas especificam etiquetas que atendem às normas UL, IEC e outras. Instalações de energia renovável, incluindo parques solares e eólicos, contribuem com crescimento incremental por meio de suas extensas redes de fiação. Do lado da oferta, o mercado permanece fragmentado, com fornecedores globais de materiais e conversores especializados competindo em desempenho de material, durabilidade da impressão e velocidade de personalização. A volatilidade dos preços de matérias-primas para polímeros e adesivos representa um risco persistente de margem, enquanto a transição para impressão digital e kits de etiquetas pré-impressas está remodelando os canais de distribuição. Regionalmente, a Ásia-Pacífico mantém a maior participação no consumo, apoiada pela fabricação de eletrônicos e pelo investimento em infraestrutura, enquanto a América do Norte e a Europa priorizam produtos de alto desempenho e certificados. A previsão aponta para um índice de mercado de 142 em 2035 (2025=100), equivalente a uma CAGR de 3,6%, com potencial de alta decorrente da aceleração dos gastos com data centers e eletrificação e risco de baixa associado à fraqueza industrial cíclica. Drivers e restrições da demanda Principais drivers de demanda - A rápida construção de data centers e a cablagem de fibra e cobre de alta densidade exigem etiquetas para fios duráveis e legíveis para instalação e manutenção. - As normas de segurança elétrica e conformidade exigem identificação clara de fios em instalações industriais, comerciais e de infraestrutura. - A automação industrial e a fabricação de painéis de controle ampliam a demanda por marcadores de fios pré-impressos e imprimíveis. - Instalações de energia renovável, incluindo parques solares e eólicos, envolvem extensas redes de fiação que exigem etiquetagem. - O crescimento da fabricação de chicotes automotivos e aeroespaciais aumenta as exigências de rastreabilidade e identificação. - A automação predial e os sistemas inteligentes de gestão de instalações impulsionam a demanda por cabeamento estruturado e etiquetagem. Possíveis restrições ao crescimento - A volatilidade dos preços de matérias-primas de polímeros e adesivos pressiona as margens dos fabricantes e pode adiar decisões de compra. - A concorrência de produtores regionais de baixo custo limita o poder de precificação em segmentos sensíveis a preço. - A adoção de sistemas digitais e de gestão de ativos baseados em RFID pode reduzir a demanda por alguns tipos convencionais de etiquetas. - A fraqueza cíclica da produção industrial e da construção pode reduzir temporariamente o consumo de etiquetas para fios. artigo.texto: A corrida pela inteligência artificial está criando um novo desafio nos Estados Unidos: encontrar energia suficiente para manter os grandes centros de processamento de dados em funcionamento. Com a demanda por eletricidade crescendo rapidamente e as conexões à rede convencional demorando anos, empresas começaram a apostar em uma alternativa pouco comum: reaproveitar motores de aviões aposentados para gerar energia. A estratégia foi apresentada pelo jornal The New York Times. De acordo com a publicação, companhias especializadas estão retirando turbinas de aeronaves antigas e adaptando os equipamentos para funcionar como geradores elétricos. A solução tem atraído principalmente empresas que precisam colocar data centers em operação sem esperar pela conclusão de obras de infraestrutura energética. Um dos principais motivos para essa escolha é o tempo de instalação. Segundo Audun Martinsen, analista da consultoria Rystad Energy ouvido pelo jornal, conectar uma estrutura de 100 megawatts à rede elétrica pode levar cerca de sete anos. Com turbinas adaptadas, esse prazo poderia cair para aproximadamente dois anos. A diferença é importante para as empresas de inteligência artificial, que precisam ampliar rapidamente sua capacidade computacional. Os data centers consomem grandes volumes de eletricidade e dependem de fornecimento contínuo para manter servidores, sistemas de processamento e equipamentos de refrigeração funcionando. Motores militares poderiam gerar 40 mil megawatts O potencial dessa tecnologia também aparece em um levantamento da Administração de Informação de Energia dos Estados Unidos. Em janeiro, o órgão estimou que os motores de aproximadamente 4 mil aeronaves militares aposentadas, armazenadas em uma base no deserto de Tucson, poderiam alcançar uma capacidade de geração de cerca de 40 mil megawatts. O volume seria maior do que toda a capacidade de geração de energia do estado do Arizona. A estimativa ajuda a dimensionar o interesse pelo reaproveitamento desses equipamentos. Originalmente projetados para impulsionar aeronaves, os motores podem passar por adaptações para operar como turbinas geradoras de eletricidade. xAI e OpenAI já utilizam turbinas adaptadas Entre as empresas que recorreram a essa alternativa está a xAI, companhia de inteligência artificial de Elon Musk. Segundo o The New York Times, oito turbinas convertidas de motores de aeronaves foram instaladas no Mississippi para ajudar no abastecimento do data center Colossus 2, em Memphis. A presença dos equipamentos foi identificada pelo jornal a partir de licenças estaduais e imagens de satélite. A OpenAI também utilizou uma solução semelhante em seu primeiro complexo Stargate, localizado em Abilene, no Texas. Em 2025, a empresa recorreu a turbinas a gás para ampliar a oferta de eletricidade necessária ao funcionamento da estrutura. O movimento acompanha a expansão dos investimentos em inteligência artificial. Com a disputa por capacidade de processamento cada vez maior, as empresas buscam alternativas para evitar que a falta de energia atrase a construção e a operação de novos centros de dados. Organizações ambientais apontam riscos de poluição Apesar da rapidez na instalação, o uso de motores adaptados tem provocado críticas de organizações ambientais e moradores das regiões próximas aos empreendimentos. As principais preocupações envolvem a eficiência energética dos equipamentos e a emissão de poluentes. No Mississippi, o Centro de Direito Ambiental do Sul (SELC) contestou a autorização para o funcionamento das turbinas utilizadas pela xAI. A entidade questionou a documentação apresentada pelo fabricante e afirmou que não havia comprovação suficiente de que os equipamentos atendiam às exigências ambientais relacionadas à emissão de substâncias como o formaldeído. O grupo também acusou a empresa de apresentar estimativas abaixo do esperado para a quantidade de poluentes liberados. Patrick Anderson, advogado do SELC, criticou a escolha de uma tecnologia considerada mais poluente justamente por empresas que estão na linha de frente do desenvolvimento tecnológico. Na avaliação dele, a expansão da inteligência artificial deveria ser acompanhada por soluções de geração de energia menos prejudiciais ao meio ambiente. Outro problema apontado é que turbinas adaptadas de motores de aviões podem apresentar eficiência inferior à de equipamentos projetados especificamente para usinas a gás natural. Com isso, seria necessário utilizar mais unidades para produzir a mesma quantidade de eletricidade. A utilização desses motores mostra o tamanho do desafio energético provocado pela expansão da inteligência artificial. Enquanto as empresas tentam garantir eletricidade em menos tempo para ampliar seus data centers, cresce também a discussão sobre os impactos ambientais das soluções escolhidas para sustentar essa expansão. Compartilhe este conteúdo do Diário da Guanabara, o melhor site de notícias do Estado do Rio.

artigo.texto: Company proposing battery storage facility, data center infrastructure site in South Bend SOUTH BEND, Ind. (WSBT) — An energy center development could be in South Bend's future. The company nextNRG is planning to develop 27 acres into a data center infrastructure, battery storage, and pharmaceutical site. The multi-million-dollar proposal is in its early stages and the deal has not officially been closed. The proposed development, would be called the Lone Wolf Energy Center. The company nextNRG is planning to acquire 33-acres located on Lone Wolf Drive near the Toll Road and US 31 on South Bend's Northwest side. This announcement came as a surprise for neighbors who live nearby. “Well, I'm very shocked first of all. What is going on, Will it affect us? So, we're, I'm sure most of my neighbors out here are going to be very not happy. You know, they're upset already that no one contacts them and stuff,” said Tom Bayer. 27 acres would be used for data center infrastructure and battery storage. It's expected to support up to 70 megawatts of capacity, but could potentially go up to 100 megawatts. But it leaves neighbors with concerns about the potential long-term effects of this development. “So we'd like to know, are we protected? I heard about water issues, you know, I've heard about noise, which noise pollution, you know. So, there's a lot of issues that haven't been come forward to us," said Bayer. The city of South Bend says they have also had no communication with NextNRG and said in a statement: "The City learned of NextNRG’s involvement and the larger project scope from Inside Indiana Business on Friday. If accurate, the city will hold this project to protections and standards in the Neighborhood’s-First framework, including zero local incentives or subsidies and a requirement that the developer pay its own way for any infrastructure and energy needs." The existing 50,000 square-foot building would be leased separately to a pharmaceutical company for 10-years. NextNRG says the proposed acquisition remains subject to negotiation and execution of transaction documents. Meaning the deal has not officially closed for the $22 million purchase. WSBT sent a list of questions to NextNRG: What does the timeline look like for this project? - What does the timeline look like for this project? - How will the company address potential noise, emissions, water use, and traffic from this project? - Why is this location being chosen in South Bend? - What can those who live in South Bend expect from the company and completion of this data center? - How does the size of this data center and impact compare to other locations the company owns? - Some residents are calling for transparency about this project. Do you plan to hold a public, in-person meeting to address potential concerns? - What are the potential costs of this project? NextNRG response: Statement: NextNRG was founded to make energy smarter and cleaner, and the Lone Wolf Energy Center in South Bend is designed to meet growing technology demand without putting the cost on the community. When our November 5 announcement referred to a data center, it meant the amount of power the site can support, not the development of a traditional hyperscale facility. Lone Wolf aims to generate its own power on site to support compact, modular computing units, so it won’t strain the local grid, raise utility rates, draw on local water or seek local tax incentives. The project remains in its early stages, with negotiations ongoing and no final agreements in place. We look forward to working alongside South Bend residents to pioneer a greener model that the community can be proud of as we spearhead the future of energy, together. FAQ Is NextNRG building a data center in South Bend? No. Lone Wolf is intended as an energy project that will generate power on site and use it to support modular computing units. These are container-sized systems set on concrete pads, with no large building, no water use and no major construction. Our announcement used the term “data center” to describe the site’s power capacity, not the type of facility. How is modular computing different from a traditional data center? Modular computing units are compact, quiet, and self-contained. They have their own cooling systems, need only limited construction, and run at a fraction of the scale of hyperscale campuses, which can span millions of square feet, draw hundreds of megawatts from the local grid, and use large amounts of water for cooling. Will this affect my utility bills, water or taxes? Lone Wolf is designed to produce its own power, so it is not expected to strain the grid or raise residents’ utility rates. It does not draw on local water and is not seeking local tax incentives. It is expected to add to the local tax base, not take from it. How will this impact the surrounding community? Lone Wolf would add to South Bend’s tax base and bring local construction jobs to the area. Because the project will generate its own power, it would reduce reliance on the local grid and would not increase residents’ utility rates. It would also not draw on local water or rely on local tax incentives, and construction would be limited to site preparation. Where does the project stand? The project is in its early stages, with negotiations ongoing and no final agreements in place. NextNRG looks forward to working openly with residents as plans develop. It’s unclear what the timeline is or when the approval process could be finalized.

A proximidade de redes de comunicação robustas e o fornecimento estável de energia elétrica tornam-se decisivos. A expansão contínua da demanda por dados garante que esse segmento continue atraindo grandes aportes financeiros nos próximos anos, redesenhando o perfil das grandes metrópoles e polos tecnológicos.

artigo.texto: Quincy data center tour offers lessons as Montana weighs development QUINCY, Wash. — As Montana debates data center development, midterm election voters are making it clear they want a say in what comes next. NBC Montana’s Laurel Staples visited one of the nation’s largest data center hubs to see how the technology is changing and what Montana could learn from it. Eight data center campuses operate in Quincy, Washington, where Montana Tech’s Robert Morris, who serves on Montana’s Energy Task Force, joined NBC Montana for a tour. Morris, who has four decades of experience in the industry, said newer facilities are becoming more efficient in how they use electricity. “More of the power goes right to the servers rather than the cooling systems and the power system itself,” Morris said. Water use is another key question. “They’ve gone from evaporative coolers that use utility supply or civil supply of water to air-cool chillers, which use no external water for cooling,” Morris said. Newer cooling technologies can reduce water use, but city officials say data centers account for about 5% to 8% of Quincy’s water use. Before entering the facility, Morris pointed to transmission lines carrying hydropower from the Columbia River system into the regional grid part of a vital energy corridor which connects to the Colstrip Plant in Montana. He also used a phone app to take a rough, uncalibrated sound reading near the campus. The app fluctuated between about 70 and 100 decibels, a range that spans from a vacuum cleaner to a loud power lawn mower. For Morris, it’s another data point in a broader effort to give communities facts as they consider data center development. “My approach is to not pick sides but to bring data. And that’s what I try to do. It is very emotionally charged, and data centers are not right for every place. But let’s understand what the real facts are, and then each community can make its own choice.” Morris said. Inside Sabey Data Centers’ newest building, representatives described a colocation model in which customers from different industries store data at the facility. Those customers include health care and agriculture businesses. One example shared during the tour was how farmers use stored data to track soil composition and apple inventory. The tour showed how the facility manages heat from its servers. Warm air moves through a ceiling plenum to a cooling area, where fans pull it across chilled coils. The cooled air then returns to the server hall. The liquid used in the cooling process is sent to outdoor chillers to be cooled and reused, according to company representatives. Morris said the newest building reflects how quickly the technology has advanced. He also noted that the air chillers were quiet during the visit. Morris said Quincy also offers a lesson in planning. He said data center developers, local leaders and Grant County Public Utility District worked together on infrastructure, which he said was paid for by the data center. In a second report, NBC Montana will examine how data center development has affected Quincy and what the community’s experience could mean for Montana.
