artigo.texto: Trending LANSING -- Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel has filed a petition for rehearing before the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC) in case U-22058, wherein the Commission approved DTE's special contracts to service a Google hyperscale data center in Van Buren Township. The Attorney General repeatedly demonstrates in her petition where DTE failed to meet its legal burdens, the MPSC ruled in error by applying incorrect standards of review and acting without reason or regard for ratepayer protections, and how the consequences of both are unnecessary risks of cost-shifting from DTE and Google to the utility's household, business, and other classes of customers. Attorney General Nessel raises in her petition several proposals for strengthening DTE's cost recoveries from Google, establishing sufficient cost and benefit tracking mechanisms, and ensuring adequate cost backstops by Google and DTE that won't ultimately fall on DTE's existing ratepaying customers. "These are massive, twenty-year, billion-dollar contracts between one of the wealthiest businesses on the planet, and one of the most powerful companies in the State," said Attorney General Nessel. "The MPSC simply didn't do their job here – failing to protect DTE's existing residential and business customers, and accepting lousy contracts with weak terms to yet again appease a utility they're supposed to keep in check. Sweetheart deals for data centers and unaccountable utilities run amok is not responsible government, and it's not good business for the State. In this petition we've outlined serious concerns about how these contracts set up DTE customers to be burned." Among the Attorney General's most significant concerns is the MPSC's decision to adopt DTE's contract-long "aggregation" approach to assessing projected ratepayer benefits against the utility's actual costs to serve the Google data center. This decision presumably accepts years-long periods where DTE's other customers will directly subsidize the operation of the hypserscale data center, and the MPSC itself concedes this will certainly happen, at least for a four-year period from 2035 to 2038. DTE proposed to the MPSC a 20-year term-long "aggregation" standard for evaluating costs and benefits to and from its other customers, and assumes only to evaluate or demonstrate whether other customers bore any net-negative cost of serving the Google data center in view of the entire 20-year term, indicating that DTE expects its other customers to pay costs to support the data center and makes difficult any challenge to those costs until the contract term concludes. The MPSC order establishes the precedent and the expectation for their acceptance of DTE passing on data center costs to other ratepayers in any number of years under the presumption of a longer-term benefit that has not been adequately supported throughout the case and that may not ever be realized. "The most shocking part of these contracts is that DTE and the MPSC are seemingly signing off on unknown ratepayer costs to support the Google data center, as long as DTE's benefit projections can keep pace for 20 years" added Attorney General Nessel. "It's imperative to keep DTE from charging Michigan households their own costs to fuel Google's data center, and that we insist that costs and benefits be accounted for and reconciled annually. This aggregation standard, on a twenty-year contract, simply swings the doors wide open for customer cost-shifting, and that's how the data center crash-lands onto your electric bill." The MPSC additionally adopted a collateral cap limiting Google and parent company Alphabet's liability for costs of service, which the Attorney General urges the MPSC to reject outright on rehearing. As it did when considering the DTE contracts to service the Oracle and Open AI data center in Saline, the MPSC also ignored in this case significant transmission costs identified by the Attorney General that DTE has refused to account for in its contracts and assessments. For these reasons, and more articulated within the petition, the Attorney General asserts the MPSC's order demonstrates a litany of errors, such as by applying an incorrect burden of proof and an incorrect standard of review, by failing to meaningfully engage with or outright ignoring important arguments from the Attorney General's briefing, and by repeatedly defaulting to acceptance of DTE's proposed terms despite DTE's failures to support the reasonableness and prudence of those terms. The consequence of these errors, argues Attorney General Nessel, is the imposition of mistaken and unnecessary cost-shifting risks onto Michigan ratepayers. The Attorney General argues that, given DTE's repeated failure throughout the contested case to meet its burden of proof under Michigan law, the MPSC must adopt on rehearing the recommendations made in her petition or instead reject the contracts outright.

artigo.texto: Statesboro’s city government, through City Attorney Cain Smith, filed a response Oct. 19-21 in Bulloch County Superior Court to a lawsuit seeking to reverse the city’s Aug. 18 rezoning of a 27-acre tract on Burkhalter Road to “O” or office at the request of data center developers. Meanwhile, Smith says that processing by the city of any further application by the property owner and potential developer, 4AM Development LLC, for a special use permit required for a data center “would continue to be stayed.” In other words, unless the court upholds the zoning or until it issues some other go-ahead, the mayor and council apparently won’t be holding a hearing to consider issuing a permit, even if 4AM Development, whose publicly identified partners are Bobby Bagwell and Charles C. Way, try to submit a completed application. The Data Centers Ordinance, enacted in June by a 3-1 vote of City Council as an amendment to the Statesboro Unified Development Code, allows data centers as a special use in four non-residential zoning classifications. However, “special use” means that a data center will not be automatically allowed. Instead, plans for any particular site must meet special requirements for a permit to be issued by the council on a majority vote. Way and Bagwell, whose company reportedly includes two other investors, propose locating a 230,000-square-foot data center on the site at 6539 Burkhalter Road, and have applied to Georgia Power for an up to 99-megawatt electrical supply. City Council’s Aug. 18 vote approving the rezoning from “R-4” high-density residential to “O” was 3-2, including the mayor’s tiebreaker. Original complaint But on Sept. 17, the nonprofit organization Coastal Communities United and 11 named individuals, including some adjacent property owners and other nearby residents, filed a petition in the county Superior Court for review of the rezoning and a declaratory judgment against the city’s action. Although worded in some ways like a standard lawsuit, the “petition for review” signed by attorney Robert Abney Fricks Sr. of Warner Robins identified his clients as petitioners rather than plaintiffs. But it named both the city, as a municipal corporation, and 4AM Development as defendants. It asserted that the petitioners would suffer damages “to be determined” but asserted no monetary amounts. In the closing paragraphs of the 30-page complaint, the petitioners asked that the court declare the city zoning decision “invalid, void or stricken.” Citing a provision of state law, the complaint also asserts that filing such a challenge should “stay all legal proceedings in furtherance of the action.” 4AM’s previous answer As previously reported, 4 AM Development LLC, though William J. Keogh III, of the Augusta-based Hull Barrett law firm, then replied with an Oct. 6 "motion to dismiss and request for expedited hearing.” Points of that motion were reported by the Statesboro Herald in an Oct. 12 story. At that time city officials had not filed a separate answer, but Smith said the city would have to do so or face a “default judgment” and would answer by a 30-day deadline from having been served notice of the suit. Notice had been served Sept. 21 at City Hall. The city’s answer, signed by Smith as submitted to the court Oct. 19 and stamped at the clerk of court’s office Oct. 21, runs to 16 pages. It parallels the 4AM Development response in some ways, such as by asserting that the nonprofit organization and the 11 property owners or neighbors at various distances from the site lack legal standing to challenge the zoning decision. The city’s answer But the city’s response differs from the developers’ in other ways, such as by asserting a defense of sovereign immunity. The city’s “first defense” is simply: “The Petition fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted and thus should be dismissed.” The “second defense” is that the petitioners allegedly lack standing. “Petitioner Coastal Community United should be dismissed from this action,” Smith has asserted in the city’s written answer. “An organization cannot obtain standing merely by asserting its members’ rights. It must establish a cognizable violation of its own rights under an available standing theory.” He cites the 2025 opinion of the Georgia Supreme Court in a case called Republican National Committee v. Eternal Vigilance Action Inc. in support of this. Smith then cites the state high court in a different decision, from 2006, as holding “that a plaintiff cannot avoid zoning-standing requirements merely by seeking equitable relief or asserting an interest in enforcing zoning laws.” The city’s fourth defense, the one claiming sovereign immunity, is aimed at an assertion in the petitioners’ complaint that the rezoning decision amounts to an “inverse condemnation” by reduction of nearby property values. “Petitioners do not allege and cannot show that private property has been taken for public use, nor does the City maintain any control or interest in the rezoned property; the city is therefore immune from claims for inverse condemnation,” the answer asserts. The city’s “fourth defense” briefly echoes a point of the developers’ motion, that petitioners “are barred from making a Constitutional attack for the first time before the Superior Court.” In other words, the defendants assert that the citizens should have stated a constitutional basis for their objections during the rezoning hearings. But then the city’s “fifth defense” claims that the petitioners’ complaints “are not ripe for adjudication” because the data center project “cannot be undertaken without the issuance of a special use permit by the Mayor and Council.” The city’s answer continues through 12 stated “defenses,” most very short and direct. But the 12th goes on to list 115 specific points from the petitioners’ complaints as “denied” or “admitted.” It ends with a request to the court dismiss the petition and require the petitioners to pay all costs of the act

artigo.texto: The Case for Prefabricated Power in AI Data Centers Key Highlights - Prefabricated power modules integrate critical electrical systems into factory-tested, cohesive solutions. - Off-site assembly can cut deployment timelines in half compared to traditional construction. - Factory testing reduces on-site complexity, commissioning delays and unexpected construction costs. - Modular infrastructure enables flexible capital investment and more efficient long-term operations. - Power skids and outdoor modules offer deployment flexibility for different site requirements. The AI boom has placed data center operators in a historic squeeze. CTOs and infrastructure managers are under pressure to bring massive, high-density computing capacity online faster than ever, even as the grid struggles to keep up. And as demands intensify, there’s very little room for error. The question now is how the industry can scale AI infrastructure without putting reliability, power availability, and the grid itself at risk. In this high-stakes environment, power-related challenges represent a massive business risk. They remain the leading cause of impactful data center outages and cost the world’s 500 largest companies an estimated $1.4 trillion annually. That makes the way power infrastructure is designed, built and deployed more important than ever. The industry is beginning to rethink the traditional approach to building power infrastructure. To scale rapidly without compromising reliability, the industry is shifting toward prefabricated, factory-tested power modules. By moving complex electrical assembly off-site, operators can balance the competing demands of deployment speed, financial risk, and total cost of ownership. The Technical Reality: A Power Module Is a Cohesive System A prefabricated power module is more than a group of components assembled on a metal floor. It’s an integrated system that is engineered and tested to operate as a single unit. In a typical deployment, a weather-proof outdoor module or an indoor structural skid houses: - Medium Voltage (MV) Switchgear: The entry point for utility power, providing robust protection and control. - Low Voltage (LV) Distribution Switchboards: Directs large blocks of power to the server rooms. - High-Efficiency UPS Systems: Industrial-grade systems operating at optimized efficiency to minimize energy waste. - Energy Storage: Long-life valve regulated lead‐acid (VRLA) or high-density Lithium-Ion battery cabinets. - Auxiliary Systems: Factory-installed direct expansion (DX) cooling, clean-agent fire suppression, security cameras, and comprehensive environmental monitoring. The critical engineering value lies in factory-level integration. When these systems are designed, wired, piped, and programmed under controlled factory conditions, the complex electrical and digital interactions between them are fully validated before shipping. For example, coordination between an MV switchgear’s circuit breaker trip settings, a UPS’s transient response, and a Lithium-Ion battery’s management system is highly sensitive. Resolving a communication mismatch or tight clearance issue on-site during commissioning can delay a project by weeks. Resolving it on the factory floor, where engineers have specialized diagnostics and direct manufacturer support, takes hours instead of weeks and eliminates on-site construction errors. Balancing the Tradeoffs: Speed vs. Cost vs. Risk Infrastructure buyers prioritize outcomes differently. Hyperscalers might value pure speed to market, while colocation providers and enterprise operators may be highly sensitive to upfront CapEx, long-term OpEx, or project risk. Prefabricated modular infrastructure shifts the traditional trade-off curve across all three variables: 1. Speed: Accelerating Time-to-Market For AI developers chasing first-mover advantages, speed is often the primary metric. By moving much of the electrical work off-site, prefabricated power modules can significantly shorten deployment timelines. For example, Schneider Electric’s power skids can be operational in half the time of traditional “stick-built” electrical rooms. A new research paper co-authored with hyperscale developer Compass Datacenters also highlights the quantitative deployment efficiency gains of shifting from traditional white space builds to prefabricated modular IT pods. According to the study performed at a Compass hyperscale data center campus, prefabricated modular pods shorten onsite installation time from 75.5 hours to just 15 hours per pod, delivering an 80% reduction in onsite installation duration. By shifting critical assembly, integration and verification to a controlled factory environment, data center operators can reduce on-site labor and complexity while bringing AI compute capacity online faster. 2. Risk: Shifting Complexity Off-Site On-site construction is inherently unpredictable, plagued by weather delays, labor shortages, and variable craft quality. Shifting assembly to an ISO-certified manufacturing facility replaces field variables with standardized quality control. Factory-tested validation ensures that the module arrives as a "plug-and-play" asset, eliminating unexpected construction expenses and ensuring the system works flawlessly from day one. 3. Cost: Granular CapEx, Reduced OpEx, and Environmental Impact From a financial perspective, modular construction also gives operators more flexibility with capital. Instead of building massive, over-engineered structures on day one to accommodate growth that may not happen for years, they can add capacity as demand materializes. That means capital can be deployed when it is actually needed, rather than tying up millions in infrastructure long before the servers — and the revenue they generate — are ready. There are operational savings, too. Pre-engineered systems can be paired with cloud-based monitoring and intelligent management platforms that give operators a much clearer view of system health in

artigo.texto: Bloomberg — A ByteDance, proprietária do TikTok, considera expandir um projeto de data center no nordeste do Brasil, uma iniciativa que reforçaria sua posição como principal player de infraestrutura de dados da América Latina. A empresa sediada em Pequim está buscando uma incorporadora para supervisionar a segunda fase de um projeto em um porto industrial no estado do Ceará, onde se beneficia de incentivos fiscais para a exportação de dados, segundo pessoas a par do processo que pediram para não ser identificadas ao discutir informações confidenciais. Está em jogo o esforço do Brasil para se manter como um player competitivo de data centers, em um momento em que países, incluindo o Chile e a Argentina, estão oferecendo incentivos e criando infraestrutura para atrair os mesmos tipos de investimentos. A expansão seria ainda maior do que o projeto de US$ 10 bilhões e 300 megawatts atualmente em construção, também no Ceará, afirmaram as fontes. A ByteDance também está em negociações iniciais com desenvolvedores para um data center de tamanho semelhante fora do porto de Pecém, acrescentaram algumas das fontes. O projeto atenderia clientes no Brasil, enquanto os data centers em Pecém são obrigados a exportar os dados para se qualificarem para isenções fiscais. ⟶ Assine as newsletters da Bloomberg Línea e receba as notícias do dia em primeira mão no e-mail. A ByteDance não respondeu a um e-mail solicitando comentários. Para apoiar sua aposta na IA como seu próximo motor de crescimento, a ByteDance está focada em aumentar os gastos com hardware para equipar melhor suas instalações. No entanto, a reação negativa dos eleitores contra os data centers nas eleições de meio de mandato nos Estados Unidos ameaça desacelerar a expansão em andamento e levar os desenvolvedores a considerar outros locais, como o Brasil. Leia também: Nubank e Mercado Pago suspendem transações com criptomoedas após falhas em fornecedores A capacidade dos data centers do Brasil mais que dobrou desde 2022, ultrapassando um gigawatt, de acordo com o grupo setorial Brasscom. A entidade prevê que a capacidade instalada cresça cerca de 20% ao ano até 2031, quase triplicando em relação aos níveis de 2025. Pecém está localizada em uma das regiões mais atraentes do Brasil para geração eólica e solar, o que torna os data centers menos dependentes de linhas de transmissão do que outros projetos no sul do Brasil. No ano passado, a ByteDance anunciou que investiria R$ 200 bilhões (US$ 36 bilhões) em um complexo de data centers em Pecém, a ser construído em fases. A construção da primeira etapa teve início no início de 2026. A cidade de Fortaleza, próxima a Pecém, abriga o maior centro de cabos de fibra óptica da América do Sul, que pode ser utilizado para exportação de dados. “A região em torno de Fortaleza, e o Nordeste em geral, se destacam porque os cabos submarinos do Brasil chegam exatamente ali”, afirmou o presidente da Brasscom, Affonso Nina. “Essa é uma localização privilegiada.” Incentivo ao investimento A construção de data centers no Brasil deve acelerar após o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ter assinado, em setembro, medidas de isenção fiscal para a importação de equipamentos. As medidas reduzem a carga tributária sobre servidores, processadores e equipamentos de rede importados em cerca de um terço, contribuindo para tornar a maior economia da América Latina um local mais competitivo para data centers. O setor ainda aguarda que o governo publique regulamentações detalhando quais produtos se qualificarão para os incentivos fiscais. Os data centers contam com apoio bipartidário no Brasil e, ao contrário dos Estados Unidos, a oposição local tem sido limitada. Lula prometeu trazer mais data centers para o Brasil em seu discurso de vitória após ser reeleito em outubro. Embora o setor tenha comemorado a aprovação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter no Brasil (Redata), ainda existem obstáculos para que o país alcance seu potencial, como a expansão das linhas de transmissão de energia elétrica para levar mais energia renovável aos centros populacionais no sul do Brasil. “Ainda temos outros desafios”, afirma a sócia especializada em energia do escritório de advocacia BMA Advogados, Bruna de Barros Correia. “Temos uma rede de transmissão que não consegue acomodar todas as usinas que buscam se conectar ao sistema.” -- Com a colaboração de Zheping Huang. artigo.texto: Publicidade O Ministério das Comunicações informou nesta segunda-feira (9) que o governo federal planeja investir R$ 46,3 milhões no desenvolvimento de uma plataforma de gerenciamento e distribuição de dados entre mini data centers no Brasil. Batizado de Prisma, o projeto utilizará inteligência artificial para identificar onde e como os dados devem ser processados, distribuindo automaticamente os recursos computacionais entre diferentes infraestruturas. Na prática, o Executivo espera que a tecnologia reduza gastos com energia e custos operacionais, acelere o acesso às informações e aumente a proteção de dados estratégicos. Os recursos serão administrados pela Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep), e o projeto será executado pelo Centro Brasileiro de Inovação em Tecnologias da Informação e da Comunicação (CPQD). O prazo de execução é de 36 meses, a partir da celebração do convênio de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação entre a Finep e o CPQD. O ministro das Comunicações, Frederico Filho, afirmou que o projeto possibilitará maior autonomia e soberania no tratamento de dados no País. “Investir em tecnologia nacional é garantir que o Brasil tenha mais autonomia para proteger suas informações e desenvolver soluções para os desafios do futuro. Estamos fortalecendo a inovação brasileira e criando condições para uma infraestrutura digital mais moderna, segura e sustentável, reduzindo nossa dependência de tecnologias desenvolvidas no exterior”, afirmou em nota.

artigo.texto: Publicidade Os protestos contra data centers continuaram neste sábado (7) em várias partes da Europa. Cidadãos foram às ruas para manifestar preocupação com os impactos dessas instalações sobre a sociedade e o meio ambiente. Cerca de 2 mil pessoas marcharam em Dublin, na Irlanda, segundo a emissora RTE. Em Helsinque, na Finlândia, aproximadamente 1,3 pessoas participaram de uma manifestação, e atos também foram realizados em várias cidades menores da Finlândia, informou a televisão YLE. Representantes do Stop Dirty Data Centres, uma coalizão de grupos locais em defesa da democracia e do clima, disseram que pretendem “interromper a expansão desenfreada dos data centers de IA e impedir que nossa democracia seja feita refém dos interesses das grandes empresas de tecnologia”. Grupos de campanha da Escócia à Espanha e da França à Dinamarca participaram dos atos. Eles pedem uma moratória que suspenda as construções “até que nós, cidadãos, decidamos democraticamente o que é necessário para garantir que a IA e os data centers atendam às pessoas e ao planeta, e não à ganância privada”. Os protestos deste sábado foram realizados após uma manifestação na sexta-feira, em Amsterdã, quando centenas de pessoas entraram em confronto com a polícia em um data center da Microsoft Corp. Uma pessoa foi presa. A construção de data centers em todo o mundo se acelerou à medida que empresas de tecnologia investem centenas de bilhões de dólares em infraestrutura para treinar e operar sistemas de inteligência artificial. O ritmo dessa expansão preocupa comunidades que temem a demanda por terrenos e eletricidade, o aumento dos custos de energia e a possibilidade de não receberem benefícios econômicos. Continua depois da publicidade A Irlanda atraiu investimentos de grande porte de gigantes americanas de tecnologia, entre elas Microsoft, Amazon e Google, da Alphabet. Isso transformou o país em um importante polo de data centers — um dos maiores da Europa. Segundo o órgão oficial de estatísticas, essas instalações responderam por 23% do consumo total de eletricidade medido no país em 2025. No sábado, manifestantes marcharam até os escritórios do Google e o Parlamento, no centro de Helsinque, informou a YLE. Em setembro, o Google anunciou seu maior investimento já feito na Europa: € 13 bilhões (US$ 14,5 bilhões) na Finlândia. O plano prevê a ampliação de um data center existente e a construção de outros dois. Segundo a Confederação das Indústrias Finlandesas, projetos de fazendas de servidores avaliados em cerca de € 80 bilhões estão em diferentes etapas de planejamento e construção no país. Continua depois da publicidade A população finlandesa tem demonstrado cada vez mais resistência aos data centers, após a revelação de que representantes do Google haviam removido árvores de uma área florestal, retirado a camada superficial do solo e construído estradas em um dos locais antes da conclusão de uma avaliação de impacto ambiental. A empresa responsável pela construção é alvo de uma investigação criminal, e o governo está elaborando uma legislação para conter a expansão da IA. A reação na Europa ecoa a crescente onda de protestos nos Estados Unidos, onde a proliferação de data centers se tornou um dos principais temas das eleições de meio de mandato realizadas nesta semana. Eleitores de vários estados escolheram autoridades locais que prometeram interromper ou suspender as construções. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P.

artigo.texto: Home › Energy Storage ›NHPC Floats Tender for BESS Integration with 1,200 MW Jalaun Solar Park in UP NHPC Floats Tender for BESS Integration with 1,200 MW Jalaun Solar Park in UP NHPC has invited bids to develop battery energy storage systems and supply solar-plus-BESS power using 1,200 MW of existing solar capacity at Jalaun Solar Park in Uttar Pradesh. November 09, 2026. By Mrinmoy Dey NHPC has floated a tender for setting up Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and supply of Solar-plus-BESS power utilising the 1200 MW Solar Project at Jalaun Solar Park of Bundelkhand Saur Urja (BSUL), Uttar Pradesh. BSUL intends to integrate BESS with the existing solar power of 2,419 Million Units (MU) in Solar + BESS configuration to meet the firm and dispatchable power requirement of the end procurer. Bidders need to pay INR 30 lakh (plus GST) for each Block. They also need to deposit INR 10 crore as bid security. The last date for submission of bids is December 12, 2026. The techno-commercial bids will be opened on December 16, 2026. The project developer will be selected through Tariff-Based Competitive Bidding (TBCB) based on a composite solar-plus-BESS tariff under two configurations. Configuration I involves scheduling 300 MW of solar power during solar hours and 800 MW/4,800 MWh of BESS capacity during non-solar hours. Configuration II involves scheduling 600 MW of solar power during solar hours and 800 MW/3,200 MWh of BESS capacity. Developers can bid for either or both configurations, with the final selection depending on the buying entity's requirements. The selected BESS developer will set up battery storage infrastructure across four blocks near three 33/400 kV pooling substations close to Jalaun Solar Park. The developer will procure solar power generated from these blocks and supply the combined solar-plus-BESS power to the designated delivery point at the ISTS CTUIL substation. Bidders can submit offers for Configuration-I, Configuration-II or both, with each location comprising 75 MW solar capacity and 200 MW/1,200 MWh of BESS under Configuration-I, or 150 MW solar capacity and 200 MW/800 MWh of BESS under Configuration-II. Bidders can secure up to 50 percent of the total contracted capacity, with allocation limited to a maximum of two locations across either or both configurations. For Configuration-I, bidders must have a minimum net worth of INR 353.20 crore per block, while the requirement for Configuration-II is INR 261.20 crore per block. To demonstrate liquidity, bidders must meet at least one of three criteria: minimum annual turnover of INR 176.60 crore per block for Configuration-I or INR 130.60 crore for Configuration-II; PBDIT of INR 35.32 crore or INR 26.12 crore per block, respectively; or an in-principle bank sanction for a fund-based credit line of INR 44.15 crore per block for Configuration-I or INR 32.65 crore for Configuration-II. artigo.texto: The Lead In: City Council coin toss, Harmony data center, Townies’ future, and Albert Lea tax aid Pine Island City Council seat, Townies Future, Harmony Data Center, Albert Lea Tax abatement ROCHESTER, Minn. (KTTC) – A city council seat is up for grabs. The future of a popular restaurant space will be decided. A data center discussion comes to a head. And a Freeborn County town could help a local company expand. Here is The Lead In, for Nov. 8-14, 2026. Pine Island: Tie for council seat to be settled by coin flip or draw Last Tuesday’s election saw several candidates win decisively in their races. The race for Pine Island City Council is a different story. According to the unofficial results, Tosca Wohl won 809 votes, or 27.9%, to claim the first of two open council seats. However, the second seat ended in a tie between incumbent Delana Weis and challenger Dominick Pahl, each earning 711 votes. According to the City of Pine Island, the decision will come down to a coin toss or drawing from a hat. It will occur at a special council meeting on Thursday, Nov. 12, at 6 p.m. at City Hall. Rochester: Park Board to decide Soldiers Field clubhouse concessions The Rochester Park Board is scheduled to make a decision on the future of concessions at the Soldiers Field Memorial Park clubhouse. Rochester Parks and Recreation is recommending Uni Uni Bubble Tea and Old Abe Coffee Shop to replace Townies Philly Kitchen + Bar as the clubhouse concessions operator. The city announced the recommendation Friday. The city said it also received a proposal for Townies to retain the space, but parks and recreation officials decided to move in a different direction. The city said Uni Uni Bubble Tea and Old Abe Coffee Shop’s proposal stood out for menu options, ideas and approach to serving customers. Townies said it was informed of the decision less than half an hour before the city sent out the announcement. In mid-July, the restaurant temporarily closed after multiple employees quit due to a broken air conditioning system, something the restaurant looked to the city to fix. Townies responded to the news on Facebook Friday, thanking the community for its support over the years. The restaurant also said that while it is closing its doors, it is not staying silent. A Townies customer started a petition on Saturday calling on the Park Board to keep the restaurant at its location. As of 11 p.m. Sunday, the petition has more than 2,000 signatures. On social media, Townies General Manager Tim Nela asked customers to attend the meeting to show support for the restaurant. The Park Board will make a final decision Tuesday at 4:30 p.m. at the Maintenance Center. Harmony: council to review data center ordinance The Harmony City Council is preparing to consider final language on its proposed data center ordinance at its meeting Tuesday at 7 p.m. at the community center. The review follows months of discussions among councilmembers and the community about how to address a possible data center in the region. According to the city, the goal is to protect public health and welfare, as well as the environment around the town. The proposed ordinance would limit data centers to a new industrial technology zone in the city and limit each data center to 55 megawatts of power. Any building would have to sit at least 500 feet from residential areas. Evaporative cooling, which uses large amounts of water, would also be banned. Unlike the planned Google data center development in Pine Island, there has been no public announcement about a specific project in Harmony. However, the city website says there has been interest from developers. Albert Lea: council to vote on tax abatement and loans for company expansion In Freeborn County, the Albert Lea City Council will vote on assisting a local business expansion with a tax abatement and loans. The council will vote on providing D & S Holdings of Albert Lea with three forms of financial aid for a $2 million expansion of Pro Manufacturing on 209th Street. The aid includes: - A tax abatement starting in 2028 that would last 10 years and not exceed $129,000. - A forgivable loan of $50,000 if the expansion brings in at least five new jobs maintained over five years. - A $300,000 loan at zero percent interest to be paid over 10 years. The loans come from a fund created for assisting businesses with job creation. The goal of the financial assistance is to increase both the number of jobs in town and the local tax base. The council will take up the items at its regular meeting Monday at 7 p.m. at City Hall. Find stories like this and more, in our apps. Copyright 2026 KTTC. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Do ronco ao silêncio: qual a diferença entre dirigir um carro elétrico e um a combustão? César Urnhani, piloto e especialista automotivo, mostra quais são essas diferenças e dá dicas para quem está fazendo essa transição. Crédito: Estadão Gerando resumo A TIM fechou um contrato com a BYD para fornecer internet a toda a frota de veículos leves da montadora chinesa no Brasil, além do seu polo industrial. Com a parceria, os diferentes modelos da marca passarão a contar com chips virtuais (eSIM) da TIM, com conexão 4G em 100% das cidades brasileiras e 5G em 1,1 mil cidades onde a operadora oferece cobertura. A previsão é de que cerca de 200 mil veículos da montadora chinesa contem com essa conectividade embarcada nos próximos 24 meses. Assim, a BYD busca avançar no desenvolvimento de novas funcionalidades que envolvam serviços conectados. Com o crescimento de serviços como inteligência artificial e uso de funções como mapas e streaming a bordo, um carro já tem consumo de dados quase equiparável a de um plano básico pós-pago, tipo ‘controle’. Do lado da TIM, o negócio representa uma expansão no setor automotivo, onde já oferece conexão para cerca de 630 mil veículos. A tele italiana possui uma parceria com a antiga Fiat Chrysler Automóveis (FCA) – hoje parte do grupo Stellantis – para fornecer conectividade 4G e eSIM em veículos das marcas Fiat, Jeep e Ram no Brasil. Leia também - TIM deixa mais ‘inteligentes’ as antenas e ajuda a tornar mais veloz o 5G - Carros elétricos são o ‘caminho natural’ em todo o mundo, diz diretor da Nissan - The Economist: Empresas correm contra o tempo para se proteger de ataques hackers turbinados por IA O contrato entre a TIM e a BYD envolve também a implantação de infraestrutura dedicada de redes 5G e 4G no complexo industrial da montadora em Camaçari, na Bahia. Essa é a maior fábrica de veículos eletrificados da América Latina, com 4,6 milhões de m². O projeto prevê a instalação de sete pontos de cobertura externa e 63 equipamentos distribuídos entre os galpões e as áreas operacionais, garantindo uma rede preparada para acompanhar o crescimento da produção e as demandas tecnológicas do complexo.

artigo.texto: A expansão de data centers para inteligência artificial, que mobiliza trilhões de dólares no mundo inteiro, enfrenta resistência crescente da opinião pública e, sobretudo, de eleitores. Nas eleições de meio de mandato dos Estados Unidos, realizadas na última terça-feira, dia 3 de novembro, eleitores rejeitaram ou restringiram projetos em dezenas de municípios de dez estados americanos. Pelo menos 38 de 41 medidas locais sobre o tema resultaram em veto ou limitações, mandando um recado que atravessa linhas partidárias e já repercute em mercados e na estratégia das empresas de tecnologia. Pesquisas de boca de urna, como a da NBC News, mostram que 57% dos eleitores acreditam que a IA fará mais mal do que bem à sociedade e que 76% se opõem à construção de data centers em suas comunidades. Uma pesquisa Gallup de março registrou 71% de oposição a instalações locais. O tema une preocupações com contas de energia mais altas, uso intensivo de água, ruído, poluição e baixa geração de empregos. No encontro Future of AI (Futuro da IA), do Financial Times, realizado nesta quinta-feira, 05 de novembro, em Londres, executivos admitiram que o próprio setor contribuiu para a hostilidade. O codiretor executivo da Prometheus, Vik Bajaj, diz que a reação não se explica apenas por resistência à tecnologia. “Como categoria profissional, passamos dois anos dizendo às pessoas, de maneira bastante irresponsável, que a IA mudaria o futuro do trabalho para pior, que elas perderiam o emprego, que seus filhos perderiam o emprego, que seus netos viveriam em um mundo irreconhecível. E, no último ano, também estivemos flertando com a ideia de que se trata de uma crise existencial”, afirma Bajaj. O fundador da Niantic Spatial, John Hanke, reconhece que o ritmo de construção foi acelerado demais. “E parte disso foi feito com a cabeça enterrada na areia”, diz. A ex-chefe de políticas globais da DeepMind e diretora do Projeto de IA e Geopolítica da Universidade de Cambridge, Verity Harding, observa que os data centers se tornaram o alvo concreto de ansiedades mais amplas sobre a tecnologia. “De certa forma, só podemos culpar a nós mesmos”, afirma. Os impactos locais são concretos. Data centers de grande porte consomem energia equivalente à de dezenas de milhares de residências e exigem volumes significativos de água para resfriamento. No primeiro trimestre de 2026, ao menos 75 projetos avaliados em cerca de US$ 130 bilhões foram bloqueados ou atrasados por oposição comunitária, segundo o Data Center Watch. Em 2025 e 2026, o volume acumulado de empreendimentos afetados chega a centenas de bilhões de dólares. A resistência não se limita aos Estados Unidos. Há protestos na Índia, no Japão e na Europa. No Brasil, o Ministério Público e a Defensoria Pública pedem a paralisação de obras em Pecém (CE), voltadas ao TikTok, até que haja consulta à comunidade indígena e estudo de impacto ambiental. Há ações semelhantes envolvendo projetos em Belém do Pará e Campinas, além de questionamentos sobre o uso de água no Espírito Santo. O setor brasileiro ainda é pequeno em capacidade global, mas cresceu rapidamente. Gargalos de energia já reduziram a carteira de projetos viáveis, segundo análise da Rystad Energy, de cerca de 21 GW para aproximadamente 7 GW. No Brasil, o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata) condiciona incentivos à eficiência hídrica e a energia renovável ou de baixa emissão, mas o acesso à rede permanece o principal entrave. As empresas respondem com mudanças. Nos Estados Unidos, OpenAI, Amazon e Microsoft anunciaram o fim de acordos de confidencialidade controversos. Mais de 200 companhias aderiram a um compromisso não vinculante da gestão Trump para que custos de eletricidade dos data centers não sejam repassados aos consumidores. O chefe da divisão de novas energias da Chevron, Jeff Gustavson, afirma que o relacionamento com as comunidades decide o sucesso dos projetos. “Se você não consegue administrar esse relacionamento, se as comunidades não se beneficiam desses investimentos, você enfrentará oposição”, diz Gustavson. O diretor-executivo da britânica Virtus Data Centres, Adam Eaton, diz que a visibilidade aumentou com a IA e que o setor precisa informar melhor as comunidades. A expansão continua necessária para atender à demanda por modelos e serviços de IA, mas o resultado das urnas e das mobilizações locais indica que o ritmo e as condições dependerão cada vez mais da capacidade de demonstrar benefícios concretos e reduzir impactos sobre energia, água e vizinhança. – Com informações de agências internacionais e do UOL/Folha de S. Paulo.

artigo.texto: A Eletronet, empresa de telecomunicações do grupo Axia Energia (ex-Eletrobras), está investindo R$ 25 milhões em um novo data center na cidade de São Paulo, localizado no bairro Chácara Santo Antônio. O empreendimento terá aproximadamente 350 m², capacidade para cerca de 90 racks de computadores e potência inicial de 0,5 MW, podendo chegar a 1 MW na segunda fase de expansão. A entrega está programada para o primeiro trimestre do ano que vem. Esse projeto é o maior já feito pela companhia, mas não é do tipo que vai brigar com os mega data centers das big techs. Em vez disso, seu objetivo é atender a demanda crescente das empresas pequenas e médias de internet e conteúdo digital - como streaming e computação em nuvem. “Não é um data center grande, mas tem importância significativa para o mercado”, afirmou o presidente da empresa, Rogerio Garchet, em entrevista à Coluna. O data center da Eletronet dá acesso não só à rede de fibra ótica própria da companhia, como também ao seu ponto de interconexão no IX.br São Paulo - infraestrutura física que permite que diferentes redes de computadores se conectem diretamente para trocar dados entre si. Para o mundo de telecom, esse é um ponto estratégico porque permite maior velocidade e menor latência no tráfego de dados. Área deve crescer no faturamento da companhia Segundo Garchet, os data centers devem ter uma participação cada vez maior no faturamento da Eletronet. Hoje, isso está em 3%. “Não podemos dar detalhes sobre em quanto deve chegar para não atrair os competidores, mas apostamos bastante no crescimento desse setor”, disse o executivo. A empresa grupo tem uma receita anual na ordem de R$ 200 milhões. A Eletronet já vem investindo na ampliação da capacidade para atender clientes da economia digital. A empresa tem, hoje, 170 edge data centers espalhados pelo País e planeja chegar a 255 unidades até o fim do ano. São data centers descentralizados, que atendem a demandas locais. Estes empreendimentos têm uma função semelhante ao novo negócio de São Paulo, mas são centros bem menores (entre 20 e 50 m²), com energia e conectividade, mas sem acesso direto ao ponto de interconexão. Eles também atendem pequenas e médias empresas que buscam infraestrutura no mercado para otimizar seus serviços. Já o negócio principal da Eletronet continua sendo a sua rede de 18 mil quilômetros de fibra óptica em 18 estados, que foi construída aproveitando a infraestrutura física das linhas de transmissão de energia elétrica de alta tensão da Axia ao longo dos anos. Essa rede de fibra é utilizada pelos provedores que levam internet para o cliente final. Desde as grandes teles até os provedores regionais são clientes da Eletronet neste segmento. artigo.texto: Patrocinado por: Repórter Publicado em 8 de novembro de 2026 às 09h28. A Anthropic, desenvolvedora de IA, investiu US$ 3,4 bilhões para garantir fornecimento de energia a seus data centers através de geradores a gás. O acordo com a OnePWR Solutions é a maior compra individual conhecida de equipamentos de geração elétrica por uma empresa de IA, refletindo a crescente demanda por eletricidade com a expansão de data centers. A empresa assegurou equipamentos encomendados anteriormente, evitando preços mais altos. A Anthropic, desenvolvedora da inteligência artificial Claude, fechou um acordo de US$ 3,4 bilhões para garantir o fornecimento de energia a seus data centers. A empresa assumiu encomendas de geradores a gás com capacidade total de 1,7 gigawatt (GW), em uma tentativa de reduzir a dependência de fornecedores de eletricidade. A operação, concluída no fim de setembro com a americana OnePWR Solutions, foi revelada pelo Financial Times. Segundo o jornal, trata-se da maior compra individual conhecida de equipamentos de geração elétrica por uma desenvolvedora de IA. O negócio mostra como a demanda por eletricidade está alterando a estratégia das empresas de tecnologia. Com a expansão dos data centers, a procura por turbinas e geradores a gás aumentou, e os prazos de fabricação de novos equipamentos passaram a se estender por anos. Em vez de depender exclusivamente de concessionárias e fornecedores especializados, companhias de inteligência artificial começaram a investir diretamente na infraestrutura necessária para manter suas operações. A OnePWR havia encomendado os geradores à Caterpillar dois anos antes, mas precisava de financiamento para concluir a compra. Inicialmente, a Anthropic pretendia contratar a empresa como fornecedora, mas decidiu assumir diretamente os pedidos, segundo uma pessoa familiarizada com a negociação ouvida pelo FT. Com isso, a desenvolvedora do Claude garantiu acesso a equipamentos encomendados antes da alta dos preços, com entregas previstas para o curto prazo e os próximos dois anos. A Anthropic não comprou a OnePWR. O acordo incluiu serviços de engenharia e construção necessários para instalar os geradores, sem transferência de funcionários da fornecedora. As empresas não comentaram a transação. A disputa por equipamentos de energia também levou outras gigantes da tecnologia a ampliar seus investimentos no setor. A xAI, empresa de Elon Musk controlada pela SpaceX, comprou turbinas móveis a gás por US$ 2 bilhões neste ano. Já a Alphabet, controladora do Google, adquiriu a desenvolvedora de energia Intersect no fim de 2025. O investimento em geradores ocorre enquanto a Anthropic amplia seus compromissos financeiros para sustentar a expansão da inteligência artificial. A empresa informou que possui quase US$ 900 bilhões em compromissos de capacidade computacional até 2045. Até então, vinha recorrendo principalmente a parceiros para garantir acesso a chips, terrenos, data centers e eletricidade. A companhia também se prepara para uma possível abertura de capital ainda em novembro, em uma operação que pode estar entre as maiores da história, segundo o Financial Times. Os planos de expansão, porém, enfrentam desafios financeiros. A Blackstone alertou investidores de que pode receber uma classificação de crédito especulativa, inferior ao grau de investimento anteriormente esperado. Glossário O que é geradores a gás? artigo.texto: Energy storage is expanding across Europe, but its growth remains constrained by obstacles that extend beyond technology. This is the conclusion of Energy Storage Deployment in the EU: Drivers, Barriers and Policy Pathways, published by the Joint Research Centre (JRC), the European Commission’s science and knowledge service. The analysis identifies grid connection delays as the most widespread barrier, while regulatory uncertainty and unpredictable revenues limit projects’ ability to secure financing. The report combines market data, policy analysis and a stakeholder consultation that received 19 responses. The JRC treats these contributions as qualitative evidence rather than a statistically representative sample. Grid connections remain the main bottleneck Insufficient capacity at targeted connection points and lengthy procedures for securing connection agreements are delaying new installations. In the report’s stakeholder consultation, insufficient grid capacity received an average severity rating of 4.1 out of 5, followed by long lead times for connection agreements, at 3.9 out of 5. The study also highlights how applications for projects that fail to progress, or reserve several potential locations, can block capacity for developments that are ready to proceed. Measures examined include prioritising projects that demonstrate maturity, improving transparency on available grid capacity and simplifying administrative procedures. Flexible connection agreements offer another route to earlier grid access. However, they may impose temporary network access restrictions that developers must account for in their business models. Predictable revenues are critical to financing The JRC warns that projects relying exclusively on market revenues still face difficulties attracting financing in many countries. Price volatility and uncertainty over future income make it harder for lenders to assess projects’ ability to repay debt. There is also a risk that the entry of additional batteries and other flexible resources will erode some revenue opportunities, particularly in markets vulnerable to saturation. The report identifies long-term contracts, capacity and flexibility remuneration mechanisms, and agreements combining renewable generation with storage as ways to improve revenue predictability. It also examines tolling agreements, under which a counterparty pays an agreed fee for commercial use of a storage facility. These arrangements can support financing, although they transfer part of the risk to the counterparty and require an assessment of its creditworthiness. Regulation still limits the value storage can capture Fragmentation across national markets represents another obstacle. The report highlights double charging when storage withdraws electricity from and injects it into the grid, high network tariffs and incomplete rules for participation in certain markets. It also finds that some services storage can provide, such as relieving local grid congestion, do not always receive adequate remuneration. The JRC therefore argues that policies should reward measurable contributions to the electricity system—including duration, availability and security of supply—while maintaining technology neutrality. Co-location with renewables creates opportunities The report highlights the potential of installing batteries alongside solar or wind farms. These configurations can share infrastructure, capture electricity that might otherwise be curtailed and shift delivery to higher-value hours. Power purchase agreements combining renewable generation and storage can provide an electricity supply profile better aligned with buyers’ requirements. However, securing financing requires clear contractual provisions on revenue allocation, operational responsibilities and risk sharing. Modelling points to 172 GW of EU storage needs by 2030 The report cites PRIMES modelling results that put the European Union’s power sector storage requirements at 172 GW by 2030, combining batteries and pumped hydropower. For 2040, projected requirements range from 213 GW to 275 GW, depending on the scenario. These figures represent modelled system requirements, rather than a specific binding storage deployment target. The JRC concludes that accelerating deployment requires action on permitting, grid connections, market rules and revenue stability. Falling technology costs support growth, but converting that potential into operating projects also depends on a framework that enables developers to finance and connect their assets.

artigo.texto: Turkey approves more than 33 GW of energy storage projects — Deutsche Welle Turkey, which is hosting the UN climate summit COP31 in Antalya, has approved more than 33 GW of battery energy storage projects since 2022. According to Deutsche Welle, these capacities could supply electricity to more than 27 million households. Storage systems are intended to complement the rapid growth of wind and solar generation. These sources currently provide 22% of Turkey's electricity, compared with 4.5% ten years ago. Solar energy's share of the country's installed power generation capacity grew from about 0.1% in 2014 to nearly 21% at the beginning of 2026. Dependence on coal At the same time, coal-fired electricity generation in Turkey has increased by about one-third over the past decade. In 2024, the country surpassed Germany and Poland in coal generation capacity; these countries had previously had the largest such capacities in Europe, but they have begun to decline. Turkey has still not set a date for a complete phaseout of coal. According to the German climate campaign Beyond Fossil Fuels, about 97% of new coal projects in the country have been cancelled over the past ten years. However, in June, Turkish authorities announced plans to expand one of the largest coal-fired power plants and nearly double its capacity. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. The Climate Action Tracker think tank notes that Turkey's current climate target allows emissions to increase until 2038. In the organization's view, this complicates the country's achievement of its carbon neutrality target by 2053. Electrification and fuel imports According to Efe Baysal, head of the Turkish team of the environmental network 350.org, Turkey imports 95% of its natural gas, 83% of its crude oil, and 60% of its coal. In September, the country launched the global “35x35” initiative, which envisages increasing the level of electrification of the world's economies from just over 20% to 35% by 2035. The initiative includes replacing fossil fuels with electricity in transport, buildings, and industry. At the same time, according to Climate Action Tracker's assessment, Turkey's national energy plan provides for the electrification of only about 25% of total energy consumption by 2035.

artigo.texto: Mercado global de ventiladores de resfriamento: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de ventiladores de resfriamento até 2035: demanda por refrigeração de data centers impulsiona expansão Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de ventiladores de resfriamento, o setor inicia 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compra mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de suprimento mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de ventiladores de resfriamento é um componente crítico do ecossistema mais amplo de gestão térmica, sustentando a integridade operacional e a eficiência de uma vasta gama de tecnologias industriais, comerciais e de consumo. No período de análise de 2026, o mercado se caracteriza por demanda robusta, impulsionada pelo crescimento contínuo do processamento de dados, da eletrificação e da manufatura avançada, embora enfrente pressões simultâneas decorrentes da reconfiguração das cadeias de suprimento e da volatilidade dos custos de matérias-primas. A transição para projetos de ventiladores mais eficientes em energia, inteligentes e específicos para cada aplicação está remodelando a dinâmica competitiva e favorecendo empresas com forte capacidade de P&D e cadeias de suprimento verticalmente integradas. Este relatório traz uma avaliação abrangente do estado atual do mercado, das principais forças de oferta e demanda, dos fluxos comerciais e dos mecanismos de formação de preços, culminando em uma previsão estratégica até 2035 que delineia os caminhos de crescimento e os desafios a serem enfrentados. A evolução do mercado está indissociavelmente ligada a megatendências globais, como digitalização, exigências de sustentabilidade e automação industrial. Essas forças não apenas ampliam o mercado endereçável, como também ditam uma mudança nas especificações dos produtos em direção a maior desempenho, menor ruído acústico e maior conectividade. O cenário competitivo está se fragmentando, e líderes consolidados em segmentos industriais amplos enfrentam concorrência intensificada de fabricantes especializados que atendem nichos de alto crescimento, como veículos elétricos e infraestrutura de energia renovável. Compreender a interação entre esses fatores tecnológicos, econômicos e geopolíticos é essencial para os agentes que buscam aproveitar oportunidades emergentes e mitigar riscos inerentes. Esta análise sintetiza dados proprietários, estatísticas comerciais e inteligência setorial para construir um retrato detalhado do mercado mundial de ventiladores de resfriamento. O horizonte de previsão até 2035 é estruturado a partir da análise da trajetória das principais indústrias de uso final, dos desdobramentos regulatórios e dos ciclos de inovação tecnológica. As implicações para fabricantes, fornecedores e investidores são profundas e exigem uma estratégia nuançada, que equilibre escala e especialização, gestão de custos e investimento em inovação, alcance global e proximidade com os mercados regionais. O cenário-base para o mercado mundial de ventiladores de resfriamento até 2035 prevê expansão sustentada, apoiada pela demanda estrutural da infraestrutura de data centers, da modernização de sistemas HVAC e da automação industrial. O índice de mercado deve alcançar 142 em 2035 (2025=100), o que corresponde a uma taxa composta de crescimento anual (CAGR) de aproximadamente 3,6% no período de previsão. Essa perspectiva pressupõe ausência de recessão global relevante, continuidade dos investimentos de capital em infraestrutura de nuvem e inteligência artificial e endurecimento gradual das normas de eficiência energética nas principais economias. Espera-se que a demanda por refrigeração de data centers seja o maior contribuinte individual para o crescimento incremental, à medida que operadores de hiperescala e de colocation ampliam a capacidade para atender cargas de IA, o que exige sistemas de ventiladores de alto fluxo de ar e alta eficiência. Os sistemas HVAC seguirão como o maior segmento em volume, com a demanda de reposição e as atualizações impulsionadas por normas para ventiladores de velocidade variável e baixo ruído sustentando o crescimento em valor. A demanda por ventilação industrial acompanhará a produção manufatureira e a atividade de mineração, com mercados emergentes na Ásia-Pacífico e na América Latina oferecendo potencial de alta. O resfriamento automotivo se beneficiará da eletrificação, já que a gestão térmica das baterias exige módulos adicionais de ventiladores, embora o crescimento da produção de veículos de passeio possa ser modesto. O resfriamento de eletrônicos de consumo terá demanda estável, puxada por dispositivos portáteis e hardware para jogos, enquanto equipamentos médicos e telecomunicações oferecem nichos menores, porém de alto valor. Do lado da oferta, a volatilidade dos custos de matérias-primas, especialmente cobre e aços especiais, segue como risco relevante, ao lado de interrupções logísticas e da incerteza na política comercial. Espera-se uma consolidação moderada do cenário competitivo, com os principais fabricantes investindo em tecnologias de ventiladores inteligentes que incorporam sensores integrados e conectividade IoT. No geral, a perspectiva-base é positiva, mas atenuada pela ciclicidade dos mercados industriais de uso final e pela pressão persistente sobre as margens nas negociações de preços com montadoras. artigo.texto: 9 de novembro de 2026, às 16:22 A TIM fechou um contrato com a BYD para fornecer internet a toda a frota de veículos leves da montadora chinesa no Brasil, além do seu polo industrial. Com a parceria, os diferentes modelos da marca passarão a contar com chips virtuais (eSIM) da TIM, com conexão 4G em 100% das cidades brasileiras e 5G em 1,1 mil cidades onde a operadora oferece cobertura. A previsão é de que cerca de 200 mil veículos da montadora chinesa contem com essa conectividade embarcada nos próximos 24 meses. Assim, a BYD busca avançar no desenvolvimento de novas funcionalidades que envolvam serviços conectados. Com o crescimento de serviços como inteligência artificial e uso de funções como mapas e streaming a bordo, um carro já tem consumo de dados quase equiparável a de um plano básico pós-pago, tipo ‘controle’. Do lado da TIM, o negócio representa uma expansão no setor automotivo, onde já oferece conexão para cerca de 630 mil veículos. A tele italiana possui uma parceria com a antiga Fiat Chrysler Automóveis (FCA) – hoje parte do grupo Stellantis – para fornecer conectividade 4G e eSIM em veículos das marcas Fiat, Jeep e Ram no Brasil. O contrato entre a TIM e a BYD envolve também a implantação de infraestrutura dedicada de redes 5G e 4G no complexo industrial da montadora em Camaçari, na Bahia. Essa é a maior fábrica de veículos eletrificados da América Latina, com 4,6 milhões de m². O projeto prevê a instalação de sete pontos de cobertura externa e 63 equipamentos distribuídos entre os galpões e as áreas operacionais, garantindo uma rede preparada para acompanhar o crescimento da produção e as demandas tecnológicas do complexo. artigo.texto: Scaling Power Electronics from Residential to Utility-Scale Energy Storage The article examines how power-conversion architecture, semiconductor selection, thermal management, protection, control, and grid integration must evolve as battery energy storage systems scale from residential installations to utility-scale plants. It focuses on the engineering implications of increasing power, voltage, current, and system complexity. November 09, 2026. By News Bureau Scaling a battery energy storage system (BESS) involves far more than increasing the power conversion system rating. It requires a coordinated evolution in electrical architecture, semiconductor topology, thermal management, protection, controls, and grid interconnection capability. BESS Application Segments BESS applications can broadly be classified into three segments: Each segment is characterised by distinct economic drivers, operating profiles, duty cycles, system requirements, technical constraints and control objectives. Electrical Architecture Residential: Integrated Solution The battery, converter and protection functions are integrated into a single enclosure. The primary objectives are compactness, safety, efficient power conversion, plug-and-play installation, low maintenance, uninterrupted power supply and a service life of 10–15 years. For example, Hoymiles HIS series converters along with LB series battery packs provide an integrated solution that simplifies installation and supports reliable long-term operation. C&I: Modular Architecture Power and energy are distributed across battery racks and multiple PCS units. Each section can be monitored, protected and maintained independently, while supervisory controls coordinate overall operation. Utility: High Power Subsystem At the multi-megawatt level, the PCS contains semiconductors, DC link capacitors, busbar, cooling, protection, sensors and control subsystems. Multiple PCS blocks share a medium voltage network and are coordinated through a BESS controller and power plant controller (PPC). The plant, rather than an individual PCS, becomes the controlled electrical resource. Power Conversion Topologies Residential: Integrated Converter Residential topologies use a two-stage conversion scheme: an isolated bidirectional DC-DC converter (e.g., dual active bridge) matching wide battery swing to a regulated high-voltage DC bus, feeding a single-phase full-bridge inverter. Moderate power throughput allows compact integration of passive LCL filter inductors and planar magnetics. C&I: Modular Converters Scaling to hundreds of kilowatts relies on paralleled three-phase two-level or three-level bridges. Paralleling requires active carrier interleaving to suppress AC ripple, common mode filtering to block zero-sequence circulating currents, and dynamic active/reactive current sharing loops. For example, the Hoymiles HESS-261 series supports modular design that allows multiple units to be connected in parallel to meet custom energy needs and easily scale up for future expansion. Utility: Multilevel High Current Topologies Utility PCS designs utilise three-level Neutral Point Clamped (NPC), Active NPC (ANPC), or T-type topologies. These lower the device dV/dt stress, reduce switching losses and shrink output LCL filter footprints. However, they demand active neutral point balancing algorithms, ultra-low stray inductance busbars and gate drives with multi-stage desaturation protection. DC Voltage and Current The selected DC link operating voltage influences the entire electromechanical stack, including switch conduction losses, conductor copper volume, creepage and clearance distances and switchgear arc extinction capability. Residential Traditional 48 V systems prioritise touch safety and simple pack balancing, but require heavy conductors. Higher voltage strings (200–500 V DC) drastically reduce I²R conduction losses and cabling weight, requiring integrated DC Arc Fault Circuit Interrupters (AFCI) and rapid shutdown. C&I Operating in the 100 kW to 1 MW range at lower voltages causes severe current penalties. Standardising on 800–1,000 V DC reduces cable size, cuts inverter conduction losses, and boosts round-trip efficiency (RTE). Utility Standard 1,500 V DC platforms maximise container energy density and minimise cabling over large field layouts. However, prospective short-circuit currents exceed 50–100 kA, creating high arc-flash energy and strict insulation requirements (As per IEC 62477-1). Fast-acting DC fuses or high-speed hybrid DC breakers are essential to clear non-zero-crossing faults. Semiconductor Technology Semiconductor selection balances switching losses, conduction losses, thermal impedance, switching frequency, and passive filter dimensions. Residential Operates at higher switching frequencies for silent operation and reduced filter size. Low-voltage topologies employ low R_DS(on) Si MOSFETs, whereas high-voltage strings use 650 V / 1,200 V SiC MOSFETs to reach peak efficiencies above 99 percent. C&I Operates between 4 kHz and 12 kHz. Converters use 1,200 V IGBT modules or hybrid configurations like Si IGBTs with SiC Schottky diodes to suppress diode reverse recovery losses affordably. Utility Operates between 1.5 kHz and 3.5 kHz to manage thermal dissipation. Power stages deploy high-power dual/half bridge modules. In three-level ANPC designs, hybrid configurations place fast SiC MOSFETs in high-frequency switching positions and low-V_CE(sat) Si IGBTs in 50/60 Hz line unfolding positions, maximising efficiency across wide power factor ranges. Hoymiles HPCS series string PCS comes with SiC technology, which offers higher efficiency. Thermal Management Thermal management becomes progressively more critical as BESS power increases. The fundamental requirement remains the same at every level. The heat generated by the battery and power electronics must be removed while maintaining the components within their allowable operating temperature range. Residential Residen

artigo.texto: Data centers become a political flashpoint after midterms, putting AI industry on notice HOBART, Ind. - The message from voters was hard for the data center industry to ignore: communities want a say in what gets built in their backyards — and they're increasingly demanding answers before those projects move forward. Data center debate The backstory: President Donald Trump has been one of the biggest supporters of the data center boom, arguing these facilities will bring jobs, investment and economic prosperity to communities across the country. On August 31, in a post on Truth Social, Trump said in part, "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want data centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let data reign." "You have to convince your community how great these things," said Trump. "You can't fight it. You have to go with it. And you're going to make a tremendous amount of money. You're going to reduce taxes." But that message hasn't necessarily resonated with residents who are worried about the potential consequences of these massive developments. And those concerns became a political talking point during the midterm elections. The Associated Press reports Democrats who campaigned on tighter restrictions on data centers made significant gains in several key gubernatorial races, including Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Nevada and Iowa. In fact, 32 of the 34 winning gubernatorial candidates in races where AP called a winner supported stronger regulations or restrictions on data centers. Twelve supported outright bans or moratoriums. At the local level, the opposition was even more pronounced. An analysis by Redbud Consulting found voters approved restrictions in 44 of 45 completed local data center referendum elections across the country. And the opposition wasn't confined to one political party or one part of the country. The AP Voter Poll found roughly three-quarters of Americans opposed building a new data center in their community. For Wannie Park, founder and CEO of Pado AI, an energy orchestration software company that works with data centers, this backlash has been building for some time. "I think the dynamics of growth sometimes, which is what we're kind of going through, is oftentimes full brute force without thoughtfulness and good planning," said Park. "And I think with that, what you have is sort of what we have now, which is the backlash, right? Moratoriums and just people saying like, 'hey, let's take a breath here and figure out what's the right way to deploy this stuff.'" Park says the issue has become increasingly bipartisan, as residents question whether the economic benefits promised by developers are actually materializing. "People are saying, well, like, 'hey, I'm not getting what I thought I was getting' or ‘the economic development is not there’ or 'you're using up and polluting all our water' or ‘my rates are going up.’ Like all those types of things started to trickle in," said Park. Hobart meetings on data centers In northwest Indiana, Fox Chicago has reported increasingly heated public meetings in Hobart over proposed data center developments, with some residents even being removed after voicing their opposition. And the concerns being raised locally mirror what is happening across the country. On Fox News, Compass Data Centers CEO Chris Crosby acknowledged that not every developer has done a good job addressing those concerns. "I think it's fair. Their questions are real. Not everybody who develops and owns data centers does a good job of it. And, you know, there is a bar that needs to be raised," said Crosby. He says developers need to be more transparent, pay their own way when it comes to electricity and provide tangible benefits to the communities where they operate. Park agrees the industry needs a different approach. And he takes issue with the idea that opposing data center development means someone doesn't understand the importance of artificial intelligence. "I think that's just the wrong position, right?" Park argues the industry has been operating inefficiently, with opportunities to get more out of existing facilities rather than simply building more. He says older data centers could be repurposed, potentially reducing the need for some of the massive new construction projects being proposed. And he pushes back against the argument that slowing development automatically means America will fall behind China in the AI race. "I don't think it's that dire. Sometimes the industry kind of speaks to it like it's a binary. We have to build, build, or we're going to fall behind China or whatever. We're not going to lead. It's not that dire," said Park. What's next: Instead, Park says the next phase should focus on making better use of existing infrastructure and proving that these projects produce meaningful benefits. He also believes the political backlash is already affecting the industry's bottom line, with stricter regulations and uncertainty making investors and lenders more cautious about financing new developments. The Source: The information in this report came from statements by President Donald Trump, reporting and polling by The Associated Press, an analysis by Redbud Consulting, interviews with Pado AI CEO Wannie Park and Compass Data Centers CEO Chris Crosby, and previous FOX Chicago reporting on data center developments in Hobart, Indiana.

artigo.texto: A world leader in the provision of battery manufacturing assembly equipment, Gloucester-headquartered TBS Engineering plays a crucial role in keeping the vehicles and infrastructure used by millions of people up-and-running, right across the globe. SoGlos looks at five of its biggest customers and the products they power, from high-end cars like Porche, Bentley and Jaguar, to everyday essential infrastructure, like rail signals and telecoms. Exide With roots going all the way back to the 19th century, Exide is a US-founded company steeped in history, having made batteries used to launch torpedoes in World War Two, and by NASA to land on the moon in the 1960s. Now split from its former North American operations, the company supplies batteries for the automotive and energy sectors, operating from facilities across Europe and Asia Pacific as Exide Technologies. Bringing in annual revenue of around €1.6 billion, it supplies world-leading vehicle manufacturers from Citroen, Volkswagen and Mini, to Alfa Romeo, BMW and Jaguar, powered by TBS Engineering's state-of-the-art battery manufacturing assembly equipment. Clarios Clarios is a global giant in the automotive battery manufacturing sector, serving 1.5 million customers across more than 100 countries – and boasting the claim that one in three vehicles worldwide are powered by a Clarios battery. Bringing in $10.6 billion in annual revenue, a long list of renowned vehicle manufacturers use Clarios batteries, from Nissan, Renault and Skoda, to Porche, Bentley and Mercedes Benz. TBS Engineering has built up a strong partnership with Clarios, providing critical battery manufacturing assembly equipment that has accelerated capacity expansion for the company globally – a valued collaboration that was recognised with an award at the Clarios Supplier Summit in 2026. Enerya Served by TBS from its Mexico office, Enerya is dedicated to the manufacture of electrical batteries for the vehicle industry. Based in Nuevo León in Mexico, it's a leading North American brand, manufacturing batteries that power everything from passenger cars and commercial trucks, to motorcycles and marine vessels. TBS established its Mexico office in Monterrey in 2024, in order to provide its customers in the region with aftermarket spare parts, technical support, service, account management and streamlined logistics. East Penn A private, family-owned business operating the largest single-site lead battery manufacturing facility in the world, Pennsylvania company East Penn serves the North America and Asia Pacific markets. Making batteries for all types of vehicles, from cars and trucks, to boats, along with reserve power for things like rail signals and telecommunications, the company boasts annual revenue of around $3 billion. East Penn and TBS have a long-standing relationship which goes back to 1987, with Robert Flicker, COO of East Penn, saying of working with the Gloucester company: 'Their commitment to customer satisfaction and their willingness to work with their customers to provide the state-of-the-art equipment with high-level quality and standards makes them a great partner to satisfy our equipment needs.' Amara Raja Indian company Amara Raja Energy & Mobility manufactures a range of batteries for the automotive and industrial sectors, bringing in annual revenue of more than £1 billion. The company is the largest automotive battery manufacturer in India, supplying major auto manufacturers like Ford, Suzuki and more, while it also makes industrial batteries for sectors including telecoms, railways and defence. This year, TBS Engineering opens its TBS India office in Pune, Maharashtra, where it will provide aftermarket and technical support services for its clients in the region. To find out more about TBS Engineering, its global operations, and the equipment and services it provides for its customers, visit tbseng.co.uk.
