artigo.texto: Patrocinado por: (VCG/VCG/Getty Images) Repórter de Inteligência Artificial e Tecnologia Publicado em 9 de novembro de 2026 às 10h01. A ByteDance, dona do TikTok, planeja expandir suas operações de data centers no Brasil. O primeiro complexo está em construção no Ceará, com investimentos bilionários, enquanto negociações avançam para uma segunda instalação voltada ao mercado brasileiro. O projeto enfrenta questionamentos jurídicos sobre licenciamento ambiental e consulta indígena. Com seu primeiro data center na América Latina ainda em construção, a ByteDance, dona do TikTok, já procura uma empresa para desenvolver a segunda fase do complexo no Pecém, no Ceará. Em paralelo, o grupo chinês abriu conversas preliminares sobre outra instalação, fora do complexo portuário, que atenderia clientes no Brasil, segundo a Bloomberg. A expansão no Pecém pode superar em porte a obra atual, estimada em US$ 10 bilhões e que terá demanda elétrica de cerca de 300 megawatts (MW). A segunda fase segue em avaliação, e o projeto voltado ao mercado brasileiro está em estágio inicial. As obras da primeira etapa começaram em janeiro de 2026. A Omnia, plataforma de data centers do Pátria Investimentos, desenvolve o projeto para a ByteDance em parceria com a Casa dos Ventos. A previsão informada pela Omnia à Reuters é iniciar a operação no terceiro trimestre de 2027 e ampliar as atividades gradualmente até 2029. O projeto original do Pecém foi anunciado em dezembro de 2025 com investimento estimado em cerca de R$ 200 bilhões para o complexo completo, previsto em fases. Na etapa em obras, os servidores terão 200 MW de capacidade de tecnologia da informação. A demanda elétrica total, próxima de 300 MW, inclui os sistemas que mantêm os equipamentos em funcionamento, como a refrigeração. A energia é uma parte do negócio que já tem contrato. Em maio, Omnia e Casa dos Ventos acertaram um fornecimento de 20 anos, avaliado em cerca de US$ 2 bilhões. A maior parte virá do complexo eólico Ibiapaba, no Ceará, com uma parcela menor de um parque no Piauí, segundo as empresas. Perto do Pecém, os cabos submarinos que chegam a Fortaleza dão ao estado conexões de fibra óptica com os Estados Unidos, a Europa e a África. O empreendimento em construção fica na Zona de Processamento de Exportação (ZPE) do Pecém. O conselho federal que administra o regime aprovou o projeto da ByteDance para prestação de serviços exclusivamente ao mercado externo. Na prática, os servidores ficam no Ceará e processam dados para operações em outros países. Já a instalação em discussão fora do Pecém teria como destino o mercado brasileiro, segundo a Bloomberg. As conversas ocorrem enquanto o governo prepara as regras do Redata, regime federal sancionado em setembro que prevê incentivos tributários para equipamentos de data centers. Entre as contrapartidas previstas na lei estão critérios de eficiência hídrica e a oferta de pelo menos 10% da capacidade beneficiada ao mercado interno, compromisso que pode ser substituído por investimento adicional em pesquisa e inovação. Na sexta-feira, 6, a ministra da Casa Civil, Miriam Belchior, disse que o governo espera anunciar a regulamentação na semana de 16 de novembro. Em setembro, o Ministério Público Federal e a Defensoria Pública da União entraram com uma ação civil pública para impedir o início da operação antes de uma consulta livre, prévia e informada ao povo indígena Anacé e da elaboração de um estudo de impacto ambiental. Os órgãos também pedem que sejam avaliados os efeitos do empreendimento sobre a água, a rede elétrica e as comunidades do entorno. Em resposta à agência eixos, a Omnia afirmou que o licenciamento segue o rito da Superintendência Estadual do Meio Ambiente do Ceará (Semace) e que possui as autorizações válidas para as atividades que exerce. No início de novembro, o Fórum Nacional pela Democratização da Comunicação divulgou as conclusões de uma missão dos conselhos nacional e estadual de direitos humanos que recomendou a revisão do licenciamento e a consulta às comunidades afetadas.

artigo.texto: Around one million high-performance batteries from e-bikes and electric scooters are prematurely discarded in Germany every year, despite often retaining a significant proportion of their original capacity. Freiburg-based startup EDENenergy aims to turn this untapped resource into industrial energy storage, developing modular systems that reuse batteries from micromobility applications. Founded by former researchers from the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE, the company has developed a technology that combines different battery modules through flexible power electronics, enabling heterogeneous batteries to be integrated into stationary storage systems safely and efficiently. The startup has recently reached an important commercial milestone: in mid-October 2026, it delivered its first industrial storage system to a customer. The installation has a capacity of 70 kilowatt-hours (kWh) and integrates 112 second-life e-scooter batteries. Power electronics overcome the challenge of battery diversity Although second-life applications have already demonstrated their potential in the electric vehicle sector, the reuse of batteries from e-bikes and e-scooters remains largely untapped. One of the main obstacles is the wide variety of battery designs, cell technologies, battery management systems and communication protocols, which makes standardised integration difficult. EDENenergy addresses this challenge through power electronics developed at Fraunhofer ISE. The technology allows different storage units to be interconnected and communicate with the system without requiring the batteries to be dismantled. Florian Bierwirth, co-founder of EDENenergy, explains that this approach makes it possible to integrate different battery modules into a single stationary storage system. Bierwirth previously worked in the Power Electronics Department at Fraunhofer ISE, alongside fellow co-founders Daniel Seeger and Hannes Kurzmann. For its initial market entry, the company is focusing on 70 kWh industrial storage systems aimed primarily at medium-sized businesses that already operate photovoltaic installations but do not yet have battery storage. The technology could also serve municipal utilities, providing applications such as increasing self-consumption of locally generated electricity, reducing peak loads and participating in electricity trading. Used batteries retain more capacity than expected The initial assessment of the batteries has produced encouraging results. Of the first 350 batteries tested by EDENenergy, their remaining capacity was significantly higher than the company had initially anticipated. The startup had estimated that second-life batteries would retain around 80% of their original capacity, measured through their State of Health (SoH). However, the tested batteries showed average remaining capacity levels that, in some cases, were well above 90%. According to the company, this makes them particularly suitable for stationary storage applications. Unlike their first life in e-bikes and e-scooters, where they are exposed to vibrations and temperature fluctuations, stationary batteries operate under conditions involving fewer mechanical stresses and temperature variations. This can allow them to remain in service for several additional years. To ensure safe and reliable operation, EDENenergy remotely monitors its battery modules through a dedicated monitoring system. When individual modules reach the end of their useful life, they can be replaced separately, even while the overall storage system remains operational. Batteries that eventually reach the end of their service life are sent for recycling through partner companies. Modular replacement aims to maintain storage capacity over time The company’s modular approach is also intended to address one of the main challenges associated with battery degradation: the gradual loss of storage capacity over time. By replacing individual battery modules as they deteriorate, EDENenergy aims to maintain the system’s nominal capacity at 70 kWh even after ten years of operation. The company contrasts this approach with conventional energy storage systems, whose manufacturers typically guarantee 80% of their original capacity after ten years, reflecting the impact of battery degradation. EDENenergy therefore seeks to turn the variability and ageing of second-life batteries into a technical advantage through individual module replacement rather than requiring the entire storage system to be replaced. Expansion plans target 300 kWh storage systems Following the delivery of its first industrial installation, EDENenergy plans to expand its storage capacity to up to 300 kWh. The startup is also seeking additional pilot customers among regional businesses. Potential customers can receive funding covering 50% of the storage system’s cost through the Baden-Württemberg state programme Mittelstand trifft Start-ups, which has already been approved. The company currently has three founders and employs an additional three part-time staff members. Its development is supported by funding from the Center of Excellence for Sustainability and the Baden-Württemberg innovation startup programme BW Pre-Seed. Ulrich Prediger, founder of JobRad, is EDENenergy’s first investor. In the longer term, the company identifies two important conditions for scaling up second-life battery storage: standardised communication protocols for battery storage systems and legislation establishing clear rules for the use of batteries originally designed for mobile applications in stationary energy storage. By combining battery reuse, modular power electronics and industrial-scale storage, EDENenergy is seeking to establish a new route for extending battery lifetimes while making stationary energy storage more resource-efficient and cost-effective.

artigo.texto: Building owners are turning to battery energy storage systems to lower energy costs, add resilience against grid disruptions and support decarbonization. Despite momentum, their adoption faces a number of persistent obstacles, said panelists at the Greenbuild conference last month. Nationwide, nearly 58 gigawatt-hours of on-site battery storage capacity was installed in 2025, the largest single year of new battery capacity on record, according to a report by the Urban Land Institute and UL Standards & Engagement, drawing on data from the American Clean Power Association. Looking ahead, the sector is expected to install 500 GWh of battery storage between 2026 and 2032, the report says. Notwithstanding the success of these models, several barriers are keeping the market from growing more quickly, according Jill Maltby-Abbott, senior environmental and sustainability standards engineer at UL Standards & Engagement, a panelist who contributed to the ULI and UL report. Location-specific challenges. Even when a project makes economic sense, it can be stopped by interconnection and permitting woes, unclear approvals, shifting local requirements and unfamiliarity with the technology, according to Maltby-Abbott. Even where interconnection and permitting processes exist, commercial-scale storage projects can take years to deliver, the report said. Long and unpredictable timelines can cause projects to accumulate soft costs — like time and money spent on community engagement or engineering fees — and be exposed to changing market conditions, incentive structures and regulatory requirements, adding to the financial risk of implementation, per the report. Risk thresholds. Another key consideration is how municipalities view the risk and governance of these assets, Maltby-Abbott said. “How are [municipalities] defining the [risk] thresholds that they’ll accept? It’s very much on a per-project, per-owner basis, and this is a challenge that a lot of people experience with multiple emerging technologies.” Concern over risk can lead to delays as local officials put up hurdles, Dean Apostoleris, practice leader of renewable energy development at Kimley-Horn, said at the conference. “What we see as a really big barrier in terms of penetration into new markets and, even in some situations, mature markets is resistance from the regulatory, zoning, land use and siting perspective of these batteries,” he said. Even in really population-dense markets, where storage development has been a priority for quite some time, there has only been increased adoption of on-site battery energy storage in the past five or so years, according to Apostoleris. “That issue stems from a lack of education and lack of knowledge about what battery energy storage really is,” he said. For example, New York state has established a mandate to procure 6 GW of battery energy storage by 2030, with Illinois and Massachusetts setting targets of 3 GW and 5,000 MW as well, respectively. But with those targets close to just three years away, New York only has 415 MW of battery storage installed, or 7% of its target, as of the presentation, Aposoleris said. State mandates aim to spur battery adoption but development "comes down to the local and community level,” Apostoleris said. “And a lot of these communities have not yet had the bandwidth, the knowledge or the education to implement some of these regulations.” “As a result, when you actually go to permit and construct BESS, ultimately the reviews and approvals are … preventing a lot of that mandate and that goal from being achieved,” he said. Fire risk. Of all the risks, fire is one of the first localities worry about, said Kara Kokernak, senior director of the ULI Lewis Center for Sustainability in Real Estate. “That is something that became very apparent” when conducting research for the report, she said. “That was tagged in most of our conversations, but having fire safety teams part of that education can help ease those concerns.” Because of this pushback, Apostoleris said, it can be much easier to implement these projects in jurisdictions that have already established BESS safety requirements and review processes, which provide more prescriptive guidance on how projects will be evaluated. He points to the Massachusetts Energy Facilities Siting Board as a good example. It “allows a lot of developers to push through their projects in a very prescriptive manner that reduces some of the risk that often comes with uncertainty of reviews and approvals they might have at the state level,” Apostoleris said. Even when requirements are stringent, this predictability can help project teams incorporate safety considerations earlier while supporting fire department preparedness and confidence in how potential incidents will be avoided or managed, the report says. Community engagement, or lack thereof, can often delay, constrain or stop otherwise viable projects, the report says. For that reason, early engagement, before formal filings, is a “consistent recommendation from those who have successfully navigated community opposition,” the report says. “This gives developers the opportunity to understand specific concerns, explain safety and emergency response approaches, and adjust the project so that community input is reflected in project planning from the start.”

artigo.texto: New power equipment for AI sites is now booked into the 2030s, so developers are paying for anything that already exists. If you're betting on AI capacity arriving on schedule, the secondhand turbine market is where that schedule gets tested. Reuters reported on Monday, November 9, that utilities, developers and data center builders are combing the world for used gas turbines, reviving mothballed machines and converting retired jet engines into power generators. The reason is arithmetic. Global orders for gas turbines are above 100 GW, against annual manufacturing capacity of 60 to 70 GW, and new US units now take about six years on average to arrive, with delivery talks focused on 2030 to 2031. Grid connections are no faster. Reuters put US data center demand at roughly 17 GW this year and said it could triple by 2028, when expected power capacity of 87 GW would still trail the 129 GW the buildout needs. A developer who waits for a new turbine from GE Vernova, Siemens Energy or Mitsubishi Heavy Industries is waiting past the point where the chips it has already ordered will be obsolete. Per Reuters, well-maintained used units go for about $1.5 million to $1.7 million per megawatt, and refurbished ones around $1.3 million. New turbines cost $2 million to $2.5 million per megawatt. Reuters cited one deal as the sharpest example: two 14.5-megawatt turbines from Solar Turbines, a Caterpillar subsidiary, sold for $12.5 million, or about $430,000 per megawatt. A new equivalent would have cost around $35 million and taken five years. That discount is the bargain. The catch is that sellers know it. "That secondary market is very, very hot right now," EthosEnergy chief executive Ana Amicarella told Reuters, adding that the company has also seen "an escalation on the prices of what people are demanding." Darayus Pardivala of Sulzer's US aftermarket business said his team now gets a request "every few weeks" to find a used gas turbine for a data center. Crusoe has canceled its $1.25 billion deal to buy 29 jet-derived turbines from Boom Supersonic, walking back a plan once pitched as a fast workaround for the AI industry's power bottleneck. The move comes weeks after Crusoe raised $3.9 billion at a $30.9 billion valuation and dropped a Wyoming campus, and lands the same week Oracle filed a force... - why Crusoe canceled Boom Superpower turbine order - AI data centers alternative power generation solutions Frankly, a market where brokers get phone calls every few weeks is not a market that can rescue anyone at scale. Reuters itself noted that the secondhand route is unlikely to offset a meaningful share of the delays, since there is little excess supply to buy. Every working turbine that comes up for sale has a line behind it. Jet engines do the rest The more inventive supply comes from aviation. Crusoe, the AI infrastructure firm, ordered 13 aeroderivative turbines from ProEnergy in April, for about 650 MW. Aeroderivatives are built on jet engines from GE Aerospace, and ProEnergy takes used CF6-80C2 cores, the engine family that powered Boeing 747s, and mounts them on trailers as 48-megawatt units, according to Tom's Hardware. The same report said ProEnergy has delivered more than 1 GW of its PE6000 systems to just two data center customers. Wartsila, the Finnish engine maker, has taken a different route around the queue. Reuters said it has booked around 3 GW of orders from US data centers since spring last year for power units that run on gas engines instead of turbines. Siemens Energy has said more than 60% of its US gas turbine orders are now tied to AI data centers, as Tom's Hardware reported. The winners here are the less famous names. EthosEnergy, ReflowX, SVI Bremco, Sulzer and ProEnergy sit in the aftermarket, and none of them needed to build a new factory to benefit. Reuters also named FTAI Power and Boom among the firms trying to turn aircraft-engine know-how into data center power, according to the Runtime Wire summary of the piece. What the scramble says about AI timelines Look at what is being bought. Trailer-mounted jet engines and second-hand industrial turbines are bridge power: loud, less efficient and meant to run until a grid connection shows up. Nobody pays a premium for stopgap equipment unless the buildout schedule is already slipping, and a developer who locks up a used unit early can switch on capacity years ahead of rivals still in the new-equipment queue. That changes how you should read the capex headlines. Spending plans assume sites go live on time. A six-year wait for new turbines says the physical side of the boom is moving slower than the financial side, and that the companies with power in hand, bought used or built from an old airliner engine, are the ones whose timelines are real. artigo.texto: Funttel destina R$ 46,3 milhões ao CPQD para desenvolver tecnologia nacional de data centers Projeto Prisma, do Funttel, terá duração de 36 meses e usará inteligência artificial para distribuir processamento entre data centers. O Conselho Gestor do Fundo para o Desenvolvimento Tecnológico das Telecomunicações (Funttel) aprovou na sexta, 6, um investimento de R$ 46,3 milhões no desenvolvimento de uma plataforma nacional de gerenciamento de data centers e infraestruturas de processamento distribuído. O projeto, denominado Prisma, será executado pelo CPQD, com recursos administrados pela Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep). A iniciativa prevê o uso de inteligência artificial para definir onde os dados deverão ser processados e distribuir recursos computacionais entre diferentes instalações, incluindo mini data centers localizados em diversas regiões do país. O projeto terá duração de 36 meses, contados a partir da celebração do convênio de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação entre o CPQD e a Finep. O comunicado não informa a data prevista para a assinatura do instrumento. A proposta busca desenvolver uma tecnologia nacional capaz de gerenciar ambientes distribuídos de processamento, com aplicações previstas em telecomunicações, saúde, defesa, segurança pública e educação. Inteligência artificial para distribuir processamento O Prisma utilizará inteligência artificial para identificar a infraestrutura mais adequada ao processamento de dados e realizar a distribuição dos recursos computacionais entre diferentes instalações. Uma das frentes do projeto é o uso de mini data centers em arquiteturas de computação de borda (edge computing), nas quais parte do processamento ocorre mais perto dos locais de geração e utilização das informações. Essa arquitetura permite reduzir a distância percorrida pelos dados entre os dispositivos e os centros de processamento, com potencial para diminuir o tempo de resposta de aplicações digitais. Para o diretor de Tecnologia e Inovação do CPQD, Gustavo Correa Lima, o processamento distribuído também permite ampliar o controle sobre as informações mantidas nessas estruturas. “Além de tornar mais rápidos o processamento e o acesso às informações, essa arquitetura permite maior controle sobre o dado que está na borda”, afirmou. No setor de telecomunicações, a plataforma está prevista entre as soluções que poderão utilizar infraestrutura distribuída de processamento. Eficiência energética e continuidade dos serviços Outro objetivo do Prisma é desenvolver mecanismos para reduzir o consumo de energia e o impacto ambiental dos data centers. A proposta contempla o gerenciamento de recursos computacionais e soluções de armazenamento de energia elétrica para ampliar a autonomia das instalações em situações de instabilidade no fornecimento. Entre os resultados esperados estão a redução da pegada de carbono, o aumento da resiliência a falhas de energia e a proteção contra ataques cibernéticos. O projeto também prevê mecanismos de governança de informações críticas, observando padrões internacionais de segurança e as diretrizes da Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD). Funttel financiará desenvolvimento tecnológico Os recursos foram aprovados pelo Conselho Gestor do Funttel, fundo vinculado à política de desenvolvimento tecnológico das telecomunicações e cuja atuação envolve o Ministério das Comunicações. A Finep ficará responsável pela gestão financeira dos recursos, enquanto o CPQD executará as atividades de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação previstas no projeto. Segundo a superintendente da Área de Saúde e Transformação Digital da Finep, Joana Meirelles, a proposta é disponibilizar uma plataforma nacional para aplicações em diferentes setores. “O objetivo é desenvolver e disponibilizar uma plataforma nacional segura e sustentável para setores como saúde, defesa, segurança pública, educação e telecomunicações”, afirmou. O ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho, relacionou o investimento à ampliação da capacidade nacional de desenvolvimento tecnológico e à soberania nacional. “Com o apoio do Funttel, estamos fortalecendo a inovação brasileira e criando condições para uma infraestrutura digital mais moderna, segura e sustentável, reduzindo nossa dependência de tecnologias desenvolvidas no exterior”, afirma o ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho. *Com assessoria de imprensa

artigo.texto: A City-County Council committee voted 11-2 Monday to recommend the full council reject about $113 million in tax breaks for data center developer DC Blox. The company previously won approval to build a two building campus on Indianapolis’ east side. The recommendation is not binding. The full council, which must also approve the tax abatements, is expected to vote in December. More than two dozen people spoke at the meeting in council chambers — nearly all opposed the tax deal. Indy Economic Development CEO Andrea Richter-Garry, whose organization negotiated the deal for the city, told the committee the project would bring in about $58 million to the local community during the abatement period: roughly $28 million in taxes plus the company’s $30 million pledge. DC Blox has not fully committed to building the $1.8 billion data center project at 305 Fintail Drive near Irvington. Asked by Councilor Andy Nielsen whether it would build the first building without the abatements, David Armistead, the company's senior vice president of sales, said it has no full tenant commitments on that building and none on the second, citing a court challenge to its land use approval. The Atlanta-based company said the project is planned to be built in two phases — a one-story, 70,000-square-foot building expected to be completed within two years, followed by a two-story, 250,000-square-foot building, in the next five years. The development would create hundreds of temporary construction jobs and 21 permanent positions. Data centers have become a major target of Indiana's economic development strategy, but the industry's need for electricity has put it at odds with a separate fight over rising utility costs. Gov. Mike Braun signed a law this year aimed at reining in utility rates, and critics argue large-scale power consumers like data centers make that harder. Members of the council’s Metropolitan and Economic Development Committee considered two abatements: a 10-year, 50% break on real property taxes on land and buildings, and a 10-year, 85% break on personal property taxes on high-tech equipment like servers. The site of the data center is on the border of two districts represented by two members of the City-County Council — Nielsen and Michael-Paul Hart. Nielsen rejected the plan. “The presentation we got is clear as mud,” he said. “It is speculative.” If the project is built as planned, the company said it would still pay about $28 million in property taxes during the abatement period. It also pledges $30 million for east side projects on top of the local taxes, including park and trail upgrades, a fire station and $5.7 million in redevelopment of Washington Square Mall. Councilor Hart, who sponsored the proposals, said the vote is about east side investment, not whether to allow a data center, which the Metropolitan Development Commission already approved. “You see convention centers in Noblesville and in Fishers — all those things are starting to take the people away from Indianapolis because we're not investing in our townships,” he said. “We're going to become a downtown of nothing if we don’t start doing it.” Residents who testified opposed the breaks. Sue Beecher, president of the Irvington Community Council, said the group voted unanimously against any abatements. Others cited concerns over contamination or said the company could afford to build the campus without tax breaks. DC Blox is one of three data centers in the city approved before the Metropolitan Development Commission voted in August to temporarily ban new developments in Marion County through 2027. The other approved centers are Sabey Data Centers’ $4.3 billion project in Decatur Township, which received more than $240 million in tax breaks in September, and Metrobloks’ project in Martindale-Brightwood. DC Blox is also planning to seek state incentives but the application is not yet complete. Eric Weddle is WFYI's education editor. Contact Eric at eweddle@wfyi.org or follow him on X at @ericweddle

artigo.texto: Changan and CATL to collaborate on 1,500 km solid state cells, establish 75 GWh battery lines Chinese automaker Changan has officially announced plans to deepen its partnership with battery giant CATL. The two firms have committed to expanding joint battery production capacity to 75 GWh and collaborating on solid-state batteries (SSBs) and sodium-ion cells. Like its previous statements on its in-house SSBs, Changan made its announcement on an interactive platform owned by the Shenzhen Stock Exchange. The automaker also expressed commitment to prospective industries, including humanoid robots and China’s “low-altitude economy”. More cells with CATL Changan and CATL are not new partners in China’s automotive sector, having established a joint venture (JV), CATL-Changan (时代长安, Times Changan), earlier in 2023. The JV supplies cells to Changan’s in-house NEV brands, including Avatr, Deepal, and Nevo. Libattery.net, a Chinese battery industry outlet, reports that CATL-Changan is on track to reach 50 GWh of battery production capacity, a plan Changan revealed at an investor relations event in May 2025. The announcement means CATL-Changan will receive an additional 25 GWh of capacity and new production lines. The JV plans to establish a 700,000-square-meter facility and invest 5 billion yuan (~750 million USD) in the expansion. According to Changan, the new facility will integrate the “latest generation of CATL battery tech” and supply cells to the automaker’s NEV brands. It’s planned to start operations in 2027 and meet the 25 GWh goal in three years. It will be situated in a high-tech zone between Chongqing City and Sichuan Province. The automaker expects the expansion to bring in annual revenue of 10 billion yuan (~1.5 billion USD), create 2,500 jobs, and generate 300 million yuan (~45 million USD) in tax revenue for the local community. Changan may also see this move as a way to cut costs. ZAKER News, a Chinese automotive outlet, reports that the Chongqing-based automaker is only earning 68 yuan (10 USD) per car, and is under heavy pressure to boost profits. A JV with CATL would give it access to cheap in-house cells, and avoid high acquisition costs for battery packs,which is one of the priciest components in an NEV. More on Changan’s SSBs Changan has joined the race for SSBs in China, announcing its Golden Bell (Jinzhongzhao) cells in November 2023. The automaker says it’s aiming for an energy density of 400 Wh/kg and claims it will be 70% safer than rivals because it uses “AI remote diagnosis technology”. It also claims the new Golden Bell cells will help EVs reach ranges over 1,500 km and says cell degradation won’t be noticeable for at least 600,000 km. Cell life will exceed 5,000 cycles, and Golden Bell packs will support 6C charging, enabling a 30-80% charge in 9 minutes. The automaker has also reiterated its development schedule for the Golden Bell cells, aiming for vehicle road tests in 2026 and ramping up to commercial production in 2027. artigo.texto: Hazle Township residents press for tougher data center zoning limits on revised ordinance HAZLE TOWNSHIP, LUZERNE CO. (WOLF) — A packed auditorium at Hazleton Area High School Monday night, as Hazle Township residents voiced their concerns over a proposed 40-page zoning ordinance that could determine where data centers are allowed to be built. Township supervisors are considering revisions to the ordinance, including a designated overlay district for data center developments. But the proposal is drawing pushback from residents who say they want a say in how these projects could impact their community. The township recently posted an updated version of its proposed data center ordinance, dated November 5, along with a map showing a proposed area called the Energy and Technology Overlay District. Under the proposal, data centers would be allowed within that designated area without needing a special exception from the zoning hearing board. However, developers would still have to meet township requirements and obtain the necessary approvals. Residents raised concerns and suggested stronger protections, focusing on noise levels, decibel limits, and potential environmental impacts. The proposed data center zoning amendment would allow the residential setback requirement to be reduced to 500 feet. One resident spoke out in favor of increasing the setback requirement to provide greater protection for nearby residents. “The 1,250 feet requirement should be enforced, if this is going to go through. 500 feet is not enough to protect property and or people from the noise, the pollution, and the activities of an active data center area,” said Margaret. Another resident stressed the importance of giving residents a voice before any decisions are made on the amendment. “We believe residents deserve a meaningful opportunity to understand, question, and discuss the proposed regulations,” said Michael Reilly. One resident cited a statistic that 71% of people oppose local AI data centers, questioning why Project Hazelnut is still being considered and referencing a recent debate involving Governor Shapiro. “Governor Shapiro stood up at his debate, and say any community that’s not for this, they will not go through with these data centers. So, I don’t even know why we’re still having this conversation,” said Jane Tadlock. The revised amendment also outlines additional approval requirements for battery storage facilities and sets standards for roads, utilities, fire protection, noise and water systems. Developers would also need to complete necessary infrastructure improvements before buildings could be occupied. The board has until December 7 to finish the amendment process.

artigo.texto: Tenaga Nasional Bhd (TNB), IOI Corp Bhd and a consortium of small and medium enterprises (SMEs) have partnered to develop a 500 MW solar power project integrated with a battery energy storage system (BESS) in Bahau, Negeri Sembilan, Malaysia. The project represents a major renewable energy investment, with TNB planning to inject up to RM424.4 million into the joint venture (JV). According to a filing with Bursa Malaysia, TNB’s subsidiary, TNB Renewables Sdn Bhd (TRe), has signed a shareholders’ agreement with IOI Corp’s subsidiary, Luminous Aspect Sdn Bhd, and CSP 500MW Sdn Bhd. The project will be developed through Bahau Energy Ventures Sdn Bhd, the joint venture established by the three partners. The proposed development will comprise a 500 MWac solar photovoltaic (PV) power plant and a 250 MW/1,000 MWh BESS. It will operate under Malaysia’s Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme (CRESS), which enables renewable energy developers to supply green electricity to corporate consumers. Under the agreed ownership structure, TRe will hold a 70% stake in the joint venture, making it the largest shareholder. Luminous Aspect will own 25%, while CSP will hold the remaining 5%. CSP represents a consortium of 12 SMEs that have established the special purpose company to participate in the development and implementation of the project. The JV has a maximum equity capitalisation of RM606.2 million. TRe will contribute RM424.4 million, while Luminous Aspect and CSP will invest RM151.5 million and RM30.3 million, respectively. The project financing is expected to combine shareholder equity and third-party project financing, with a debt-to-equity ratio of up to 80:20, subject to market conditions and funding availability. The project will be supported by TNB’s long-term renewable energy offtake agreement with DayOne Data Centres Ltd, a Singapore-headquartered digital infrastructure company. Under the agreement announced on June 11, 2025, DayOne is expected to procure up to 500 MWac of renewable energy over 21 years to support its data centre operations in Malaysia. TRe will act as the project’s asset manager and oversee engineering and procurement arrangements. Meanwhile, IOI will participate as an investor and provide the project site through a land lease arrangement. IOI Group Managing Director and Chief Executive Datuk Lee Yeow Chor said the partnership would support the company’s renewable energy portfolio and generate stable long-term recurring income. For TNB, the project is expected to strengthen its renewable energy portfolio and support Malaysia’s energy transition. The company highlighted growing corporate demand for renewable electricity and the implementation of CRESS as important factors supporting the project’s prospects. TNB also stated that the transaction is not expected to have a material impact on the group’s earnings per share, net assets per share or gearing for the current financial year. The eventual financial impact will depend on the final project cost, financing arrangements and commercial operations. The partnership also aligns with IOI’s Five-Year Strategic Roadmap for 2025–2029, which aims to expand its renewable energy business and strengthen its participation in Malaysia’s low-carbon energy transition. artigo.texto: A Eletronet, empresa de telecomunicações do grupo Axia Energia (ex-Eletrobras), está investindo R$ 25 milhões em um novo data center na cidade de São Paulo, localizado no bairro Chácara Santo Antônio. O empreendimento terá aproximadamente 350 m², capacidade para cerca de 90 racks de computadores e potência inicial de 0,5 MW, podendo chegar a 1 MW na segunda fase de expansão. A entrega está programada para o primeiro trimestre do ano que vem. Esse projeto é o maior já feito pela companhia, mas não é do tipo que vai brigar com os mega data centers das big techs. Em vez disso, seu objetivo é atender a demanda crescente das empresas pequenas e médias de internet e conteúdo digital - como streaming e computação em nuvem. “Não é um data center grande, mas tem importância significativa para o mercado”, afirmou o presidente da empresa, Rogerio Garchet, em entrevista à Coluna. O data center da Eletronet dá acesso não só à rede de fibra ótica própria da companhia, como também ao seu ponto de interconexão no IX.br São Paulo - infraestrutura física que permite que diferentes redes de computadores se conectem diretamente para trocar dados entre si. Para o mundo de telecom, esse é um ponto estratégico porque permite maior velocidade e menor latência no tráfego de dados. Área deve crescer no faturamento da companhia Segundo Garchet, os data centers devem ter uma participação cada vez maior no faturamento da Eletronet. Hoje, isso está em 3%. “Não podemos dar detalhes sobre em quanto deve chegar para não atrair os competidores, mas apostamos bastante no crescimento desse setor”, disse o executivo. A empresa grupo tem uma receita anual na ordem de R$ 200 milhões. A Eletronet já vem investindo na ampliação da capacidade para atender clientes da economia digital. A empresa tem, hoje, 170 edge data centers espalhados pelo País e planeja chegar a 255 unidades até o fim do ano. São data centers descentralizados, que atendem a demandas locais. Estes empreendimentos têm uma função semelhante ao novo negócio de São Paulo, mas são centros bem menores (entre 20 e 50 m²), com energia e conectividade, mas sem acesso direto ao ponto de interconexão. Eles também atendem pequenas e médias empresas que buscam infraestrutura no mercado para otimizar seus serviços. Já o negócio principal da Eletronet continua sendo a sua rede de 18 mil quilômetros de fibra óptica em 18 estados, que foi construída aproveitando a infraestrutura física das linhas de transmissão de energia elétrica de alta tensão da Axia ao longo dos anos. Essa rede de fibra é utilizada pelos provedores que levam internet para o cliente final. Desde as grandes teles até os provedores regionais são clientes da Eletronet neste segmento. artigo.texto: Cabot Corporation Major manufacturer with extensive R&D and production capacity According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Wood Activated Carbon market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global wood activated carbon market is entering a phase of structural expansion rather than cyclical recovery, with the forecast horizon 2026-2035 shaped by regulatory tightening in water safety, air emissions, and pharmaceutical purity. Wood-based activated carbon occupies a distinct position within the broader adsorbents industry because its renewable feedstock and pore structure suit high-value purification duties, yet it competes directly with coconut shell and coal-derived carbons on cost and performance. The 2026 baseline shows a fragmented supply chain, from sawdust and wood chip sourcing through carbonization and activation to sizing and distribution, with demand concentrated in water treatment, air purification, food and beverage processing, pharmaceutical purification, and industrial recovery applications. The central analytical question for the next decade is not whether demand grows, but where it grows fastest and which producers can defend margins as feedstock variability and energy costs persist. This report provides a data-driven view of market size, structure, trade flows, and competitive dynamics, with a transparent product definition aligned to HS 380210 and 380290. It is designed for manufacturers, distributors, investors, and advisors who need a consistent baseline and a clear read on the drivers and restraints that will determine the market's path to 2035. The baseline scenario for the world wood activated carbon market through 2035 assumes moderate volume growth and a gradual shift in value toward higher-grade and impregnated products. Demand is anchored by municipal and industrial water treatment, where stricter discharge and drinking-water standards raise adsorbent dosing rates and replacement frequency. Air purification, particularly in industrial settings and automotive evaporation controls, adds a second structural layer of demand, while food and beverage and pharmaceutical purification support premium pricing for low-contaminant grades. The baseline does not assume a breakthrough that displaces competing carbons; instead, wood-based carbon holds share in applications where its adsorption kinetics and renewable origin are valued, while ceding price-sensitive segments to coconut shell and coal variants. Supply-side conditions remain a constraint: feedstock costs for sawdust and wood chips are volatile, activation is energy-intensive, and capacity additions require long lead times. The market index, set at 100 in 2025, rises to 138 by 2035, implying a compound annual growth rate of 3.3% over the forecast period. This trajectory reflects steady rather than explosive expansion, with the strongest incremental demand coming from Asia-Pacific water infrastructure and from tighter industrial emission rules in Europe and North America. Producers with secure feedstock, efficient kilns, and certification for food and pharmaceutical grades are best positioned to capture value, while sub-scale operators face margin pressure from energy and compliance costs. Water treatment is the largest and most defensible outlet for wood activated carbon. Municipal utilities and industrial wastewater plants use powdered and granular carbon to remove organic contaminants, taste and odor compounds, and trace micropollutants. Through 2035, the demand mechanism is regulatory: as discharge limits and drinking-water guidelines tighten, utilities increase carbon dosing and replacement frequency rather than relying on existing media. Industrial users, including chemical and petrochemical plants, add carbon polishing stages to meet permit conditions. Demand-side indicators to watch include municipal capital spending on treatment upgrades, per-capita water consumption in urbanizing regions, and the pace of micropollutant regulation. Wood-based carbon competes with coal and coconut variants here, but its renewable origin supports procurement preferences in regulated markets. The segment grows in line with infrastructure investment rather than GDP alone, making it relatively resilient to cyclical downturns. Current trend: Steady expansion supported by stricter drinking-water and wastewater standards. Major trends: Stricter micropollutant and disinfection by-product rules, Upgrade of aging municipal treatment plants, Industrial wastewater reuse and zero-liquid-discharge targets, and Shift toward granular and pelletized media for longer service life. Representative participants: Calgon Carbon Corporation, Jacobi Carbons AB, Haycarb PLC, Donau Carbon GmbH, and Kuraray Co., Ltd. Air purification covers industrial off-gas treatment, solvent recovery, and automotive evaporation controls. Wood activated carbon is used in fixed-bed adsorbers and canisters where its pore structure captures volatile organic compounds and odorous substances. The demand mechanism through 2035 is driven by tightening industrial emission standards and the expansion of solvent recovery in coating, printing, and chemical operations. Automotive evaporation controls, including canister systems, add a volume base tied to vehicle production, though electric vehicles reduce this outlet over time. Demand-side indicators include industrial production growth in chemical and coating sectors, regulatory timelines for VOC limits, and vehicle production volumes. Wood-based carbon faces competition from coal-derived and impregnated carbons in specialized applications, but granular and pelletized wood grades remain competitive in general VOC removal. The segment is expected to grow moderately, with the strongest gains in Asia-Pacific as industrial emission rules tighten. Current trend: Growing demand from industrial emission controls

artigo.texto: Nove ONGs, incluindo o Greenpeace, exigem suspensão de projetos de data centers no Brasil até que sejam feitos estudos de impacto e criadas leis rigorosas. Ações ocorreram em Fortaleza, Belém e Pindamonhangaba para alertar sobre os altos consumos de água e energia. Nove organizações da sociedade civil lançaram a mobilização nacional "Parem os mega data centers! O Brasil não é colônia das Big Techs". O grupo pede que nenhum projeto de centro de dados de hiperescala avance no país enquanto não houver estudos de impacto, licenciamento ambiental completo e uma lei que garanta participação das comunidades atingidas. O lançamento aconteceu em 6 de novembro com atos em Fortaleza (CE), Belém (PA) e Pindamonhangaba (SP), onde há projetos desse tipo. A iniciativa integra o Dia de Ação Global contra mega data centers, que mobilizou mais de 100 organizações de diferentes países nos dias 6 e 7 de novembro. - Nove ONGs assinam o manifesto: Instituto Terramar, Amazônia Sem Data Center, CTRL+Z, Data_Labe, Instituto Decodifica, Mulheres pelo Clima do Vale do Paraíba, Coding Rights, Filha do Sol e Greenpeace Brasil. - As entidades exigem o fim das isenções fiscais concedidas ao setor pelo regime Redata. - Ações ocorreram em Fortaleza, Belém e Pindamonhangaba, cidades com projetos de data centers em andamento. - Os projetos consomem grandes volumes de energia e água, gerando preocupação com a fatura de luz e abastecimento. - O movimento faz parte de uma ação global que envolve mais de 100 organizações internacionais. Críticas à falta de transparência e impactos sociais As organizações pedem ainda o fim das isenções fiscais concedidas ao setor pelo Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata). Esse regime foi sancionado em setembro e deve ser regulamentado pelo Governo Federal ainda neste ano. Na avaliação das entidades, o país oferece benefícios fiscais, energia e água a essas empresas antes de ter análise dos riscos, planejamento territorial, regras socioambientais e contrapartidas sobre a soberania digital. Julia Catão, especialista em Tecnologia do Greenpeace Brasil, alertou para a interferência dos bilionários da tecnologia no processo eleitoral. "Acabamos de testemunhar a interferência dos bilionários da tecnologia no nosso processo eleitoral. Se por um lado precisamos regulamentar essas plataformas, por outro, precisamos impedi-las de construir suas casas de máquinas - os data centers - no nosso território da forma como têm feito, transferindo para a nossa população os seus custos socioambientais, sem ganho nenhum pro país", disse Catão. Vozes locais repudiam projetos na Amazônia e no Rio João Paulo Guimarães, ativista do Amazônia Sem Data Center, declarou: "É um absurdo um data center na Amazônia. O Pará já lidera números de mortes pelo calor extremo. Nós repudiamos esse projeto.". Mariana Ceres, ativista da Mulheres pelo Clima do Vale do Paraíba, ressaltou a falta de participação social. "A principal questão para nós está na falta de transparência e total ausência de participação social. Em 2026, é inaceitável um empreendimento desse porte e com grande impacto ambiental, sem que haja um rigoroso licenciamento ambiental", afirmou Ceres. Andréa Camurça, coordenadora de Incidência Política do Instituto Terramar/CE, destacou a questão energética. "A ação é fundamental para que as vozes dos territórios cheguem ao mundo e denunciem a ofensiva das big techs sobre os bens comuns do Sul Global. Não podemos gerar insegurança energética num país que ainda enfrenta pobreza energética: queremos água e energia para o povo, não para big techs!", declarou Camurça. Polinho Mota, diretor do Data_labe, comentou sobre a situação no Rio de Janeiro. "Aqui no Rio de Janeiro estamos acompanhando a chegada de um mega empreendimento que vai afetar a vida de toda a população da cidade, mas que em momento nenhum ouviu o que tínhamos para falar. Por isso, junto com o Decodifica e Coding Rights, estamos enfrentando a falta de transparência e exigindo mais estudos de impacto", relatou Mota. Detalhes das ações em três capitais brasileiras As mobilizações no Brasil começaram no dia 6 pela manhã, em Belém. A campanha Amazônia Sem Data Center esteve na comunidade Residencial Miramar Shalon, para uma roda de conversa com os moradores que podem ser impactados pelo projeto BEL1, da Elea Data Centers e Axia Energia. No Ceará, onde o data center do TikTok está em fase avançada de construção, ativistas se reuniram para conversar com a população na orla da Praia de Iracema, em Fortaleza. A atividade foi realizada pelo Instituto Terramar e Greenpeace Brasil. Um caminhão de LED percorreu as ruas da cidade com informações sobre os impactos no aumento da conta de luz e na poluição sonora. O caminhão exibiu ainda o documentário "Inteligência Natural", realizado pela Coding Rights sobre o empreendimento que está sendo construído pelas empresas Omnia e Casa dos Ventos em território indígena Anacé, em Caucaia, na região metropolitana. Já em Pindamonhangaba, a ação foi organizada pelas Mulheres pelo Clima do Vale do Paraíba. Moradores da região se reuniram em uma praça de grande circulação para alertar a população sobre o projeto Riverhook Village 18, planejado para a cidade. O que são data centers e por que geram preocupação Os mega data centers, ou centros de dados de hiperescala, são complexos industriais voltados sobretudo ao treinamento de modelos de Inteligência Artificial (IA) pelas grandes empresas de tecnologia, as Big Techs. Funcionam sem pausa, ocupam áreas extensas e consomem volumes muito altos de energia e água para refrigeração. Nas cidades que recebem esses projetos, a preocupação dos moradores vai do barulho contínuo das máquinas à pressão sobre o abastecimento de água e a conta de luz.

artigo.texto: O Governo do Brasil vai investir R$ 46,3 milhões no desenvolvimento de uma tecnologia nacional capaz de tornar os data centers mais eficientes, seguros e sustentáveis. A iniciativa, aprovada pelo Conselho Gestor do Fundo para o Desenvolvimento Tecnológico das Telecomunicações (Funttel), prevê a criação de uma plataforma inteligente para gerenciar e distribuir dados entre diferentes estruturas de processamento, incluindo mini data centers instalados em diversas regiões do país. Batizado de Prisma, o projeto utilizará inteligência artificial para identificar onde e como os dados devem ser processados, distribuindo automaticamente os recursos computacionais entre diferentes infraestruturas. Na prática, a tecnologia poderá reduzir gastos com energia, diminuir custos operacionais, acelerar o acesso às informações e aumentar a proteção de dados estratégicos. “Investir em tecnologia nacional é garantir que o Brasil tenha mais autonomia para proteger suas informações e desenvolver soluções para os desafios do futuro. Com o apoio do Funttel, estamos fortalecendo a inovação brasileira e criando condições para uma infraestrutura digital mais moderna, segura e sustentável, reduzindo nossa dependência de tecnologias desenvolvidas no exterior”, afirma o ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho. Os recursos serão administrados pela Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep), e o projeto será executado pelo Centro Brasileiro de Inovação em Tecnologias da Informação e da Comunicação (CPQD), em Campinas (SP). Uma das frentes do projeto é estimular a expansão de mini data centers em diferentes regiões do Brasil. Essas estruturas permitem processar informações mais perto de onde são geradas e utilizadas, reduzindo o tempo de resposta dos sistemas e melhorando o desempenho de serviços digitais. A tecnologia poderá beneficiar áreas estratégicas como saúde, defesa, segurança pública, educação e telecomunicações, contribuindo para proteger informações sensíveis e ampliar a capacidade nacional de armazenamento e processamento de dados. “O objetivo é desenvolver e disponibilizar uma plataforma nacional segura e sustentável para setores como saúde, defesa, segurança pública, educação e telecomunicações, apoiando, assim, a transformação digital de setores estratégicos”, explica a superintendente da Área de Saúde e Transformação Digital da Finep, Joana Meirelles. Para o diretor de Tecnologia e Inovação do CPQD, Gustavo Correa Lima, a distribuição de mini data centers pelo país também representa um avanço na aproximação da infraestrutura digital dos usuários. “Além de tornar mais rápidos o processamento e o acesso às informações, essa arquitetura permite maior controle sobre o dado que está na borda”, destaca. Eficiência energética e autonomia tecnológica Além de ampliar a capacidade de processamento de dados, o Prisma busca reduzir o impacto ambiental dos data centers, estruturas que demandam grandes quantidades de energia elétrica para funcionar e manter seus sistemas de refrigeração. Entre os resultados esperados estão a redução do consumo energético e da pegada de carbono, o aumento da resiliência contra falhas no fornecimento de energia e a proteção contra ataques cibernéticos. A plataforma também contemplará soluções de armazenamento de energia elétrica para garantir maior autonomia e continuidade dos serviços em situações de instabilidade no abastecimento. A proposta prevê ainda o fortalecimento da governança nacional de informações críticas, seguindo padrões internacionais de segurança e as diretrizes da Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD). O prazo de execução é de 36 meses, a partir da celebração do convênio de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação entre a Finep e o CPQD.

artigo.texto: Not all technology companies stand to lose from a slowdown in data center construction. In fact, it could be exactly what Amazon needs to pull ahead, according to Jim Cramer . "If it's going to be slower, that does work for the incumbents, hence why I would buy Amazon," Jim said Monday morning on CNBC. A divide in the artificial intelligence trade has become increasingly apparent since last week's midterm elections , as growing opposition to new projects raises concerns about future infrastructure spending. Amazon shares have surged 7% since the election, including Monday's intraday gains. Other cloud incumbents such as Microsoft and Google parent Alphabet are solidly higher too. Meanwhile, semiconductor and neocloud stocks have suffered steep losses, with Micron tumbling 14.1%, Sandisk plunging 21.2% and CoreWeave falling 8.9%, when including Monday's intraday bounce-back rallies. The strength in hyperscalers has helped fuel a broader technology rebound following last week's sell-off. Despite weakness in Nvidia and other chipmakers, the Nasdaq has gained a combined 3.3% over Friday and Monday, recovering much of Thursday's 5.5% plunge. "I think the Amazon move is very right," Jim said. "I was talking about it going to $300." That would represent nearly 10% upside from current levels. The recent rally marks a turnaround for Amazon, which had slumped over the last few months as investors grew tired of enormous AI spending. The stock briefly got hot in late July and into August, following the forced unwind of Situational Awareness and an encouraging second-quarter earnings report . But after closing at $284 apiece on Aug. 3, shares lost more than 15% through the end of October, ending that month at roughly $240. Cramer argued that a slowdown in development could benefit established cloud providers, which already operate extensive data center networks and could have the corporate heft needed to navigate any new bureaucratic obstacles. He compared the situation to a yellow flag in Formula One racing. "Everyone has to go slower, no one's allowed to pass," he said. "If that's the case, that's Microsoft and that's Amazon winning." Demand for AI computing power isn't going away, even if new data centers become harder to build. Unlike smaller neocloud providers that rely on continued expansion to grow, Amazon and Microsoft already have massive infrastructure networks in place, positioning them to capture a larger share of demand as new capacity becomes harder to bring online. Jim also said that he likes that Amazon has been less reliant on neocloud providers to secure extra capacity to meet demand. A slower buildout would also ease pressure on the hyperscalers to keep accelerating capital spending, potentially allowing their free cash flow to recover and improving returns on their existing infrastructure investments. For investors, that makes the established hyperscalers better positioned to weather a slowdown than companies whose growth depends more directly on new data center construction. artigo.texto: How data center demand is reshaping electricity costs across the US By Lucas Winter for Shipley Energy Three years ago, U.S. utilities expected peak electricity demand to grow by about 24 gigawatts over the following five years. Their most recent forecasts put that figure at roughly 166 gigawatts, 6.9 times the earlier estimate, and about 90 gigawatts of the increase is tied to data centers. That growth is beginning to show up in electricity costs for businesses and households, though the effect looks very different depending on where a customer is located. Data centers used about 4.4% of U.S. electricity in 2023, according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and the lab projects that share could reach 6.7% to 12% by 2028. The U.S. Energy Information Administration expects record national electricity sales in 2026, driven by data center development and manufacturing, with the average U.S. residential price rising from 17.3 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2025 to 18.2 cents in 2026. Whether data centers raise costs in a given area depends on three things: - How much spare power supply the region had before they arrived - How its electricity market recovers the cost of new demand - What rules regulators have set for very large customers Before looking at how those factors play out region by region, it helps to understand how data center demand turns into charges on an electricity bill. For instance, if you’re doing business in Pennsylvania, Ohio, Maryland, or D.C., capacity charges are now one of the fastest-growing parts of commercial electricity bills in the PJM region. Below, Shipley Energy explains what the latest auction results mean for your next budget. A large data center campus can need as much power as a small city, running around the clock. Grid operators and utilities have to secure generation and build transmission for that demand, often years before the facility opens. Those costs reach customers through three main channels. The first is capacity costs, which pay power plants to be available during the hours when demand peaks. Some regions buy this capacity through auctions held years in advance, so forecasts of future data center demand can raise prices before the facilities exist. The second is wholesale energy prices, which rise when added demand calls more expensive power plants into service. Researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas estimate that existing data centers have already raised wholesale electricity prices by 2% to 6% on average nationwide. The third is transmission and distribution, the lines and substations needed to deliver power to new load, which are often paid for by all customers in a utility’s territory. Because wholesale power typically makes up about half of the retail price of electricity, a given increase in wholesale prices reaches retail bills at roughly half its size. A Region-by-Region Look The same kind of demand growth is producing very different results across the country. PJM The grid operator serving 13 states and Washington, D.C., runs a capacity auction about three years ahead of delivery. Its clearing price rose from $28.92 per megawatt-day for 2024/2025 to $269.92 for 2025/2026, then hit a federally approved cap in each of the next three auctions. The 2028/2029 auction cleared at $325 per megawatt-day and still came in 6,831 megawatts short of PJM’s reliability requirement. PJM’s independent market monitor attributes about 46% of capacity costs across the last four auctions, or $29.4 billion, to data center demand. MISO The Midcontinent grid operator saw summer capacity prices reach a record $666.50 per megawatt-day for 2025/2026 as its surplus shrank. A year later, the picture shifted. Capacity offered into the 2026/2027 auction grew 3.4%, led by solar additions, and annualized prices fell to between $116 and $126 per megawatt-day, down from $212 to $217 the year before. Texas ERCOT has no capacity auction, so data center demand shows up mainly in wholesale prices during high-demand hours and in transmission spending. In August 2026, Gov. Greg Abbott directed state regulators and ERCOT to audit every data center seeking a grid connection before any project moves forward, citing more than 474 gigawatts of requests, more than five times the state’s record peak demand, with about 90% coming from data centers. Southeast Georgia Power’s pipeline of prospective large-load projects grew from about 16,000 megawatts in 2023 to roughly 69,000 megawatts by December 2025, about 80% of it from data centers. The utility and its regulators disagree on the electricity bill impact. Georgia Power projects that new large-load contracts will produce about $950 million a year in customer savings beginning in 2029, while state commission staff cautioned that the related generation buildout could add around $20 a month to residential bills. Pacific Northwest Data centers account for roughly 15% of the current load of Oregon’s investor-owned utilities, according to the state’s utility commission. Under a 2025 state law, Oregon regulators approved new rates for Portland General Electric in July 2026 that raised data center rates by an average of 29% while lowering residential rates by 1.3% and commercial rates by 2.1%. Surplus-Supply States In states that had extra generation before data centers arrived, new demand has often spread fixed grid costs across more customers. North Dakota saw electricity demand grow almost 40% while inflation-adjusted prices fell by about 3 cents per kilowatt-hour. Researchers at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and The Brattle Group, who documented that pattern, describe the overall relationship between load growth and prices as mixed and uncertain in their 2026 update. Forecasts Versus What Gets Built Not every announced data center will be built, and forecasts disagree about how many will. artigo.texto: 247 – O governo federal planeja destinar R$ 46,3 milhões ao desenvolvimento de uma tecnologia nacional de inteligência artificial (IA) para gerenciar e distribuir dados entre pequenos centros de processamento de informações espalhados pelo Brasil. A iniciativa pretende modernizar a infraestrutura digital do país, reduzir custos operacionais e ampliar a autonomia brasileira no tratamento de informações estratégicas. O plano do Ministério das Comunicações prevê que o investimento seja direcionado ao desenvolvimento do projeto Prisma, uma plataforma capaz de identificar automaticamente onde e como os dados devem ser processados, utilizando inteligência artificial para otimizar a distribuição dos recursos computacionais. A proposta é permitir que diferentes estruturas de armazenamento e processamento de dados operem de maneira integrada, com maior eficiência na utilização de energia e capacidade computacional. O sistema deverá identificar as melhores condições para executar determinadas operações e distribuir as demandas entre os chamados mini data centers. Além da redução de despesas com energia elétrica e manutenção das operações, o governo espera que a plataforma acelere o acesso às informações e fortaleça a proteção de dados considerados estratégicos. Governo busca reduzir dependência de tecnologias estrangeiras Um dos principais objetivos do investimento é ampliar a soberania tecnológica brasileira, diminuindo a necessidade de utilização de soluções desenvolvidas fora do país para administrar infraestruturas digitais. O ministro das Comunicações, Frederico Filho, destacou que o desenvolvimento de tecnologias nacionais é fundamental para garantir maior autonomia no tratamento de informações e preparar o Brasil para os desafios da transformação digital. “Investir em tecnologia nacional é garantir que o Brasil tenha mais autonomia para proteger suas informações e desenvolver soluções para os desafios do futuro. Estamos fortalecendo a inovação brasileira e criando condições para uma infraestrutura digital mais moderna, segura e sustentável, reduzindo nossa dependência de tecnologias desenvolvidas no exterior”, afirmou o ministro, em nota. A declaração coloca a redução da dependência tecnológica externa entre as prioridades do projeto, ao lado da modernização dos sistemas de processamento e da segurança das informações. A iniciativa também busca estimular o desenvolvimento de soluções brasileiras de inteligência artificial aplicadas à infraestrutura digital, área considerada estratégica para o armazenamento, a circulação e o processamento de grandes volumes de dados. Projeto será executado pelo CPQD e terá duração de 36 meses A administração dos R$ 46,3 milhões ficará sob responsabilidade da Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep), instituição federal de fomento à pesquisa e à inovação. A execução técnica caberá ao Centro de Pesquisa e Desenvolvimento em Telecomunicações (CPQD), instituição brasileira especializada em pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação tecnológica. O prazo previsto para a realização do projeto é de 36 meses, contados a partir da assinatura do convênio de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação entre a Finep e o CPQD. Durante esse período, o trabalho será direcionado ao desenvolvimento da plataforma Prisma e de suas funcionalidades de gerenciamento inteligente de dados. A tecnologia deverá permitir que as demandas computacionais sejam distribuídas automaticamente entre diferentes infraestruturas, levando em consideração as condições necessárias ao processamento das informações. Inteligência artificial será utilizada para otimizar recursos O funcionamento previsto para o Prisma tem como elemento central a utilização de inteligência artificial na administração dos recursos computacionais. Em vez de concentrar necessariamente o processamento em uma única estrutura, a plataforma deverá avaliar a distribuição das demandas entre diferentes mini data centers, buscando melhorar o aproveitamento da capacidade disponível. Esse modelo poderá contribuir para reduzir o consumo de energia e os custos associados ao funcionamento dos equipamentos, além de tornar mais eficiente a circulação das informações. A proteção de dados estratégicos também integra os objetivos anunciados pelo Ministério das Comunicações. Ao desenvolver uma solução nacional de gerenciamento, o governo pretende fortalecer a capacidade brasileira de administrar informações em infraestruturas digitais.

artigo.texto: Solutions for Diverse Energy Applications As Australia expands renewable energy deployment, energy storage is increasingly important for grid flexibility, energy cost optimization and reliable power supply. OneMatrix Solution addresses utility-scale applications, including renewable energy projects, standalone grid-side storage and electricity market operations. Featuring flexible modular design and LONGiBank 3.0, it supports 2–8-hour duration and customized system configurations. Cluster-level independent management, AI-powered battery health diagnostics and intelligent O&M help improve operational efficiency and support long-term asset performance. The solution has received TÜV Rheinland certifications under IEC 62619, IEC 63056, and an IEC/EN 60730-1 Annex H report, reinforcing its safety credentials for international markets. Hi-MO One Pro supports C&I applications with flexible 2-24-hour configurations for solar-plus-storage, peak-valley arbitrage, and backup power. Featuring LONGi's proprietary iCCS and liquid-cooling technology, it supports grid-connected and off-grid operation, helping businesses optimize energy costs and enhance power supply security. OneNexus H2 and M5 serve remote areas, mining operations and other locations with limited grid access. By coordinating solar, battery storage and diesel generation, they help increase renewable energy utilization, reduce diesel dependence and strengthen power supply resilience. Project Experience Demonstrates Local Market Value In Strathalbyn, South Australia, the Lunio Energy BESS project was connected to the grid in September 2026. Comprising four LONGiBank 2.0 systems with a total capacity of 5 MW/20 MWh, the project participates in Australia's National Electricity Market (NEM), optimizing charging and discharging in response to electricity demand and market prices. Advancing LONGi ONE Through Localized Services LONGi continues to integrate proprietary technologies, system solutions and intelligent O&M under its LONGi ONE strategy, providing support from solution design and delivery through lifecycle operations. Through its "2830 Plan," LONGi aims to establish 30 comprehensive local service centers worldwide by the end of 2028, strengthening local responsiveness and lifecycle support. With its full-stack capabilities, diverse solution portfolio and expanding local service network, LONGi Energy Storage will continue working with Australian customers and partners to deliver flexible, reliable and sustainable energy solutions. artigo.texto: NHPC Limited has issued a tender on behalf of Bundelkhand Saur Urja Limited (BSUL) to select a Battery Energy Storage System Developer (BESSD) for developing two Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS). NHPC's two BESS projects comprise a 300 MW/800 MW/4,800 MWh system and a 600 MW/800 MW/3,200 MWh system. It has sought bids until December 12, 2026. By seeking over 4 hours of supply during non-solar hours, the tender seeks to push the boundaries of solar plus storage in UP for the first time. BSUL is a joint venture between NHPC Limited and the Uttar Pradesh New and Renewable Energy Development Agency (UPNEDA). The selected developer will procure the entire solar energy generated by the existing solar plants, establish co-located BESS projects, and utilise the solar power to charge the BESS. The remaining solar power, along with the power discharged from the BESS, will be scheduled for supply. Scope of Work BSUL intends to integrate BESS with its existing solar power generation capacity to meet the firm and dispatchable power requirements of the End Procurer. It has invited proposals for setting up BESS projects that will use energy generated by the existing solar plants to charge the storage systems and schedule Solar-plus-BESS power under either of the two configurations. The projects are intended to meet the solar and non-solar hour power requirements of the Buying Entity/Distribution Companies (DISCOMs). Under the first configuration, the project involves scheduling 300 MW of solar capacity during solar hours, coupled with an 800 MW/4,800 MWh BESS for supplying power during non-solar hours. Under the second configuration, 600 MW of solar capacity will be scheduled during solar hours, supported by an 800 MW/3,200 MWh BESS during non-solar hours. Under this framework, BSUL, acting as an Intermediary Procurer, has selected Coal India Limited (CIL) and NLC India Renewables Limited as Solar Power Developers (SPDs) to develop a total solar generation capacity of 1,200 MW across Tehsil Orai and Tehsil Madhogarh. BSUL will execute Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) to procure the entire 1,200 MW of solar power generated from the park. Integrating ESS With Solar Projects Energy Storage Systems (ESS) play a critical role in managing fluctuations in renewable energy generation and helping grid operators maintain reliability while facilitating the smooth integration of renewable energy into the grid. Additionally, ESS connected to Solar Photovoltaic (SPV) plants can enhance the utilisation of renewable energy transmission systems. It has been clarified that the BESSD will procure the entire power generated by the co-located solar projects in Jalaun Solar Park from the Solar Power Project Developer (SPPD), BSUL, at the tariff detailed hereunder.

artigo.texto: Sodium-ion batteries are moving into commercial production, supported by growing interest in diversified supply chains and reliable performance across a wide range of temperatures, according to new analysis from Wood Mackenzie. The report, Sodium-ion batteries: commercialisation begins, economics to follow, examines developments in China, the United States, Germany and India. It finds that supply agreements now exceed 70 GWh, signalling growing confidence among downstream customers. Wood Mackenzie expects leading manufacturers to achieve cell-level cost parity with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries by the end of 2026. However, parity at module and complete system level is not expected until after 2030. Supply security and temperature performance support adoption The consultancy identifies supply chain security, cycle life and a broad operating temperature range as key advantages of sodium-ion technology. Its performance in cold conditions strengthens its appeal for applications where low temperatures can affect battery operation. According to Ankita Chauhan, Director of Global Supply Chain and Integrated Power & Renewables Research at Wood Mackenzie, these characteristics, alongside geopolitical supply advantages, are driving near-term commercialisation. China leads manufacturing expansion China is leading the development of sodium-ion manufacturing capacity. Wood Mackenzie reports that BYD has 30 GWh of planned capacity in the country, while CATL is targeting at least 1 GWh of sodium-ion battery shipments by the end of 2026. China, the United States and Europe have significant offtake agreements, while India remains at an early stage of commercial validation. Manufacturing capacity, however, is expanding ahead of demand. The consultancy estimates a learning rate of 18–20% for China during 2026–2035, reflecting the potential for costs to decline as production scales and manufacturers gain experience. Higher upfront investment, lower lifetime costs The analysis puts average global upfront costs for sodium-ion systems at US$229/kWh, compared with US$200/kWh for LFP. Despite this initial premium, it estimates that sodium-ion can deliver a 21% lower total cost of ownership over a 20-year project. The projected savings stem from lower operating expenditure and avoiding capacity additions needed to compensate for battery degradation. According to Wood Mackenzie, system economics remain stable across storage durations of two to four hours. Near-term deployment nevertheless faces several obstacles. The report highlights Chinese export controls, India’s underdeveloped supply chain, slow gigafactory expansion in the United States and German trade policies as potential constraints on growth. Policy plays a central role in commercialisation Wood Mackenzie finds that taxation, trade measures and domestic manufacturing incentives are shaping sodium-ion deployment alongside technological progress. According to the report, China’s reintroduction of a consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries in July 2026 exempts sodium-ion technology through the end of 2028. LFP batteries face a 2% levy from September 2026, rising to 4% from September 2027. In the United States, the consultancy identifies Section 301 tariffs of approximately 58% on Chinese energy storage cells as an incentive for domestic sodium-ion production, complemented by manufacturing credits under Section 45X of the Inflation Reduction Act. In Europe, carbon-footprint disclosure requirements under the EU Battery Regulation provide further support. India is developing local capacity through a US$1.25 billion incentive programme and duty exemptions on manufacturing equipment, the report notes. The economics could shift decisively between 2030 and 2035 Wood Mackenzie identifies 2030–2035 as the period when sodium-ion economics could become significantly more competitive. For projects being deployed today, however, it considers LFP the established, bankable choice for storage assets with durations of two to four hours. Sodium-ion manufacturers still need to scale production, refine cell materials and establish a consistent operating track record. The consultancy therefore expects several battery technologies to coexist, each serving different applications and storage durations.
